docs.title: C-STREAM Framework
docs.text:
• Catholic · Science · Technology · Religion · Engineering · Arts · Math

    A local Catholic C-STREAM program integrating faith and reason, hands-on inquiry, responsible design and service.

    Quick Start Guide

docs.title: Welcome to C-STREAM
docs.text:
2026-27 curriculum review

Start with the curriculum review for verified sources, local standards, grade progression, lesson audits, low-tech materials and revised teaching plans. All 251 documents have complete written pathways; actual kit, school approval and classroom-pilot checks remain conditional. Local program standards are not official Archdiocesan or Minnesota standards.

C-STREAM represents Catholic STEM education that intentionally weaves together faith and reason throughout every aspect of the curriculum. Rather than treating religion as a standalone subject, this framework integrates Catholic identity like "yeast that causes everything to rise."

Our Vision

"Science and faith are complementary – the beautiful harmony of faith and reason so students can be a light in the secular world."

docs.title: What Makes C-STREAM Special
docs.text:
The "A" in C-STREAM encompasses Arts (both visual and musical), with hands-on creation first:

  • Visual Art: Observational drawing, pattern, purposeful model design, composition and visual communication

  • Music: Rhythm, sound investigation, composition and attentive listening

Digital art, animation and music tools are optional extensions when they materially improve the learning objective, not prerequisites for arts learning.

docs.title: The 12 Success Factors
docs.text:
These twelve design principles guide the local program. Consult the source register before making an official standards or accreditation claim.

1. Faith-Reason Integration

Present faith and reason as complementary, while distinguishing scientific evidence, theological teaching and a classroom metaphor.

2. NCEA's 10 Characteristics

Use a local STREAM reflection checklist. Exact NCEA publication alignment and accreditation status are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

3. Hands-On, Project-Based Learning

Students apply leading-edge technology to "hands-on, minds-on projects" that build critical thinking and collaboration.

4. Service-Oriented STEM Applications

Connect STEM skills to Catholic social teaching through "Hands and Feet of Christ" projects.

5. Cross-Curricular Integration

Intentionally connect disciplines – math, science, art, music, religion, and language arts.

6. Balance with Traditional Subjects

STEM receives emphasis but not at the expense of other subjects; maintain the whole-child approach.

7. Start Early

Begin high-quality STEM education as soon as children enter elementary school.

8. Teacher Professional Development

Investment in educator training on bringing faith and reason together in the classroom.

9. 21st Century Skills Focus

Emphasize problem-solving, communication, collaboration, and critical thinking.

10. Catholic Heritage in Science

Leverage the Church's rich scientific legacy (Mendel, Copernicus, Pasteur, Lemaître, and more).

11. Community and Industry Partnerships

External connections with parishes, universities, and industry partners enhance programs.

12. Wonder and Curiosity as Foundation

Approach education from the perspective of wonder, exploration, and faith.

Choose one sequence, not an additive menu:

  • Weekly: A 34-slot planning calendar; holiday and multi-week document counts require the grade-band pacing check.

  • Extensions: Use additional meetings for retesting, data, artistic revision and communication; do not add every optional project to the year.

See the scope and sequence for learning priorities and the lesson map for document-level counts.

docs.title: 🎨🎵 The "A" in C-STREAM: Arts
docs.text:
Hands-on creation first. Arts include purposeful visual and musical communication. These digital tools are possible extensions, not requirements:

Art (Visual) Music (Audio) Drawing/painting apps (Tayasui Sketches, Procreate) Music composition apps (GarageBand, Chrome Music Lab) Animation (Scratch, FlipaClip) Sound design and effects Graphic design (Canva, Google Drawings) Audio storytelling (podcasting) 3D modeling (Tinkercad, SketchUp) Coding music (Sonic Pi, Scratch) Digital photography Rhythm and pattern coding

docs.title: Seasonal Structure
docs.text: Season Weeks Focus Lesson Types Foundation Slots 1-13: 13 meetings Wonder, tools, structures, service Use the selected grade-band track Investigation Slots 14-27: 13 meetings + slot 17 break Light, inquiry, design and computing Indoors; preserve evidence and revision time Application Slots 28-34: 6 meetings + slot 32 break Measurement, life/creation care, reflection Move seasonal/liturgical contexts to actual school dates

docs.title: Count meetings, not project labels
docs.text:
For the weekly scaffold: 13 + 13 + 6 = 32 teaching meetings, plus two break slots. The earlier single-week/multi-week/long-arc quotas double-counted time and must not be added together.

Choose the actual grade/rotation documents, total their planned meetings, then compare with the school's calendar. Use unexpected spare meetings for retesting, individual evidence and artistic revision. If meetings are lost, reduce project scope rather than removing assessment or cleanup.

For Robotics/Coding Weeks: - "Can you show me how you programmed the robot?" - "What went wrong and how did you fix it?" - "How can robots help people?"

For Building/Engineering Weeks: - "What made your structure strong?" - "If you could rebuild it, what would you change?" - "Who might use something like what you built?"

docs.title: Parent Quick Explanations
docs.text:
What is C-STREAM?

C-STREAM stands for Catholic Science, Technology, Religion, Engineering, Art & Music, and Mathematics. It's like STEM, but with Catholic faith woven throughout. Your child learns that faith and science work together to understand God's amazing world.

Why Catholic STEM?

Catholic education has always valued both faith and reason. We help students see that the same God who inspired the Psalms also created the laws of physics. Learning about creation helps us know and love the Creator.

How can I help at home?

Ask questions! Show curiosity about what your child is learning. Point out science and engineering in everyday life. Wonder aloud about how things work. Most importantly, help your child see God in the amazing world around them.

docs.title: Evidence of learning, not participation percentages
docs.text:
Evidence What to assess Individual oral explanation, drawing or demonstration The stated science, mathematics, computing or design objective Test record and revision Whether the student uses evidence to explain an improvement Ethical or stewardship choice An age-appropriate reason about people/resources, not the child's personal piety Collaboration and effort Record separately from mastery; successful group work does not prove every student's understanding

Use a simple objective-linked rubric and the local progression. Do not grade handwriting, artistic polish or reading proficiency unless it is the actual objective.

docs.title: Contributing to C-STREAM
docs.text:
🤝 Contributing to C-STREAM

Catholic Science, Technology, Religion, Engineering, Arts, and Math

Thank you for your interest in contributing to the C-STREAM Framework! We welcome your input, whether it's submitting new lesson plans, improving existing resources, or helping us better integrate Catholic values into STEM education.

Before editing curriculum, read the curriculum review, local standards and teaching-release priorities. Preserve baseline findings when recording a revision; a changed file is not automatically classroom-ready.

docs.title: 1. 🐛 Reporting Issues
docs.text:
If you notice any issues with the framework, lesson plans, templates, or resources (e.g., broken links, typos, or inaccuracies), please help us by reporting them:

  1. Go to the Issues tab in the repository
  2. Click on New Issue
  3. Provide a clear description with as much detail as possible:
  4. The file where the issue exists
  5. What needs to be corrected
  6. Any suggested fixes

docs.title: 2. 📝 Submitting New Lesson Plans
docs.text:
We'd love your help creating new C-STREAM lessons! Follow these steps:

  1. Fork the Repository Fork this repository to your own GitHub account.

  2. Create a New Branch Create a branch specific to your changes: 

    git checkout -b add-new-lesson-plan

  3. Use Our Templates Build your lesson using the C-STREAM Lesson Plan Template. Ensure your lesson:

  4. Integrates faith and reason (the "R" in C-STREAM)
  5. Specifies grade-appropriate timing (K: 25min, 1-2: 30min, 3-4: 40min, 5-6: 45min)
  6. Includes materials from the CSCOE Library where applicable

  7. Connects to Catholic values and/or Catholic Social Teaching

  8. Submit a Pull Request Submit a pull request to the main branch with a clear description of your lesson.

docs.title: 3. ✨ Improving Existing Resources
docs.text:
If you have suggestions for improving current materials:

  1. Identify the Resource Locate the file in the appropriate folder (Templates/, Rubrics/, Resources/)

  2. Fork and Branch Fork the repository and create a branch

  3. Make Changes Edit to improve clarity, expand activities, or better integrate Catholic values. Be sure to reference:

  4. CSCOE Library materials where appropriate
  5. Grade-level time frames

  6. The 12 Success Factors outlined in the framework

  7. Submit a Pull Request Include a description of what you changed and why

docs.title: 4. 👨‍🔬 Adding Catholic Scientist Profiles
docs.text:
Help expand our Catholic Scientists Heritage resource:

  1. Research a Catholic scientist not yet profiled
  2. Include:
  3. Biographical information
  4. Scientific contributions
  5. Faith journey and how faith influenced their work
  6. Discussion questions for students
  7. Grade-level adaptations

docs.title: 5. 📦 Contributing CSCOE Library Integration
docs.text:
If you have experience with CSCOE Library materials:

  • Share lesson ideas using specific equipment

  • Document setup procedures for materials

  • Suggest alternative activities when materials aren't available

docs.title: Respect Catholic Values
docs.text: All lesson plans, resources, and materials must align with Catholic values and teachings. C-STREAM is built on the foundation that faith and reason are complementary.

docs.title: Maintain Grade Appropriateness
docs.text: Grade Time Approach Kindergarten 25 min Wonder, exploration, simple hands-on Grades 1-2 30 min Guided exploration with structure Grades 3-4 40 min Independent work with collaboration Grades 5-6 45 min Complex projects, student-led inquiry

docs.title: Follow the 12 Success Factors
docs.text: Ensure contributions align with the 12 Success Factors for Catholic STEM education.

docs.title: Use Consistent Formatting
docs.text:
• Follow existing file naming conventions

  • Use provided templates

  • Include proper YAML frontmatter

  • Add breadcrumb navigation

docs.title: Test Your Contributions
docs.text:
If contributing a new lesson plan:

  • Test in a classroom setting if possible

  • Note any challenges or modifications needed

  • Include setup time and preparation requirements

Also provide exact, scalable supplies for 10/15/20/25 students, numbered steps within the native period, an individual objective-linked evidence check, visible safety/stop rules, support/challenge, cleanup and an indoor alternative when weather matters. For early readers, demonstrate directions and accept oral, drawn or manipulated evidence.

Use hands-on/unplugged methods first. Categorize technology as None, Optional, Recommended or Required and explain any required use. A device-free fallback must state what changes in the objective; it cannot certify actual hardware/software execution. Family work and donations must not be prerequisites.

docs.title: Update the curriculum maps
docs.text:
Add/update the corresponding band-audit CSV in Review/ for every lesson. Use the documented schema, the actual schedule/rotation, the native period as integer minutes per meeting, and 2-5 relevant local codes linked to planned individual evidence. Keep the baseline status/priority and record the subsequent revision separately.

From the repository root:

.\scripts\Build-CurriculumMaps.ps1
.\scripts\Build-CurriculumMaps.ps1 -ValidateOnly
mkdocs build

Include the regenerated maps with the curriculum change. Schema validation does not establish safety, developmental fit or standards mastery. Report desk walkthroughs and actual classroom trials separately.

For current Kindergarten version-3.0 references, keep metadata, actual teaching steps and the individual-evidence definitions in the K sync script consistent:

.\scripts\Sync-KindergartenAudit.ps1
.\scripts\Test-KindergartenReferences.ps1
.\scripts\Build-CurriculumMaps.ps1

The K validator checks the current 37-document/29-autonomous-reference contract, 25-minute sequences and supply scaling. An intentional structural revision must update the corresponding contract/tests, not merely bypass their failures.

docs.title: Verify sources and claims
docs.text: Use authoritative sources and record the URL, applicable version and review date. Official benchmark alignment needs the exact benchmark, student task and assessment evidence. Label locally created standards as local. Unverified Church/history/Archdiocesan/state/accreditation claims are VERIFICATION REQUIRED; do not invent identifiers or quotations.

docs.title: Integrate Faith Meaningfully
docs.text: Don't just add a prayer at the beginning—weave Catholic identity throughout like "yeast that causes everything to rise."

docs.title: 🔄 Review Process
docs.text:
Once your pull request is submitted:

  1. Initial Review - The C-STREAM team reviews your contribution
  2. Feedback - You may receive suggestions for improvements
  3. Revision - Update your pull request based on feedback
  4. Merge - Approved contributions are merged into the main branch
  5. Recognition - Contributors are acknowledged in release notes

docs.title: 💡 Ideas for Contributions
docs.text:
Not sure where to start? Here are some ideas:

  • Add more Catholic scientist profiles

  • Create grade-specific activity variations

  • Develop Digital Art/Music integration lessons

  • Write family engagement activities

  • Translate resources to Spanish

  • Create video tutorials for complex setups

  • Document CSCOE equipment procedures

  • Develop assessment tools

  • Add seasonal/liturgical connections

docs.title: 📫 Questions?
docs.text:
If you have questions about contributing:

  • Open a Discussion in the repository

  • Review existing Issues for similar questions

  • Contact the C-STREAM team through GitHub

docs.title: 🙏 Thank You!
docs.text:
Your contributions help us continue to inspire students to explore STEM through a Catholic lens. Together, we can help students see how science and faith work together to understand God's amazing creation.

"Science and faith are complementary – the beautiful harmony of faith and reason so students can be a light in the secular world."

Happy Teaching and Creating! ✨

docs.text:
Location: Our Lady of the Prairie Catholic School · Belle Plaine, MN · Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis

docs.title: 🔄 Curriculum Flexibility Options
docs.text: C-STREAM offers flexible scheduling to meet your school's needs:

docs.title: Year A / Year B Rotation (Grades 1-6)
docs.text:
For schools with combined grade classrooms (1-2, 3-4, 5-6), we provide a two-year rotation:

  • Year A: Complete curriculum with one set of projects and contexts

  • Year B: Same skills and concepts with different projects, saints, and applications

Core competencies intentionally recur with increasing independence. Contexts vary, but the grade reviews identify actual overlaps and prerequisites. Kindergarten does not require Year A/B since students advance to 1st grade.

docs.title: Weekly vs. Bi-Weekly Scheduling
docs.text:
• Weekly (34 calendar slots): Check multi-week meetings and holidays against the grade review; this is not 34 lesson files.

  • Bi-Weekly (17 sessions): Condensed curriculum for schools with STREAM every other week

docs.title: 🎯 STREAM Focus Areas
docs.text:
Each lesson integrates multiple STREAM elements:

Letter Focus Area Description S Science Scientific inquiry, observation, experimentation T Technology Tools, systems, algorithms, data, responsible use; digital creation when valuable R Religion Faith integration, Catholic identity, ethics E Engineering Design process, problem-solving, building A Arts Visual arts, digital creation, music M Mathematics Measurement, patterns, data, computation

docs.title: 🙏 Catholic Identity Integration
docs.text:
Catholic integration is expressed through age-appropriate truth, wonder, dignity, stewardship and service. Prayer or a saint reference alone does not establish a meaningful connection. Review and verify any historical or scriptural attribution. Existing lessons may include:

  • Opening Prayer — Connected to lesson theme

  • Scripture Connection — Relevant Bible verse

  • Wonder Question — Sparking curiosity about God's creation

  • Catholic Scientist — When applicable, historical Catholic STEM contributors

  • Faith Reflection — Closing connection to Catholic teaching

docs.title: 🔬 Grades 1-2 Year A Bi-Weekly C-STREAM
docs.text:
17 Sessions | 30 Minutes Each | Every Other Week

This folder contains the condensed Grades 1-2 Year A C-STREAM curriculum for schools with bi-weekly STREAM classes. Year A focuses on foundational engineering, coding with ScratchJr/Dash Robots, and exploring God's patterns in nature.

docs.title: Audit and entry conditions
docs.text:
See the Grades 1-2 review and downloadable audit. There are 17 actual meetings in 17 files = 510 minutes, compared with 32 weekly meetings/960 minutes. This is a reduced-contact alternative, not equal robotics/science mastery in half the time.

Year A need not precede Year B. New Grade 1 students learn through oral directions, pictures, pointing and drawing; returning Grade 2 students add evidence-based explanations and revisions. Before Session 15 recheck Session 04 stored-code start/stop and simple sequence, rather than assuming expertise after one encounter. Revisit skills briefly between biweekly meetings where ordinary class routines permit, but do not count extra C-STREAM sessions as existing inventory.

All 17 files are complete documented packages: Bridge Building and Robot Friends are preserved references, and the remaining 15 plans are rebuilt. Supplies, native timing, Grade 1/Grade 2 evidence and cleanup are explicit. Weather Watchers now makes three actual same-window checks within its period; Sound Engineering includes physical vibration and purposeful musical composition. A brief Mendel/abbey context is source-checked; unsupported history and quotations are omitted. Documentation checks are not classroom certification or official benchmark alignment.

For trio-based lessons, 10/15/20/25 pupils use ⅘/7/9 groups: two trios and two pairs; five trios; six trios and one pair; seven trios and two pairs. Optional reference routines support kit checks and individual evidence but do not replace the lesson's complete sequence, supplies or safety. Pair-based lessons keep their own allocation/reserve plan. Fewer devices use the lesson's stated waves/shared tests, not groups of four or credit for watching.

docs.title: 🎯 Year A Learning Goals
docs.text:
Target outcomes, demonstrated individually when the relevant primary path is taught:

  • ✅ Follow the design process: Ask → Imagine → Plan → Create → Improve

  • Run/debug a short stored Dash/Blockly sequence; manual Go driving is not programming evidence.

  • ✅ Create simple coding projects with ScratchJr

  • ✅ Identify patterns in God's creation

  • ✅ Connect Catholic faith to scientific discovery

  • ✅ Work collaboratively on engineering challenges

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher plan Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly A / Structures Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE Domains / big idea C, E, M / A first engineering question names a need and a test. Student objective / why "I can build a low structure that stands and explain a changed support." New pupils can enter either rotation with concrete design routines. Catholic connection Share blocks fairly, save reusable materials and explain how careful work helps the group. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard. Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-E1: needs, criteria and constraints; CST-E2: build, test and redesign; CST-M1: count, compare and measure. Only the evidence below supports these local claims. Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
  2. Inspect planks, mark a 30 cm ceiling and choose a 10-second standing test. Draw ask/plan/try/change icons; do not prepare a tallest-tower contest.
  3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: plan or prediction / actual result / reason or revision. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
  4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

docs.text:
Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
Engineer = designs solutions; criterion = must do; base = bottom support.

A low structure can solve a stability problem. Failure identifies a weak part, not a weak child.

Common misconception: An engineer must make the tallest structure.

If asked: "What if it falls?" Record that useful result and change a support.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Tabletop under 30 cm, hands clear during the standing test, no heavy loads or furniture climbing. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

docs.title: Meeting 1: First useful structure - 30 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3: State the need: a structure that stands 10 seconds in its tabletop space.
  2. 3-7: Model a broad base, measure from table level and show a plan -> test -> change record.
  3. 7-20: Teams use 18 planks to build/test, record height and change one support. Every child adds/directs a part and counts or measures.
  4. 20-26: Each child explains the need, first/revised result and a reusable-material care action.
  5. 26-30: Dismantle top-down and count all 18 planks; retain individual records. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

docs.title: Questions to ask
docs.text:
• Which support did you change after the test?
  • How did we care for shared materials?

docs.title: Individual evidence and success
docs.text:
Grade 1: Show a standing test, count/compare height and point to a changed support.

Grade 2: Name the criterion and limit, compare measured results and explain a test-based change.

Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

docs.title: Support and challenge
docs.text:
Support / nonreader access: Prebuilt base example and large picture steps; accept equal-unit height counting. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

Challenge: Maintain height while using fewer planks and test the tradeoff. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor alternative
docs.text:
No planks: use equal clean blocks and pretest a feasible low height. Immediate falls: widen base rather than add unsafe weight.

Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

docs.title: Family copy - optional, no routine homework
docs.text: We began engineering with a clear standing test and careful shared-material work. Ask: "Which support did you change after the test?" Optional: notice a stable base in a pictured object. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

Student objective / why "I can make, extend and repair a pattern and explain its purpose." Pattern rules support mathematics and genuine artistic choices. docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
  2. Count 30 existing large pattern shapes or batch-precut colored paper shapes per kit, enough for up to three 9-shape patterns. Draw AB and ABB examples plus one intentional error. Use paper crayons for a silent rhythm route.
  3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: unit / next two elements / corrected pattern. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
  4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

docs.text:
Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50 Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25 Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9 Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1 Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1 Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1 Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1 Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1 Pattern shape / kit / large reusable shapes 120 150 210 270

Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
Unit = repeated part; predict = say what comes next; rhythm = timed pattern.

A repeated-looking natural feature is not always a strict mathematical repeat. Assess a constructed rule, not a claim that everything in nature repeats perfectly.

Common misconception: Any decorative arrangement is a repeating pattern.

If asked: "Must every leaf match exactly?" No; nature has variation. Our constructed pattern has a stated rule.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Large cards only; no beads, food props or loud compulsory clapping. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

docs.title: Meeting 1: Pattern communication - 30 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3: Show a patterned border intended to welcome a viewer; ask which part repeats.
  2. 3-7: Model AB twice, then an incorrect next card; explain how the unit predicts the correction.
  3. 7-20: Each child makes AB twice (Grade 1) or ABB/AAB three times (Grade 2), chooses a color/shape purpose and trades a next-two prediction. Partners insert one error; each author repairs it.
  4. 20-26: Each child identifies the unit, next two elements and purposeful visual choice; return reusable cards thoughtfully.
  5. 26-30: Count 30 cards per kit and save each child's drawn pattern before dismantling. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

docs.title: Questions to ask
docs.text:
• Which part of your pattern repeats?
  • Why did you choose those shapes or colors?

docs.title: Individual evidence and success
docs.text:
Grade 1: Identify AB, extend by two elements and explain one purposeful choice.

Grade 2: Identify ABB/AAB, repair an error and explain the prediction using the unit.

Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

docs.title: Support and challenge
docs.text:
Support / nonreader access: Use two high-contrast or tactile shapes with teacher oral rhythm; avoid color-only distinctions. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

Challenge: Show the same rule using a silent four-beat finger/tap representation. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor alternative
docs.text:
Cards missing: draw shapes on allocated paper. Sound sensitivity: use a silent pointing pattern with the same rule; no music performance claim on that route.

Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

docs.title: Family copy - optional, no routine homework
docs.text: We created purposeful patterns, predicted their continuation and repaired an error. Ask: "Which part of your pattern repeats?" Optional: tell or point to a two-part pattern indoors. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

docs.text: These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register. Catholic care, dignity and honest-inquiry applications follow that register; no unsupported scientist/saint biography, Scripture quotation or devotional history is required to execute this lesson. docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Structures / Bridge Building Time / domains One native 30-minute meeting, session 3 of 17 / C, E, M Big idea Shape can change how a bridge supports a load; fair tests compare evidence. Student objective "I can test two paper shapes and explain one improvement." Why Bridges serve people; engineers test safe models before trusting designs. Catholic connection Include neighbors and build relationships; this is a teacher metaphor, not Scripture or an attributed papal quotation. Service and dignity: CCC 2407. Standards Local CST-C2: explain who crossing helps; CST-E1: span/load criteria; CST-E2: two tests/redesign; CST-M1: count load; CST-M2: record/compare results. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path: physical paper tests answer the question. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class / supplies
docs.text:
1. On each table place two identical-height books 10 cm apart, measured between inside edges. Test ordinary A4/letter paper across gap; do not promise a flat sheet must fail. Make pairs, with one trio at odd enrollment: 5/7/10/12 active teams for 10/15/20/25 pupils. The table budgets ⅝/10/13 kits, retaining one reserve at 15/25.
  2. Cut/choose identical paper sheets; prepare equal broad wooden blocks as loads, maximum five, one at a time. Do not use pennies or heavy weights.
  3. Draw two-result chart (flat/folded). Demonstrate accordion folds; Grade 1 can use a teacher-started fold.
  4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, individual evidence check.
  5. Per pair: two support books, two paper sheets, five identical broad blocks; ruler shared.
  6. Class: timer, class comparison board; optional bridge pictures.
  7. Teacher-only: scissors if paper needs cutting, model-preflight materials.
Students Pairs / bridge kits Test sheets Broad blocks 10 5 10 25 15 8 16 40 20 10 20 50 25 13 26 65

At 25 partners test simultaneously on low tables while teacher checks individuals; no 13-group sequential whole-class loading queue. In a trio, rotate builder, loader and observer so every child predicts, handles a safe test step and explains the result; the extra kit is not a lone child's pair.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Span = gap crossed; support = holds bridge at ends; load = what bridge holds; criterion = success requirement; redesign = change after testing. Beam bridges carry loads across supports. Folding can stiffen paper, but paper type, span and placement affect results. Model behavior is not proof a real bridge is safe. Misconception: the strongest student's bridge matters most. Same conditions and explaining evidence matter. If asked "Is a bridge a Bible verse?" No. Our relationship metaphor is a teacher illustration; the removed "bridges, not walls" quotation was not Scripture. Optional service reference: Galatians 5:13 in school-approved Bible, wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Show a bridge purpose; ask who needs safe access and how a design includes them. Optional original prayer asks for kind cooperation.
  2. 4-8: Demonstrate fixed 10 cm span and loading one equal block at center for five seconds, stopping at five or failure. Clear hands before loading.
  3. 8-14: Partners test flat paper; each predicts and counts/points to result. Record actual supported load before failure, not total dropped blocks.
  4. 14-21: Fold second sheet, keep supports/load alike, test again; swap loader/observer roles. If needed redesign one fold and retest within block.
  5. 21-26: Each child draws/shows a changed feature and compares two results; Grade 2 names what stayed the same. Partner explains who a real bridge serves.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: What stayed the same? Which shape held more, or were they equal? What would you change next? Who benefits from crossing safely? - Grade 1: count/point to two loads, show one change and orally explain a user need; drawing replaces writing. - Grade 2: record two counts, identify same span/load, explain improvement from evidence, not appearance. - Record not yet / prompted / independent per child for comparison, change and criteria. Failed models can still demonstrate learning.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Both hold five: record ceiling "at least five"; narrow paper equally or widen span slightly for a second comparison, labeling changed conditions. Neither holds one: reduce span equally. Missing books: identical boxes. All work indoors with no devices; no extended curing/glue time.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: Models on tables only, no student weight, floor crossings, climbing, heavy loads or loose coins. Broad loads maximum five; hands out during collapse. Never apply model capacity to a real bridge. Support: prestarted folds, four picture steps, adult scribing and oral count. Challenge: Grade 2 compare two fold patterns under identical criteria, not an unlimited load contest.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text:
Count loads/books, flatten/recycle usable paper, return ruler, retain comparison sketch. We tested two paper bridge shapes and compared honest load counts. Catholic connection: designs that help neighbors cross safely. Ask: "What changed, and how did you know it helped?" Optional: notice a bridge in a picture or fold scrap paper with an adult; no supplies purchase or routine homework. CCC 2407. John Nepomucene patronage/history: VERIFICATION REQUIRED, optional and not needed for lesson; no attributed quote is used.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Robot Friends Time / domains One 30-minute meeting, session 4 of 17 / C, T Big idea Remote control and a stored program are different ways to give input. Student objective "I can predict and run two stored actions, then fix one instruction." Why A useful program runs in order and is checked against its purpose. Catholic connection Share tools fairly and choose a helpful purpose; teacher application of CCC 2407. Human dignity is not machine obedience. Standards Local CST-C2: fair partner turn/helpful purpose; CST-T1: run/stop and input/output; CST-T2: order two actions/debug. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Required primary path: Dash plus compatible tablet and Blockly to run stored instructions. Go driving alone does not meet programming objective. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes initial setup plus charging; 4 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Confirm actual loan, compatibility/permissions and model charging instructions. Open Blockly, not just Go.
  2. Test drive forward 20 cm at low speed -> change light color using installed block names; write tested settings on board. Show Run and Stop.
  3. Mark a dry 1 m floor bay for each active kit, clear of exits; have a forward/light picture card and table token.
  4. Assign teams of 2-3; rotate programmer, observer and checker after every run. No prior Year A/B coding assumed.

docs.title: Supplies
docs.text:
• Per student: half-sheet, crayon.
  • Per team: one charged Dash/tablet kit, two cards, token.
  • Whole class: floor tape, timer, board; reusable trays.
  • Teacher-only: chargers, installed help, roster.
Students Teams / kits for simultaneous practice Papers 10 4 10 15 5 15 20 7 20 25 9 25

With three kits at 25, use three 4-minute waves (three teams/wave) at a teacher-supervised station; other teams predict with tokens. With one kit, not all children can receive adequate independent practice in 30 minutes: record missing device opportunities and repeat later. Do not count watching as operating/programming.

docs.title: Vocabulary / teacher background
docs.text: Program = stored instructions; input = what we send; output = movement/light; sequence = order; debug = correct a mismatch. Blockly is a stored block-based programming tool. Go joystick input steers in real time; it can illustrate input/output but cannot certify stored-code learning. Misconception: pressing a drive button proves programming. Require a connected stored sequence. If asked about Carlo Acutis: saint title/biography is optional; current official source is VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching details. A helpful technology choice can be assessed without a biography.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: State objective, bay/stop rules, fair turns and helpful-purpose question. Optional original prayer asks for wise use.
  2. 4-7: Every child predicts two picture actions; partner moves a tabletop token and points to light picture.
  3. 7-11: Teacher contrasts manual Go steering with Blockly two-block stored run; shows how to stop. Do not say driving was programming.
  4. 11-23: Each child predicts/runs the tested sequence, swaps a color or movement amount and reruns. Observer says what changed; rotate after each run. Teacher records individual run/stop, sequence and one change.
  5. 23-26: Each child points/draws two actions and explains why the second run differed; state one fair turn/helpful purpose.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: Can it run without steering? Which instruction changed output? Did your partner get an actual turn? Grade 1: orally/visually order two actions, run/stop under supervision and point to one changed output. Grade 2: assemble two or three actions, predict, change one block and explain before/after. Both name a responsible use. Score not observed / prompted / independent per child. Unplugged evidence never earns physical-robot operation credit.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: After two minutes checking charge/selected robot, use cards and token. Child orders two actions, partner follows, child fixes reversed order. Assess CST-T2 conceptual sequence/debug only; no real robot programming or operation mastery. Poor travel: shorten/lower speed on same dry surface. All work indoors.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: No racing, chasing, running on tables or touching a moving robot; stop outside bay. Teacher-only charging; keep cables out of routes. Consent before physical assistance. Support: picture blocks, narrate each action, adult scribing and two-action starter. Challenge: Grade 2 add a short wait/light action; postpone maze/loops to a later measured opportunity.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text:
Stop programs, power down, count kits/cards, clear tape and store labeled trays; teacher charges. We distinguished steering from stored code, predicted a sequence and changed one instruction. Our Catholic connection was responsible sharing. Ask: "What ran without steering?" Optional: two spoken instructions for a paper token; no device/purchase or routine homework. Blockly official app; CCC 2407. Colossians 3:23 is an optional school-approved Bible reference, no unverified quote.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher plan Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly A / Observation Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE Domains / big idea C, S, A, M / Observation distinguishes living, once-living and never-living examples. Student objective / why "I can draw details, sort three examples with reasons and compare a feature count." An indoor sample table gives every child safe observation time. Weather = conditions at a time/place; precipitation = rain/snow falling; observation = noticed condition; forecast = prediction.

docs.text:
Vibration = back-and-forth motion; pitch = high/low sound; volume = loud/soft; rhythm = timed phrase.

A shorter freely vibrating part generally has higher pitch. Change length while using similarly gentle plucks; this is a guided comparison, not precise acoustic measurement.

Common misconception: Louder means higher pitch, or a pupa/balloon instrument is needed for music.

If asked: "Why can I feel sound?" Sound involves vibration; our strip lets us see/feel a vibration safely without putting anything in mouths.

No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

docs.title: 🌟 Grades 1-2 Year B Bi-Weekly C-STREAM
docs.text:
17 Sessions | 30 Minutes Each | Every Other Week

This folder contains the condensed Grades 1-2 Year B C-STREAM curriculum for schools with bi-weekly STREAM classes. Year B features different projects, saints, and contexts than Year A while building the same foundational skills.

docs.title: Audit and entry conditions
docs.text:
See the Grades 1-2 review and downloadable audit. This track has 17 actual meetings/17 files = 510 minutes; weekly has 32 meetings/960 minutes. Fewer contacts mean fewer independent device turns and science observations, not equivalent mastery.

Year A is not a prerequisite. Teach safe handling, observation and picture sequences before challenges. Grade 1 can point, draw or respond orally without reading; Grade 2 should justify a feature/measurement and revise using evidence. Session 14 rechecks Session 03 stored-code start/stop rather than declaring students experts.

All 17 files are complete documented packages: Meet Sphero and Garden Engineers are preserved references; the remaining 15 plans are rebuilt. Mathematics progresses through same-start measurement, repeated counts, two-part/equal-group operations and interpreted data, with distinct Grade 1/Grade 2 checks in the actual steps. Maria Agnesi's brief context is source-checked; unsupported quotations/history are omitted. School stock/policy and classroom pilots remain conditional, not documentation gaps or observed outcomes.

For trio-based lessons, 10/15/20/25 pupils use ⅘/7/9 groups: two trios and two pairs; five trios; six trios and one pair; seven trios and two pairs. Optional reference routines support kit checks and individual evidence but do not replace the lesson's complete sequence, supplies or safety. Pair-based lessons keep their own allocation/reserve plan. Fewer devices use the lesson's stated waves/shared tests, not groups of four or credit for watching.

docs.title: Before class / supplies
docs.text:
1. Confirm real inventory/loan and school permissions. Check the exact model supports chosen blocks; do not assume Mini/BOLT features identical.
  2. In Blocks test light-color -> roll at heading 0 for 0.5-1 second at low speed -> stop; write model-specific working settings on board. Aim heading 0 away from children.
  3. Mark dry 1 m floor bays; prepare light/roll/stop picture cards, tabletop tokens and safe stop signal.
  4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, individual roster check.
  5. Per team of 2-3: one robot/tablet kit and picture cards/token.
  6. Class: floor tape, timer, board, storage trays.
  7. Teacher-only: chargers, installed help and model screening. No attached pens.
Students Teams / simultaneous kits Papers 10 4 10 15 5 15 20 7 20 25 9 25

If only three kits exist, at 25 supervise one station with three 4-minute waves of three teams; off-device teams predict cards. With one kit, record unobserved individual runs and repeat assessment later. Do not infer mastery from watching another child's robot.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; input/output = code/result; aim = set direction reference; debug = fix a mismatch. Manual Drive mode is remote control. A connected stored sequence that executes hands-off is programming. Floor, charge and aim influence travel. Misconception: every rolling robot run matches an exact path. Observe before promising accuracy. If asked "Are we experts now?" We are beginning programmers; evidence shows specific skills, not expertise.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Show robot, purpose and care/turn rule. Optional original prayer asks for wise tool use.
  2. 4-7: Children predict color then forward movement using cards/token, orally or by pointing.
  3. 7-11: Teacher contrasts Drive with a stored Blocks sequence; demonstrate aim, Run and Stop.
  4. 11-23: Each child predicts and executes starter, changes a color or roll duration and reruns. Roles rotate after each run; teacher records each child's observed actions.
  5. 23-26: Individual exit: point to two ordered actions, name an output and one change; identify safe equipment care.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / measurable evidence
docs.text: What is stored before Run? Why aim again? What changed after your edit? How did you protect shared equipment? Grade 1: order two action cards, personally Run/Stop under supervision and point to changed output. Grade 2: assemble at least two stored actions, predict, change a block and explain mismatch or change. Record not observed / prompted / independent for each criterion; care assessed through an action, not a saint fact.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Connection failure: check selected robot/charge once, switch after two minutes. Token alternative: arrange two cards, have partner follow, fix one intentionally wrong card. Record algorithm/debug evidence only; no real robot operation/programming mastery. Mis-aim: stop/re-aim/shorten movement. All work indoors, no winter/outdoor condition.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: Low-speed marked bays; stop if out of area; no chasing/racing or holding running robots. Teacher handles chargers and small removable model components. Dry floor only, no art paint/markers attached to ball. Support: picture starter, narration, large cards, adult scribing and accessible tabletop token; Grade 1 needs no independent reading. Challenge: Grade 2 adds light/wait action or compares two durations, not expert mazes.

docs.text:
Feature = characteristic; camouflage = reduced visibility against surroundings; model = representation.

Shape, background, lighting and observer affect detection. Actual adaptations develop across populations; children drawing a trait do not engineer a living species.

docs.text:
1. 0-3: Discuss a visible feature and a labeled model, distinguishing a prediction from a result.

docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Growth and design / Garden Engineers Time / domains One 30-minute meeting, session 5 of 17 / C, S, E, A Big idea A garden needs light, safe space and responsible care; design has constraints. Student objective "I can plant a seed and show where our pots and care path fit safely." Why Designers consider living needs and people who care for plants. Growth will not happen during today's meeting. Catholic connection Stewardship of plants/resources, CCC 2415; service through a shared accessible garden. Standards Local CST-C3: care plan/resource use; CST-S3: seed/seedling needs; CST-E1: light/access constraints; CST-E2: test/revise layout; CST-A1: garden plan. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path: physical pot-layout model and planting suffice. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20 minutes initial setup plus 2-3 minute adult school-day care checks; 5 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Verify one untreated seed variety's packet, allergy/school potting-mix guidance and suitable bright indoor space. No outdoor planting or grow light required.
  2. Teacher makes drainage holes in plastic pots and places them in leakproof trays. Premeasure about 200 mL mix/team.
  3. Draw a 30 x 40 cm tray model with light-side mark and a 10 cm-wide care access strip at its front. Use three paper pot circles/team; do not block an exit or window route.
  4. Name an adult to check moisture on school days, weekends/break plan and watering when needed. No daily automatic watering or required home care.
  5. Prepare a prestarted seedling/photo for showing future growth. Explicitly identify it as earlier/teacher evidence.

docs.title: Supplies / scaling
docs.text:
• Per student: half-sheet garden sketch, crayon.
  • Per team of 2-3: one pot, two seeds, 200 mL commercial potting mix, tray space, three paper pot circles and 30 x 40 cm paper mat.
  • Class: water jug, scoop, spill cloth, seedling/photo, whiteboard care log, handwashing.
  • Teacher-only: hole tool, seed packet, water distribution, care responsibility.
Students Teams / pots Seeds plus 4 backups Mix Student sheets 10 4 12 0.8 L 10 15 5 14 1.0 L 15 20 7 18 1.4 L 20 25 9 22 1.8 L 25

At 25 trays stay on tables; one teacher distributes water and collects pots. A small school garden can use team pots; no need for 25 individual live plants.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Seed = young plant with stored food; seedling = growing young plant; constraint = limit; access = reaching safely; care plan = who checks needs and when. Seeds may germinate without light depending on variety; green seedlings need light to make food. Soil provides support and nutrients, not the plant's food itself; suitable soilless growth is possible. No causal experiment or same-day growth is claimed. Misconception: a plant needs exactly the same water daily. Check moisture/packet guidance. If asked "Will mine sprout by next class?" Maybe; variety, conditions and viability matter. Record what actually happens.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Show seed versus earlier seedling and explain today's design/planting objective. Optional original prayer asks for responsible care.
  2. 4-8: Model pot circles on tray mat: three fit without overlap, face light-side, keep care strip clear. Deliberately block strip then revise.
  3. 8-14: Teams arrange three circles, partner checks constraints, revise one feature. Each child sketches/points to light and access path.
  4. 14-21: Demonstrate packet-based planting depth; teams fill pot, plant two seeds, lightly water and label date/team. Each child participates safely.
  5. 21-25: Individual exit: show two seedling needs and one layout/care choice. Identify adult moisture checker and record a prediction as a prediction.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

docs.title: Questions / success and later observation
docs.text: Where does light reach? Can the caretaker reach without knocking pots? How do we know when water is needed? Which result is still a prediction? Grade 1: oral/drawn two needs, point to clear access path and one care action. Grade 2: explain both layout constraints and one revision after checking; distinguish germination from later seedling growth. Record not yet / prompted / independent for needs, criteria, revision and care. One planted seed does not prove growth or experimental mastery. Before Session 06, the named adult adds one dated drawing/photo or height observation during normal plant care (about 2-3 minutes, not an extra C-STREAM meeting). Session 06 may spend its opening minute comparing it; if unavailable, use labeled teacher data and do not certify firsthand observation.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: No safe growing space or allergy clearance: use empty pots/paper circles and teacher seedling pictures. Assess layout/needs, not live planting/care mastery. docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grade Band: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes per session | Sessions: 17 over the school year | Rotation Year: A

This bi-weekly schedule provides a condensed C-STREAM experience for schools with alternating week schedules. Each 40-minute session delivers high-impact learning with Catholic integration.

docs.title: Audit status and prerequisites
docs.text:
These are 17 represented meetings / 680 minutes in 17 files, not half the weekly sequence compressed without loss. See the Grades 3-4 review and 71-lesson audit. All packages have complete quantities, native timelines and individual checks. Fourteen were completed in the all-60 follow-up; Dash, the updated Light & Circuits and Plants references remain unchanged. Document completion is not classroom certification.

Either rotation may be a pupil's first year. Teach Grade 3 supported counts/measurement and Grade 4 repeat-test/limitation reasoning in either. Scratch Intro is the prerequisite for animation; verify that learning rather than assume attendance. Plants has a within-meeting evidence path; living growth still takes days and an assigned adult caretaker.

CSCOE loan stock/dates, models, batteries, software and privacy permissions are VERIFICATION REQUIRED, not guaranteed. Paper route fallbacks evidence CT, not Dash operation. Circuits require approved low-voltage kits for real electrical outcomes; paper models do not light. No loose coin-cell cards are sent home. Weather and plant work have indoor/no-homework paths.

New packages supply needed source facts or omit unneeded biographies/quotes. Gratitude/Easter slides and Scratch animation include concrete executable workflows; paper fallbacks explicitly shift objectives. LittleBits needs its own matching approved modules, not guessed Snap wiring. Home activities and donations remain optional.

Optional preparation aid: Grades 1-6 reference routines. The complete lesson-specific supplies, individual checks and 40-minute sequence still govern. Dash retains its pair/trio budget; Light & Circuits retains the eight reported Snap kits and its actual station/wave plan. Waiting work is reasoning/design evidence, not a physical turn; groups never increase to four.

  3. Mark two 1 m square floor areas away from doors/stairs, each with start/direction and a soft cardboard boundary. Do not make pupils walk through a maze.
  4. Pair pupils, final trio if odd. Assign teams to seven one-minute testing rounds at most (two teams per round); all other work occurs at desks.
  5. Board: predicted path | actual endpoint | one correction. Draw a 4 by 4 grid for paper work. No printer required.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth paper kit is spare. Seven testing rounds cover up to thirteen teams, more than the twelve needed with a trio.

  • Per student: pencil and 1 evidence half-sheet.
  • Per team: 2 paper sheets (grid/record), ruler, paper token, 6 command cards hand-drawn on the sheets.
  • Class: 2 robots, 2 tablets, 2 chargers, 2 soft boundary sets, timer, 4 m floor-safe tape.
  • Teacher: kit instructions, stop control, charge access. No child plug handling.
Students Teams / rulers / tokens Team paper Cards Evidence slips / pencils Robots / tablets / chargers 10 5 each 10 sheets 30 10 each 2 each 15 8 each 16 sheets 48 15 each 2 each 20 10 each 20 sheets 60 20 each 2 each 25 13 each 26 sheets 78 25 each 2 each

Devices/rulers/cards/tokens reusable. Paper/tape consumable. One robot permits a teacher demo and limited operation checks; record missing pupil operation, not universal mastery.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text:
Algorithm: ordered instructions. Input: instruction/start action. Output: movement or light/sound. Debug: compare prediction to actual and correct. Relative turn: right/left from the robot's current facing direction.

Dash does not read the floor tape in this route; tape marks our reference. Blockly programs are distinct from steering it by remote control. Two forward movements separated by one right turn form an L. A whole square needs four sides and turns.

Misconception: "It knows where we want it to go." It follows the code using its hardware. If asked: "Why missed the target?" Answer: "Check the start/facing direction, units and turn. Change one setting, then run the same test."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Low-speed motion only, no races or intentional collisions. Teacher starts/stops demonstration; only scheduled teams enter a testing area. Hands off moving robots; retrieve after stop. Dry floor, no stairs/doorways; sound low. Teacher handles batteries/chargers. Stop if an area is no longer clear.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Purpose. Original prayer: "God, help us use tools responsibly and include each classmate." Ask: "Is steering by hand the same as running saved instructions?"
  2. 4-9: Demonstration. Identify robot, Blockly blocks, start and stop. Run the pretested L. Ask: "Which instruction changed its direction?"
  3. 9-14: Paper rehearsal. On a grid, one forward command means one square. Trace forward; right turn; forward; swap executor/reader. Draw expected endpoint. Explain that the grid is a model, not a physical centimeter measurement.
  4. 14-27: Build/run slots. Teams plan code on paper, then use a one-minute robot slot. First child enters forward; second adds right turn/forward; run and measure endpoint difference from the taped target. A trio's third child starts/stops and explains output. Teacher logs observed operations. Waiting teams find a deliberately wrong left-turn card in a paper route.
  5. 27-32: One correction. Teacher chooses a route that missed, checks start and facing, then adjusts one distance/turn. Predict and retest. "What changed? Which part did we keep the same?"
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Every child draws the L and identifies the turn, a debug change and its reason. Actual operators additionally identify start/stop and one measured result. Mark paper only when appropriate.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup/exit. Stop programs, teacher powers off/stores robots/tablets, pupils gather cards/tokens/rulers and restore lanes. Collect slips. Ask: "What does our paper test fail to test?"

docs.title: Low-tech substitute path / indoor alternative
docs.text: Use the same time windows; replace steps 2/⅘ with teacher/partner token execution on grids. Give a wrong-turn route, identify the first mismatch, replace one instruction and retest. Record computational-thinking sequence/debug evidence. Do not claim CST-T1 Bluetooth/device operation, robotics or sensor mastery. All pathways are indoors; Minnesota winter has no effect.

docs.title: Success, troubleshooting, support and challenge
docs.text:
Success: child traces a sequence, identifies the wrong turn and explains a testable correction. Device success is separately observed editing/running/stopping, not merely watching a partner. Score 1 guess; 2 trace with help; 3 independent trace/debug reason; 4 explains model-versus-device limitations using a measured result.

  • Pairing fails after 2 minutes: announce paper path and notify regular teacher of missing operation evidence.
  • Wrong turn: check relative left/right and robot starting direction; no floor-line sensing assumed.
  • Support / Grade 3: three cards, oral prompts, turn one's own paper token, ruler assistance; no angle calculations required.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: repeat test and compare whole-number endpoint errors, explaining why traction/units may matter.
  • 25 pupils: thirteen teams, two areas, seven one-minute rounds within the thirteen-minute window; no five-mission race.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text:
We planned and debugged an L-shaped sequence. Paper tracing demonstrates computational thinking; robot use adds measured input/output evidence. Our Catholic connection was sharing skills and safe tools fairly. Ask: "Which command changed direction?" Optional at home: trace three arrow directions with a token; the original scratch.mit.edu resource is optional, not required. No devices or homework.

docs.title: Starter, vocabulary and background
docs.text:
On one sprite:

when green flag clicked
go to x: (0) y: (0)
point in direction (90)
repeat (4)
  move (20) steps
  turn clockwise (90) degrees
  wait (1) seconds
end
say [Welcome!] for (2) seconds

Stage = display; sprite = character; loop = repeated enclosed blocks; event = trigger. Misconception: a block below the loop repeats. If asked "Why not forever?" Finite repeat permits an exact prediction and clear end. Scratch steps are screen coordinates, not physical centimeters.

docs.title: SAFETY/privacy
docs.text: Dry seated devices/counters; no public accounts/media, passwords or downloaded assets. Counters off bodies/away from mouthing pupils. Stop/report damaged gear. God-as-programmer is not a literal scientific model. Indoor primary.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "Which action happens four times?" Optional inclusive-work prayer.
  2. 4-10: Tour stage/sprite/Code; model starter and Stop.
  3. 10-21: Every child edits/runs in a three-minute turn; peers trace with four counters and record four moves/turns.

  5. 29-35: Each explains inside/outside loop and actual result; roster logs individual edit/run/stop. Four 90-degree turns total 360, no ratios.
  6. 35-40: Stop/save/reopen, count counters, return devices, file dated trace.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: four-repeat prediction, correction/retest and observed operation/ fair turn. Grade 3/support: copied stack/token trace/scribing. Grade 4/challenge: compare ¾ repeats and total turns. Sprite drifts: reset position/direction, check block enclosure, rerun. Half stations: two waves of three-minute turns within work blocks; fewer means reschedule operation. No device: same times token/block cards, CT/counting only, Scratch operation not observed. Early finish: new message, not unbounded program.

Family: We executed and checked a finite dance loop. Ask, "What repeated?" Optional: trace four turns verbally; no home device.

docs.text: Slide = display page; audience = reader; contrast = visible difference; consent = permission. Slide 1 "Thank you, classroom helpers"; slide 2 "You prepare our shared tools." Adult checks recipient consent/school approval first; this lesson assesses local display, not delivery. Dry devices, no names/photos/voices/passwords/cloud upload; stop/report damage. Grade 4/challenge: contrast/space tradeoff. Wrong text box: select slide/box then edit; no audio workaround. No app/device: two paper slides and same reader test, communication/privacy only, digital operation not observed. Half devices allow two waves of turns within work windows; below that reschedule. docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit Grades 3-4 / Circuits / Light & Circuits Time One 40-minute meeting, including 5-minute cleanup Domains Catholic audience care, science systems, technology tools, artistic communication Big idea / objective "I can trace and test an open/closed light circuit, then communicate what the light means." Why Safe testing helps us understand everyday tools. Catholic connection Advent light symbolizes hope in Christ (John 8:12); electricity does not prove Christ's divinity. Use the school's approved Scripture translation and design a respectful message without judging the reader's circumstances. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C2 (respectful message), CST-S3 (circuit model), CST-T1 (test/repair), CST-A3 (message feedback/revision). Technology None: no computing device or software. Approved electrical hardware is required for actual operation; paper is a model, not circuit mastery. Prerequisites No prior circuit lesson or Year B assumed Prep / cleanup First kit inspection 30 minutes; repeat prep 15 minutes; missing instructions/approval extra. Cleanup 5 minutes included.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text: Complete the OLP Snap Circuits guide preflight for the eight individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits (OHM-135). Use the actual model's documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project. Leave the approved diagram and counted station list ready for a substitute. Do not assume holder protection, a two-AA allocation or LED current limiting.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
• Per pupil: pencil, evidence half-sheet, art/message half-sheet.
  • Per team: diagram sheet, shared marker, dry work area.
  • Per hardware station: approved Snap kit with only project parts, grid and tray. Battery type/count and checked reserves follow the guide.
  • Teacher/class: approved instructions, setup card, board, timer, roster, dry storage and adult-controlled cells; demo uses a station kit.
Pupils Teams / diagram sheets Kits / trays Waves Student half-sheets / pencils 10 4 4 1 20 / 10 15 5 5 1 30 / 15 20 7 7 1 40 / 20 25 9 5 2 50 / 25

Reuse the same hardware for Year B Christmas Circuits; no second kit purchase.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and safety
docs.text:
Circuit: complete conducting path, including return. Open: interrupted. Closed: complete. Switch: opens/closes the path. Current: charge flow. The battery supplies energy; light symbolism is not an electrical explanation of faith or human dignity. A lamp project does not establish LED polarity mastery.

Misconception: touching any two conductors makes a safe circuit. If asked: "Why is it off?" Trace the approved path while power is isolated; ask the adult to check contacts/cells. Never short the supply.

SAFETY: follow the guide's manufacturer/school gate, adult source isolation before snap changes and adult inspection before power is restored. No pupil battery access, coin cells, mains/USB power, extra loads, fan blades, live shorts, bare LED substitutions or take-home circuits. Warm/smelly/leaking/damaged: stop/report, adult isolates and marks OUT OF SERVICE.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Purpose/symbol. Prayer: "Jesus, help us share hope and care for one another." Explain symbol versus physical explanation and the real-turn rule.
  2. 4-8: Model safely. Teacher traces the approved full path, demonstrates OFF/ON and models source isolation/inspection.
  3. 8-10: Predict individually. Each child traces battery -> switch -> light -> return and predicts both states.
  4. 10-22: Wave A. Follow the guide's isolated team build, adult checks, each child's two OFF/ON cycles and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Waiting teams draw diagrams and draft an Advent message with a named reader.
  5. 22-23: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
  6. 23-35: Wave B / communicate. Remaining teams get the identical hardware routine; finished teams peer-check and revise one message detail, record repair evidence and answer individual path/state questions. At smaller enrollment all teams use this window for retests/feedback. Ask: "Where is the gap? What showed the repair worked? What does your message mean?"
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Isolate/count/return parts and cells, store dry kits and collect sheets. Record any missing physical turns explicitly.

docs.title: Success, support, troubleshooting and indoor fallback
docs.text:
Each child traces a full path, predicts and operates both states twice, explains a repair using observed evidence and revises a respectful message. Record physical contribution/test observed / prompted / not yet separately from reasoning/art. Score 1 decoration only; 2 prompted path; 3 independent path/state/repair and message evidence; 4 explains a model limitation or two possible open-path faults without unsafe live testing.

  • Grade 3/support: traced diagram, large words/symbols, oral responses, motor help for snaps; still collect each child's prediction and switch turn.
  • Grade 4/challenge: compare two drawn faults; no extra branches or loads.
  • 25 pupils: nine pairs/trios, five stations, two 12-minute waves. Each child must have an observed turn; defer unfinished evidence rather than rush inspection. No four-person hardware groups.
  • No working kit: isolate/report, use a checked reserve or the guide's verified protected-AA route. Never connect Snap parts to that supply.
  • Paper route: use identical times with drawn paths and an on/off token. Record circuit reasoning/art only; electrical operation not observed. A demonstration alone does not prove each child's assembly/testing.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text:
We traced, predicted and tested a switched light, then revised a hopeful Advent message. Physical light is a symbol of Christ, not a theological experiment. Describe the actual hardware or paper route. Ask: "Where is the gap when the light is off?" Only paper goes home; no electrical homework or purchases.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Grades 3-4; Bi-Weekly A; Faith and evidence; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: cite a verified heritage fact, use visible plant-model details to classify/tally six records and revise the explanation after peer checking. Why: inquiry uses observations and honest records, not biographical praise alone. Catholic/CST-C1 distinguish history/model/faith; CST-S1 observed detail/ question; CST-T3 source responsibility; CST-A3 visual explanation/revision; CST-M2 labeled tally/table. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; introductory. Prep 15 minutes first use, 10 with ready cards; cleanup 5 included.

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Use the Mendel and Albert cards in verified Catholic scientific heritage. Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9): two markers/two prepared half-sheet cards, made from one ordinary sheet. Per pupil: two sheets/pencil; teacher board/timer.

  1. Mendel card, original teacher read-aloud: "Mendel belonged to a Catholic religious community. He also studied pea plants. His museum preserves evidence of that scientific work. A person can have a religious vocation and also investigate nature." Masaryk University Mendel Museum verifies Augustinian membership/abbacy and pea experiments.
  2. Albert card, original teacher read-aloud: "Albert was a Dominican who studied many subjects, including living things and the natural world. He described and grouped what he studied. Science methods have developed since his time; we should not call a medieval practice the same as every modern experiment." Benedict XVI, March 24, 2010 explicitly describes observation/classification and historical method limits.

These are original classroom paraphrases, not quotations from the historical people. Both sources were directly checked October 4, 2026. On the cards' backs or board draw six MODEL PLANTS, NOT MENDEL'S DATA: A:2 leaves; B:3; C:2; D:3; E:2; F:3. Show that number of leaf shapes on each. Demonstrate classification into two/three-leaf groups using one item only. Reuse cards; if no copies, read the supplied text and draw the six models once on the board. No hidden source preparation, live plants or home research.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Cards; markers (2/team each) 8 10 14 18 Card preparation paper (1/team) 4 5 7 9 Pupil paper (2/pupil) 20 30 40 50 Pencils (1/pupil) 10 15 20 25

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Observe = notice a shown detail; classify = group by a stated rule; tally = count record; source = origin of historical information. The model has three items per group, six total; this does not establish inheritance, a plant-growth result or Mendel's experimental outcomes. Misconception: matching categories proves why traits occur. If asked "Did faith cause Mendel's discovery?" Religious membership and scientific work are supported facts; this lesson cannot establish his personal motivation. No unverified Pasteur/Jesuit quotation or genetics priority claim. Paper indoors; no seeds/allergy handling, animal/human trait tests, personal family data or public accounts. Report damaged tools.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "What records help people compare plants honestly?" Read short source cards; optional original prayer for honest inquiry.
  2. 4-10: Identify publishers and historical limits; model the visible grouping rule. Mark the six drawings as classroom models, not living plants.
  3. 10-22: Each child cites one supported heritage fact, records two visible details, sorts A-F on paper and creates a labeled two-row tally/table. Ask a question needing actual plant observations rather than pretend growth.

  6. 35-40: Count/cap/store cards/tools, retain dated tables, clear desks.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: supported fact/citation, visible-detail explanation, correct labeled three/three tally and six total, peer-backed correction/revision and honest model limit. Biography recall alone is insufficient. Grade 3/support: two pictured group headings/read-aloud/scribing. Grade 4/challenge: total all shown leaves (15) and explain why classification is not a controlled causal or inheritance investigation. Missing cards: use the complete board version. Miscount: touch each leaf/item once, correct the record visibly. Unsupported history: omit it rather than invent a quote. Early finish: identify evidence needed for the unanswered real-plant question; no genotype or ratio exercise.

Family: We credited heritage sources, then classified model observations and checked our records. Ask, "What did you observe yourself, and what was a source fact?" Optional conversation only.
