docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Life inquiry / Plants & Growth Time One 40-minute meeting, including cleanup; real germination takes days Domains Catholic truth/stewardship, life science, investigation, measurement Big idea A living seed needs suitable conditions to germinate; observing takes time. Student objective "I can observe a seed, plan a one-change test, and compare labeled practice data." Why Gardeners and scientists separate predictions from observations and plan reliable care. Catholic connection John 12:24 uses a seed image to teach about Jesus' self-giving; it is a theological metaphor, not a claim that a seed must die to germinate. Care for living things and tell the truth about evidence. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C1 (distinguish metaphor/evidence); CST-S1 (observations); CST-S2 (one variable/controls); CST-M1 (length/count comparisons). Technology None; photos optional, not required Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; compare whole millimeters and identify one changed condition. No Year A/Year B prior sequence required. Prep / cleanup 15 minutes for dry kit/data; 5 minutes cleanup. Optional actual sprout samples need days of advance growth, not concealed in prep estimate.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Check school seed/legume allergy guidance; substitute paper seed drawings if needed. No seed tasting or sending loose seeds to younger children.
  2. Pair pupils, final trio if needed. Give each team two clear cups labeled moist and dry, two folded paper towels, and four untreated bean seeds (two per cup).
  3. Board the practice table below, labeled SIMULATED DATA; NOT OUR OBSERVATIONS. Draw lines 4 mm and 9 mm long for ruler practice.
  4. Decide whether a regular teacher has accepted daily care for a real optional test. Write caretaker name and check dates. If no caretaker, leave seeds dry and assess the plan/data today; do not start an unattended living experiment.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth kit is spare. The water budget includes those spare cups and is a maximum.

  • Per student: pencil, evidence half-sheet.
  • Per team: 4 untreated bean seeds, 2 clear plastic cups, 2 paper towels, 2 labels, 1 ruler, 2 recording sheets.
  • Class: jug with 100 mL maximum water; 1 teacher measuring spoon; 1 tray/bin to hold all cups; board/timer.
  • Teacher only: water dispensing, optional live sample and care calendar. No soil, fertilizers or grow lights needed.
Students Teams Seeds Cups / towels / labels Rulers Team paper Slips / pencils 10 5 20 10 each 5 10 sheets 10 each 15 8 32 16 each 8 16 sheets 15 each 20 10 40 20 each 10 20 sheets 20 each 25 13 52 26 each 13 26 sheets 25 each

Use 5 mL water per moist cup initially only if care is arranged: 25/40/50/65 mL for the four class sizes, from the 100 mL supply. Damp, not pooled. Cups/rulers/bin reusable; seeds/towels/labels/paper consumable.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background, misconception and answer
docs.text:
Seed: contains a living embryo and stored resources. Germinate: begin growth from a viable seed. Variable: condition intentionally changed. Control conditions: things kept the same. Prediction: expected result, not data.

Beans need water, oxygen and suitable temperature for germination; they can germinate on a damp towel without soil/burial. Many germinating seeds use stored food before leaves develop; growing green plants need light and nutrients. Needs vary by species; do not claim every seed has identical light needs.

Misconception: "The seed dies or must be buried to sprout." A viable embryo remains alive while growing. If asked: "Will it grow today?" Answer: "Not visibly during our class. Today we observe, plan and practice measuring; actual changes must be checked over days."

docs.title: Practice data: two seeds per condition
docs.text:
Condition / seed Day 0 root length (mm) Day 3 (mm) Day 5 (mm) Moist / 1 0 4 9 Moist / 2 0 3 8 Dry / 1 0 0 0 Dry / 2 0 0 0

Invented instructional values, not guaranteed bean growth or observed evidence. They illustrate comparison; two seeds do not prove a universal rule. Keep seed type, cup/towel, location, temperature and observation time the same; vary added water only. Do not test several variables at once.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No eating seeds, rubbing eyes, handling mold or using chemicals. Teacher pours water. Keep cups open to air; no tight bags around faces. Wash hands after contact; wipe spills. Adult discards moldy samples without student handling. No outdoor requirement or classroom heat equipment.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Observe. Short original prayer: "God, help us care for living things and speak truthfully." Show a dry bean. "What can you actually see? What are you guessing is inside?"
  2. 5-10: Explain life and metaphor. Draw embryo/stored food/coat. Clarify that an alive seed grows; John 12:24 is not a botany rule. "Could a dead embryo grow?"
  3. 10-17: Plan a test. Each team states question: "How does added water affect these seeds?" Write prediction; circle changed condition and list two controls. Ask: "Why use the same kind of seed in both cups?"
  4. 17-23: Set up model. Place towels and two seeds in each labeled cup. If care is arranged, teacher adds 5 mL to moist cup; otherwise all remain dry and are labeled planned setup only. Every child sketches both conditions. No growth result claimed.
  5. 23-29: Read practice evidence. Teacher labels simulated table. Pupils compare day 5 moist and dry counts/lengths, and measure the drawn 4/9 mm lines. "Did our class grow these roots? What would real observations need?"
  6. 29-34: Individual evidence. Child records one observation, the variable/two controls, and a correct whole-number comparison: 9 mm versus 0 mm, difference 9 mm. Grade 4 also compares the two moist seeds (1 mm difference) and names a reason more seeds could help.
  7. 34-35: Check success. Teacher asks two children: "What do we know today, and what remains a prediction?"
  8. 35-40: Cleanup. Store any cared-for cups in adult-approved spot with caretaker/date card; otherwise return dry seeds to teacher storage. Collect rulers, wipe cups/desks and wash hands. Collect slips.

docs.title: Success, troubleshooting, support, challenge and indoor fallback
docs.text:
Success: each child distinguishes observation from prediction/simulated data, identifies water as one variable and two kept-same conditions, and reads/compares whole-mm values. Growth itself is not today's assessment. Score 1 unsupported growth claim; 2 identifies water with prompts; 3 observation/variable/controls/comparison correct; 4 adds replication or species/model limitation.

  • No seed supplies or allergy restriction: sketch two labeled cups with seed drawings; the same timed planning/data work remains. Record direct seed observation as unavailable.
  • No care between bi-weekly meetings: use dry planning setup and supplied simulated data; no failed forgotten plants or required home care.
  • No sprout appears later: log "no visible root"; check water/temperature/viability without inventing a result.
  • Support / Grade 3: oral explanations, pre-drawn cups, adult ruler placement and tally/whole-number comparison.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: propose more seeds per condition and a consistent check schedule; no multi-variable "challenge" that ruins the fair test.
  • Indoor alternative / winter: the primary plan is entirely indoor and includes data now. No spring weather or greenhouse needed.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text:
We observed seeds, planned a fair water test and compared clearly labeled practice data. We learned that germination is growth of a living embryo, not a resurrection experiment. Our Catholic connection was honest inquiry and care for life. Ask: "Which condition changed, and which stayed the same?" Optional at home: notice a growing plant with an adult. No planting supplies, daily log or homework required.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grade Band: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes per session | Sessions: 17 over the school year | Rotation Year: B

docs.title: Audit status and availability
docs.text:
17 represented meetings / 680 minutes in 17 files. Read the Grades 3-4 review and lesson audit. All packages have complete quantities, native timelines and individual checks. Fifteen were completed in the all-60 follow-up; Ozobot Coding and the updated Christmas Circuits reference remain unchanged. No classroom/substitute certification is inferred.

Year B can be a first rotation: do not require prior Year A circuits or Scratch. Grade 3 uses supported counts and labeled models; Grade 4 adds test comparisons, limits and justified revisions. No guaranteed loans or installed software. Verify models/stock, official code chart, batteries and approved connections in advance. Ozobot paper fallbacks are CT, not sensor operation. Christmas Circuits retains its updated Snap primary route, matching-manual/power gates and eight-individual-kit wave plan, plus the separate protected-AA alternative. New packages supply required source facts or omit unneeded unverified biographies/quotes. docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Computing / Ozobot Coding Time One 40-minute meeting, including cleanup Domains Catholic truthfulness, technology/computing Big idea A sensor reads a physical input; a command only works when its representation and hardware are compatible. Student objective "I can predict, test and debug one verified command on a line route." Why A reliable programmer checks documentation and actual output, rather than guessing commands. Catholic connection Honest claims and patient shared testing respect other people. St. Carlo Acutis is an example of service with technology; use the verified 2025 Vatican canonization homily, not a fabricated quotation. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C1 (record verified versus unverified claims); CST-T1 (optical input/output/troubleshooting); CST-T2 (command sequence/debugging). Technology Required primary: 2 charged Ozobots, a model-matched official color-code chart, markers. Tablets/OzoBlockly not required. Paper fallback assesses CT, not sensor calibration, color-code operation or real robot programming. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; no Year A, OzoBlockly or prior Ozobot experience assumed Prep / cleanup 20 minutes with charged kits and chart already obtained; charging and first model verification are advance work. 5 minutes in class.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Confirm model and loan; do not assume CSCOE inventory. Obtain its official chart from the kit or Ozobot color-code resources (also keep the existing family resource ozobot.com).
  2. VERIFICATION REQUIRED: code order, entry direction, line/segment widths and calibration procedure for the actual model. The previous unsourced U-turn/spin/turbo color list has been removed. Do not replace it with guessed colors.
  3. Choose one speed-change command from that chart, copy its exact colors/label to the board and record model / chart title / command / teacher observed output. Test it twice. Choose a slow setting, not a race/turbo challenge. If chart/testing unavailable, announce line-following observation only; command programming not observed, or use the paper pathway.
  4. Draw one smooth, unbranched black line on white paper, roughly 30 cm long, with rounded bends and clear start/end. Start around 5 mm width, then adjust to the model's instructions. Prepare a second line with the verified code on a straight portion. Follow the model guide for calibration; do not guess power-button timing.
  5. Pair pupils, final trio if odd. Two desk testing trays; assign seven one-minute rounds at most for thirteen teams.

docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth kit is spare. Seven two-robot rounds are an upper capacity bound.

  • Per student: pencil, evidence half-sheet.
  • Per team: 2 white paper sheets, paper robot token, 1 ruler, 4 markers (black/red/blue/green), 6 hand-drawn command/condition cards on team paper.
  • Class: 2 Ozobots, 2 chargers, 2 shallow testing trays, 1 official model chart, 2 teacher-demo paper sheets, timer/board.
  • Teacher: charging/calibration access and model guide. No tablet or internet during teaching.
Students Teams / rulers / tokens Team paper + 2 demo Markers (4 per team) Cards Slips / pencils Robots / chargers / trays 10 5 each 12 sheets 20 30 10 each 2 each 15 8 each 18 sheets 32 48 15 each 2 each 20 10 each 22 sheets 40 60 20 each 2 each 25 13 each 28 sheets 52 78 25 each 2 each

Share marker sets between adjacent teams if needed; it does not require shared robots to be increased. Robots/markers/rulers/cards/trays reusable; paper consumable.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
Sensor: hardware detecting information. Input: sensed line/color. Output: movement/light response. Command: instruction represented by a verified color pattern. Calibration: adjusting sensing for the surface. Debug: compare expected and actual, change one thing and retest.

Ozobot does not "think" like a person; onboard programs respond to sensor readings. A line-following demonstration is not proof that a pupil programmed it. A pupil-created, tested, compatible color command is additional programming evidence. Branch choices are not guaranteed without verified instructions.

Misconception: "Any colorful stripe is code." The model expects particular patterns and spacing. If asked: "Why didn't it obey?" Answer: "Check the model chart, entry direction, colors, spacing and calibration one at a time. An invented command cannot be fixed by trying harder."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Use only desk trays; prevent falls at table edges. Teacher handles charging and calibration controls; dry paper/clean hands. Keep robots/small parts out of mouths and away from younger children. No racing, stairs, liquids or marker ink on the robot. Cap markers during tests; stop motion before retrieval.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Purpose. Original prayer: "God, help us be truthful and patient with one another." Ask: "What does a sensor detect? Does a robot understand kindness the way a person does?"
  2. 4-10: Model input/output. Teacher shows baseline line-following, then the preverified speed-change command. Point to model chart. "What input changed? What output did we actually see?" If not verified, explicitly teach only observed line following.
  3. 10-15: Paper prediction. Partners trace a line with a token and sequence cards: follow route, read named command, change speed. Use "slow" as a paper rule, not a claim about an unverified color combination. Swap reader/executor.
  4. 15-27: Draw/test slots. Teams draw a smooth line and the exact verified code, with correct entry direction from the chart. In one-minute slots across two trays, one child places/starts, another observes output, then swap on a retest. Trio adds chart checker. Teacher logs each child's real operation/command evidence; waiting teams trace and label route.
  5. 27-32: Debug one thing. Teacher chooses a failed line or code. Change line width, segment spacing or calibration one at a time, per guide. Retest. "Which change is supported by the result?"
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Child names input/output, points to the documentation used, and explains one expected/actual difference. Paper-only children identify a sequence bug; do not claim real color decoding.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Teacher switches off/stores robots and counts kits; pupils cap markers, collect paper/tokens/rulers, clear trays and hand in slips.

docs.title: Unplugged / indoor alternative
docs.text: Use the same sequence/time windows. Teacher follows named paper rule cards with a token; partners insert a wrong instruction, find the first mismatch, replace it and retest. No invented color chart. Label CT sequencing/debugging observed; sensor/robot programming not observed. All pathways are indoor, independent of winter and internet.

docs.title: Success, troubleshooting, support and challenge
docs.text:
Success: child predicts a sequence, identifies input/output and documentation, and explains one debug change. Actual robot programming additionally requires that child's verified command construction/test, not simply watching line following. Score 1 guess; 2 trace with help; 3 independent prediction/debug/evidence distinction; 4 explains a hardware/model limitation.

  • No chart / unexpected response: stop the color-code claim; use observed line following or paper sequence and report missing programming evidence.
  • Leaves line: smooth solid width, plain white surface, gentle curves, calibration per model. No guessed "connect Ozobot" tablet requirement.
  • Support / Grade 3: pre-drawn route and adult marker assistance; child chooses/checks command and predicts.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: compare two trials, explain why successful sensing differs from successful paper execution; OzoBlockly is a later optional extension with separate setup.
  • 25 pupils: thirteen stationary teams, two trays, seven rounds; no multi-mission race. With one robot, use a teacher demonstration and log who actually tests.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text:
We checked a robot's documentation, predicted a route and debugged one input. Paper tracing shows computational thinking, not actual robot sensing. Our Catholic connection was honest evidence and respectful shared work. Ask: "What did you verify before calling it a command?" Optional at home: create and test three named paper rules with a token; ozobot.com has optional resources. No robot purchase or homework.

docs.title: Complete starter, vocabulary and background
docs.text:
Four stacks on target:

when green flag clicked
set [Score] to (0)
say [Click or tap space. Three ends scoring; flag restarts.]

when this sprite clicked
broadcast [point] and wait

when [space] key pressed
broadcast [point] and wait

when I receive [point]
if <(Score) < (3)> then
  change [Score] by (1)
end
if <(Score) = (3)> then
  say [Three reached. Flag restarts.]
end

Input = action; variable = stored score; condition = test; boundary = limit. Distinct taps, not simultaneous inputs/held keys. Trace 0,1,2,3,3; reset 0. Misconception: <=3 also stops at 3. If asked "Why no catching?" Continuous contact needs additional guarding; this discrete game is complete within today's period.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and safety

Open/closed: interrupted/complete conducting path. Output: light response. Troubleshoot: isolate a fault, make one approved correction and retest. The battery supplies energy; current is charge flow. A resistor alone does not make a light blink. This lesson claims neither blinking nor series/parallel. Lamp results do not establish LED polarity understanding.

Misconception: extra lights can always be attached to the same supply. If asked: "Is our light the Bethlehem star?" No; it is an artistic symbol. The electrical test cannot reconstruct or prove the religious event.

SAFETY: obey the guide's model/age/holder gate. Adult isolates the battery holder before snap changes and checks before reconnecting. No pupil cell access, coin cells, household/USB power, live shorts, bare LEDs, extra branches, motors, fan blades or take-home circuits. Warm/smelly/leaking/damaged -> stop/report, adult isolates, OUT OF SERVICE. Keep paper beside, not over, the circuit.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Audience/meaning. Prayer: "Jesus, help us share hope with care." Ask how a message can include a reader who cannot distinguish colors.
  2. 4-8: Teach from the beginning. Trace the approved return path; teacher tests OFF/ON and models isolation/inspection.
  3. 8-10: Predict. Each child draws the path and predicts both states; identify a gap in a drawn fault, not a live short.
  4. 10-22: Wave A. Follow the guide's isolated build, inspection, each child's two OFF/ON cycles and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Waiting teams draw a readable Nativity message labeled "light as a symbol of hope."
  5. 22-23: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
  6. 23-35: Wave B / revise. Remaining teams get the identical hardware routine. Finished teams explain the repair, peer-check their scene/message and revise one detail; at smaller enrollment use the window for retesting and individual checks. Ask each child: "Where was the gap? What did the retest show? What change helped your reader?"
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store all parts and cells, collect evidence and paper artwork. Note any physical turns still outstanding.

docs.title: Success, support and alternatives
docs.text:
Each child contributes to the isolated team build, operates both states twice, explains the full return path and observed repair, and revises a purposeful message. Record physical evidence separately as observed / prompted / not yet. Score 1 scene only; 2 prompted path; 3 independent path/repair and message evidence; 4 explains two possible open-path faults or model limits.

  • Grade 3/support: labeled diagram, words/symbols not color alone, oral record and motor assistance; keep each child's prediction and switch turn.
  • Grade 4/challenge: compare drawn faults one at a time; no additional loads.
  • 25 pupils: nine pairs/trios, five stations, two 12-minute waves. Inspection/access overruns mean deferred physical evidence, not rushed checks.
  • Failed kit: isolate/report, use a checked reserve or the guide's separate verified protected-AA route. Never mix the two systems' supplies.
  • Paper route: same timed windows using drawn paths/on-off tokens, modeled repair and message revision. Record circuit reasoning/art only; electrical assembly/operation not observed. All work is dry/indoors.

Ask: "What broke the path, and what showed the repair worked?" Paper only goes home; no electrical homework or purchases.

docs.text: Conductive = permits charge flow; input = closure; event = key signal; beat = steady pulse. Misconception: any object conducts sufficiently. If asked "Does foil make the music?" docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grade Band: 5-6 | Duration: 45 minutes per session | Sessions: 17 over the school year | Rotation Year: A

This bi-weekly schedule delivers advanced C-STREAM experiences for intermediate students with Catholic integration throughout.

docs.title: October 2026 review and teaching conditions
docs.text:
17 lesson documents, 17 planned 45-minute meetings (765 minutes). This is an alternative to weekly, not an additional full curriculum. Service implementation, extended programming, and invited exhibitions require separately approved time; they are not silently included in the 17 meetings.

Read the Grades 5-6 review and 69-lesson audit. Scratch Advanced and Christmas Electronics are fully rebuilt. Other lessons have targeted fixes and individual local checks but are not fully substitute-certified. Shortened research/app/invention sessions need tighter scope and prepared materials.

Check measurement, sequencing, comparison, and diagram-reading prerequisites. Grade 5 uses reference cards/numbered steps; Grade 6 adds independent tracing, uncertainty, and tradeoff justification. Neither A nor B assumes the other has already been taken. A 45-minute introduction is not platform mastery.

Sphero/Little Bits loans, compatible devices, and accounts are not confirmed. Protected-AA circuit kits are the inexpensive primary electronics path; no button cells. Paper coding/app routes teach algorithms/interfaces, not actual device programming. Biology uses prepared images/models, not body samples, cultures, or alcohol extraction. Outdoor work has an indoor alternative.

Unsourced Scripture translations, saint sayings/biographies, historical superlatives, current roles, and numerical statistics are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching; prefer verified paraphrase. Acutis and Frassati were canonized September 7, 2025; older resources may still have outdated "Blessed" labels. Local CST codes are not official benchmarks; official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. No routine homework or required home device/donation.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY

docs.text:
Review accommodations/contact; seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Copy reading cards 12/48/30/18 and two word-output labels NEEDS LIGHT / ENOUGH LIGHT. docs.title: Optional shared-kit turn plan
docs.text: Choose one hardware row, not both. With three approved working BOLT/tablet/tray setups, teacher preloads the exact finite program below with the documented actual threshold/units. Keep ⅘/7/9 balanced groups <=3: two trios/two pairs, five trios, six trios/one pair, seven trios/two pairs. Teams 1-3 use 11-19, 4-6 19-27, 7-9 27-35; 10/15 use two waves, then retest. Each pupil has up to two minutes to change one approved LED-output block, personally run the four-read cycle and record actual input/output; two minutes/team allow reset/checking. Waiting pupils trace 12/48/30/18 and the strict 30 boundary. Pretest this access/turn plan and record the actual child, assistance or NE; watching is not operation. One/two setups serve that many teams per window, with later hardware checks for the remainder. Never rush access or form groups of four. Invented card values remain separate from live readings, and a uniform live output is recorded honestly.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Sensor: input-reading tool. Threshold: dividing value. Conditional: rule with alternatives. Loop: repeated instructions. Common misconception: sensor knows where light is. If asked, "Will it seek a light?" No; one brightness value gives no direction. Key: 12 -> NEEDS, 48 -> ENOUGH, 30 -> ENOUGH, 18 -> NEEDS; four checks, two each. Strict < versus <= matters at 30. Optional finite BOLT program: repeat 4 {read ambient light; if reading<30 set main LED blue, else green; wait 2 seconds}; stop. Pair display colors with spoken/written words; preflight detects if actual ambient range requires teacher-documented different threshold. No motion blocks.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "What can one reading tell us?" Introduce fairness/limits.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model threshold and exact-boundary 30; show paper versus optional real run.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Rotate operator/reader/checker; execute four paper cards; optional teams assemble/run finite program, each edits/runs or reads actual sensor once. Shared hardware teams begin their stated waves.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Deliberate paper bug <=30, compare boundary, fix/retest. Finish shared waves; each device operator records four actual readings/outputs separately from card traces.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Each student independently gives four correct outputs, loop count, input/output and an equitable role/measurement limit.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Stop optional program, return inspected devices, save traces and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Which branch at 30? Were readings invented or measured?" Each has four correct card outputs, debug boundary and input/output/access reason. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 uncertainty near threshold; NE for unobserved device operation, separate from paper reasoning.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: No compatible/approved robot -> complete paper core, defer hardware evidence. Live output never changes -> inspect actual range/threshold with adult, no shaking or chasing light. No motion, collisions, battery access, public accounts, bright lights in eyes or private data. Stop/isolate/report warm/damaged equipment.

Common misconception: tested load is breaking strength. If asked, "Is our bridge safe for people?" No; tabletop model only. Key: two packets = 20 g, four = 40 g, not 400 g. docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations; do not ask health/disability stories. Seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Copy complete cards below; draw simple lung/heart/body boxes. Prepare paper arrows, word labels and four-chamber heart inset; no tubes, shared breathing, fluids or specimen sourcing. Adult checks arrow direction.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper model/evidence; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Cardstock arrow sheet; fact sheet; ruler; red/blue marker set 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper consumable; tools reusable. Use words/patterns with colors.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
Respiration: processes involving gas exchange/energy use; distinguish breathing movement from cellular respiration. Circulation: blood transport. Alveoli: small lung air sacs. System: interacting parts. Common misconception: blue diagram means real blue human blood. Blood is red; color/pattern indicates relatively more/less oxygen, both streams carry gases. If asked, "Does the brain start every heartbeat?" Specialized pacemaker cells initiate beats; nerves help regulate rate.

Complete cards/key: Air moves through nose/mouth, trachea, branching airways to alveoli. Oxygen moves into nearby blood; carbon dioxide moves toward air and is exhaled. Heart's right side pumps toward lungs, left toward body; vessels return blood. Cells use oxygen/nutrients and produce carbon dioxide. Digestive system supplies absorbed nutrients; muscles help breathing/movement; nervous system helps regulation. Model arrows: BODY -> right HEART -> LUNGS -> left HEART -> BODY. Four chambers (two atria/two ventricles); boxes omit capillaries/valves/relative size/time. No clinical numbers measured.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "How does oxygen get from air to cells?" State dignity boundary.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Read cards, model full loop and correct red/blue misconception.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each draws lungs/heart/body and labeled directed arrows, heart inset and one other-system connection; teams check cards.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Move a paper oxygen label along path, carbon dioxide back; every pupil traces without pretending to be a patient. Peer asks one model question; revise drawing.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual function/connection, five-part path, blood-color/model limit and dignity independent of health explanation.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save diagrams, cap/count tools, sort scraps and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Where do gases exchange? What does a blue arrow mean? What did boxes omit?" Each has correct directed loop, functions, four chambers/model limit and dignity statement. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 adds accurate system connection; NE if missing. Not a clinical/anatomy certification.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Arrow backwards -> reread cards, retain correction. Confusing detail -> simplify to loop before inset. Missing colors -> words/hatching preserve objective. No pulse/breath counts, exercise challenges, breath holding, body samples, disease diagnosis, shared mouthpieces or private health discussion. Stop/report distress or unsafe condition; do not diagnose in class.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Computing A / Scratch Advanced Time One 45-minute meeting Domains C, T, M Big idea A variable changes according to explicit rules, not the programmer's wishes. Student objective I can trace a score, stop it at three, and debug reset or condition logic. Why Programmers and players need predictable rules and respectful feedback. Catholic connection Inclusive play, honest tests, and shared roles express dignity; verified sources. Local standards / evidence CST-T2: individual loop/condition trace and bug correction; CST-M1: individual score table; CST-C2: individual respectful-feedback/access decision. Local codes, not official. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Recommended: primary paper trace is complete without devices. Optional Scratch desktop/web path requires an approved computer/team, no student account. Paper work is not actual programming/operation evidence. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; count to three, compare "less than," follow sequence. Advanced here means state/condition reasoning, not building a whole game in twelve minutes. Prep / cleanup First packet 15 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; cleanup 4 minutes included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
Optional approved platform: Scratch, or an installed desktop editor. The primary paper path needs neither account nor connection.

  1. Make teams of three maximum (⅘/7/9); rotate input caller, operator, checker.
  2. Make score cards 0,1,2,3/team; draw two buttons: green flag/reset and sprite click. Copy the complete reference below on board or team sheet.
  3. Optional devices: pre-open blank Scratch project, one sprite with two costumes, create variable score for all sprites; test saving locally. No public studio, names, or home login.
  4. Write criterion: after reset, clicks ½/¾ produce scores ½/3/3; feedback is welcoming, not a rating of people.

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text: Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25 Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Individual trace sheet 1/student 10 15 20 25 Reference/button/score-card sheet 1/team, cut into cards 4 5 7 9 Marker; blunt scissors 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Timer; board example 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1 Approved computer with Scratch, optional 1/team 4 5 7 9

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Variable: named stored value. Event: trigger. Condition: test deciding a branch. Loop: repeated instructions. Reset: return to starting state. Bug: mismatch between intended and actual behavior.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND / COMPLETE STARTER
docs.text:
when green flag clicked
  set score to 0
  say "Try three clicks"

when this sprite clicked
  if score < 3 then
    change score by 1
    if score = 3 then
      repeat 3
        next costume
        wait 0.2 seconds
      say "Thanks for trying!"

On paper the operator swaps score cards and flips the sprite card three times instead of changing costumes. if score = 3 is inside the guard: the fourth click causes no change or repeat. Record this precise behavior, not an assumed extra celebration.

Common misconception: reset only changes the picture. Here reset must change the score.

If asked, "Is this a complete game?" Answer: It is a small tested interaction. A full game needs more design and time; custom blocks, falling objects, lives, and levels remain later extensions.

Teacher key: reset -> 0; four clicks -> 1,2,3,3; reset again -> 0. Celebration loop occurs once on the third click.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce respectful game rules and the score-limit criterion; differentiate simulation from real programming.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Model reset and first two clicks; teach variable, guard, and nested condition.
  3. 12-20 (8 min): Teams assemble paper model or exact Scratch blocks. Each member explains a different event/branch.
  4. 20-30 (10 min): Run reset, four clicks, reset again; rotate operators, log expected/actual scores and loop count.
  5. 30-38 (8 min): Intentionally omit reset or change guard to score < 4 in a copy. Predict, test, correct, and retest; preserve original working version.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Each independently gives five score states, says why click four stops, and explains one respectful/access decision.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Save approved local work, collect individual traces, count cards, tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: What is stored before the event? Which condition blocks click four? How many costume changes occur? Why would a player need a clear reset? Which test revealed your bug?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student correctly gives 0/½/3/3, traces the three-iteration loop, and corrects a reset/guard bug with one before/after test. Grade 5 uses the reference. Grade 6 changes the limit to four, predicts the new boundary, and justifies both edits needed (guard and celebration condition). Team success alone earns no individual programming credit.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: Device unavailable: paper operator executes all events; mark algorithm simulation, not device programming. Score does not reset: check green-flag event and variable name. Repeated click animation surprises: inspect nesting. Too difficult: keep the same rule with highlighted guard and a checker, not a different unassessed task.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Adult checks device/charging condition. No personal/public accounts, private entries, online chat, or publishing. Keep sounds optional/off for sensory access. Never use game score to rank worth or religious commitment.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: large score cards, less-than symbol spoken aloud, oral exit. Challenge: predict missing reset. Grade 6: same scaffold; challenge limit-four trace with tests at ¾/5. Keyboard-accessible trigger may replace sprite clicking on device with stated event change and retest.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: The paper state machine is complete at desks, with no device/internet or weather dependency.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: Save/sign out per school policy; collect score cards and scissors; retain individual trace and bug explanation, not screenshots alone.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Explored: score variables, loops, and conditions. Did: tested a three-click interaction and debugged it. Learned: boundary rules and reset matter. Catholic connection: welcoming, accessible play. Ask: "Why didn't the fourth click change the score?" No routine homework; optional conversation needs no account.

docs.text: Service: action for others. Consent: free permission. Criterion: checkable success. Pitch: supported recommendation. docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Physical Computing A / Christmas Electronics Time One 45-minute meeting Domains C, S, T, A Big idea Physical light needs a closed powered circuit; Advent light is a theological symbol, not an electrical claim. Student objective I can explain push/release behavior and design a clear light-symbol display. Why Switches and accessible visual signals are useful everyday technologies. Catholic connection Reflect on Christ as light using the school's approved Advent teaching; daylight in Minnesota generally decreases until the winter solstice, not throughout Advent. Stewardship/dignity: sources. Local standards / evidence CST-S3: individual complete-path diagram; CST-T1: input/output state predictions; CST-A2: purposeful label/symbol tested by peer; CST-C3: individual reuse/safe-resource decision. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; four local codes only. Technology None: no digital or programmable device is needed. Protected AA kits remain required materials for physical circuit operation. Optional Little Bits uses its manufacturer supply. Paper fallback demonstrates reasoning/symbol design, not actual circuit operation. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; open/closed circuit introduced here. No previous electronics assumed. Prep / cleanup First kit 30 minutes, repeat adult inspection 15 minutes; cleanup 4 included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Make ⅘/7/9 teams of at most three and rotate connector, observer, recorder.
  2. Adult prepares one enclosed-contact protected two-AA holder with built-in current/short-circuit protection, matching cells, a push switch, and a red LED with a 220-ohm ¼-watt series resistor and sleeved joints. A plain holder is not adequate.
  3. Pre-test path: holder + -> push switch -> resistor -> LED anode (+) -> LED cathode (-) -> holder -, using three insulated clip leads. Connections change only with holder OFF; adult checks each before ON.
  4. Put kits on dry trays and display paper symbols. All circuits remain at school; no real candles or wearable electronics.

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text:
Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25 Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Individual diagram/state sheet 1/student 10 15 20 25 Protected enclosed 2-AA holder; push switch; sleeved red LED/resistor assembly 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Matching AA cells 2/team 8 10 14 18 Insulated clip leads 3/team 12 15 21 27 Clean recycled 20 x 20 cm cardboard base; cardstock label 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Marker; ruler; blunt scissors 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Tape 0.5 m/team 2 m 2.5 m 3.5 m 4.5 m Timer; spare protected kit 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Optional Little Bits: one tested power/button/light kit/team using only its specified supply. No loan availability promised. Do not combine supplies or treat the colored signal chain as the physical return-path diagram.

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Input: push action. Output: light response. Closed path: conducting route including return to source. Resistor: limits current. Symbol: image conveying meaning, not scientific evidence.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
A single push switch closes the path while pressed; releasing opens it. The resistor and holder protection have different purposes. The LED transfers energy into light and thermal energy; current is not "used up." A paper Advent star/wreath label can be purposeful communication without building four powered candles.

Common misconception: brighter light proves stronger faith.

If asked, "Does the circuit explain Jesus?" Answer: No. It explains an electrical system; light can be a meaningful faith symbol without treating Christ or people as circuit components.

Teacher key: holder OFF/released -> off; OFF/pressed -> off; ON/released -> off; ON/pressed -> light.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce Advent light symbolism and stewardship; explicitly correct daylight misconception.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Adult demonstrates OFF assembly, inspection, and four-state test.
  3. 12-20 (8 min): Each student sketches complete path; team connects OFF and waits for adult approval. Other members prepare purposeful symbol/large label while circuits are inspected.
  4. 20-30 (10 min): Adult-approved teams run four states, rotate operator, record expected/actual. Mount circuit without covering holder/protection.
  5. 30-38 (8 min): Another team interprets symbol/label without coaching. Revise one unclear label; retest push/release twice, adult reinspects after wiring changes.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: explain path interruption, one visual choice, and one responsible material decision.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Turn OFF; adult controls battery removal and storage.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: Why does release turn the LED off? Where is the return path? What does your label communicate? Why aren't seasonal daylight and an Advent symbol the same kind of claim?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student labels five path components, predicts all four states, and explains a peer-tested visual choice. Grade 5 uses open/closed explanation; Grade 6 additionally explains why bypassing resistor/protection is not a valid brightness improvement. Record actual operation separately from paper reasoning.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: No light: OFF first; adult checks polarity, assembly, cells. Hot kit: stop/remove from use. No safe kits: draw state model and label; mark circuit reasoning only, no operation evidence. Too slow: omit enclosure complexity, keep one LED and label.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Protected AA holders, no button/coin cells, bare terminals, shorting, mains experiments, or supply substitutions. Adult inspects before every energizing. Never connect battery leads directly, bypass resistor/protection, mix cells, recharge disposable cells, or use water near circuits. No candles, soldering, wearable electronics, or take-home powered gifts.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: preprinted path, tactile switch label, oral exit. Challenge: identify interruption in a diagram. Grade 6: same core path; challenge compare diagram versus optional module signal chain. Use high-contrast symbols, not color alone; allow observer/recorder roles for fine-motor needs.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Dry indoor primary path; paper reasoning fallback is complete for shifted objectives in any season.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: OFF before handling. Adult counts cells and holders, isolates damaged components, separates leads from battery terminals, stores kits at school, and saves individual diagrams.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Explored: switches and light symbolism. Did: tested push/release and revised a clear display. Learned: circuits need a complete path. Catholic connection: meaningful Advent symbols and stewardship. Ask: "How is a circuit explanation different from a faith symbol?" No routine homework or home battery project.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Confirm school contact/accommodations. IT verifies current platform age/privacy policy, approved individual school-managed access, local/school save and tested Companion/emulator connection. Never share passwords or require home accounts. Seat ⅘/7/9 teams; rotate editor/operator/tester every five minutes in the simultaneous route or by the shared turns below. Pretest exact starter; if setup fails choose paper before class, not live login hunt.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper trace; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Computer plus tested Companion device/emulator, simultaneous route 1 working setup/team 4 5 7 9 Computer plus tested Companion device/emulator, shared route instead 3/class alternative 3 3 3 3 Paper screen/event/test sheets 3/team 12 15 21 27 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper consumable; equipment reusable. App Inventor/Companion are access resources; emulator does not require an additional physical phone.

docs.title: Shared-route kit and turn plan
docs.text: Choose one setup row; each setup includes the stated computer/test connection, not an extra teacher device. If three approved setups work, preload the complete Designer/events below with Reset's output intentionally wrong on a turn copy. Keep balanced groups <=3: 10 two trios/two pairs; 15 five trios; 20 six trios/one pair; 25 seven trios/two pairs. Teams 1-3 use 11-19, 4-6 19-27, 7-9 27-35; at 10/15 use the last window for retests. Each pupil has up to two minutes to restore Reset to "Ready", execute Reset/Help/Help/Reset and record actual outputs; allow two minutes/team for approved account transition/reset/checking. Waiting pupils label their own screens, trace events and prepare privacy/access reasons. IT must pretest this actual individual-access workflow; never share passwords. Record each child's edit/run or assistance/NE, not watching. One/two setups serve that many teams per window; schedule remaining device checks later and retain paper reasoning without an app-execution claim. If account switching or accessibility overruns, defer checks rather than compress safe turns. This route edits a provided starter, not a fresh complete app from blank.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Component: interface part. Event: trigger. Output: response. Reset: return to starting display. Common misconception: attractive screen already functions. If asked, "Can we publish?" Not in this class; school review first. Complete Designer: TitleLabel "Supply helper"; HelpButton "Show paper location"; ResetButton "Reset"; ResultLabel initially "Ready". Large vertical labels. Blocks: when HelpButton.Click set ResultLabel.Text "Paper: tray A"; when ResetButton.Click set ResultLabel.Text "Ready". No text input, storage, sound, camera, GPS or external link. Key sequence Reset/Help/Help/Reset -> Ready/Paper: tray A/Paper: tray A/Ready; four events, two unique display states. Physical tray A is fictional here.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Read supply-help purpose; ask "Why doesn't it need your name?"
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Demonstrate Designer component names and two Blocks events.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Teams assemble exact screen/events and execute through tested setup; each pupil edits or runs one event. Shared teams begin the stated waves; waiting pupils draw/trace components.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Run four-event key; deliberately wrong Reset output on copy, predict/fix/retest; finish shared waves and have a peer find both controls without coaching.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Each independently traces outputs, explains trigger/result, privacy boundary and accessible label choice; record runtime turn separately.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save school-only if approved, disconnect/close, save traces and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "What happens on second Help? Which test finds reset bug?" Each has four correct outputs, corrected test, input/output/privacy/access reason and observed execution when device route chosen. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 predicts another event sequence; NE for unexecuted app evidence.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: No response -> check component names/event connection before cosmetic edits. No approved setup -> paper operator moves ResultLabel by same rules; defer actual programming. No private data, public upload, shared login, permissions, patient app or personal account. Stop/report unsafe device/data behavior.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: component checklist, large block reference, oral trace. Grade 6/challenge: compare input-free design against a hypothetical unnecessary name field; no persistence/multiscreen scope. Indoor seated plan.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Record actual versus paper, save evidence and report setup failures. Explored: app events. Did: assembled/run or simulated two controls. Learned: reset/privacy. Catholic connection: dignity in useful tools. Ask: "Which event changed the label?" No routine homework.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Bi-Weekly / A / Research Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes Objective / why / big idea I can cite a supported scientist claim, compare two model-data samples and revise a clear evidence poster with limits. Source learning includes inquiry, not biography recall alone. Domains / Catholic connection C, T, A; faith/reason and honest sourcing, not a predetermined conflict rebuttal. Local standards CST-C1: historical/model-data claim and limit; CST-T3: provenance/data interpretation; CST-A3: revised evidence message. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement None; complete printed/board packet; optional approved source viewing only. Difficulty / entry Developing; teach source author/title/date and paraphrase. Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Mendel Source Study.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations; tool teams ⅘/7/9. Copy the three complete cards and the two model-data rows below onto one reference sheet/team. These facts were checked October 4, 2026. No unsourced quotations, world-first claims, open-web search or broader biography homework. Draw claim/source/limit poster columns and a sample/R count/W count/total table. Each pupil owns their counts, comparison and poster even when reading together.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper poster/evidence sheets 2/student 20 30 40 50 Pencil 1/student 10 15 20 25 Paper source/data packet; ruler; marker 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper consumable; tools reusable.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
Provenance: origin. Paraphrase: own wording preserving meaning. Claim: statement needing support. Limit: what source does not establish. Common misconception: religious identity verifies every scientific claim. If asked, "Did faith cause his discovery?" These cards show his role/work, not establish a causal account of his private motives.

Card A - verified heritage/history: Adapted from the original Mendel heritage card. Masaryk University's Mendel Museum identifies Mendel as a member and abbot of the Augustinian order, his pea experiments, and preserved original objects/work on plant hybrids. A religious role and scientific work can coexist; this record does not establish private motives or prove a faith claim. Its historical facts are separate from our invented classroom data. Card B - archive: Villanova Library, Rediscovering Gregor Mendel lists holdings of Mendel's plant-hybridization paper and monastery archive materials. A holdings list establishes preserved sources, not every quoted belief. Card C - faith: Fides et Ratio, opening affirms faith/reason in pursuit of truth; this is Church teaching, not pea data. All cards are paraphrases, not attributed quotations.

docs.title: Complete model dataset and inquiry key
docs.text:
Invented classroom labels, not Mendel's measurements or observations of real plants. R means round and W wrinkled in a paper pea-trait model:

Sample A: R R R R R R R R W W
Sample B: R R R R R R R W W W

Question: "Do these two equal-sized samples have identical category counts?" Each student tallies directly from the labels: A has 8 R / 2 W / 10 total; B has 7 R / 3 W / 10 total. A has one more R and one fewer W. Combined counts 15 R / 5 W / 20 total give a 3:1 count ratio (divide both counts by 5). This arithmetic describes only the invented dataset; it is not an inheritance experiment, a guaranteed offspring ratio or evidence about human traits. The individual poster distinguishes museum fact, classroom model-data result and an unanswered question about real plant observations.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "Which source supports which kind of claim?"
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Read the short heritage card and source cards; model history versus invented data, one tally and the sample-comparison question.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each counts both rows, records R/W/total and compares equal sample sizes; records one museum fact/source and one limit. Make a poster with original pea symbols and separate source/model-result panels.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Partners check counts against labels, not memory; each explains 15/5 and its 3:1 ratio. Ask "Where did that result come from?" Revise a misleading caption while retaining the original; name a question the model cannot answer.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual A/B counts, one numerical comparison, supported historical claim/source/date/limit and revised caption; distinguish model arithmetic from historical or biological evidence.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save posters/notes, cap/count tools, reuse scraps and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Which result did you count yourself? What real records would compare plants honestly? Does our model prove inheritance? Does a catalog prove a quotation?" Each has both correct 10-item tallies, a supported A/B comparison, a sourced historical claim, provenance/date, model/history limit and reader-driven revision. The combined count ratio must be checked against 15/5, not recalled as biography. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 distinguishes source types and explains a further observation needed; NE if missing.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Source page offline -> supplied verified packet; do not invent fresh claims. Count mismatch -> mark each R/W once and compare the printed labels; keep the correction. Too much text -> one historical fact and one model-data result. Missing markers -> pencil. No plants, food, biological sampling, personal-trait or belief interviews, copied images/quotes, public media or browsing without school policy. Never infer a pupil's genes or Mendel's private faith motives. Stop/report unsafe data or device use.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: read cards aloud, point/tally each of ten labels, use a table and comparison stem; scribing permitted. Grade 6/challenge: check 15/5 as 75%/25% of the 20 labels and explain why model proportions do not establish real inheritance; distinguish a museum record from a catalog referring to the same work. No simplistic "always supported" history. Indoor source study.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Save claim/source records and changes, count tools, log unanswered questions. Explored: Mendel, sources and model-data inquiry. Did: counted two invented samples and revised an evidence poster. Learned: historical facts and our model results have different sources/limits. Catholic connection: faith/reason and honest evidence. Ask: "What did you count yourself, and what came from the source?" No routine homework or home trait survey.

If asked, "Can we sort bins?" No; supplied clean paper/pictures only. Key totals 36/30 sheets; difference 6; means 12/10 if taught. Counts could change with attendance/workload; no causal savings claim.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Bi-Weekly / A / Service Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes; outside service separately approved/booked Objective / why / big idea I can define/test a useful kit handoff and complete its safe in-class implementation. Local standards CST-C2: consent/access; CST-E1: criterion/constraint; CST-E3: evidence/limit explanation. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Service Handoff.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review accommodations/contact. Teacher is the consenting in-class recipient: request "Please prepare counted paper/ruler kits with a clear return label for the next class." Confirm available storage table; if teacher cannot accept, use fictional handoff and explicitly record implementation deferred. Seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Each kit: three blank paper sheets, one ruler, one label RETURN RULER / KEEP YOUR WORK. Criterion: peer finds return action without coaching and kit matches inventory. No external organization needed for this bounded in-class work; no assumed community outcome.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper evidence; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Blank kit paper 3/team 12 15 21 27 Cardstock label; folder; ruler; marker 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster; acceptance checklist 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper/cardstock consumable; folders/tools reusable. No family supply obligation.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Implementation: carry out approved action. Output: prepared/delivered kit. Outcome: later user effect, not assumed. Consent: accepted choice. Common misconception: delivering nine kits proves improved learning. If asked, "Can we contact a shelter?" Adults arrange any outside partner/ date/review separately. In-class task is actual service only when accepted. Key kit totals: at 25, 9x3=27 sheets, 9 rulers/folders/labels; individual evidence adds 25 sheets, total paper 52. Counts are not "people helped."

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Read teacher request; connect Lenten service to careful work.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model counted kit, label/access criterion and acceptance record.
  3. 11-24 (13 min): Each drafts criterion/constraint, teams assemble counted kits; rotate counter/label maker/checker.
  4. 24-35 (11 min): Neighbor tests return label and inventory; revise; teacher accepts/checks kits placed on designated table. Each logs actual handed-off or deferred status.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual count, test evidence, consent/access decision and "delivered does not prove used/helped" limit.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Store accepted kits, return other tools, save logs and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Was the recipient asked? Is it delivered or planned? What remains unknown?" Each has criterion/constraint, checked handoff evidence and dignity/impact limit. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 identifies follow-up evidence; NE for unfinished implementation, never disguised as completed service.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: No storage/consent -> prototype/tabletop handoff only, log deferred delivery. Missing folder -> flat stacked kit on approved table, record changed constraint. Label unclear -> larger action words, retry. No clinical/food-contact gifts, private data, donations, fasting requirement or off-site visit. Stop/report unsafe handling; adult owns recipient/event approval.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Record accepted/deferred kits and individual tests; replenish supplies later. Explored: service handoffs. Did: prepared/tested and, if accepted, delivered classroom kits. Learned: outputs aren't outcomes. Catholic connection: Lenten care and dignity. Ask: "How did you know the kit was ready?" No routine homework or compulsory family service.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Bi-Weekly / A / Life Science Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes Objective / why / big idea I can model a typical cell's parts and pair eight DNA bases, naming an exception/limit. Biology models simplify, not replace observation. Domains / Catholic connection S, A, C; wonder at life with accurate reasoning; biological renewal is not proof of Resurrection. Local standards CST-S3: cell/DNA; CST-A1: annotated model; CST-C1: exception/faith distinction. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement None; prepared diagram not microscope operation. Difficulty / entry Developing; teach complementary pairing and membrane/nucleus here. Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Cell/DNA Models.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations; tool teams ⅘/7/9. Draw cell reference from facts below; prepare eight-letter base cards/team and arrows. No bodily sampling, pond water, extraction, alcohol, slides or live cultures. Teacher verifies pairing key before distribution; each pupil makes own model.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper model/evidence sheets 2/student 20 30 40 50 Pencil 1/student 10 15 20 25 Cardstock base sheet; reference sheet; ruler; marker 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper consumable; tools reusable; no food models.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Cell: basic unit of living organisms. Membrane: boundary regulating movement. Nucleus: compartment containing much DNA in typical plant/animal cells. Base pair: complementary DNA letters. Common misconception: every cell has a nucleus/DNA. Bacteria lack membrane-bound nuclei; mature human red blood cells lack nuclei and DNA. If asked, "Is DNA a tiny ladder?" Ladder is a flat model; DNA has three-dimensional structure and chemistry omitted here. Complete reference: typical animal cell has membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria; typical plant cell additionally wall/chloroplasts/large central vacuole (not every plant cell has chloroplasts). DNA pairing A-T/C-G; ATCGTAAC -> TAGCATTG, eight pairs. Model letters do not measure actual DNA.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "What does a model leave out?" Introduce honest life/faith distinction.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model cell compartments/exceptions and A-T/C-G key.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each draws typical cell, labels four shared parts, marks plant differences; pairs eight-letter strand on second sheet.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Peer checks eight pairs and diagram against reference, not aesthetics; revise one mistaken label and explain exception.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual function of membrane/nucleus, 8-base complement, model limit and natural-process versus faith-symbol statement.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save models, cap/count tools, sort paper and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Does every plant cell photosynthesize? What pairs with C? Is this observation?" Each has four correct shared labels, at least ⅞ pairs with correction, one accurate exception/limit and faith distinction. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains another omission; NE for missing.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Pairing reversed -> point to key, preserve correction; confusing cell detail -> four shared parts first. No cardstock -> write letters on paper. No biological sampling, chemicals, unknown soil/water, food/tasting or microscope claims. Stop/report unsafe substitute equipment or disclosure.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: preoutlined cells, base key, tactile letters and oral response. Grade 6/challenge: explain exceptions/compartments and 2D model limits. Indoor dry-model plan; ecosystem fieldwork not added as unsafe choice.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Keep individual pairing/cell evidence, count tools, log reteaching. Explored: cells/DNA. Did: labeled and paired models. Learned: complements/exceptions. Catholic connection: honest wonder. Ask: "What did your DNA model omit?" No routine homework.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations; tool teams ⅘/7/9. Religion teacher confirms seasonal use. Supplied original paraphrase content: scene 1 "Catholics celebrate Christ's Resurrection at Easter"; scene 2 "We can share hope through kind, respectful service." Reference John 20:1-18, not an invented direct quotation. Use original abstract sunrise/helping-hands drawings, not photographs of pupils. Optional IT-pretested editor/save school-only; no public accounts/publication.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Storyboard: ordered visual plan. Caption: message text. Source: content origin. Audience: intended readers. Common misconception: spring growth proves Resurrection. If asked, "May I add music/photos?" Not needed; use original silent visuals and no identifiable media. Paper does not demonstrate digital production. Digital starter: two slides with supplied texts and original drawings, advance/ back; or Scratch one sprite: green flag say scene 1; space key say scene 2. Each digital pupil edits/runs if chosen. Two scenes, not a full narrative/game.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "How can a message be hopeful without exaggerating?" State faith claim/source.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model two scenes, contrast/readable caption and original-media rule.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each sketches two-scene composition; optional teams create actual slides/Scratch starter with rotating editor/operator.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Peer reads message at seated distance and asks one question; record/revise caption or visual order; retest.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual old/new message, source/paraphrase status, audience access choice and actual paper/digital route.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save school-only if digital, close devices, cap/count tools and save evidence.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Which words are paraphrase? What will a reader notice first? Why no photos?" Each has coherent two scenes, specific feedback/revision and safe media/ access reason. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains visual tradeoff; NE for missing. Do not score personal piety.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: No devices -> complete paper communication objective, digital production deferred. Content unclear -> supplied two sentences, no fabricated quote. Too much animation -> static panels. No public sharing, personal accounts, private prayer/health data, unlicensed media, flashing effects or real-user claims. Stop/report unsafe content/data use.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: predivided panels, large words, oral/scribed caption. Grade 6/challenge: defend accessible visual sequence and faith-symbol limit. Indoor seated production; no outdoor/Easter-event prerequisite.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Bi-Weekly / A / Computing Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes; one mission, not five rushed contests Objective / why / big idea I can trace a route, diagnose a wrong turn and retest a justified correction. Accuracy/evidence matter more than speed. Domains / Catholic connection T, E, C; equitable turns and respectful cooperation, no winners ranked by wealth/device access. Local standards CST-T2: trace/debug; CST-E2: revision/retest; CST-C2: roles/safety. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement Recommended; paper primary algorithm route, optional approved BOLT actual program/run separately evidenced. Difficulty / entry Developing; teach heading frame and duration; no previous robot session assumed. Prep / cleanup Light paper first 15 min/repeat 10; device lane/preflight 25 min extra; cleanup 4 min.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations. Seat ⅘/7/9 teams; rotate operator/tracer/checker. Draw 5x5 paper grid: start (0,0), goal (2,2), right/up positive. Commands RIGHT 2 / UP 2; intentional bug RIGHT 2 / DOWN 2 reaches (2,-2), outside grid, so mark invalid instead of moving off table. Paper token remains seated. Optional actual setup/team: adult-approved Sphero Edu, charged BOLT/tablet, clear 1 m lane, 50 cm observer boundary; mark 30 cm straight target. Pretest low-speed roll at aimed heading 0, speed <=20, duration <=1 second, Stop. Adjust duration using actual endpoint; heading zero is aimed frame, not north. No directional light-seeking or collision mission. Adult checks the actual removable floor-marking tape's adhesion/removal compatibility on the school's surface; generic masking/painter adhesive is not an automatic substitute.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper trace; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Grid/rule sheet; large paper token; ruler 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 BOLT; tablet, optional simultaneous route 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 BOLT; tablet, optional shared route instead 3/class alternative 3 3 3 3 Removable floor-marking tape, optional simultaneous route 2 m/team 8 m 10 m 14 m 18 m Removable floor-marking tape, optional shared route instead 6 m/class alternative 6 m 6 m 6 m 6 m Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper/tape consumable; tools/devices reusable. Choose simultaneous or shared hardware/tape rows, never add them. No device/lane holding is assumed.

docs.title: Optional shared-kit turn plan
docs.text: With three approved BOLT/tablet setups and three safe marked lanes, preload the exact bounded roll/Stop program above. Keep ⅘/7/9 balanced teams <=3: two trios/two pairs, five trios, six trios/one pair, seven trios/two pairs. Teams 1-3 use 11-19, 4-6 19-27, 7-9 27-35; 10/15 then retest. Each pupil has up to two minutes to personally run the original duration, measure its stopped endpoint, edit duration within the <=1 second/speed<=20 caps, rerun and record the second endpoint. Three operators produce three baseline/retest pairs/team; a two-pupil team uses the spare third turn to repeat one pair, preserving three trials/condition. Two minutes/team cover stopped reset/checking. Waiting pupils complete their independent grid trace and debug reason. Adult pretests access, lane coverage, safe retrieval and turn timing; the demo uses an issued station. Never count watching as operation. If only one/two safe staffed setups exist, that many teams use each window and others book later hardware checks, recording paper-only/NE without enlarging groups or compressing safety/accommodations. No paper endpoint is called measured robot motion.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Algorithm: instructions. Heading: aimed direction reference. Debug: locate/fix error. Retest: repeat criterion. Common misconception: same roll duration always travels identical distance. If asked, "Can we go faster?" No; change within safe duration/precision limits. Paper Manhattan steps total 4; wrong/down has invalid endpoint. Real endpoint error = measured distance from target, e.g. 28 versus 30 cm -> 2 cm; do not call this theoretical speed calibration or paper distance a robot measurement.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "What evidence finds a wrong route?" Introduce cooperative roles.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model paper endpoint and optional real Stop/boundary setup.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each traces buggy/correct route; optional teams assemble finite roll/Stop, each edits/runs a supervised short trial. Shared hardware teams begin their stated waves.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Paper pupils fix DOWN and repeat from start; optional pupils record three endpoints, revise one duration within cap and retest. Finish shared waves; keep each pupil's measured pair distinct from paper traces.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual trace, revision/result/limit and safe equitable-role reason; log device turn only if observed.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Stop before adult retrieval, save records, return devices/tokens and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Did you reset start? What changed? Was endpoint measured or modeled?" Each has valid trace/debug/retest and access/safety decision. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains repeat variability; NE for unobserved actual robot operation.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: No device/approval/lane -> paper core, record real programming deferred. Robot drifts -> Stop, re-aim/check surface with adult, no speed increase. No races, collisions, shaking, moving retrieval, battery handling, bright lights in eyes or public accounts. Adult isolates/reports damaged/hot equipment.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: arrow cards, large grid, oral/scribed trace. Grade 6/challenge: compare real endpoint variation or paper alternate route with same goal; no speed prize. Indoor seated/lane plan only.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Keep original/retest data and route labels; count tools, report gaps. Explored: precise instructions. Did: fixed/retested one mission. Learned: reset and evidence. Catholic connection: cooperation. Ask: "How did you find the error?" No routine homework.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Bi-Weekly / A / Physical Science Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes Objective / why / big idea I can measure a ramp outcome and identify an equal/opposite force pair on different objects. Motion needs careful physical explanations. Domains / Catholic connection S, M, C; order in creation invites inquiry, but Catholic moral natural law is not Newton's physical laws. Local standards CST-S3: force-pair model; CST-M1: measured cm; CST-C1: faith/physical distinction. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement None; actual ramp/ball/tray required for measurement. Difficulty / entry Developing; teach forces versus motion and ruler zero. Prep / cleanup Moderate: first 20 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Motion Models.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations. Seat ⅘/7/9 teams; pilot ramp at 3/6 cm book heights into 60 cm tray, same soft ball release point. Ball must stop before tray end; reduce both heights if necessary and record. Copy force cards: gravity Earth on ball / ball on Earth; foot pushes ground back / ground pushes foot forward. No live rocket/balloon or tablecloth stunt.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper evidence; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Low cardboard ramp; soft ball; long tray; ruler; force sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Stable books 2/team 8 10 14 18 Masking tape 0.2 m/team 0.8 m 1 m 1.4 m 1.8 m Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper/tape consumable; kit tools reusable; adult cuts ramp.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Force: push/pull interaction. Inertia: resistance to changing motion. Acceleration: change in velocity. Force pair: forces on different objects. Balanced forces on one object differ from third-law pair. Common misconception: gravity gets stronger on a steeper ramp. Same ball's weight essentially same; downhill component changes. If asked, "Did distance measure acceleration?" No; stopping distance is an outcome influenced by release, friction and surface. We haven't measured time/velocity to calculate acceleration. F=ma is conceptual context only. Worked fictional distances 12/14/13 and 19/21/20 cm; compare 13/20 cm means if taught, not expected results.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "What changes a resting ball's motion?" Introduce honest physics/faith distinction.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model release/ruler, gravity pair and why two forces act on different objects.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Rotate releaser/measurer/recorder, run three rolls at each height; each records six values with cm and controls.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Compare outcomes, draw Earth/ball and foot/ground arrows; peer checks objects, correct same-object mistaken pair.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Each student independently explains one accurate force pair, cites a measured outcome/limit and distinguishes physical law from moral/theological reflection.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Retrieve balls, stack supports, remove tape, save records and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Which object receives each force? Did we measure acceleration?" Each has six values/units, correct two-object pair, limit and faith distinction. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains a confound; NE for unmeasured operation.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Wall hit -> invalid trial, adult reduces both heights. Missing kit -> fictional data analysis/diagrams, measurement deferred. No launches, balloons, glass, coins, crashes, pushing balls, students in paths or high ramps (>15 cm). Stop/report unstable supports or injury.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: ruler guide, two-object arrow template, oral/scribed answer. Grade 6/challenge: explain why a stopping-distance trend doesn't isolate force/ acceleration. All tests indoors with catching trays.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Count kit pieces, store dry ramps, save actual/fictional labels. Explored: motion/forces. Did: measured rolls and drew force pairs. Learned: forces act on different objects. Catholic connection: honest reasoning. Ask: "What did your distance not measure?" No routine homework.

Originality means a reasoned choice, not claiming patent novelty. Domains / Catholic connection E, C; creativity used to support classmates without ranking abilities.
