docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Community communication / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, T, A; a visual message can honor a contribution without exposing private information Objective / why "I can explain a helpful school action and revise a message about it." Communication helps communities appreciate each other. Catholic connection Every person's dignity and gifts matter; do not rank families or private religious practice. Local standards CST-C2: respectful contribution; CST-T3: private-information/adult-help scenario; CST-A3: communication/revision. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional approved photography; no device needed / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Offer complete examples: teacher explains; custodian keeps space usable; librarian helps find books; classmates share a tool. Child chooses an action, not a private name/photo. Use actual school event dates, or ordinary community learning.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Student: drawing/message sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Teacher: two hypothetical sharing cards 2 2 2 2

Teacher timer/roster and class envelope/display space; pair with final trio. No block-school model, visitor, mural, biography or photo collection required. Draw a fictional-home-address icon and an anonymous shape-pattern card. Explain the meanings aloud; never use or ask for real personal details.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Community = people working/living together; contribution = helpful action; message = communicated idea; revise = clarify it. Misconception: only a visible job is valuable. Ask about an action and include many kinds of contribution. If asked about a saint's school history, use a verified school source later; the lesson does not assert an unverified biography. If asked about sharing, keep a person's home address private and ask a trusted school adult before public posting; an anonymous pattern is not personal information. School-approved paper/crayons; no public identities/images without consent.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Invite thanks for the school community and name a concrete helpful action.
  2. 4-8: Model drawing that action; listener says what it means; add a clarifying detail. Read the two hypothetical cards and model the private-address/adult-help choice.
  3. 8-17: Each child draws/directs a message, partners interpret, then child revises a feature or explanation. Rotate trio listening turns; begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child identifies an action, explains respectful meaning and the change that helped another person understand, then chooses the private hypothetical card and identifies the adult to ask before sharing.
  5. 21-25: Share in neighboring pairs, retain evidence/display with permission, return crayons and clear. No long whole-class queue.

docs.title: Success, access, troubleshooting and family copy
docs.text: Check specific contribution, respectful message and communication revision, not excitement, handwriting or prayer participation. Record the individual private-information and adult-help choices separately; do not request a real address, name or photograph. Ask "What did this person do? What helped your listener understand?" Support: two pictured actions, pointing and scribing. Challenge: explain another person's contribution without assuming all people in that group act alike. No display space: keep individual sheets. No photo permission: use drawings. Fully indoors; no family purchase or home task. Family: We explained a helpful school action and clarified a message. Ask, "What detail made your message clear?" Optional conversation only.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Weather evidence / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea S, M; dated observations are different from forecasts and favorite-weather drawings Objective / why "I can record sky conditions and compare two records." Weather records help us describe change without guessing. Catholic connection Truthful inquiry and responsible care; no storm legend or claim that every condition is safe. Local standards CST-S1: actual observation; CST-S3: weather representation; CST-M2: two-record comparison. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 5 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and quantities
docs.text:
Read K routines. Choose an indoor sky view away from the Sun. Prepare mostly clear, partly cloudy and mostly covered symbols per kit. Bring a dated actual prior class/ teacher sky record if available; label its observer and time. If absent, make records at minutes 0-4 and 17-21 today, with times; do not invent earlier weather. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: three large sky symbols 15 24 30 39 Student: two-row record sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster and class record sheet. No thermometer, video or outside trip.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Weather = conditions at a place/time; observe = notice evidence; compare = identify alike/different; predict = expectation, not observation. Two records cannot establish a season or reliable forecast. Room temperature does not measure outdoor air. Misconception: sunny always means warm. If asked why records agree, say unchanged results are useful evidence. No outdoor exposure, Sun viewing, climbing to windows, spinning/storm movements or forced sensory task. Adult-described observations support access.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Observe/dictate actual sky condition; date/time today's first record if there is no previous one. Distinguish a preferred picture from evidence.
  2. 4-8: Model symbol choice and labeled observer/time; explain the two-record comparison.
  3. 8-17: Each child represents today's sky, compares an existing actual prior record when available, and explains a same/different feature. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: If using today's two-time route, observe/record again now. Each child compares the labeled records and names what was actually observed.
  5. 21-25: Save dated evidence/class records, collect symbols/crayons and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text: Check actual-condition symbol, observation/prediction distinction and valid comparison; a preferred-weather drawing is not data. Ask "Who observed this? When? What is alike or different?" Support: two symbols, tactile cloud shapes, adult scribing/report with source label. Challenge: explain what the record cannot tell about tomorrow. No sky view/report: use a clearly invented model-data example and defer actual-weather evidence. Do not infer wind/temperature from a picture. The whole primary pathway stays indoors in Minnesota winter. Family: We compared two labeled observations, including no change. Ask, "What did your record show, and was it a prediction?" No routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / title K / Plant observation / Growing Things Time / domains One 25-minute meeting / C, S, A Big idea A seed contains a young plant and stored reserves; an observation is different from a prediction. Student objective / why "I can show a seed detail, tell what I think may change, and choose a care action." Decisions about plants should follow evidence. Catholic connection Responsible care of resources, CCC 2402, paraphrase. Local standards CST-C3, CST-S1, CST-S3, CST-A1; local, never official. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty None / Beginner Prep / cleanup Moderate: 20 minutes initially plus school care / 3 minutes inside class

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Seat 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 children (pairs/final trio). Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment; table totals include it. Draw a seed, root and shoot as examples, explicitly not today's results.
  2. Adult prepares one clear 240 mL lidded cup per team with two towel squares, 15 mL water and two fresh untreated bean seeds visible against the side. Do not flood. Close securely; pupils only handle exterior.
  3. Make two teacher cups similarly: one today, one 5-7 days earlier. Growth is not guaranteed. Keep away from freezing windows and direct hot sunlight.
  4. Fold one half-sheet per child into "eye: see now" and "question: might happen." Adult can draw the symbols; no printed worksheet or reading needed.
  5. Name a school adult to check daily and through any break. If care is unavailable, use labeled seed/stage drawings instead of starting live seeds. Do not send care home as an obligation.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Allocation 10 15 20 25 Per student: observation half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Per team: clear 240 mL cup with secure lid 5 8 10 13 Per team: two untreated bean seeds; two towel squares 10 each 16 each 20 each 26 each Initial team water (15 mL/cup) 75 mL 120 mL 150 mL 195 mL Teacher: two backup cups/lids; four seeds; four towel squares; 30 mL water 1 set 1 set 1 set 1 set

Class/teacher for any size: one tray for all cups, 250 mL jug, 5 mL measuring spoon, marker, timer, roster; reserve six seeds and 100 mL water. Total cups 7/10/12/15; seeds including reserves 20/26/30/36; initial water 105/150/180/225 mL. Children do not handle loose seeds, soil, fertilizer, or cup lids.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and misconception
docs.text:
Seed: young plant with stored reserves. Germinate: begin growing. Root: takes in water/minerals. Prediction: what we think might happen. Point to real features or sketches while teaching each word.

Seeds need appropriate water, oxygen and temperature; different kinds have different light requirements. Soil is not food. A seed can begin on moist paper using stored reserves; leaves later need light to make sugars, and sustained growth needs nutrients. This short-term cup is not a permanent plant habitat. University of Minnesota Extension explains moisture, stored reserves and light.

Misconception: "Planting means a sprout appears today." No promised germination day; observations may show no change.

If asked, "Can it grow without soil?" "This seed can start on damp paper. To keep growing, plants need support, water, light and nutrients; these can be supplied in different ways."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Adult handles all seeds, opening/watering and disposal; no eating or smelling seeds/sprouts. Confirm allergy needs; use drawings when safer. Keep lids secure; adult checks for mold and removes affected cups without pupil handling. Dry spills immediately. No heated equipment or outdoor soil. Do not place plants where children can open cups unsupervised.

docs.title: Timed numbered sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Brief stewardship prayer; show a closed seed cup and ask "What can we see now?"
  2. 3-7 (4 min): Adult models one setup and compares with dated older cup or labeled drawing. Explain stored reserves and the difference between observation and prediction.
  3. 7-15 (8 min): Each child observes exterior view and draws/dictates one current detail in the eye box. Partners alternate holding and describing; final trio gives every child a turn. Teacher begins observation/prediction/care checks while circulating.
  4. 15-20 (5 min): Each child chooses/draws a possible root/shoot change in the question box and a care action. Teacher finishes remaining checks while peers rehearse with pictures; no 25-child exit line.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Ask "Which box is evidence from today? Which is a prediction? Who will check our cups?"
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Return cups to tray, collect pages, wipe any moisture, return crayons.

docs.title: Individual evidence and what success looks like
docs.text: Record actual detail, distinct prediction, and care action as independent / prompted / not yet. Success: child points to a real seed detail, identifies predicted growth as not yet observed, and chooses appropriate moisture/air/light care. Drawing quality and sprouting are not graded. With picture-only pathway, label evidence "model observation," not live growing.

docs.title: Between meetings and cleanup
docs.text:
Named adult inspects daily, briefly opens for air away from children, adds 5 mL only when towel is drying, drains standing water and records changes. At the next classroom calendar time, children may observe for two minutes only if that teacher agrees; this is not an eighteenth STREAM session or a homework prerequisite. No growth data mastery is claimed from this single session.

After 10-14 days adult transplants healthy seedlings under a school plan or disposes of seeds/towels; do not keep moldy cups. Clean reusable trays and cups according to school procedures.

docs.title: Questions, support, challenge and fallback
docs.text:
• "What changed in the older sample? Can we promise our seed will do exactly that?"
  • Support: child points to two large choices; adult scribes; offer oral/tactile paper models for low vision, no loose-seed handling.
  • Challenge: explain why flooded paper might not be appropriate; compare observation with prediction.
  • No growth/mold: remove unsafe sample; record no change or use honestly labeled demonstration drawings.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: classroom shelf is primary; no spring planting, outdoor trip, new device or special lamp is required.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text:
We observed a seed and separated what we could see from what we predicted. Ask: "What did you actually see today?" School adults manage care. No seeds, equipment, donations or home activity required.

Previous: Session 10 - Weather Wonder

Next: Session 12 - Animal Homes

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Habitat model / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, E, A; a habitat supplies more than a place to sleep Objective / why "I can model food, water, shelter and space and name a limit." Models explain needs without disturbing animals. Catholic connection Care for living things and resources rather than collecting or moving nests. Local standards CST-C3: care/reuse; CST-S3: habitat needs; CST-E1: model criteria; CST-A1: representation. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes first kit / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use one fictional insect-eating bird family with young. Model must let a viewer identify insect food, water, shelter/nest and surrounding space. Draw one >=8 cm bird-family picture per kit; precut six 15 cm paper strips. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: 20 cm cardboard base; bird picture; glue stick 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Kit: six paper strips 30 48 60 78 Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster and a demonstrated kit returned before practice. School cardstock replaces donated cardboard; no donation prerequisite.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Habitat = place supplying needs; shelter = protection; criterion = required feature; model = representation. Nests often serve eggs/young, not a bird's permanent house. Different species use different resources; not every rabbit burrows or bear lives in a cave. Misconception: a nest alone is the entire habitat. If asked about using it outside, explain our paper model is not approved wildlife shelter. No live animals, nest collection, twigs, feathers, food or unknown specimens.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Read the fictional bird-family needs and four-feature model criterion.
  2. 4-8: Demonstrate a paper-strip nest plus drawn insects, water and surrounding space. Explain why the nest alone is insufficient.
  3. 8-17: Teams build the model, rotate construction/choice turns and each sketch a needed resource; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child points to all four needs, states the model criterion, names a limit and identifies a care/reuse action.
  5. 21-25: Retain drawings, cap glue, reclaim dry paper and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text: Check four needs, model/criterion explanation and responsible care, not model beauty. Ask "What is outside the nest? Could a real bird use this?" Support: four large resource pictures, adult placement directed by child. Challenge: explain what would happen if one resource were unavailable. No glue: use a drawn model with the same four identifiable features. No cardboard: school cardstock. Fully indoors; no wildlife feeding or outdoor testing required. Family: We modeled a habitat, not just a nest. Ask, "What does the bird family need besides shelter?" No home collection.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Life-cycle model / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, A; a living insect changes stages, not through death/resurrection Objective / why "I can order four stages and explain my picture's limits." Accurate models help us understand living things. Catholic connection Easter Resurrection teaching and biological metamorphosis are distinct; a hope symbol is a classroom interpretation. Local standards CST-C1: truthful distinction; CST-S3: cycle; CST-A1: visual model. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes first pictures, 5 reset / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and quantities
docs.text:
Read K routines. Draw each child's four >=5 cm cards: egg on leaf; segmented caterpillar; hanging pupa/chrysalis; adult butterfly. Prepare a large teacher set. The reverse can carry teacher labels; no pupil reading or printer required.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Student: four stage cards 40 60 80 100 Student: model sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Teacher: additional stage cards 4 4 4 4

Teacher timer/roster. No pasta, paper plates, glue, live butterfly kit or release.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background, sources and SAFETY
docs.text: Cycle = stages across generations; larva = caterpillar; pupa = living changing stage; model = representation. Key: egg -> caterpillar -> pupa -> adult; next-generation eggs come from adults, not an adult turning into an egg. USDA monarch biology supports the four stages. CCC 638-645 supports the separate Catholic teaching, not a biological equivalence. Misconception: a chrysalis is dead/a tomb. If asked, state it is alive and changing. Use the actual school calendar, not a presumed Easter date. Large paper only, no specimens, food, tiny decorations or outdoor prerequisite.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Introduce living change and the faith/biology distinction.
  2. 4-8: Model four-stage ordering and a limit: pictures are not actual insects.
  3. 8-17: Each child orders cards, draws arrows and indicates one changed feature; partner interprets. Teacher begins individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child independently shows four stages, a living change and a model limit. Record prompts; craft completion is not the assessment.
  5. 21-25: Save dated models, count four cards per child into envelopes and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text: Check order, living change and clear representation/limit separately. Ask "What follows the caterpillar? Is this a real animal? Is the pupa alive?" Support: adjacent picture pairs, pointing and adult scribing. Challenge: explain next-generation arrows. No pictures: draw described stages on the board; child directs a model. Child equates biology and Resurrection: restate they are different processes; do not claim the experiment proves a belief. Fully indoors. Family: We ordered a living insect's stages and explained a model. Ask, "What does your picture show, and what does it not show?" No homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Vibration and rhythmic design / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, A; vibrating objects produce sound and silence can be a purposeful musical choice Objective / why "I can show a vibration and communicate a four-beat phrase." Evidence and intentional patterns support science and music. Catholic connection Include listeners and respect sensory needs; music can express gratitude without forced performance. Local standards CST-C2: accessible role; CST-S1: vibration observation; CST-A2: purposeful rhythm choice. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Pretest a sound, smooth plastic ruler held firmly on a desk with 10 cm overhang; adult gently plucks while holding it, never releasing the ruler. Establish soft conversation-level tapping. Model four boxes: circle = tap, square = rest.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Student: dry paper cup; phrase sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Teacher: smooth ruler; timer; roster 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each

Children use their own inverted cup with fingertips; no tape or loose filler. Pairs/final trio share interpretation, not mouth instruments.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Vibration = back-and-forth motion; beat = regular time point; rest = silence for a beat; phrase = designed pattern. Misconception: louder means better. Judge purposeful rhythm, not volume/hearing ability. If asked about sound, identify the vibrating ruler; do not claim a cup is a professional instrument. No rice/beans, latex bands, kazoos, bells/loose parts, sticks or collective noise blast. Offer silent pointing/gesture; no forced humming or body contact.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Explain inclusive volume and demonstrate the adult-held vibrating ruler.
  2. 4-8: Model tap-rest-tap-rest while counting four steady beats; indicate the same phrase silently. A rest still occupies a beat.
  3. 8-17: Each child chooses four symbols, softly performs or points the phrase and explains a sound/silence choice to a partner. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child indicates a vibrating object seen/heard/felt through an accessible description and reproduces their intentional four-beat pattern.
  5. 21-25: Share softly in pairs, save phrase sheets, keep cups dry/reusable, return crayons and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text: Record vibration evidence, intentional pattern and accessible collaboration separately; do not assess loudness or forced singing. Ask "What vibrated? Why put silence there? How can your partner participate?" Support: two repeated symbols, adult counting and pointing. Challenge: explain how another four-beat phrase changes the effect. Ruler demo unavailable: children may voluntarily feel their own soft hum or observe a teacher's described vibration; record the evidence source. Sound too intense: stop tapping and use silent symbols for the musical target; do not invent a vibration observation. Indoors, no device or home instrument. Family: We noticed vibration and chose sound/silence in a phrase. Ask, "Where did you put a rest, and why?" No routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Service and algorithms / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, T, A; a useful message and clear instructions both consider a recipient Objective / why "I can explain a kind design choice, predict two moves and fix a step." Service benefits from tested communication. Catholic connection Ask what is welcome; do not assume every elderly/disabled person wants the same gift. Local standards CST-C2: recipient/dignity; CST-T2: correction; CST-A2: purposeful design; CST-A3: message. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes first paper kit / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and quantities
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use a school-library welcome card with prior librarian permission; otherwise keep a fictional recipient/model in class. Draw a 3-by-3 grid, START lower-left, RECIPIENT one square right/one up; RIGHT/UP/DOWN/STOP cards. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: grid; >=8 cm token; four cards 5 / 5 / 20 8 / 8 / 32 10 / 10 / 40 13 / 13 / 52 Student: message/result sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster, demonstration from one kit; no glue, photo or delivery trip.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Recipient = audience; purpose = intended meaning; algorithm = ordered instructions; debug = find/fix a wrong step. The paper route represents delivery; it is not a real robot, software or an actual service visit. Misconception: a kind intention means every recipient wants our gift. If asked about delivery, teacher arranges only school-approved acceptance. Large paper pieces, seated grids, no body maze, tiny tokens, public identities, physical-contact promises, food, sequins or ribbon.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Name the agreed/fictional recipient and a welcoming message.
  2. 4-8: Model a clear picture choice and RIGHT, DOWN, STOP; reset and change DOWN to UP to reach the target. Explain that a person names the goal, breaks delivery into two moves and puts those moves in order.
  3. 8-17: Children create a simple message, predict/test RIGHT, UP, STOP, and correct the wrong path in full individual turns. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child explains intended design meaning, predicts an endpoint and identifies the tested correction. Each child shows the human-chosen goal, smaller steps and their order; the paper model does not decide for a person. Trio's third child gets a planner turn.
  5. 21-25: Save evidence, arrange only approved delivery, return four-card kits, collect crayons and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check recipient/choice, communicated meaning and algorithm correction, not drawing polish or actual hardware mastery. Ask "What would be welcome? Which card changed? Did it reach the target?" Support: two visual choices, adult motion directed by child and scribing. Challenge: predict reversed order and test the same grid. Recipient permission absent: model stays at school. No cards: draw arrows; no printer or home supplies needed. Fully indoors.

Family: We made a respectful message and corrected two picture instructions. Ask, "Which step did you fix, and why?" No homework or home-service requirement.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / title K / Buoyancy and redesign / Water Wonder Time / domains 25 minutes / C, S, E, M Big idea Test predictions; an object's shape can change how it behaves in water. Student objective / why "I can predict, test, record what happened, and try a new foil shape." Evidence is more useful than guessing rules from one example. Catholic connection Use water sparingly and share tools, CCC 2402, paraphrase. This is not a baptism simulation. Local standards CST-C3, CST-S2, CST-E2, CST-M2; local, never official. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty None / Beginner Prep / cleanup Light: 15 minutes, including a teacher trial / 4 minutes inside lesson

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Seat 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 children (pairs/final trio). Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment; totals include it. Put one shallow tray at each active team table; mark a 2 cm maximum water depth. Keep reserve water in the jug rather than filling an unused tray.
  2. Adult adds 300 mL tap water to each approximately 20-by-15 cm tray, no deeper than 2 cm. Test the same large wooden block and all-metal tablespoon to confirm observable behavior; record actual results, not a guarantee.
  3. Cut one 20-by-20 cm foil square per team and keep a second reserve. Teacher tests folding a shallow open boat with turned-up edges; a tightly pressed ball and boat may behave differently, but floating is never promised.
  4. Fold each student's half-sheet into two rows with eye and up/down arrows: predicted / observed. Pupils point while adult reads. No worksheet reading or coins needed.

docs.title: Exact materials
docs.text:
Allocation 10 15 20 25 Per student: record half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Per team: shallow tray; wooden block at least 5 cm; all-metal tablespoon 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Per team: two foil squares, 20-by-20 cm 10 16 20 26 Per team: two paper-towel sheets 10 16 20 26 Water at 300 mL/team 1.5 L 2.4 L 3 L 3.9 L

Teacher/class any size: one demonstration tray/block/spoon, two additional foil squares, 300 mL additional water, one measuring jug, one stable clean collection container of at least 5 L, one surface-cleanup cloth, timer and roster. Total prepared water 1.8/2.7/3.¾.2 L; foil squares 12/18/22/28. Adults collect/empty water at the approved sink; pupils never lift the filled collection container. The cloth is not a shared hand towel; follow the school hygiene/handling plan. Reuse trays, spoons, blocks. Do not require pennies, corks, caps, tiny rocks, family supplies or a large shared testing tub.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and misconception
docs.text:
Float: remain supported at the surface. Sink: go below the surface toward the bottom. Prediction: what might happen. Redesign: change a design and test again. Use hand gestures and pictures.

Water pushes upward on objects. Floating depends on displaced water and the object's overall density/shape, not simply "light floats, heavy sinks." A foil boat can enclose air and displace water; filling with water or pressing flat can change the result. Keep the foil piece and water the same when comparing shapes; this is a limited comparison, not a universal rule.

Misconception: "All metal sinks." Metal ships float; shape and enclosed space matter.

If asked, "Why did our boat sink?" "Water may have entered, or its shape may not have pushed enough water aside. Let's check the edges and try one change."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Adult fills/empties trays; never leave water unattended. No drinking, mouth contact, splashing, glass, electronics, sharp foil edges, coins or small test pieces. Teacher folds sharp foil edges inward. Stop testing when spills occur and dry immediately. Use fresh clean water and clean tools. Children handle dry parts with a spoon or adult help; follow school handwashing procedures after water play. Default low-contact pathway uses tools and adult-only wet handling; if a class requires full handwashing, reserve a supervised sink transition after the session rather than claim 25 children wash at one sink in four minutes.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Brief stewardship prayer and safety demonstration. Ask "How can we test without wasting water?"
  2. 3-6 (3 min): Model predicting, gently placing one large object, observing and recording up/down. Never drop from a height.
  3. 6-12 (6 min): Each child predicts one block/spoon trial, observes partner/teacher placing it and marks or dictates actual result. Swap roles; the third child gets a full prediction turn.
  4. 12-17 (5 min): Team tests one foil piece as a ball, opens the same piece into a boat, tests again and changes one edge if needed. Reserve foil only for tears; if replaced, record that material also changed. Teacher begins individual prediction/result/change checks.
  5. 17-21 (4 min): Finish remaining checks during paired retelling: child reports one prediction versus actual result and identifies a foil change or suggests a retest. Teacher records evidence without a 25-child serial exit.
  6. 21-25 (4 min): Pupils return dry tools/records; adult collects water into pitcher, empties at sink, wipes trays/tables. Do not rush a heavy water-carrying trip; keep pupils seated while adult collects.

docs.title: Evidence and what success looks like
docs.text: Record prediction/result, two-row representation, and identified redesign as independent / prompted / not yet. Success is an honest report and reasoned retest, not necessarily a floating boat. Child may point, dictate or arrange picture arrows instead of drawing/writing.

docs.title: Questions, support, challenge, troubleshooting, indoor fallback
docs.text:
• "Did your observation match your prediction? What changed in the foil? What stayed the same?"
  • Support: choose one of two large objects; adult performs wet handling; use picture response and a pre-folded boat.
  • Challenge: explain why comparing a torn new piece would not isolate shape.
  • No contrast in foil tests: honestly report both floating/both sinking; adult demonstrates gently tipping water into an existing boat and names water entry as another changed condition.
  • No trays/water access: adult demonstration for the whole class using one tray, with simultaneous individual picture predictions; no claims that each child tested directly.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: all work is indoors. No lake, snow or tap outside is needed.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text:
We tested predictions and changed a foil shape. Ask: "What did the water test show, and what did you change?" We learned that heavy/light alone does not explain floating. No bathtub task, homework or supplies required.

Previous: Session 15 - Helping Others

Next: Session 17 - Year Celebration

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Evidence celebration / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, A; a celebration honors every child without overstating learning Objective / why "I can show one actual result and explain a next step." Dated evidence informs continued teaching. Catholic connection Truth and dignity; neither a certificate nor prayer participation measures readiness. Local standards CST-C1: honest claim/limit; CST-A3: communicate. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional approved documentation camera; no device needed / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Retrieve one dated result per child; two comparable dates are needed to claim growth/mastery at a local checkpoint. Missing work uses a fresh route: 3-by-3 grid, START lower-left, target right/up, RIGHT/UP/DOWN/STOP. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: grid; large token; four cards 5 / 5 / 20 8 / 8 / 32 10 / 10 / 40 13 / 13 / 52 Student: reflection/record sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster/envelope; no food, decorations, certificate, slideshow or summer work required. No assumption every child attended all 17 meetings.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Evidence = real dated work/result; demonstrate = show; next step = skill to practice. Misconception: attendance proves Grade 1 readiness. If asked whether a child is ready, report observed skills/supports only. Fresh paper correction is not proof of software execution or a year's growth. Large desk pieces, no public names/photos without consent or food celebration.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Invite gratitude and celebrate belonging; introduce the evidence target.
  2. 4-8: Model a truthful explanation. For missing work, demonstrate the right/up route and correction of a deliberately wrong DOWN.
  3. 8-17: Each child explains a real record or performs a fresh dated demonstration. Rotate full turns; teacher begins checks.
  4. 17-21: Child points to evidence, explains support/independence honestly and chooses one next practice action. Record unobserved skills as such.
  5. 21-25: Pairs share concurrently; save handoff evidence, count materials, return crayons and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Assess actual claim/evidence, understandable communication and next step. Ask "What does this show? What does it not show yet?" Support: two explanation choices, pointing and scribing. Challenge: compare two dated records with the same criterion and note a limit. No portfolio: fresh evidence, not a fabricated memory. No successful test: record support needed and teach next time; don't issue a mastery-shaped claim. All work indoors; optional photography follows school rules.

Family: We celebrated a demonstrated skill and named what to practice. Ask, "What can you show, and how will you check your next step?" No routine homework, purchases or compulsory summer activities.

docs.title: 📚 Grades 1-2 C-STREAM Lessons
docs.text:
Session Length: 30 minutes Teaching Meetings: 32 meetings in 20 lesson files; 34 calendar labels include two breaks

Grade Level: Grades 1-2 (ages 6-8)

docs.title: Audit, prerequisites and outcomes
docs.text:
See the Grades 1-2 review and downloadable audit. All 74 packages across four tracks are complete documented references: 61 remaining plans were rebuilt and the 13 earlier references preserved. This folder has 20 complete files. Stock, policy and classroom use remain conditional, not certified outcomes.

Year A is a rotation, not Grade 1 only, and is not required before Year B. Reintroduce observation, safe tool use and picture sequences each fall. Grade 1 may point, tell or draw without independent reading; Grade 2 should explain choices, compare same-unit measurements and revise from evidence. Use each rebuilt lesson's individual checks; participation does not establish mastery.

At 30 minutes, this collection supplies 960 minutes, not 1,020. Weeks 17 and 32 are breaks. If the school requires 34 actual teaching meetings, schedule two evidence/reteach opportunities locally; they are not additional existing lesson files. Liturgical events follow the actual school calendar, not guaranteed numbered dates. The biweekly option is 17 meetings/510 minutes and does not promise equal depth.

For trio-based lessons, 10/15/20/25 pupils use ⅘/7/9 groups: two trios and two pairs; five trios; six trios and one pair; seven trios and two pairs. Optional reference routines support kit checks and individual evidence but do not replace the lesson's complete sequence, supplies or safety. Pair-based lessons keep their own allocation/reserve plan. Fewer devices use the lesson's stated waves/shared tests, not groups of four or credit for watching.

Student objective / why "I can draw two things I notice, ask a question and choose a first learning step." Scientists and artists use attention rather than guesses. Catholic connection Practice truthful noticing as a way to study and care about creation; distinguish a taught belief from an observed feature. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard. Local standards CST-C1: honest evidence and faith/reason; CST-S1: observations, questions and evidence; CST-A1: observational representation. Only the evidence below supports these local claims. Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
  2. Choose three familiar dry objects per kit: a leaf picture, pencil and smooth block. Draw eye/question/footstep icons. Keep biographies and acronym memorization out of the assessment.
  3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: noticed detail / question / next practice step. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
  4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
Observe = notice with senses; question = something to investigate; goal = an action to practice.

A question such as "Does this roll?" can be tested; "It looks happy" is an interpretation. Briefly name C-STREAM areas, then let children investigate.

Common misconception: A drawing or guess automatically explains why something happens.

If asked: "Can faith and science go together?" Say that Catholic schooling values both faithful living and careful reasoning; the object test answers a testable question, not every question about meaning.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Only screened dry classroom objects; no tasting, sharp specimens or unknown plants. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

docs.title: Meeting 1: Wonder and first goal - 30 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3: Show an object and offer an original short prayer for careful learning. Name one observed detail and one guess.
  2. 3-7: Model looking, drawing two visible details and asking "What happens if I turn it?" Show a picture-step goal.
  3. 7-20: Each child chooses an object, draws two details, asks a partner a testable question and tries a safe turn/roll test on a tray. Teacher checks each child.
  4. 20-26: Children point to what they actually saw, distinguish it from their prediction and draw one practice goal; partners suggest a clearer detail.
  5. 26-30: Return the three objects to each tray; save goal pages for Week 18. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

docs.title: Questions to ask
docs.text:
• What did you notice rather than guess?
  • How could we check your question?

docs.title: Individual evidence and success
docs.text:
Grade 1: Point to two represented details and ask one oral question; choose one concrete first step.

Grade 2: Distinguish observation from prediction, ask a testable question and give a reason for a useful next step.

Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. No scientist-name, acronym-recall or all-domain mastery is inferred.

docs.title: Support and challenge
docs.text:
Support / nonreader access: Offer two objects and eye/question icons; teacher repeats each question orally. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

Challenge: Suggest what evidence would answer a second question without inventing an explanation. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor alternative
docs.text:
No leaf picture: use a second familiar dry object. A broad question: help narrow it to turning, rolling or comparing without supplying the answer.

Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

docs.title: Family copy - optional, no routine homework
docs.text: We practiced observation, drawing and honest questions, then chose a learning action. Ask: "What did you notice rather than guess?" Optional: describe two visible details on a familiar object. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

No external historical or official numeric claim is made.

Student objective "I can predict a short program, run it, and change one instruction." Why Programmers check results rather than blaming people or guessing. Catholic connection Share equipment fairly and report results honestly; teacher application of stewardship, CCC 2407 and 2415. Local standards CST-C3: equipment care/turn record; CST-T1: connect/run/stop demonstration; CST-T2: ordered program and one debug; CST-M1: compare two travel lengths. These are local, not official benchmarks. Official standards VERIFICATION REQUIRED; no Minnesota/Archdiocesan/CSTA benchmark claimed. Technology Required primary path: one compatible charged Sphero and Sphero Edu tablet per team, to execute stored code on a physical robot. Paper fallback assesses algorithms only. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes first setup plus manufacturer charging time; 4 minutes cleanup within each meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Confirm loan/inventory, exact robot model, current app compatibility, school-approved permissions and charging instructions; do not assume a class set exists.
  2. On each device create a tested Blocks starter: roll at heading 0, low speed for 1 second; stop; delay 1 second; roll at heading 180 for 1 second; stop. Labels vary by app version: use its installed help. Do not invent a "turn right" block.
  3. Aim/calibrate heading 0 away from students. Test on the actual surface; shorten duration/speed until travel stays inside a 1 m square. Teacher records working settings on the board.
  4. Mark dry floor bays with clear walking aisles, never across an exit. Make arrow cards for forward, wait, return, stop; no printing needed.
  5. Assign teams of 2-3: programmer, observer, safety checker. Swap after each run; teams of two combine observer/checker.

docs.title: Supplies and class sizes
docs.text:
• Per student: one half-sheet and crayon; an individual evidence box on teacher roster.
  • Per team: one robot/tablet pair, four arrow cards, one 1 m paper measuring strip with equal hand-width marks.
  • Class reusable/consumable: floor tape, timer, whiteboard; one dry bay per active robot.
  • Teacher-only: charger, model-specific help, roster. No water, paint, attached markers, or robot disassembly.
Students Teams of at most 3 / kits for simultaneous work Paper sheets 10 4 10 15 5 15 20 7 20 25 9 25

With fewer kits use one supervised robot station, not nine unsupervised moving robots. In the 12-minute practice block use three 4-minute waves (three teams per wave for 25 students); other teams predict on paper. With only one kit, this is a demonstration/partial practice lesson: record children not yet assessed and schedule another opportunity. Do not certify everyone from a group run.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; input = our code; output = observed movement; debug = change an instruction after comparing prediction and result; loop = repeat instructions.

docs.title: Teacher background
docs.text: Heading is a direction measured from the robot's calibrated aim; rolling at 180 reverses travel relative to 0. Actual distance depends on speed, time, surface and calibration. A joystick is remote control, not evidence of a stored program. Misconception: a failed path means the child failed. Treat it as information. If asked "Does it think like me?" This classroom robot runs human-written instructions and sensors; people remain responsible. Avoid claims about every kind of robot.

docs.title: Exact sequence: meeting 1 (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3: State objective, stop signal and sharing rule. Optional original prayer: "God, help us use tools carefully and tell the truth about our tests."
  2. 3-7: At tables move a paper token for forward-wait-return cards. Each child predicts the ending by pointing.
  3. 7-11: Teacher shows aim, stored blocks, Run and Stop. Contrast one joystick movement with a hands-off stored run.
  4. 11-23: Teams run the tested starter. Each child points to the next block before their own run; observer compares start/end. Shorten one roll duration and rerun. Teacher records each child's run/stop or "not yet observed."
  5. 23-26: Individual oral/drawn exit: show the three actions in order; identify one observed difference between two runs.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup below; partners check care and equitable turns.

docs.title: Exact sequence: meeting 2 (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Re-aim robots and retell one sequence; newcomers receive a two-card demo rather than assumed prior mastery.
  2. 4-8: Model a deliberate too-long roll. Ask which instruction should change; show one shorter duration.
  3. 8-20: Each child predicts, runs and changes one parameter. Compare travel on the same surface using the marked strip. Grade 2 may repeat a short out-and-back sequence twice in a finite repeat block; this is not a guaranteed square.
  4. 20-24: Partner demonstration: original run, change, rerun. Teacher asks each child what changed and why.
  5. 24-26: Individual exit and roster check; identify anyone still needing a device opportunity.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions and measurable evidence
docs.text:
• What happens without touching the joystick? Which block changes the result? What stayed the same? Did every partner get a turn?
  • Grade 1: point to/orally order three action cards; personally Run and Stop under supervision; name/draw one change. Compare longer/shorter travel with a marked strip.
  • Grade 2: create a three-action stored sequence, predict ending, change one parameter and explain both observed results; count equal travel units. Finite loop is challenge, not universal mastery.
  • Use 0 not observed / 1 with prompt / 2 independently for each criterion. A successful team path or enthusiasm alone earns no individual code credit.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor and no-device fallback
docs.text: Connection failure: check charge and selected robot once; after 2 minutes use arrow cards and a tabletop token with the same timed blocks. Mis-aim: stop, re-aim, lower speed; change only one parameter. Finish early: make a second prediction, not a speed race. No devices: each child orders three cards, another follows literally, then the child repairs one deliberately wrong card. Mark CST-T2 algorithm evidence only; CST-T1 physical robot operation is not assessed. All work is indoors; no weather requirement.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Only low-speed floor runs inside marked bays; seated/kneeling observers outside the bay; never chase or stand in a moving path. Teacher stops any robot leaving its area. Cords remain teacher-only and off walking routes. Follow model age/use guidance, especially small Mini components. No direct-contact assistance without consent.

docs.title: Support / challenge
docs.text: Support: two actions first, picture cards, adult scribing, accessible table token, peer explains buttons but does not take the child's turn. Grade 1 needs no reading or writing. Challenge: Grade 2 compares two trials at one changed duration or explains a finite repeat; no variables or autonomous navigation claim.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: Stop all programs, power down per model instructions, count kits/cards, peel only lesson tape, return devices to labeled trays; teacher handles charging. Retain each child's prediction/change sketch.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text: What we explored: instructions that control a robot. What we did/learned: predicted a stored sequence and used observations to fix it. Catholic connection: fair turns and careful use of shared tools. Ask: "What did you change after your first test?" Optional at home: give three spoken directions to move a paper token; no purchase or device needed. No routine homework.

docs.title: Sources / verification
docs.text: Sphero official education site is the model/app reference; exact installed block labels and compatibility require teacher preflight. CCC 2407 and 2415 ground stewardship. No attributed quotation is used.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Observation / Wonder Walk Scientists Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, A Big idea Observation describes evidence; a question is different from an answer. Student objective "I can show two details, sort with a reason, and ask a question." Why Careful observations help us understand and care for living things. Catholic connection Observe without harming habitats; practical stewardship, CCC 2415-2418. Standards Local CST-C3: choose a protective action; CST-S1: two observations/question; CST-S3: living/formerly living/never living reasoning; CST-A1: sketch visible details. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path. A teacher camera is optional documentation, never needed to meet the objective. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes scouting/screening; 4 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Choose indoor by default if weather, air quality, clothing, mobility access or staffing is unsuitable. Never require an outdoor walk at -10 F.
  2. Outdoor route: a short accessible loop wholly on school grounds with two nearby stops; follow school supervision policy and count students at departure, each stop and return. If 25 cannot be supervised, choose indoor.
  3. Indoor route: prepare a live classroom plant, fallen dry leaf and smooth washed stone for each table, or draw clear pictures showing their origins. Screen for allergy, sharp edges, mold and unknown plants.
  4. Fold each child's paper into two observation boxes and one question box. Draw three sorting icons: living now / once part of a living thing / never living. No worksheet reading.
  5. Model a plant sketch with two specific details, not a generic green scribble.

docs.title: Supplies
docs.text:
• Per student: one paper, pencil/crayon; clipboard only outdoors.
  • Per pair: one plastic magnifier, optional; looking closely works without it.
  • Class: timer, three sorting icons, screened specimen/picture trays; one handwashing station.
  • Teacher-only: roster, route/weather decision, specimen screening. No collection bags: leave habitats undisturbed.
Students Pairs / optional magnifiers Table trays (up to 5/table) Papers 10 5 2 10 15 8 3 15 20 10 4 20 25 13 5 25

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Observe = notice using a safe available sense; detail = a particular feature; living = alive now; formerly living = once alive or part of something alive; evidence = what we noticed. Plants are living even when they do not move from place to place. A fallen leaf was part of a living plant; a rock was never alive. Some examples are uncertain: "need more evidence" is acceptable. Misconception: anything moving is alive. A toy car moves but is not alive. If asked about a winter tree: dormancy slows growth; a bare tree may still be living. Do not break branches to test it.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Explain safe observation and stewardship. Optional original prayer: "God, help us notice carefully and protect your creation." Show what a detail sounds like: "three pointed edges."
  2. 4-7: Model two details, one drawing and one genuine question: "Why are the edges different?" Student points to evidence rather than copying an answer.
  3. 7-17: Outdoor: travel to two nearby stops, observe, then return within this block. Indoor: examine two tray examples at tables, with the same noticing prompts. Children draw two details and tell a partner; do not require four outdoor stops.
  4. 17-22: Sort the plant/leaf/stone examples using three icons. Each child places or points to one example and gives a reason. Grade 2 discusses an uncertain example. At 25 pupils, collect the first five individual roster checks during observation/sorting, using their drawings for the two details.
  5. 22-26: Complete individual checks at tables: two drawn details, one oral question and one care action. Up to 20 remaining children receive a brief check (five per minute); peers rehearse while waiting. Earlier checks plus this block cover 25, not 25 full speeches in four minutes.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup and handwashing; headcount if outdoors.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: What did you actually see? Is that a guess or an observation? Was this once part of a living thing? How did leaving it in place protect it? - Grade 1: draw/point to two observable features and ask one oral question; sort one clear example with oral reason and choose "leave it" rather than disturb. - Grade 2: label or dictate two features, distinguish three categories and justify an uncertain classification using what further evidence is needed. - Record not yet / with prompt / independently for details, question, reasoning and stewardship. Do not score handwriting.

docs.title: If things go wrong / fallback
docs.text: Rain, ice, extreme cold, allergy or staffing concern: use the prepared indoor trays/pictures without reducing the objective. No live specimens: clearly mark pictures as evidence from pictures, not a firsthand field observation. No magnifiers: use unaided eyes. Student unsure: let them say "I need to find out," then name an observation that could help.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No tasting, close sniffing, wildlife handling, unknown plant touching, sun viewing through magnifiers, climbing, roadside routes or collecting feathers/droppings. Outdoors keep group within boundaries and follow school weather limits; indoors use seated accessible trays. Students may observe visually without touching.

docs.title: Support / challenge
docs.text: Support: teacher narration, tactile safe replica by choice, picture responses and scribing; Grade 1 never reads instructions alone. Challenge: Grade 2 compare two leaf shapes or explain why movement alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: Return magnifiers; teacher collects trays; wash hands; count students and equipment; keep sketches as evidence. Store dry materials, not mold-prone specimens.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text: We observed two details and asked a scientific question, then practiced caring for habitats. Ask: "What did you notice that you had not noticed before?" Optional: observe a plant or a picture indoors and tell two details; no outdoor trip or supplies required. No routine homework.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: CCC 2415-2418 addresses care for creation and animals. Romans 1:20 is an optional Scripture reference, not a quoted scientific explanation; use a school-approved Bible (translation/verse wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED). Hildegard's biography is not needed for this investigation; any added historical claim requires verification.

  3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: plan or prediction / actual result / reason or revision. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
  4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
Base = bottom support; stable = stays standing; span = gap crossed; redesign = change after a test.

A broad base often helps stability, but overlap and alignment also matter. Equal loads and an unchanged span make comparisons interpretable.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
Source = makes light; shadow = blocked light region; reflect = redirect light; symbol = represents meaning.

Moving the object changes shadow size when lamp and screen remain fixed. A mirror redirects incoming light; it does not create more light.

Common misconception: A mirror or a shadow makes its own light.

If asked: "Is being kind measurable like brightness?" We can observe a kind action, but spiritual worth is not measured by a flashlight.

docs.title: Meeting 1: Shadow size - 30 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3: Identify flashlight as a source and cardboard as an object that blocks light.
  2. 3-7: Model fixed lamp/screen; put cardboard at near and far marked positions and trace shadow edges.
  3. 7-20: Teams test the two positions with the same source/screen. Each child predicts and traces or points to one actual outline; rotate lamp/object/recorder roles.
  4. 20-26: Each child compares near/far shadow outlines and names the kept-same positions; distinguish observation from the hope symbol.
  5. 26-30: Switch off lights, count mirrors/cardboard, store drawings and remove tape from tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

docs.title: Meeting 2: Reflection - 30 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3: Retrieve outlines; recall source versus reflected light.
  2. 3-7: Aim light at a mirror toward a paper screen, keeping beams away from faces; tilt slightly to move the spot.
  3. 7-20: Teams compare two mirror angles with lamp fixed. Each child directs an angle and sketches arrows from source to mirror to screen.
  4. 20-26: Each child explains which part redirected light and one model limitation; name a concrete kind action without calling it a light measurement.
  5. 26-30: Switch off lights, count mirrors/cardboard, store drawings and remove tape from tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Redesign = change after a test; stable = stays standing; symmetry = matching across a line; repeating unit = the part repeated; unit = same-size measuring amount; data = recorded results. Different hand spans are not interchangeable units. Drawings can show design decisions without writing. Misconception: finishing a passport proves learning. docs.title: Four exact 30-minute meetings
docs.text:
Meeting 1: Stable structure 1. 0-4: Show challenge: tabletop structure at least five equal blocks tall, stands 10 seconds, height below 30 cm; discuss reusing planks. 2. 4-8: Model a narrow/wide base and height measurement; each child sketches a possible base. 3. 8-20: Teams build, test for 10 seconds, change one feature and retest; each child helps one test/measurement. 4. 20-24: Record two results and show changed base. 5. 24-26: Individual: explain a change using test evidence. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

Meeting 2: Symmetry studio 1. 0-4: Show matching versus nonmatching designs. 2. 4-8: Fold paper; teacher marks matching points across fold. 3. 8-20: Each child makes a purposeful symmetric design; partner checks two matching features. 4. 20-24: Revise one mismatch or explain intentional asymmetry; never equate beauty with perfection. 5. 24-26: Individual points to line and two matching features. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

Meeting 3: Pattern communication 1. 0-4: Recall a two-color AB example. 2. 4-8: Model repeating unit and intentional broken pattern. 3. 8-20: Children make two AB units (Grade 1) or three ABB/AAB units (Grade 2), trade predictions and repair one broken pattern. 4. 20-24: Draw pattern and explain what comes next. 5. 24-26: Individual identifies unit and predicts next two shapes. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

Meeting 4: Measurement gallery 1. 0-4: Choose one object to compare; recall equal units. 2. 4-8: Teacher models no gaps/overlaps from endpoint. 3. 8-20: Children measure three objects with same units; Grade 2 nearest whole cm if ready; record/draw lengths. 4. 20-24: Compare longest/shortest and represent results as aligned strips. 5. 24-26: Individual demonstrates measuring start and justifies one comparison. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Before class / supplies
docs.text:
1. Choose two smooth round lids about 8 cm and 12 cm across (neither wider than 15 cm), so their boundaries fit the 60 cm yarn. Remove sharp metal edges. Trace a square to compare.
  2. Cut 60 cm lengths of yarn; prepare one equal-size block chain per team. Demonstrate wrapping yarn once with no overlap or stretching.
  3. Draw AB and AAB circle patterns on the board. Do not use food rewards.
  4. Per student: one sheet and crayon.
  5. Per team of 2-3: two round lids, two yarn lengths, 20 equal blocks about 2 cm wide (or 20 equal 2 cm paper squares) and scrap paper for comparing laid-out yarn. Check that the unit chain spans the longer boundary before class.
  6. Class: tape and board, circle/square examples; reusable lids/yarn.

docs.title: Vocabulary / teacher background
docs.text: Circle = flat round shape; circumference = distance around its boundary; diameter = distance across through the center; approximate = close, not exact; repeating unit = part that repeats. Pi is a finite number about 3.14, the ratio of circumference to diameter. Its decimal representation does not terminate or repeat. Endless digits do not mean infinite magnitude. No ratio calculation is required of Grades 1-2. Misconception: every round-looking object is a flat circle. A ball is a sphere; its flat outline may look circular. If asked "Is pi as big as God?" No. Mathematics describes a finite quantity; a devotional analogy is not a mathematical or theological measurement.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Find a circle versus square. Explain Pi Day's 3/14 date briefly without digit recitation or theology claims.
  2. 4-8: Model wrapping yarn around one lid, marking the join, laying it flat and comparing to the same equal blocks.
  3. 8-18: Team members each help measure both lids. Align yarn starts; predict then compare. Grade 2 counts equal blocks, including "a little more than" if needed; Grade 1 points to longer/shorter. Repeat once to notice small measurement differences.
  4. 18-23: Each child traces circles in an intentional AB (Grade 1) or AAB/ABB (Grade 2) pattern. Partner extends it and explains the repeating unit.
  5. 23-26: Individual exit: identify the longer boundary, explain one measurement step and point to the repeating unit; say why a measure may be approximate.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: Which yarn is longer when starts line up? What made our two attempts differ? What part of your pattern repeats? - Grade 1: correctly compare two boundaries; demonstrate lining up endpoints; create two complete AB units and predict the next circle. - Grade 2: record two approximate counts in the same units and justify comparison; create/extend three units of AAB or ABB; identify one uncertainty. - Teacher records not yet / prompted / independent for comparison, measurement method, pattern and honest uncertainty. No coding credit from circle artwork.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Slipping yarn: tape the starting end or teacher models a paper strip. No lids: use two teacher-drawn circles and paper strips; describe these as drawings. No equal blocks: use identical paper squares. Entire lesson works indoors without devices. Early finishers compare a third circle, not speed.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No food/treats, loose coins, sharp can lids, neck loops or strings tied to students. Precut yarn; teacher manages scissors. Accessible tabletop work only.

docs.title: Support / challenge / cleanup
docs.text: Support: pretraced circles, oral prompts and partner stabilization without taking the child's decision. Grade 1 responds by pointing/drawing. Challenge: Grade 2 compare around/across lengths informally; no required division. Cleanup: count reusable lids/blocks, coil yarn into bags, recycle scraps and retain each child's pattern.

docs.title: Family snippet / sources
docs.text: We compared circle boundaries with yarn and designed a repeating circle pattern. Catholic connection: honest measurement, including uncertainty. Ask: "How did you decide which circle was bigger around?" Optional: point out two circles in a room or picture; no materials/device required. No routine homework. Pi explanation gives definition and approximate value. CCC 159 concerns faith and science; the classroom honesty connection is an application, not an official benchmark. Ecclesiastes 3:11 may be read from a school-approved Bible; no unverified quotation is reproduced.

Catholic connection Care for plants/resources, honestly report no growth too; CCC 2415. The Sower is a faith parable, not an experimental explanation. Standards Local CST-C3: care/resource choice; CST-S1: dated observation/question; CST-S3: seed/seedling model; CST-M1: height comparison; CST-M2: dated record/class display. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path. A teacher photo of changes is optional, not required. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20 minutes first setup plus 2-3 minutes school-day care check; 5 minutes cleanup each meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Check school seed/potting-mix allergy guidance. Select one untreated bean or radish variety; read packet depth/water guidance. No fertilizer, pesticides or edible harvest in class.
  2. Prestart two teacher backup pots 7-10 days earlier. Draw three dated backup observations if live growing conditions are unavailable; clearly identify teacher/picture data.
  3. Teacher makes drainage holes before class. Put pots in leakproof trays by a safe bright indoor window, not on a freezing sill/heater. No electrical grow light required.
  4. Mark a height baseline at the soil surface. Assign a named adult to check moisture on school days and before weekends; water when needed, not automatically daily. Keep care at school, including school breaks or arrange approved adult care.
  5. Make a three-column record: date / drawing / height. Leave "no shoot yet" distinct from a missing measurement.

docs.title: Supplies
docs.text:
• Per student: one folded record sheet, pencil/crayon, individual roster check.
  • Per team of 2-3: one pot with drainage, two seeds, about 200 mL commercial potting mix, tray space, ruler or equal cubes; measuring tool reused.
  • Class: one small water jug, scoop, spill cloth, handwashing access, board display.
  • Teacher-only: seed packet, hole tool, backup pots, plant care log; optional plant pictures.
Students Teams / pots Seeds plus 4 teacher backups Potting mix including 2 backup pots Student sheets 10 4 12 1.2 L 10 15 5 14 1.4 L 15 20 7 18 1.8 L 20 25 9 22 2.2 L 25

At 25 keep materials on nine table trays. Teacher controls the water jug; no queue carrying wet pots. Rotate observer, measurer, recorder roles and still collect each child's record.

docs.title: Vocabulary / teacher background
docs.text: Seed = contains a young plant and stored food; germinate = begin growing; seedling = young plant; nutrient = substance needed for growth; data = recorded observations. Many seeds need water, oxygen and suitable temperature to germinate. Seedlings need light for making food, plus water/air/nutrients and support. Soil is a useful growing medium, not plant food or a universal requirement; plants can grow without soil under appropriate conditions. This is a longitudinal observation, not a controlled experiment proving needs. Misconception: an unsprouted seed means its caretaker was bad or lacked faith. If asked "Why did mine not grow?" Seed viability, temperature, water and other factors may matter; our records do not isolate the cause.

docs.title: Meeting 1: plant and predict (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Show seed/seedling; state objective and care boundary. Optional original prayer asks for careful stewardship.
  2. 4-8: Explain seed food versus seedling needs; demonstrate packet-based planting depth and soil-surface ruler baseline.
  3. 8-18: Teams scoop mix, plant two seeds, lightly water according to packet and label pot/date. Each child draws what is visible and predicts a future change orally.
  4. 18-22: Make a care log and place pots in trays; choose an adult checker. Explain that not every seed will sprout.
  5. 22-25: Individual evidence: point to seed/seedling, name one care action and one observation.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

docs.title: Meeting 2: observe and measure (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve pots; compare to first dated drawing, not another team's tallest plant.
  2. 4-8: Teacher models height from soil surface to top of shoot, same tool each time. Grade 1 may use equal cubes; Grade 2 nearest whole cm. Do not include pot height.
  3. 8-19: Each child measures or points to the baseline and records one observation; record "no visible shoot" truthfully. Compare own two dates. Teacher checks individuals while partners work.
  4. 19-23: Inspect moisture with teacher and update care log; discuss what we know versus what we cannot yet explain.
  5. 23-25: Optional Sower paraphrase (Matthew 13:3-9) and care reflection: plant growth is not a score for anyone's faith.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

docs.title: Meeting 3: communicate changes (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Recall measurement baseline and previous record.
  2. 4-13: Final measurement/drawing using same units; each student compares two dated observations.
  3. 13-19: Display one current height per team on class chart; separate "no shoot" from "not recorded." Grade 2 explains why different heights do not identify one cause.
  4. 19-23: Pairs present change/no change and a question. Keep plants at school unless a family chooses a free take-home plant; provide teacher care instead where needed.
  5. 23-25: Individual exit: show two dated observations and one responsible care decision.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: What changed since that date? Where does the ruler start? What if a seed does not sprout? Does our evidence prove why plants differ? - Grade 1: two dated drawings, correct baseline demonstration, longer/shorter/same comparison and one care action, all oral/drawn. - Grade 2: at least two dated measures in the same units and explanation of change; distinguish observation from an untested cause. - Score not yet / prompted / independent for observation, measurement, comparison and care; never grade germination success or home participation.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: No sprouts: retain genuine record and measure backup plant; do not relabel teacher data as student's. Mold: teacher removes affected pot sealed, cleans tray per school policy, supplies pictures. No bright window/no live growing allowed: use the three dated teacher drawings and equal-length paper plant models; assess reading/comparing observations, not live plant care mastery. Indoor work remains available all Minnesota winter; no outdoor planting required.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: No tasting seeds/plants/mix, unknown soil, spraying faces, standing water near electronics, student puncturing or glass pots. Wash hands. Teacher handles spill/mold and packet safety. Support: prefilled pots, picture steps, accessible table, adult scribing, thick equal blocks; nonreaders point/draw/tell. Challenge: Grade 2 use differences between two heights or propose a future fair test without claiming this one proves it.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text: Return tools, wipe trays/tables, put labeled pots safely back, wash hands and store records; adult checks care outside meetings. Family snippet: We kept dated plant records and compared change honestly, including no growth. Our Catholic connection was stewardship. Ask: "What did your evidence show, and what are you still wondering?" Optional: notice a plant or picture at home; no seed purchase, watering homework or device required. CCC 2415; optional Matthew 13 and 1 Corinthians 3:6 references use school-approved Bible (wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED). Seed-specific timing/depth must be verified against the selected packet; no universal sprouting deadline is promised.

docs.text: Dry objects only, no tasting or unknown outdoor specimens. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

docs.title: Meeting 1: Scientists begin again - 30 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3: Show leaf and block; model a visible feature and a prediction separately.
  2. 3-7: Demonstrate drawing two details and asking whether changing the block's face changes rolling.
  3. 7-20: Each child closely observes, draws two details, asks an oral question and tries a safe tray turn/roll test. Partner checks the drawing against the object.
  4. 20-26: Each child points to an actual detail/result, states one question and revises a guessed detail that was not observed.
  5. 26-30: Return objects/pictures and save first evidence in private folders. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

docs.title: Questions to ask
docs.text:
• What did you actually notice?
  • How could you check your question?

docs.title: Individual evidence and success
docs.text:
Grade 1: Show two observed details and ask one question.

Grade 2: Ask a testable question and distinguish its prediction from an actual result.

Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

docs.title: Support and challenge
docs.text:
Support / nonreader access: Two object choices, eye/question icons and oral dictation. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

Challenge: Explain what evidence would answer a cause question. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor alternative
docs.text:
No leaf image: use another dry classroom object. Vague question: offer turn/compare/roll choices without supplying its result.

Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

docs.text: We began Year B with detailed observation and honest inquiry. Ask: "What did you actually notice?" Optional: notice two features of a familiar indoor object. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.
