docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Embryo = young plant in viable seed; dormancy = reduced activity; metamorphosis = developmental change; reproduction = new generation. Misconception: pupa/seed dies to transform. Viable embryos/pupae are alive; dead embryos do not germinate. If asked "Does every seed grow?" No; viability and conditions matter, and appearance alone does not test viability. Easter celebrates Jesus' Resurrection; growth is a metaphor of hope, not proof. No tasting, broken seeds, animal handling/releases or outdoor collection. Count seeds away from mouthing pupils; wash hands, report loss/allergy concern. Photo/drawn-card seed observation substitutes if allergy gate fails, labeled.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "Can something alive look still?" Optional prayer of Easter hope.
  2. 4-10: Model observed seed surface versus inferred embryo; read four stages.
  3. 10-22: Each observes seed with lens, draws two visible details, then orders stage cards and explains living pupa.
  4. 22-30: Draw arrows through stages and adult-to-new-eggs reproduction. Peer checks labels; revise one unclear arrow/detail.
  5. 30-35: Each identifies pupa/embryo as living, generation link, actual observed detail and separate Easter metaphor. "What did we not test?"
  6. 35-40: Count seeds/cards/lenses, file dated diagrams, wash/clear.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: visible detail, ordered living stages/generation link, labeled visual revision and science/faith distinction. Grade 3/support: pictured stages, dictation. Grade 4/challenge: explain observation cannot prove a seed viable. Wrong order: compare source card and revise; never call a pupa dead. Missing lenses: individual turns with shared lens or unaided observation. Early finish: identify what longer-term evidence a growth investigation would need. Indoor primary works without spring specimens.

Family: We studied living development and Easter symbolism. Ask, "Why is a pupa not dead?" Optional: notice a plant picture, no planting homework.

Objective: support a learning claim with two dated artifacts, demonstrate reasoning individually and revise an explanation for a peer. Why: an expo should show what changed, not certify attendance as mastery. Catholic/CST-C3: stewardship of gifts/work; CST-E3: evidence/tradeoff/limit; CST-A3: display critique/revision. Per pupil: portfolio, two paper sheets (evidence caption/fresh demonstration), pencil. Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9) share ruler. Teacher board/timer; choose safe paper artifacts, not live circuits/robots. Missing work: fresh tower folding/measuring task, labeled today's evidence, never invented history. Board: earlier date/result | later date/result | fresh explanation | limit. Tools reusable; evidence retained. No certificate/treat supplies required.

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Evidence = actual record; growth = supported change; demonstration = individual showing; limit = what record cannot establish. Misconception: a photo proves each child programmed. If asked "Can I say mastered all STREAM?" Not without individual evidence across those skills; local mastery requires two dated observations on separate occasions, including changed context/explanation. No live hardware, food, balloons or public private photos; report missing artifacts. Indoor desk displays, no weather dependency.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Optional gratitude prayer. "Which records show a changed decision?"
  2. 4-9: Model qualified claim: actual dates/results; separate paper/real operation, prediction/measurement and faith reflection.
  3. 9-20: Select two artifacts, prepare caption and independently re-trace code or explain/recreate a design. Without work, fold/test tower ten seconds, measure cm, change base/retest; label fresh evidence only.
  4. 20-29: Parallel teams: two minutes per child to show evidence/demonstrate; peers ask a specific question. At 25, nine simultaneous groups, not 25 serial two-minute speeches.

  6. 35-40: File dated captions, count rulers, return portfolios, clear desks. Optional recognition says "participated/explored," not certified mastery.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: evidence-referenced claim, fresh individual reasoning and critique-backed caption; growth not credited without two genuine records. Grade 3/support: pointing/dictation/caption stems. Grade 4/challenge: defend a tradeoff and what transfer evidence would be needed. Missing earlier work: report growth not evidenced; today's task still assesses reasoning. Overlong speech: use prompt card/task-result-limit within two minutes. Early finish: answer new peer question.

Family: Our Expo used evidence and individual explanations. Ask, "What can your records show, and what can't they show?" Optional: listen to one explanation.

docs.title: Audit status and availability
docs.text:
Read the Grades 3-4 review and lesson audit. All 17 packages have complete native meeting directions, quantities and individual evidence. Fourteen were completed in the all-60 follow-up; Flight, Game Design and Weather remain unchanged. Document completion is not whole-year classroom, substitute or official-standards certification.

Do not assume equipment, loans, software compatibility or trained helpers. Verify in advance. New packages omit unneeded unverified biography/quotation/theme claims. Optional preparation aid: Grades 1-6 reference routines. Use the actual lesson's complete supplies/times, not a generic nine-kit issue. docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Foundations; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: observe/draw three details and pose a testable question, separating what was seen from a guess. docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Flight / Flight Fundamentals Time Two 40-minute meetings, cleanup included Domains Catholic honest inquiry, physical science, measurement Big idea Air exerts forces on a moving glider; evidence about one changed feature helps us improve it. Student objective "I can label forces and compare three flights before and after one change." Why Pilots and designers use careful tests, not one lucky result. Catholic connection Faith and reason support honest inquiry; give credit for another person's design and report inconvenient results. See the Vatican's Fides et Ratio, paraphrased, not a scientific proof of faith. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C1 (honest evidence); CST-S2 (one changed feature and repeated trials); CST-S3 (force model); CST-M1 (measure/compare). Technology None; teacher photos/video optional, not needed Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; count and compare whole centimeters. No mean, percentage, formal force calculation or prior Year A required. Prep / cleanup 15 minutes plus obtaining an approved indoor flight area; 5 minutes each meeting

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Arrange pairs, one trio for odd enrollment. Tape two parallel 3 m lanes, 1 m wide, with a launch line and stopping boundary. Obtain approval for hall use; block through-traffic. If unavailable, use the short-flight alternative below.
  2. Fold one sample as described below and make the nose blunt. Prepare a large paper plane outline and four arrow labels.
  3. Board: A: trials 1/2/3 | one change | B: trials 1/2/3. Have pupils copy tables instead of printing.
  4. Mark paper with team ID and A/B. Set storage tray for meeting 2.

docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth kit is spare. Thirteen-team timing is an upper capacity bound.

  • Per student: pencil, 1 evidence half-sheet each meeting.
  • Per team: 2 letter-paper sheets for gliders, 2 paper recording sheets across the unit, 1 ruler.
  • Whole class: 2 measuring tapes marked in centimeters, 6 m floor-safe tape for launch/boundary markers, timer, 1 storage tray.
  • Teacher only: 2 demonstration paper sheets, 4 paper force labels and board; scissors if trimming a damaged nose. No clips, hair dryers, hot-air devices or fans needed.
Students Teams Paper: 4 per team + 2 demo Evidence half-sheets across unit / pencils Team rulers Measuring tapes / storage tray 10 5 22 20 / 10 5 2 / 1 15 8 34 30 / 15 8 2 / 1 20 10 42 40 / 20 10 2 / 1 25 13 54 50 / 25 13 2 / 1

Reusable rulers/tapes/tray; paper and marking tape consumable. No family material donations required.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background, misconception and answer
docs.text:
Weight: Earth's downward gravitational force. Lift: aerodynamic force roughly perpendicular to motion through the air. Drag: aerodynamic force opposing that motion. Thrust: propulsion force; the hand pushes a paper plane during launch, not after release. Trial: one repeated test.

Wings change airflow and pressure; a curved upper surface is not required. Do not teach that split air must meet again at the back of a wing, or that lift must exceed weight in every climb. The force arrows here are a simplified model. A released glider has no engine thrust; gravity helps sustain its descending motion.

Common misconception: "Paper planes fall only because they run out of thrust." They glide while aerodynamic forces and gravity act.

If asked: "Why does flat paper fly?" Answer: "At an angle to moving air, a flat wing changes the air's motion and experiences lift. We can test its flight without claiming to measure every force."

Accuracy source: NASA Glenn's Incorrect Airfoil Theory. Bartolomeu de Gusmao is not presented as a Blessed or saint; his biography and devotional status are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before a historical extension.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Only paper gliders with folded-back blunt noses. No clips, pins, hard weights, elastic launchers, hair dryers, standing on chairs or throwing toward anyone. Teacher gives launch/retrieve signals. Operators stand at the line; everyone else stays behind it. Retrieve only after both lanes stop. Stop testing when traffic enters the area. Do not go outdoors in ice, storms, unsafe wind or cold.

docs.title: Fold the baseline glider: teacher demonstration
docs.text:
1. Place letter paper portrait; fold lengthwise, then open.
  2. Fold the two top corners to the center crease.
  3. Fold each new sloping top edge toward the center crease.
  4. Fold the whole plane closed along the center.
  5. Fold each side down to make matching wings; align the top wing edge with the lower body edge.
  6. Open wings to a shallow V, keeping them equal.
  7. Fold the nose back 1 cm; do not cut it to a point. Mark A.

An adult may precrease for accessibility. Students still choose the test change.

docs.title: Meeting 1: forces and baseline, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Wonder. Original prayer: "God, help us seek truth and learn patiently." Drop a flat paper sheet. "What pushes or pulls on it?"
  2. 4-10: Force model. Draw weight down, lift roughly up and drag opposing travel. Show the hand's launch push; remove the thrust arrow after release. Ask: "Does our paper plane have an engine?" "What is still acting after release?"
  3. 10-17: Fold together. Demonstrate the seven steps. Partners alternate folds; each child labels forces on a separate drawing.
  4. 17-21: Fair-test plan. Same paper, plane, launch spot, launch height and launcher for three trials. A gentle level push, not an overhead throw. Measure from line to first ground contact, not slide distance. Record whole centimeters; human throws still vary.
  5. 21-30: Three flights. Two lanes operate concurrently. Each of 13 teams takes at most a 1-minute slot (7 rounds across two lanes); reserve 2 minutes for resets. Teacher signals launch then retrieval. Partner measures; launcher remains the same for all A/B trials; rotate other roles so all children contribute.
  6. 30-35: Individual evidence. Copy three observed distances and circle shortest/longest. "Did every trial match? Why might they differ?" Grade 3 compares values; Grade 4 also calculates the whole-number range, largest minus smallest. No mean required.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Store labeled planes flat, return rulers/tapes, clear floor markings if the space must reopen, collect force drawings and tables.

docs.title: Meeting 2: one change and comparison, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Retrieve. Review three A results. "Why isn't one flight enough?"
  2. 5-10: Choose one feature. Keep the same plane and fold both trailing wing edges up 5 mm using the ruler. Label B. Predict the effect; equal changes on both wings count as one feature, not a change in paper/launcher.
  3. 10-16: Build and rehearse. Teacher shows the fold and checks blunt noses. Record "upturned trailing edges" and a prediction. Do not promise that it improves distance.
  4. 16-27: Three B trials. Use the same launcher, height, lanes and first-contact measurement. Teacher runs two concurrent lanes, up to 7 one-minute rounds plus resets. Waiting teams annotate force diagrams.
  5. 27-32: Compare. Line up the A/B tables. Grade 3: compare shortest and longest, using whole-number differences if ready. Grade 4: compare ranges; explain overlap and why results do not prove one design always wins. Ask: "What evidence supports your recommendation? What would another trial tell us?"
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Each child names the changed feature and two kept-same features, identifies evidence for a next test, and explains that unexpected results must be kept.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Return instruments, recycle or store paper as local rules permit, remove trip hazards and collect slips. No required flight at home.

docs.title: Success, troubleshooting and differentiation
docs.text:
Success: each child labels weight/lift/drag and identifies the launch push, records actual repeated distances, and distinguishes a change from a control. Score 1 assertion only; 2 diagram/data with prompts; 3 correct force model and fair comparison; 4 level 3 plus explains variation or model limitations. Teacher notes absent measurements rather than substituting invented data.

  • Nose dives: check equal wings/nose; log a repair before restarting trials. Repairs change conditions, so compare a new baseline.
  • Beyond 3 m: record at least 300 cm, shorten the gentle launch consistently for a new set. Do not fabricate a landing distance.
  • No approved long area / winter indoor alternative: launch from a seated desk into a 1 m clear tray-lined floor lane, with the teacher as launcher for all trials. Record the new lane cap and compare only within it. No corridor test amid foot traffic.
  • Support / Grade 3: precrease, read labels aloud, let children dictate counts and point to controls; use a tape with whole-centimeter marks.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: repeat one design, compare ranges, propose a better control for launch force. Do not infer lift magnitude from distance alone.
  • 25 pupils: thirteen teams, two approved lanes; at most seven one-minute rounds per test window. If only one safe lane exists, teacher tests a selected design while every child uses the explicitly labeled class dataset; personal plane performance is not assessed.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text: We modeled flight forces and tested one wing change using repeated measurements. Each child compared evidence, not just a favorite plane. Our Catholic connection was honest investigation and patience. Ask: "Which feature changed, and what stayed the same?" Optional at home: explain the force arrows using hands. No throwing, devices or homework required.

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Lift/drag = aerodynamic forces; gravity = downward attraction; trial = repeat; criterion = desired result. After hand release, no engine thrust. Distance alone does not measure lift. Misconception: change everything to improve. If asked "Can a shorter flight still teach?" Yes; record it and compare fairly. No clips/hard loads, sharp noses, overhead throws, racing, people in lane or retrieval during flight. Teacher clears lane/signals stop/retrieve; report hazards. One team active, others seated with records.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "What counts as a fair distance test?" State 2 m cap, same paper/ release height/method; effort honesty, not winning, is Catholic application.
  2. 4-10: Fold/demo starter and safe lane; criterion: farther within lane, same conditions, not unlimited maximum.
  3. 10-21: Each sketches, team builds version 1, marks fixed launch method.
  4. 21-30: Nine or fewer one-minute slots, three launches/team; every child launches in a trio, pair's third is repeat. Record actual/capped distances.
  5. 30-35: Each copies three results/units and names two controls.
  6. 35-40: Store gliders flat, count rulers, collect dated records/clear.

docs.title: Meeting 2: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve baseline ranges; "What feature might account for drift?"
  2. 4-9: Model changing wing-fold width only; keep blunt nose/paper.
  3. 9-21: Each proposes change; build version 2 with one agreed feature.
  4. 21-30: Same three-launch slots/test; compare shortest/longest and actual whole-number changes, not required mean.
  5. 30-35: Each gives six readings across versions and change/control reason.

docs.title: Meeting 3: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Choose final design using repeated evidence, not "best throw."
  2. 4-9: Model qualified claim when trial ranges overlap or cap is reached.
  3. 9-21: Build version 3; prepare prediction and same test plan.
  4. 21-30: Three final launches/team in same slots; record results.
  5. 30-35: Parallel peer explanations and individual recommendation/limit; recognize careful tests, not four serial category awards.
  6. 35-40: Count/store paper/rulers, remove approved tape, archive dated data.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: nine readings, clear version change/controls and evidence-supported recommendation. Grade 3/support: precreased starter/oral counts. Grade 4/challenge: overlapping ranges/censored cap reasoning. Nose dives: check symmetry, choose one fold change; do not add clips. Indoor fallback: no safe lane -> teacher-controlled 1 m short lane at desk, identical release, same slots; capped distance criterion explicitly shifts, not actual full-lane performance. If no safe launch space, paper force/design model only; flight evidence not observed. No unsafe winter outdoor flight.

Family: We compared repeated glider tests. Ask, "What stayed the same across versions?" Optional: explain the force arrows, no home launches required.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: three understandable views, criteria/limits, actual retest and purposeful welcome/form explanation. Grade 3/support: view frames/precut parts/dictation. docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Gratitude data; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: tally one voluntary/practice choice, graph three category counts and explain a whole-number comparison without ranking gratitude. Why: displays communicate what data actually measure. Catholic/CST-C2: privacy/no judgment of feelings; CST-M2: tally/bar chart; CST-M3: total/difference; CST-A3: critique/revision of chart message. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Per pupil: ballot scrap, graph sheet, pencil. Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9) share ruler/ two markers. Teacher board/timer; three category headings: people/places/ experiences. Ask "Which fictional thank-you card topic would you choose?" One answer, no names; abstention allowed. If no actual survey consent, use clearly labeled practice counts 4/⅗. Board tallies, no five serial lists or medical claims. Retain charts, reuse tools.

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Category = grouping; tally = count marks; scale = value per unit; anonymous = not named. Misconception: larger bar means more grateful/healthier. If asked "Who chose people?" Anonymous tally does not tell us who; counts are not faith/happiness measurements. Catholic thanks is a practice, not scored personal emotion. Paper work indoors; no food, private blessings or public names. Report damaged tools; ballots handled by adult.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Optional prayer of thanks. Explain choice/privacy/abstention.
  2. 4-10: Model one ballot/one tally, zero baseline, one square = one response.
  3. 10-20: Collect all anonymous ballots simultaneously; teacher/volunteer count each category, class checks total equals valid responses.
  4. 20-29: Each draws three bars/title/labels/scale; peer checks counts and misleading caption, pupil revises.
  5. 29-35: Each child reads two bars, gives total/difference and a limitation. Practice key: total 12, experiences exceed places by 2.
  6. 35-40: Collect dated charts, adult disposes ballots, count/cap tools.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: accurate counts/labels, correct comparison and privacy/interpretation limit with visible revision. Grade 3/support: 0-25 pre-drawn axis/scribing. Grade 4/challenge: explain abstention/sample limitations, not percentages. Total mismatch: recount ballots, mark invalid double answers; do not silently adjust numbers. No participation: use labeled practice dataset. Early finish: ask which question these counts cannot answer.

Family: We graphed anonymous choices, not gratitude levels. Ask, "What does a bar actually count?" Optional: share a thanks if comfortable.

docs.text: Recipient = intended user; sequence = order; contrast = visible difference; criterion = success. Misconception: nice appearance proves comprehension. docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "How does listening make a gift useful?" Optional service prayer.
  2. 4-9: Model two numbered actions with word/symbol; criterion reader names both in order at 50 cm within ten seconds.

Meets: user/criterion, actual four test counts and justified layout revision. Grade 3/support: large numbered boxes/pictures/scribing. docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Light; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: compare transmission through one/two tissue layers and revise an Advent symbol for reader clarity under equal light conditions. Why: optical evidence supports design, while Advent light signifies hope. CST-C1 measured/symbolic distinction; CST-S1 observation; CST-S3 light path; CST-A2 purposeful form; CST-A3 critique/revision. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. docs.text:
Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9): enclosed flashlight, three tissue squares, cardstock frame, glue stick. Adult precuts window, checks secured batteries. Per pupil: paper/ pencil. Teacher board/timer; pretest at fixed 20 cm light-to-frame distance, demo from kit. Use star or simple branch as classroom devotional convention, not claim about every Jesse Tree. docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Transmission = light passes through; absorption = energy taken up by material; symbol = image communicating an idea; contrast = visible difference. docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Advent as preparation/hope; "What can physical light tests tell us?"

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting

Meets: accurate comparisons/path and critique-backed symbolic design, not beautiful decoration alone. Grade 3/support: precut frame/arrow stems/dictation. docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Marine systems; four 40-minute meetings. Objective: label ocean-light zones, explain a food-to-eater model and improve a collection tool using equal ten-token tests. Why: ocean stewardship needs system knowledge, evidence and honest limits. Catholic/CST-C3 creation care; CST-S3 zone/feeding models; CST-E1 criteria/limits; CST-E2 actual retest; CST-M2 labeled before/after count display. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; developing. Prep 20 minutes; cleanup 5 each. No voyage legends, unverified statistics, soap/oil/cocoa experiments or universal energy-transfer percentages.

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9). Per unit kit: three cardstock sheets (zone strip/tool), ruler, tray, plastic spoon, 40 cm tape, twenty 3 cm paper debris squares (ten per test). Per pupil: four record sheets/pencil. Teacher board/timer; adult pours 100 mL fresh water per test, 200 mL/team for two tests, in meeting 4 only; demo from issued kit. Class: one graduated plastic pouring cup and one roll of paper towels for drying/spills. Pretest spoon/card scoop and paper pickup within 30 seconds, use a fresh ten-square set each test; soaking/sinking is recorded, not replaced silently. Reuse tools, retain charts, dispose wet paper after drying.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kits; rulers; trays; spoons (1/team each) 4 5 7 9 Cardstock (3/team) 12 15 21 27 Debris squares (20/team) 80 100 140 180 Tape (40 cm/team, cm total) 160 200 280 360 Water (200 mL/team, mL total) 800 1000 1400 1800 Records (4/pupil) 40 60 80 100 Pencils (1/pupil) 10 15 20 25 Graduated cup; towel roll (fixed each) 1 1 1 1

Copy these ready cards to board, no separate research required: NOAA light zones, retrieved October 4, 2026: sunlight 0-200 m; twilight 200-1,000 m; below 1,000 m no sunlight. Deeper subdivisions: midnight 1,000-4,000 m, abyss 4,000-6,000 m, hadal 6,000 m and deeper. Boundaries are teaching divisions, not equal-width physical layers. Draw a not-to-scale strip. Food-model cards: hypothetical photosynthetic producer P; small consumer Q eats P; larger R eats Q; decomposer D breaks down remains. These stipulated relationships teach arrow direction, not unverified species diets.

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Zone = depth/light region; producer = makes food; consumer = eats organisms; decomposer = breaks down dead matter; model = limited representation. Misconception: removing one card proves all organisms will die. If asked "Are all producers sun-powered?" No; some use chemical energy; this simplified model uses photosynthesis. Religious creation care motivates responsibility, not predicted cleanup success. No actual pollution, animals, chemicals, glass, tasting or stagnant water. Adult pours/empties, dry spills immediately, stop/report unsafe setups. Indoor paper/water work, no winter outing or unseen home research.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Wonder/care question: "What changes with depth?"
  2. 4-10: Read NOAA cards, model five labeled depth bands, not stacked liquids.
  3. 10-22: Each labels five zones/depth bounds on not-to-scale strip and marks which regions permit sunlight; team compares cards.
  4. 22-30: Peer checks boundaries/model scale; revise one misleading spacing or caption. "Does equal paper spacing mean equal ocean depth?"
  5. 30-35: Individual three light regions, five labels and scale limitation.
  6. 35-40: Save dated strips/count/clear.

docs.title: Meeting 2: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Recall light/producer relationship.
  2. 4-9: Model P -> Q -> R, arrows food-to-eater; D receives remains.
  3. 9-21: Each draws stipulated feeding web, labels roles/arrows and states what is hypothetical; add light as energy source, not an organism.
  4. 21-30: Remove Q card on paper; identify represented links lost and an uncertain possible effect, not a guaranteed cascade.
  5. 30-35: Each explains arrow/role and a model limitation; "What source would we need to name real species?"
  6. 35-40: File diagrams/count tools/clear.

docs.title: Meeting 3: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "How can collecting debris help people and creation?"
  2. 4-9: Criterion >=8 of ten paper squares collected in 30 seconds; limit one spoon/card tool/40 cm tape, no claim about dissolved contaminants.
  3. 9-21: Design two scoop shapes and build dry prototype from cardstock.
  4. 21-30: Dry-tray ten-square practice; every pupil operates/records, choose one change for wet test.
  5. 30-35: Individual criterion/constraint, practice count and design reason.
  6. 35-40: Save tools/remaining squares, count/clear.

docs.title: Meeting 4: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve dry-test plan; distinguish paper debris from real marine waste.
  2. 4-9: Adult water setup/safety; fixed ten squares, 30 seconds, spoon/tool.
  3. 9-21: Test version 1, record collected 0-10 and sinking; rotate operator/ counter/recorder. Revise one scoop edge, not water volume.
  4. 21-30: Adult empties/resets with fresh 100 mL, fresh ten-square set, same setup/time; retest. Each draws two bars and makes whole-number comparison.
  5. 30-35: Individual results/limit and stewardship choice; "Does clear water mean safe drinking water?" No.
  6. 35-40: Adult empties clean water, collect wet paper, dry trays/count/store.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: zone/food models with limits, criterion and real repeated counts/chart. Grade 3/support: read-aloud depth labels/0-10 graph. Grade 4/challenge: zone scale error and collection-versus-contamination tradeoff. Sinking paper: record limitation, no replacement during a timed test. Water not approved: same ten-token dry tray/time tests, clearly dry debris model, no flotation evidence. No tray: dry desk boundary, same criterion. Early finish: explain what a real ocean trial would need. Creation-care source: paraphrased Laudato Si'.

Family: We studied marine models and retested debris collection. Ask, "What did your model leave out?" Optional: discuss reducing waste.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Reflection; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: select one evidence-recording goal, practice twice and compare checked features to decide a next step. Why: purposeful effort needs observable follow-through, not four ambitious promises. Catholic/CST-C3 stewardship of work; CST-M2 dated tracker; CST-M3 count/change. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; introductory. Prep 10; cleanup 5 included. No five-project target, required family tracker or rating spiritual growth.

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Per pupil: portfolio, two sheets/pencil. Teacher board/timer; source on board simulated flight cm data: first 40/50/40; second 50/60/50. Goal example: "By minute 30 I will copy a three-trial table with title, cm unit and all three readings correct." Three features, checked 0-3. Missing portfolio uses supplied data, not invented first-semester history. Teams <=3 confer at desks (⅘/7/9); no team-specific hardware.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Portfolios; pencils (1/pupil each) 10 15 20 25 Paper (2/pupil) 20 30 40 50

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: SMART = specific/measurable/achievable/relevant/time-bound; tracker = actual record; action = practice step; evidence = observed result. Misconception: meeting a goal once proves permanent mastery. If asked "Does prayer guarantee success?" Prayer accompanies effort, not a performance guarantee or measure of a child's worth. Desk paper only, no private faith/service/family disclosure or peer rankings. Report missing records; indoor primary.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Optional prayer for patient work; "Which saved task needs a clearer record?" View portfolio briefly, no forced personal confession.
  2. 4-10: Model one SMART goal and tracker attempt/time | 0-3 | next action.
  3. 10-20: Write goal/relevance/two actions; copy first simulated table, peer checks title/unit/values, each records actual feature count.
  4. 20-30: Apply action to missing feature, copy second table; recheck/record.
  5. 30-35: Each child compares counts, identifies action from evidence and states simulation label/limit. "What changed in your practice?"
  6. 35-40: Date/file tracker, return portfolios/pencils, clear. Teacher schedules optional next-class check without hiding extra required meetings.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: one measurable goal, two real check counts, accurate comparison and next action tied to result. Grade 3/support: goal stem/dictation/three boxes. Grade 4/challenge: explain later transfer check needed. No improvement: record same count and propose support, not invented progress. Too ambitious: reduce to three table features today. Early finish: new data/table, same criteria.

Family: We practiced and tracked one goal. Ask, "What did evidence tell you to try next?" Optional conversation, not compulsory home monitoring.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Computing / Game Design Studio Time Four meetings, 40 minutes each, including cleanup Domains Catholic dignity, computing, purposeful visual communication, whole-number reasoning Big idea A game is a rule system whose code and instructions must be tested for the people using it. Student objective "I can build or trace a three-point game, prevent extra scoring, and improve it from a user's test." Why Software designers debug behavior and make tools usable by different people. Catholic connection Respect players' dignity: clear controls, fair rules, no humiliating losing messages, privacy and accessible alternatives. St. John Bosco is a model of caring for young people; no invented quotation is needed. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C2 (inclusive user testing); CST-T1 (device input/output); CST-T2 (events/conditions/debugging); CST-A3 (test and revise instructions); CST-M3 (score reasoning within 0-3). Technology Required for primary pathway: Scratch 3 on one computer per pair, preferably offline. It enables executable event code and input/output testing. Paper trace evidence is computational thinking, not Scratch operation/programming. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; novices welcome. Meeting 1 explicitly teaches sprite, event, score and condition. No Year A prerequisite, coordinates, clones or negative-number math required. Prep / cleanup 20 minutes for first meeting once software works; 10 minutes for later meetings; initial installation is advance work. 5 minutes each meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Open Scratch on compatible school computers; use guest/offline projects and local saves, not shared pupil logins. Test the two complete scripts below. No public posting, names/photos/voices or online studios without school approval.
  2. Make pairs; an odd trio rotates planner, operator and tester. Prepare labeled local save folders by team ID; confirm reopen works.
  3. Board: input | score before | score after | message. Display the scripts or read them aloud. Students copy three game-rule cards onto paper.
  4. If computers/software fail, announce the paper pathway before class. Keep the same four meeting times, but mark operating evidence absent.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits/devices. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth device is spare. Thirteen-team showcase timing is a conservative capacity bound.

  • Per student: pencil, one evidence half-sheet each meeting (4 total).
  • Per team: 1 Scratch-capable computer, 1 paper sheet each meeting (4 total), 1 paper token; 3 small scoring squares cut/folded from the first team sheet.
  • Whole class: timer, board, local save storage already on computers; 1 teacher computer for demonstration (may share an available team computer).
  • Teacher: optional display/projector, not needed if demonstrating in a small group; no purchased game assets.
Students Teams / team computers / tokens Team paper across unit Half-sheet slips across unit / pencils 10 5 each 20 sheets 40 / 10 15 8 each 32 sheets 60 / 15 20 10 each 40 sheets 80 / 20 25 13 each 52 sheets 100 / 25

One device per pair is the primary plan. With fewer devices, paper-test while rotating; maintain a named operation log and schedule missed operation later. Existing devices are reused; paper is consumable.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background, misconception and question/answer
docs.text:
Sprite: programmable character/object. Event: trigger that starts code. Variable: named stored value, here Score. Condition: true/false check. Broadcast: message that starts matching receiver code. Debug: test and correct behavior.

The game uses one sprite called Token and a variable Score for all sprites. The goal is three deliberate inputs. Continuous touching inside a forever loop is not used: it can add points every program cycle. A guard prevents input number 4 from making the score 4.

Misconception: "A finished picture means the game works." If asked: "Why did the score jump?" Answer: "Check which event adds points. We want one deliberate input to add one point, not every instant two sprites touch."

docs.title: Complete native Scratch starter
docs.text:
Create variable Score for all sprites. Rename the default sprite Token. Set its costume/position by dragging it on stage. Place these stacks on Token, using actual Events/Variables/Control/Looks blocks:

when green flag clicked
set [Score] to (0)
say [Click Token or press space. Collect 3 points!]

when this sprite clicked
if <(Score) < (3)> then
  change [Score] by (1)
  if <(Score) = (3)> then
    say [Complete! Press the green flag to restart.]
  else
    say [One point collected. Keep going.]
  end
end

In meeting 3, add keyboard access without copying the scoring body:

when this sprite clicked
broadcast [collect]

when [space] key pressed
broadcast [collect]

when I receive [collect]
if <(Score) < (3)> then
  change [Score] by (1)
  if <(Score) = (3)> then
    say [Complete! Press the green flag to restart.]
  else
    say [One point collected. Keep going.]
  end
end

Replace the earlier clicked scoring stack with the broadcast stack; leaving both adds twice per click. Keep the green-flag reset stack. No imagined "when score > 10" event. Arrow-key enrichment, if later taught, uses up change y by 10, down change y by -10, left change x by -10, right change x by 10; not part of this core unit.

docs.title: SAFETY and privacy
docs.text: Stay at assigned desks; clean dry hands only, no liquids near devices. Teacher handles plugs/charging. Low sound, no flashing effects, no public uploads or identifying media. Save to school-controlled storage with team IDs. Paper tokens stay on desks; no student acts as a running target.

docs.title: Meeting 1: rules and traces, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: User need. Original prayer: "God, help us create fairly and include others." Ask: "What makes a game confusing or unkind?"
  2. 5-12: Demonstrate goal/input/feedback. Open Scratch, identify sprite and green flag, show Score. Teacher runs three clicks then a fourth; expected values 0,1,2,3,3. "Why shouldn't input 4 earn point 4?"
  3. 12-18: Paper model. Partners write three rules: start at 0; input adds 1 only if below 3; at 3 show complete. Move a token on squares 0-3. Swap reader/executor.
  4. 18-28: Build first stack. Students create Score and the green-flag reset, then the clicked stack above with help. Each child takes an operator turn; waiting partners trace.
  5. 28-32: Test boundary. Try four clicks, then green flag. Record actual values, not assumed correctness.
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Predict score after two inputs and after four; explain "below 3." Record which children actually edited and ran code.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup/save. Save locally by team ID, reopen one file as a class check, stop projects, store slips/tokens, close computers as school practice requires.

docs.title: Meeting 2: debugging, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Retrieve/reset. Reopen saved project; absent files are rebuilt using the short starter, not assigned as homework.
  2. 5-11: Demonstrate a bug. Teacher temporarily removes the if Score < 3 guard in a separate demo. Four clicks produce 4. "Which rule failed?"
  3. 11-17: Trace and propose fix. Individually mark the first input where expected/actual differ; partners agree on guard location.
  4. 17-28: Edit and run. Verify each team's complete starter; test zero inputs, one, three, four, then restart. Switch operator. Record expected/actual and the fix.
  5. 28-32: Explain. "Why reset to 0? Can we keep changing decorations instead of fixing this bug?" One team demonstrates a corrected trace.
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Write/dictate the guard and one passed boundary test; children with paper-only work report the trace, not an executed program.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Save/reopen locally, stop, clear desks, collect bug records.

docs.title: Meeting 3: accessible controls and visual instructions, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Consider users. "How could someone who finds mouse control difficult play?" Accept keyboard input and partner-assisted input as access choices.
  2. 5-12: Teach broadcasts. Teacher replaces the clicked scoring body with broadcast collect, adds space-key sender and matching receiver as above. Show the old scoring stack is removed.
  3. 12-24: Implement/test. Teams edit, swap operators halfway, test click-only and space-only runs. Holding a key may repeat inputs on some systems; demonstrate deliberate press/release and log observed behavior. No claim that all keyboards behave identically.
  4. 24-29: Purposeful art. Design clear readable instructions, contrast and a symbol plus words; color alone cannot communicate success. One partner tests whether the message makes sense.
  5. 29-32: Debug double scoring. "Did one click add 2? Which old stack remains?" Test again after removing it.
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Each child identifies an input, output and access improvement, and traces which broadcast starts scoring.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup/save. Save locally, stop, collect sketches and access-test notes.

docs.title: Meeting 4: user testing and showcase, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Criteria. Game starts at 0, deliberate inputs reach 3, extra inputs stay 3, restart resets, instructions readable and respectful.
  2. 5-12: Paired testing. Neighboring teams exchange places only on teacher signal or exchange paper versions. Test all five criteria; record passed/not yet with a specific observation.
  3. 12-22: Revise one feature. Fix code or instructions from feedback, then repeat the relevant test. "What evidence shows the change helped the user?"
  4. 22-29: Showcase in pairs. Half the teams present at desks, then reverse after 3 minutes; each child explains their own contribution. No twenty-five sequential presentations.
  5. 29-32: Reflect on dignity. "Whose needs did your improvement address? What should stay private?"
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Trace 0,1,2,3,3 and reset to 0; explain one test-backed revision and one input/output relationship.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup/archive. Save local final and bug record, stop, return tokens/paper, collect individual evidence. No accounts or uploads required.

docs.title: What success looks like
docs.text: Each child independently traces boundary behavior, identifies a condition and explains a test-based revision. Device programming evidence additionally requires an observed edit/run by that child; record it separately. Score 1 decoration only; 2 trace with prompts; 3 independent trace, correct condition and revision evidence; 4 level 3 plus identifies an accessibility or restart limitation and retests it.

docs.title: Unplugged, troubleshooting, differentiation and indoor alternative
docs.text:
No devices: in each meeting, replace on-screen building/testing minutes with paper script assembly, token execution, intentional bug and user-tested instruction card. Reuse the exact times. Meetings ½ trace score/guard; meeting 3 uses sender/receiver cards; meeting 4 tests/revises rules. Mark CT observed; Scratch operation not observed. A paper game is worthwhile but not an executed Scratch program.

  • Missing save: rebuild the two short stacks; save to verified school folder. If permissions fail, report to teacher and keep paper evidence.
  • Score jumps twice: remove the obsolete clicked stack, then retest. Score above 3: confirm guard encloses addition.
  • Support / Grade 3: numbered paper blocks, oral reading, score counters 0-3; adult/partner assists typing but child predicts and explains.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: devise a boundary test not shown, compare expected/actual, then explain why one receiver avoids duplicate scoring logic.
  • Indoor alternative: all meetings already indoor, no winter/weather constraint.
  • 25 pupils: thirteen pairs/trio, thirteen devices primary; desk-based pair showcase fits seven minutes. A shared-device rotation requires separate missing-operation records.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text: We designed a three-point game, tested its score boundary and restart, and revised instructions for a real user. Paper traces show computational thinking; children who used Scratch also practiced executable code. Our Catholic connection was fair, inclusive design and privacy. Ask: "What happens on input number four, and why?" Optional at home: play a three-point paper game and check its rules. The original resource scratch.mit.edu remains optional; offline classroom work needs no home account. No homework, devices or public sharing required.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Community data; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: make a three-category class survey chart, read two bars and revise a caption to respect privacy/sample limits. Why: appreciation and truthful data communication can coexist. Catholic/CST-C2 no coerced disclosure; CST-T3 data/privacy; CST-M2 chart; CST-M3 counts/difference; CST-A3 caption critique. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; introductory. Prep 10; cleanup 5. No dated national theme/history statistics required.

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Question on board: "Which classroom appreciation activity would you choose: thank-you drawing, helpful cleanup, quiet prayer?" One anonymous choice, abstention permitted; not a holiness survey. Per pupil: ballot scrap, graph sheet/pencil. Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9) share ruler/two markers. Teacher board/timer. If survey unsuitable, simulated practice counts 6/4/3, labeled not class data. No family finances/years of attendance questions. Save charts, reuse tools.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Ballots; graph sheets; pencils (1/pupil each) 10 15 20 25 Rulers (1/team) 4 5 7 9 Markers (2/team) 8 10 14 18

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Survey = question with recorded responses; anonymous = unnamed; sample = responding group; caption = explanatory label. Misconception: choices measure faith. If asked "Can we say all Catholic children prefer drawing?" No; this group/simulation cannot represent all pupils. Paper indoors; adult keeps ballots private/destroys after tally, no public names/ media, no obligatory prayer disclosure. Report broken supplies.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Optional gratitude prayer; explain Catholic appreciation/privacy.
  2. 4-10: Model one response/one tally; valid total excludes blank/double marks.
  3. 10-20: Simultaneously collect ballots, tally/check counts on board.
  4. 20-29: Each graphs three bars 0-based scale, title/unit/source label; peer critiques misleading caption and pupil revises.
  5. 29-35: Each child reads two bars, total/difference and privacy/sample limit. Practice key: total 13; drawing exceeds cleanup by 2.
  6. 35-40: Collect dated charts, adult handles ballots, cap/count/clear.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: accurate chart/comparison, responsible caption/source and access choice. Grade 3/support: pre-drawn 0-25 axis/oral evidence. Grade 4/challenge: nonresponse/sample bias in words, no required percentages/pie chart. Mismatch: recount, label invalid ballots; never adjust silently. No survey: labeled practice data. Early finish: explain an unanswered question.

Family: We used school-appreciation data responsibly. Ask, "Whose responses does your graph represent?" Optional: thank a school helper.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Stewardship design; four 40-minute meetings. Objective: plan/build a city within twenty resource tokens, test access and revise a system using countable criteria. Why: sustainability involves tradeoffs, people and resources, not green decoration. Catholic/CST-C3 stewardship; CST-E1 criteria/budget; CST-E2 test/retest; CST-A1 labeled plan/model; CST-M3 whole-number budget/remainder. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; developing. Prep 20; cleanup 5 each. Creation-care paraphrase: Laudato Si'. No Kateri stereotype/quote, real power/water savings or hidden home materials.

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9): 30 x 30 cm cardboard base, three cardstock sheets, twenty drawn large paper resource tokens, ruler/scissors, two markers, 100 cm tape/unit. Per pupil: four evidence sheets/pencil. Teacher board/ timer; demo from kit. Inspect recycled edges, reserve dry storage on bases. Post hypothetical planning costs, not dollars or measured energy: housing 4, shared community space 3, walking/public-transport route 3, water-management model 3, waste-management model 2, green space 2, energy-system model 3. Required set total 20, remainder 0. Symbols label water/waste/energy functions; no real generators or plants. An alternative upgrade costs 2 extra; choose what to reduce and explain lost function, never imply free benefits.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Bases; rulers; scissors (1/team each) 4 5 7 9 Cardstock (3/team) 12 15 21 27 Tokens (20/team) 80 100 140 180 Markers (2/team) 8 10 14 18 Tape (100 cm/team, cm total) 400 500 700 900 Evidence sheets (4/pupil) 40 60 80 100 Pencils (1/pupil) 10 15 20 25

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Sustainable = meeting needs while considering future resources; tradeoff = gain with a cost; system = interacting parts; budget = finite allowance. Misconception: labeled solar roof proves energy savings. If asked "Does our rain garden clean drinking water?" No; this is a nonworking system model, actual performance requires separate tests. Dry paper only; no moss/mold, glass/metal, wiring, stagnant water or real construction. Scissors seated; stop/report hazards. Indoor primary.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "Who could be left out of a resource-saving city?"
  2. 4-10: Read seven feature costs, count twenty tokens; distinguish budget units from money/energy.
  3. 10-22: Each draws labeled plan, team assigns tokens to all seven features.
  4. 22-30: Peer checks sum/layout; criterion continuous >=2 cm route joining housing/community/water/waste/green space; revise one plan gap.
  5. 30-35: Individual sum/remainder, one stewardship choice and plan limit.
  6. 35-40: Count tokens/tools, save dated plans.

docs.title: Meeting 2: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve budget/route criteria.
  2. 4-9: Model water/energy/waste labels with input/process/output arrows; conceptual functions, not certified machinery.
  3. 9-21: Each details one system and annotates a user/resource tradeoff; complete seven-feature plan.
  4. 21-30: Try the two-token upgrade on paper; rebalance or reject with reason, retaining required feature functions.
  5. 30-35: Each records baseline/alternative budget and justified choice.
  6. 35-40: Save/count; no family research assigned.

docs.title: Meeting 3: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve final plan/material allowance.
  2. 4-9: Show low card buildings and route width ruler check.
  3. 9-21: Build dry city model, rotating roles; every pupil adds system label.
  4. 21-30: Trace route to five destinations and measure narrowest width; record reached 0-5/cm, identify revision.
  5. 30-35: Each compares built model to plan and cites test result.
  6. 35-40: Store bases, count tools/tokens, clear scraps.

docs.title: Meeting 4: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "Which evidence makes a route change necessary?"
  2. 4-9: Model one relocated building, keeping budget/fixed base.
  3. 9-21: Revise/retest five destinations and width, same conditions.
  4. 21-30: Parallel peer tours; each explains system, cost and tradeoff; no serial seven-team five-minute speeches.
  5. 30-35: Individual before/after, sum/remainder and limit: model route is not a real accessibility-code or resource-savings certification.
  6. 35-40: Count/archive dry models/plans, cap markers/clear.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: correct twenty-token budget, labeled model, real route retest and stewardship tradeoff. Grade 3/support: token piles/copied cost card/scribing. Grade 4/challenge: compare two whole-number alternatives and explain displaced function. Over-budget: reject/adjust on paper, no invented zero-cost upgrade. Missing base: paper 30 cm plan model, label reduced 3D evidence. Early finish: new reader traces route, same criterion. No savings outcomes inferred.

Family: We balanced resource budgets and retested a city model. Ask, "What did your design gain and give up?" Optional: discuss a shared resource.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Grades 3-4; Weekly B; Mathematics; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: compare around with three across-lengths on two circles and compose a four-part radial pattern with an explained visual choice. Why: mathematical relationships can support purposeful art and honest wonder. CST-C1 approximation/faith distinction; CST-M1 measurements; CST-M3 three equal lengths/remainder; CST-A2 radial pattern purpose. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; developing. Prep 10; cleanup 5. No digit memorization contest, forced decimal division or unsupported sacred geometry/biography claims.

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9): two smooth plastic circles under 15 cm diameter, ruler, four 50 cm strings, two markers. Per pupil: two paper sheets/pencil. Teacher board/timer, demo from kit; check strings reach around circles. Model folding a traced circle into four sections for repeated motif. Tools/string reusable; retain measurements/art.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Rulers (1/team) 4 5 7 9 Circles; markers (2/team each) 8 10 14 18 Strings (4/team) 16 20 28 36 Paper (2/pupil) 20 30 40 50 Pencils (1/pupil) 10 15 20 25

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Diameter = across center; circumference = around; radial = arranged about center; motif = repeated design. Pi is finite between 3 and 4, nonterminating/ nonperiodic decimal representation. Misconception: endless digits mean infinite size. If asked "Does pattern prove God?" Mathematical evidence and faith reflection are distinct; accurate reasoning can inspire wonder. Short desk strings only, no sharp lids, compasses, beads, food or neck loops. Stop/report damaged tools. Indoor primary.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: "How can around/across help us organize a design?"
  2. 4-9: Model center/across, string around, three equal diameter portions.
  3. 9-21: Each measures a circle; team records two whole-cm pairs and compares three across-lengths plus remainder.
  4. 21-30: Each traces/folds four-section circle, repeats chosen motif for balance or emphasis; peer identifies intention, revise one section.
  5. 30-35: Individual pairs/remainder demonstration and explained visual purpose/finite-pi distinction.
  6. 35-40: Count/coil strings, cap markers, save dated data/art, clear.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: measurements/comparison and intentional repeated design, not polish. Grade 3/support: center mark/premarked portions/pre-folded sheet/dictation. Grade 4/challenge: explain measurement error and radial balance tradeoff. Wrong result: recheck zero/center/string stretch and record correction. No circles: traced teacher-selected circular object; no arbitrary oval. Early finish: change motif while keeping four-section constraint.

Family: We compared circles and composed radial art. Ask, "Why did you repeat that shape?" Optional: notice a circular pattern in a picture.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Weather data / Weather Station Time Three 40-minute meetings, including cleanup Domains Catholic care for neighbors, Earth science, tool use, mathematics Big idea A measurement needs a suitable tool, units and context; a few observations do not establish climate or a certain forecast. Student objective "I can read a tool, label the source of data, and make an evidence-based comparison." Why Meteorologists use instruments and many observations; communities use forecasts to protect people. Catholic connection Plan safe help for people affected by weather; do not suggest storms punish victims. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C2 (safe/inclusive weather response); CST-S1 (observations/evidence); CST-S2 (test a measurement method); CST-T1 (tool use/troubleshooting); CST-M2 (labeled graph/data comparison). Technology None for the supplied indoor pathway; an adult may optionally obtain current weather data. Thermometer/ruler are measurement tools, not device programming. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; count/read whole millimeters and whole-number Celsius values; no negative-number arithmetic, mean, percentage or pie chart required. Prep / cleanup 20 minutes before meeting 1; 10 minutes before meetings ⅔ with reusable kit; 5 minutes each meeting

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Seat pairs, one final trio if needed. Keep water trays away from outlets/books. Set a class room thermometer at a readable height, away from heater/sunlight; label its reading "indoor air."
  2. Use uncut, clear, flat-bottomed straight-sided plastic cups, at least 5 cm tall and inside diameter at most 4.5 cm. This keeps each 20 mm-deep fill under 32 mL and the thirteen-cup plus demonstration water budget under 500 mL. Tape a ruler with zero at the inside bottom. If the cup tapers, use it only as a water-container model, not a rainfall gauge.
  3. Cut 20 cm tissue strips for wind indicators; no pins, balloons, glass or cut bottles. Put a tray, cup, ruler and paper in each team's kit.
  4. Copy the supplied dataset onto the board. Label it SIMULATED PRACTICE DATA, not observed local weather. It makes the core unit independent of weather and unscheduled between-class monitoring.
  5. Outdoor observations are optional only with school approval, supervision, accessible route and safe conditions. Do not require outdoor access to meet the objective.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth tray is spare. Thirteen-tray capacity is conservative.

  • Per student: pencil, 1 evidence half-sheet per meeting.
  • Per team: 1 clear straight-sided cup (inside diameter <=4.5 cm, height >=5 cm), 1 shallow tray, 1 ruler, 1 tissue strip (20 cm), 1 scrap-cardboard handle (15 cm), 20 cm tape, 3 recording/graph paper sheets across unit.
  • Whole class: room thermometer, timer, board, 1 water jug with 500 mL maximum, towel, dry-material storage bin.
  • Teacher only: scissors for strips, water dispensing jug and towel. Optional printed actual weather report must include source, station, date/time and units.
Students Teams Cups / trays / rulers / strips / handles Team paper across unit Tape Evidence half-sheets / pencils Water / thermometer 10 5 5 each 15 sheets 1 m 30 / 10 500 mL max / 1 15 8 8 each 24 sheets 1.6 m 45 / 15 500 mL max / 1 20 10 10 each 30 sheets 2 m 60 / 20 500 mL max / 1 25 13 13 each 39 sheets 2.6 m 75 / 25 500 mL max / 1

Water is distributed in small pours, never all 500 mL into one tray. Cups/rulers/trays are reused; strips/tape/paper consumable. No purchased weather station needed.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text:
Weather: atmospheric conditions over a short time at a place. Climate: patterns over many years, not this week's graph. Precipitation: rain/snow/sleet/hail. Gauge: a measurement tool. Source: where data came from. Forecast: evidence-based estimate of future conditions.

Rainfall depth is read in a straight-sided collector with matching collection/storage cross-section; an uncalibrated tapered bottle is not a reliable rain gauge. Our cup test is indoor water-depth practice, not rainfall or snow measurement. A tissue strip shows air movement, not wind speed in miles per hour. Snowfall depth is not the same as melted-water depth.

Misconception: "A spinning homemade cup device tells exact wind speed." It needs calibration; this unit does not claim that. If asked: "Will rain come tomorrow?" Answer: "Our five practice days cannot tell us for sure. A forecast uses wider, current information; follow school alerts and official forecasts, not this model."

docs.title: Supplied dataset
docs.text:
Practice day Temperature (degrees C) Rain (mm) Monday 6 0 Tuesday 8 4 Wednesday 7 0 Thursday 10 6 Friday 9 2

These are invented values for learning, not a source claim. Total rain = 12 mm; warmest = Thursday; largest temperature difference = 4 degrees C. They describe neither Minnesota climate nor a real forecast.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No glass, latex balloons, exposed pins, cut bottle edges, outdoor storms/ice or unsupervised movement. Teacher pours water, maximum 20 mm depth per cup; students report spills immediately and stop movement until dried. No tasting. Tissue strips are handheld by the cardboard, not tied to wrists/necks or placed at faces. No electrical fan needed; teacher may move a card gently to create airflow. Outdoor work stops under school weather restrictions; -10 degrees F means use the indoor pathway.

docs.title: Meeting 1: observations and model tools, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Weather or climate? Original prayer: "God, help us care for neighbors and observe carefully." Ask: "Does one snowy day describe the whole climate?" Teach the time-scale distinction.
  2. 5-11: Observe safely. Look through a window; record date/time, sky and visible precipitation. If the view is blocked, write "not visible," not a guess. Read the room thermometer as indoor, not outdoor weather.
  3. 11-17: Tool demonstration. Show cup/ruler zero alignment. Pour to 10 mm; read at eye level at the bottom of the curved water surface. Ask: "Where is zero? Which unit are we using?" Show how a tapered cup would mislead.
  4. 17-27: Build/test indicator. Teams tape strip to cardboard handle, predict its direction and gently wave a card nearby. Record still/moving and direction relative to their hand. No numeric wind speed. Teacher checks one kept-same condition in each team.
  5. 27-32: Compare observations. "Which observation was direct? Which came from a tool?" Draw the tool and identify one limitation.
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Each child reads the demonstrated 10 mm cup, labels the room temperature location, and explains weather versus climate orally or in writing.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Teacher empties water; children dry cups/trays, store strips/rulers, collect slips, clear floor.

docs.title: Meeting 2: measurement consistency, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Recall. "Why can't room temperature be called today's outdoor temperature?"
  2. 5-10: Demonstrate fair reading. Teacher prepares two levels, about 5 and 15 mm. Read first with ruler zero misplaced, then aligned. Ask: "Was the water changed, or the measuring method?"
  3. 10-22: Team depth trials. Teacher pours team cups to a depth below 20 mm; both partners independently read and record to nearest whole mm, then compare. Change the water depth once and repeat. A trio adds a third reader. Record disagreements instead of forcing identical numbers.
  4. 22-28: Investigate error. Reset ruler alignment/eye height; reread one cup. "What adjustment made our reading more dependable?"
  5. 28-32: Label datasets. Introduce the practice table above. Contrast measured classroom water with simulated rainfall; they are different kinds of evidence.
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Draw zero alignment, record own two readings with units, name one cause of differing measurements.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Teacher drains cups into sink, students dry trays and store supplies; collect measurement slips.

docs.title: Meeting 3: graph and communicate, exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Source check. "Did we collect Monday's data outdoors?" Expected: no, these are simulated.
  2. 5-11: Model a graph. Draw rain bar graph, days along bottom, mm scale 0-6 by ones. Tuesday's bar reaches 4. Label title and "simulated practice."
  3. 11-23: Make graph. Grade 3 draws five rain bars and adds 0+4+0+6+2 = 12 mm. Grade 4 also draws a temperature graph, 0-10 by ones; connecting points describes sequence, not measurements between days. No average, percentages or pie chart.
  4. 23-28: Compare evidence. "Which day had most rain? What data justify that? Does Thursday's warmest temperature cause its rain?" Expected: coincidence here cannot establish causation.
  5. 28-32: Neighbor-care design. Plan a safe indoor message for school weather alerts: readable text, no color-only warning, tell an adult rather than venture into storms. Peers check clarity. This is an ethical communication decision, not forecasting certification.
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Child reads two graph values, states one comparison and labels the source as simulated. Grade 4 also states a limitation of forecasting from five days.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup/share. Two volunteers explain comparisons; collect graphs and slips, return tools, recycle spare paper, wipe trays. No ongoing home log required.

docs.title: Success, troubleshooting, support and challenge
docs.text:
Success: every child reads a tool with units, distinguishes indoor/simulated/actual data, creates an accurate labeled graph, and gives a supported comparison. Score 1 guessed data; 2 correct values with help but missing source/units; 3 accurate values, source and comparison; 4 level 3 plus explains a method or forecast limitation.

  • No thermometer: teacher displays a clearly labeled picture scale with 18 degrees C as practice, not a room observation. Tool-reading is observed; actual temperature measurement is not.
  • Cup tapered or zero inaccessible: do not certify rain measurement; use a teacher's straight-sided cup for the class depth demo.
  • Spill: stop; adult dries it. Return to dry graph work if repeated.
  • Support / Grade 3: pre-draw axes, read orally, allow finger-point/oral response, pair for handling but collect separate interpretations.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: compare two readers' values and differences; explain why a weather rhyme or this small table cannot guarantee a forecast.
  • Indoor alternative / winter: all three core meetings already work indoors; no between-meeting weather, growth, network or family labor required.
  • 25 pupils: thirteen stationary trays; teacher makes small pours during the twelve-minute work window; no four-station tool-building queue.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text: We used safe tools, labeled where our data came from, and graphed a practice weather week. Each child explained a comparison and a limit of the evidence. Our Catholic connection was caring for neighbors in severe weather. Ask: "Was your graph observed or simulated, and how can you tell?" Optional at home: discuss an adult's forecast and a safe plan. No outdoor exposure or homework.

Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; introductory. Prep 10; cleanup 5. No raw eggs, drop devices or spring launchers.

If asked "Is a butterfly the same as Jesus rising?" No; metamorphosis develops while alive, Easter is belief about Resurrection. Scene is not an archaeological reconstruction. No stones, moss, eggs, springs, bands, flames or sharp cutting. Adult cuts, children move low desk paper. Stop/report torn guides; indoor primary.

docs.title: Vocabulary/background/SAFETY
docs.text: Growth = supported change; artifact = saved work; demonstration = individual showing; limitation = inference not supported. Misconception: four years of attendance equals mastery. If asked "Can I say programmed?" Only if actual operation was individually observed; otherwise say traced/planned. Local mastery requires two dated observations on separate occasions including individual demonstration/changed context, not this showcase alone. Dry indoor paper only, no restarted devices/circuits, food/balloons or private photos. Report missing artifacts openly.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Optional gratitude prayer; "Which evidence shows a changed choice?"
  2. 4-9: Model dated-result caption and observed/simulated distinction.
  3. 9-20: Select two artifacts; read table/graph independently; compare Week 18 goal tracker if present. Missing artifacts: draw/read backup bars, total 8/difference 2, label new simulated practice.

docs.title: Success/access/troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meets: attributable explanation/data reading, accurate evidence label/limit, critique-backed caption. Growth credit requires actual dated records. Grade 3/support: two-caption stems/scribing. Grade 4/challenge: transfer check/ tradeoff explanation. Missing tracker: do not invent goal success. Long shares: task-result-limit within two minutes, not serial speeches. Early finish: explain what next evidence would resolve a gap.

Family: We shared Year B evidence honestly. Ask, "What does your record support?" Optional: listen to one explanation, no summer homework.

docs.title: October 2026 review and teaching conditions
docs.text:
This directory contains 20 lesson documents covering 32 planned 45-minute meetings (1,440 minutes), not 34 lesson files. Weeks 17 and 32 are breaks. The Expo adds a separately scheduled 60-75-minute event; buddy-class teaching also needs separate adult-supervised time. Calendar dates, Easter, Catholic Schools Week, and Pi Day must be fitted to the actual school year.

Read the Grades 5-6 review and 69-lesson audit before selecting lessons. Three documents here are fully rebuilt: Sphero Mastery, Little Bits & Electronics, and Environmental Science. Other documents have targeted fixes and individual local checks, not full substitute-readiness certification. Local codes are not Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmarks; official alignment is VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

Prerequisites are checked, not inferred from age or Year B attendance: centimeter measurement, sequence/loops, short written/oral explanations, and comparison of trial data. Grade 5 receives templates and worked arithmetic; Grade 6 adds means, uncertainty, tradeoffs, and defensible redesign. No trigonometry assumed. Year A/B may be taken in either order; provide a short entry check and teach missing skills. They revisit design, coding, service, and environment; they are not wholly unique or proven equivalent in standards coverage.

Loan stock, compatible apps, approved accounts, protected circuit holders, and school devices are not confirmed available. Paper paths assess reasoning, not actual robot/app operation. Circuits need inspected protected AA holders, not button cells. The indoor environment dataset is fictional and sufficient in winter; no unsafe fieldwork or home collection required.

For retained content, all unsourced exact Scripture translations, saint sayings, biographical/current-role details, historical superlatives, and scientific statistics are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching. Use verified paraphrase instead of unchecked quotation. No routine homework, required family purchasing, or public student media.
