docs.text: Teacher records actual versus paper operation and missing tests; return devices. Explored: functions/clones. Did: two sizes and three finite copies. Learned: parameters/local state matter. Catholic connection: honest, useful work. Ask: "Which test found the bug?" No routine homework.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit Grades 5-6 / Physical Computing A Time Two 45-minute meetings, 90 total, including 4-minute cleanup each Domains Catholic inclusive design, science systems, technology tools, engineering Big idea A complete powered path lets a switch control a light; a usable signal also needs clear communication. Student objective I can explain a closed path, test an ON/OFF indicator twice and justify an accessibility improvement. Why Safe testing and user feedback matter more than a flashy display. Catholic connection Respect each user's dignity and access, not just successful builders; sources. Local standards / evidence CST-S3: full path; CST-T1: state predictions/repair; CST-E2: before/after test; CST-C2: access decision. Local program codes only. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None: no computing device or software. Approved electrical hardware is required for operation; paper shows reasoning only. Prerequisites Open/closed is taught here; no earlier electronics or Ohm's-law arithmetic required. Prep / cleanup First inspection 30 minutes; repeat prep 15 minutes; missing instructions/approval extra. Cleanup 4 minutes per meeting included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
Release the hardware route only after completing the OLP Snap Circuits guide. Use the actual model's documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project from the eight individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits (OHM-135). Do not assume a push button, protected holder, LED/resistor specification or battery count. The filename is retained for existing links, not LittleBits wiring.

User brief: "A classroom model needs an ON/OFF light and a label readable from 1 m by someone who cannot rely on color alone." It is not a medical, emergency or real safety device, and it will not be distributed to patients.

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text:
• Per pupil: pencil/journal, one circuit/state/design sheet for both meetings.
  • Per team: diagram sheet, cardstock label, ruler and shared marker; dry work area. Keep the circuit on its supplied grid; label stands beside it.
  • Per hardware station: approved Snap kit with selected project parts, diagram/grid and tray. Cells/reserves follow the guide's setup card.
  • Teacher/class: manufacturer instructions, setup card, board, timer, evidence roster, adult-controlled cells and dry storage. Demo uses a station kit.
Pupils Teams / diagrams / labels / rulers Hardware kits / trays Waves Individual sheets / pencils 10 4 4 1 10 15 5 5 1 15 20 7 7 1 20 25 9 5 2 25

No separate LED/resistor harness, mounting tape, extra base, app or new workbook purchase for the Snap route. The protected-AA alternative remains separate.

docs.title: VOCABULARY, BACKGROUND AND SAFETY
docs.text:
Circuit: full conducting return path. Input/output: switch action/light. Load: component transferring electrical energy. Open: interrupted path. Criterion/constraint: success requirement/limit. Tradeoff: a choice with benefits and costs. Battery chemical energy becomes electrical energy and then light/thermal energy; current is not "used up" at the lamp.

Evidence change: Snap's slide switch has two states tested twice, not the old independently controlled supply/button four-state test. Teach ON/OFF, not push/release. LED polarity/current-limiting evidence is not claimed from a lamp project. The separate protected-AA option retains its four-state key.

Misconception: a lit lamp proves any wiring is safe. If asked: "Can I join the battery terminals?" No; that is a dangerous short. Trace a safe open path on paper instead.

SAFETY: follow the guide's manufacturer/age/holder gates; adult isolates the source before snap changes and inspects before restoring power. No pupil cell access, loose/button cells, mains/USB substitutions, shorts, bypassed protection, extra branches, fan blades, soldering or take-home circuits. Warm/damaged/smelly/leaking -> stop/report, adult isolates, OUT OF SERVICE. Keep labels beside the grid, not over parts or contacts.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 45 minutes - path and troubleshooting
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Purpose. Read the user brief; discuss why a clear signal can support dignity and access.
  2. 4-9: Model. Trace the approved return path, demonstrate OFF/ON, source isolation and adult inspection. Explain the two-state evidence change.
  3. 9-12: Predict. Each child labels source/switch/light/conductors/return, predicts OFF/ON and identifies a drawn gap.
  4. 12-26: Wave A. Guide routine: isolated team build, adult check, each child's two OFF/ON cycles, one teacher-managed open-path repair and checked retest. Waiting teams label diagrams and draft an accessible ON/OFF label.
  5. 26-27: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
  6. 27-41: Wave B / individual evidence. Remaining teams get the same hardware routine. Finished teams record predicted/actual results and explain one repair and safe resource choice; smaller classes use the window for repeat tests and individual checks.
  7. 41-45: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store parts and cells, save data and note unfinished physical evidence.

docs.title: Meeting 2: exactly 45 minutes - accessible indicator
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve. Revisit each child's state/path record without assuming prior mastery.
  2. 4-9: Define criteria. Two correct OFF/ON cycles; a peer reads/interprets the label from 1 m, without color-only cues. Constraints: supplied grid, unchanged approved circuit, paper label beside it.
  3. 9-12: Plan. Each child predicts an access obstacle and sketches a justified label/layout change.
  4. 12-26: Wave A. Build/check/test; peer reads label at 1 m without coaching. Record pass/not yet, revise one paper feature and repeat the same test. No electrical redesign outside the documented project.
  5. 26-27: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers station kits.
  6. 27-41: Wave B / explain. Remaining teams run the same routine. Finished teams document before/after results; each child explains path, observed change, user benefit and limitation/tradeoff. Do not claim a real alert device is safe.
  7. 41-45: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store; collect individual diagrams/state/revision records. Paper only goes home.

docs.title: SUCCESS, SUPPORT AND TROUBLE
docs.text:
Each child contributes to the isolated build, operates the switch, labels the full path, predicts two states, records two cycles and explains test-backed repair/redesign evidence. Log observed / prompted / not yet for physical contribution/testing separately from diagram reasoning; a functioning team kit does not certify every child's operation.

Score 1 participation only; 2 prompted path/test; 3 independent path, state and before/after explanation; 4 additionally defends an access tradeoff and the model's limitations.

  • Grade 5/support: traced diagram, large word/symbol labels, oral records, motor assistance; still collect each child's prediction and switch turn.
  • Grade 6/challenge: justify label size/layout/readability tradeoffs using feedback. Compare two drawn faults; no undocumented loads or V=IR requirement.
  • 25 pupils: nine teams, five stations, two 14-minute hardware waves. Inspection/access overruns defer evidence, never compress safety checks.
  • No light: isolate/report; adult compares approved diagram/contacts/cells, then supplies a checked reserve. Never bypass protection or improvise parts.

docs.title: ALTERNATIVES / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: The guide retains the original separate protected-AA push-switch/LED-resistor route and its four-state evidence key; no Snap/LittleBits components are attached to that supply. Use the same waves, replacing slide-switch tests with the specified supply/button states. Record which hardware and state table were used. Without safe hardware, retain the timed paper diagram/state/design work; record reasoning/design only; electrical operation not observed and schedule supervised completion. All work is dry and indoors.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Explored: switched circuits and accessible signals. Did: tested ON/OFF twice and revised a label using peer feedback. Learned: a complete path and clear communication matter. Catholic connection: dignity in design. Name the actual Snap, protected-AA or paper route; for the AA route describe its four-state test instead. Ask: "What did your test show, and how did the label change?" No homework, family purchases or take-home powered circuits.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / A / Mathematics Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes Objective / why / big idea I can measure three circles, calculate C/D with equal units and explain measurement uncertainty. The mathematical circle ratio is constant, our measurements approximate it. Domains / Catholic connection M, S, C; truthful numerical reasoning; mathematical philosophy is not required Catholic doctrine. Local standards CST-M3: ratios; CST-S2: repeated measurement; CST-C1: numerical versus philosophical claim. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement None; calculators are arithmetic tools; Monte Carlo coding not a core objective in this single meeting. Difficulty / entry Developing; teach diameter through center, decimal division and units. Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Circle Measures.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations. Seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Select three flat rigid plastic circular lids 6-12 cm diameter/team; no cans/sharp edges or food. Adult verifies string can wrap each circumference without stretching and pilots center diameter. Copy table Object / C cm / D cm / C divided by D. Pi Day calendar date is school-selected, not guaranteed by week number.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Plastic circular lids 3/team 12 15 21 27 Nonstretch string 0.5 m/team 2 m 2.5 m 3.5 m 4.5 m Ruler; calculator; table sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper consumable; string/lids/tools reusable; adult cuts string.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Circumference: distance around. Diameter: across center. Ratio: division comparison. Uncertainty: limits in measurement. Pi is irrational (decimal neither terminates nor eventually repeats); that is a mathematical fact, not evidence that a physical measurement has infinite precision. Common misconception: measure radius instead of diameter. If asked, "Did we discover exact pi?" No; our tool estimates are rounded. Worked fictional C/D: 18.9/6 = 3.15; 25.⅛ = 3.1375; 31.4/10 = 3.14. All compare to about 3.14, not expected actual values.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "Why might every circle give a similar ratio?" Discuss honest estimates.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Demonstrate string circumference, straight centered diameter and equal-unit division.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Rotate wrapper/measurer/recorder across three lids; each pupil measures one and records all three values/ratios.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Repeat one C/D pair; compare original/repeat and possible string gaps/center error. Keep both, no data correction to 3.14.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Each student independently calculates one ratio with units, explains the three-object pattern and uncertainty, and distinguishes evidence from a philosophical view of mathematics.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Coil string, count lids/tools, save tables and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Did you cross the center? Would a stretched string increase C? Why not erase an unexpected ratio?" Each has three measured pairs, one checked division, repeat/uncertainty and claim distinction. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains error direction; NE for missing measurement.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Ratio near 6 -> check radius/diameter. No lids -> adult-drawn circles measured as drawings, not manufactured objects. No calculator -> use worked long division scaffold. No string around bodies, tasting, sharp cans, rolling objects or device uploads. Stop/report unsafe handling.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: center-marked lid, ruler guide, calculator/scribed reasoning. Grade 6/challenge: compare absolute difference from 3.14 and explain precision; more measurements need not get closer every time. Indoor tabletop primary.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Keep raw/repeated values, count kit pieces; record incomplete checks. Explored: circle ratios. Did: three measurements and a repeat. Learned: units/uncertainty. Catholic connection: honest reasoning. Ask: "Why wasn't your ratio exact?" No routine homework.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Environment A / Environmental Science & Stewardship Time Three meetings of 45 minutes; 135 total Domains C, S, M, A; tools support observation Big idea Responsible environmental decisions need comparable measurements and honest limitations. Student objective I can graph a weather dataset and propose a small stewardship action without claiming more than the evidence shows. Why Residents, farmers, and caretakers interpret weather and use resources responsibly. Catholic connection Care for people and our common home; paraphrase Laudato Si' and stewardship sources, not proof of a scientific prediction. Local standards / evidence CST-S2: individual comparison/control explanation; CST-M2: individual labeled graph and range; CST-A3: revised visual message tested by a peer; CST-C3: individual action and resource tradeoff. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; these four codes are local. Technology None for the primary paper-data path. Non-glass thermometers optional for live indoor practice; spreadsheet optional after paper analysis. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; read integer temperatures including negatives, plot points, add/subtract. Grade 6 mean is scaffolded. No prior Year B required. Prep / cleanup First cards 20 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; optional thermometer equilibration 10 minutes before class. Cleanup 4 minutes/meeting included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Use teams of at most three (⅘/7/9). Copy the complete dataset below once/team; identify it as fictional Minnesota winter practice data, never as observed school weather.
  2. Draw graph axes: five dates on horizontal axis, temperature -15 to 5 degrees C vertically. Make high-contrast large copies available.
  3. If using thermometers, adult checks non-glass instruments and places two side-by-side indoors for 10 minutes before class. They measure room conditions, not outdoor weather.
  4. Read aloud: "We will not go outside, touch unknown water or trash, open an electrical meter, or infer drinking-water safety from pH."
  5. Prepare action brief: "The school wants a classroom reminder to shut exterior doors promptly without obstructing access or exits. Test clarity, not actual energy savings."

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text: Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25 Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Graph sheet; individual exit sheet 1 each/student, reused across unit 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Dataset sheet 1/team 4 5 7 9 Ruler; marker; blunt scissors 1 each/team, reusable 4 5 7 9 Reused paper sign, A4 or letter size 1/team 4 5 7 9 Masking tape 0.5 m/team, classroom display only 2 m 2.5 m 3.5 m 4.5 m Timer; large board graph 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1 Non-glass thermometers, optional 2/class, not per team 2 2 2 2

docs.title: SELF-CONTAINED DATA
docs.text:
All readings in this invented example are at 12:00 noon using comparable shielded instruments at the same height; site A is a fictional paved area, B a fictional grassy area. Snow/cloud cover and location could still confound interpretation.

Date A air temperature (degrees C) B air temperature (degrees C) Practice context Jan 6 -10 -11 Cloudy Jan 7 -8 -9 Cloudy Jan 8 -4 -6 Sunny Jan 9 -12 -12 Cloudy Jan 10 -6 -7 Sunny

Teacher key: A range = 8 degrees C; B range = 6 degrees C. A mean = -8; B mean = -9. A-B differences = 1, 1, 2, 0, 1 degrees C; mean difference = 1. These five points cannot establish climate change, an urban heat island, or a causal surface effect.

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Weather: conditions over a short time. Climate: long-term patterns. Variable: a factor that may change. Range: highest minus lowest value. Uncertainty: limits on what is known. Stewardship: responsible care and use of gifts/resources.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
Surface temperature and air temperature differ. Comparable air measurements need consistent height, shielding, time, and instrument. A small difference may be instrument uncertainty. Graphs communicate evidence; they do not create new evidence. Never erase an inconvenient value.

Common misconception: one cold week disproves climate change. Climate requires long-term records, not five invented days.

If asked, "Did grass make it colder?" Answer: We can describe this dataset's difference, but cannot isolate cause without more controls and repeated observations.

docs.title: Meeting 1 - measurement protocol
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce common-home stewardship and ask why accuracy is a responsibility to neighbors.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Distinguish weather/climate, air/surface; label practice data fictional.
  3. 12-20 (8 min): Each student reads two negative values, computes their difference, and identifies time/height/shield controls.
  4. 20-30 (10 min): Teams compare five A/B pairs. Optional indoor instruments: record both readings at 20 and 25 minutes without moving them; distinguish real room readings from invented outdoor data.
  5. 30-38 (8 min): Draft a repeatable outdoor protocol on paper, including adult weather permission, instrument checks, same time, and missing-data notation. Do not execute outdoors.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: state two controls and one reason the comparison cannot prove cause.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Store data and tools.

docs.title: Meeting 2 - graph and interpret
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Check controls; keep the raw data intact.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Model an axis and one plotted pair; use symbols plus labels, not color alone.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Everyone independently plots all ten points, titles graph, labels degrees C, and keys A/B.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Compare ranges and differences. Grade 5 uses a number line. Grade 6 computes means using the worked key only after trying.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Partners critique graph accuracy and clarity; each revises one label/scale or explains why no revision is needed.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual claim: cite two actual numbers and a limitation; no climate trend claims.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): File individual graphs and clean up.

docs.title: Meeting 3 - communicate a bounded action
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Read action brief. This action is a stewardship choice, not an energy saving proven by the weather data.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Set criteria: readable at 1 m; no blame; explicitly keep entrances accessible.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams make one purposeful visual sign and include a small truthful data graph/caption.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Exchange with a neighboring team. Each tester states the action without coaching; record number interpreting correctly out of testers.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Revise and retest. For nine teams use paired exchanges, not nine full-class talks.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: explain the stewardship tradeoff, one visual revision, and a proposed real measurement needed before claiming energy savings.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Classroom display only with teacher permission; clean up.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: Which values are real observations here? How would a sunlit thermometer bias a reading? What does a range tell us that a mean does not? Who might be excluded by a rushed door-closing rule? What data would test energy savings?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student names two controls and one uncertainty, plots at least 9 of 10 points correctly with units, gives a supported comparison, and explains an accessible action. Art evidence is a purposeful visual choice and a recorded revision, not neatness. Grade 6 additionally computes both means and identifies the limited sample.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: Thermometers disagree: report both and uncertainty; do not average away the discrepancy. No tools/printing: board-copy dataset and draw graph. Negative numbers overwhelm: provide number line and begin with differences. Sign misread: enlarge/action-label it, test again. Never invent "measured savings."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No outdoor requirement; no -10 F exposure, road/parking-lot sampling, unknown water, trash handling, or electrical access. Adult manages instruments and spills; no glass/mercury thermometers. A pH strip cannot determine potability. Student plans are classroom proposals only, not permission to alter doors, thermostats, wiring, or habitat.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: premarked axis and number line; dictate limitation. Challenge: compare ranges. Grade 6: scaffold signed sums; challenge redesign the measurement protocol to reduce one confound and explain why more data may still not establish cause. Provide seated work and large symbols.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: The dataset, protocol, graphs, and sign tests are the primary complete indoor path. Live indoor readings practice tool use only; neither path proves real outdoor monitoring.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: Keep original datasets, collect rulers/instruments, cap markers, remove test signs from exits, recycle drafts, and retain individual graphs for the portfolio.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Explored: weather data and stewardship. Did: graphed fictional practice readings and tested a clear, inclusive reminder. Learned: honest comparisons include limitations. Catholic connection: care for people and resources. Ask: "What could your five-day graph not prove?" No routine homework; optional conversation only.

Melting or growth may symbolize change, never prove Resurrection. Local standards CST-S3: changes/model; CST-A3: visual revision; CST-C1: faith/evidence distinction. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement None; no circuit or light-sequence option. Difficulty / entry Introductory; teach categories with complete cards. docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review accommodations/contact; seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Adult seals a small ice piece in clear bag/tray and seals a second bag of liquid water as endpoint reference. Pilot visibility; actual melting within the period not guaranteed. Copy cards: ice -> water (same water, physical); iron -> rust (new substances, chemical, diagram only); caterpillar -> butterfly (living development, biological, not death/resurrection). No chemical demonstration or body data.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper panel/evidence sheets 2/student 20 30 40 50 Pencil 1/student 10 15 20 25 Marker set; ruler; card sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Sealed clear bags 2/teacher 2 2 2 2 Ice piece; water endpoint; tray; board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper/bags consumable; tools/tray reusable. Teacher controls water.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Physical change: form/state changes without new substance. Chemical change: new substances form. Biological development: living organism changes through growth. Symbol: represents meaning, not mechanism. Common misconception: every change creates a new substance. If asked, "Is ice dead?" No; water is not an organism; Resurrection is not a phase change. Melting absorbs thermal energy from surroundings; no heating required. Two panels must show same substance plus changed state/shape.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Introduce Easter/change distinction; ask "What changed, what remained?"
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Adult shows sealed bags; pupils record actual ice appearance and endpoint-reference status.
  3. 11-24 (13 min): Each sorts three cards with reasons, makes ice/water two-panel diagram with labels/arrows and caption.
  4. 24-35 (11 min): Inspect actual bag again; record observed/not yet melted. Partners ask a science question; revise caption/arrow to avoid claiming unobserved change.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Each correctly identifies three categories, explains same-water limit and distinguishes chosen faith symbol from scientific evidence.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Adult removes bags/wipes tray, pupils cap markers, save panels and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Which panel is an observation versus reference? Is a butterfly a new substance?" Each has three correct category reasons, labeled physical-change panel, reader-driven revision and faith-symbol limit. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 adds energy/model limit; NE for unobserved change.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: No melting -> record honestly; use labeled prepared endpoint, not claim live result. No ice -> dry card model, physical observation deferred. No leaks near power; adult isolates spill and reports. No tasting, steam, fire, reactions, pressure containers, circuits or forced spiritual disclosure.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK

Learned: categories and limits. Catholic connection: Easter distinct from natural mechanisms. Ask: "What stayed the same?" No routine homework.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Curate: choose evidence for purpose. Caption: explanation beside work. Tradeoff: benefit/cost. Limit: untested claim. Common misconception: celebration proves growth for every pupil. docs.text: Adults release only after checklist approval; otherwise in-class rehearsal is the completed objective. docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Missing work -> labeled practice record, not invented personal achievement. Missing event approval -> keep rehearsal; no unplanned visitors. Unreadable caption -> fewer words/larger title. Unsafe crowding -> adult stops rotation/reports. No live circuits, robots, clinical models on people, refreshments, sharps or private spiritual records.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK

docs.title: Year Overview
docs.text: This is the Year B curriculum for Grades 5-6, alternating with Year A in either order. Contexts differ, but design, coding, service, data, and environmental topics recur. Equivalent official standards coverage and nonrepetition are not established.

docs.title: October 2026 review and teaching conditions
docs.text:
15 lesson documents; 33 planned 45-minute meetings (1,485 minutes), not 34 files or meetings. Week 32 is unrepresented/break; the five-meeting app unit includes nominal week 17, so schedule instructional meetings around any winter break rather than assuming five uninterrupted calendar weeks. Check liturgical and school-event dates locally.

See the Grades 5-6 review and 69-lesson audit. Biotechnology, Renewable Energy, Biomimicry, and App Development are fully rebuilt. Retained lessons have targeted fixes and individual local checks, not complete substitute readiness. Local CST codes are not official standards; official benchmarks are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

Entry checks: measurement, compare/count, model versus evidence, sequence and if/else. Grade 5 uses reference cards and worked examples; Grade 6 adds controls, uncertainty, means, and design/ethical tradeoffs. Neither year requires prior attendance in the other. Check advanced-unit prerequisites before use.

The complete rebuilt primary paths are indoor and device-free. Paper App Development teaches design/event reasoning, not actual programming/operation. Physical wind tests are models, not measured electrical efficiency. Real apps require approved school-managed access and a tested compatible setup. Loans, inventory, platform permissions, and any specialty equipment are unconfirmed.

Unsourced Scripture wording, saints' sayings/biographies, historical priority claims, current institutional roles, company practices, and scientific statistics in retained content are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching. Do not repeat unchecked quotations or promise medical/social/energy impact. No routine homework, family purchase requirement, patient-use prototypes, or public student media.

Review accommodations/contact; seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Copy source and fictional school-task cards below; teacher checks a sample three-word label at 50 cm. Provide each pupil journal/record; rotate listener/designer/reader rather than assign "expert" partners permanent technical control.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Innovation: changed method/product serving a purpose. Evidence: support. Criterion: checkable success. Constraint: real limit. Common misconception: a famous person's faith proves their science. If asked, "Did Mendel explain every trait?" No; this source describes particular pea experiments; inheritance can be more complex. Verified card, paraphrase of NHGRI Mendel's Peas, checked October 4, 2026: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian monk; he studied pea inheritance, carefully pollinating plants and comparing generations. Source does not establish "all traits blend" or a private quotation/belief. Fictional user: "I need a clear shared-tool label, not my name on a public display." Criterion: read RULER / TAPE / PAPER from 50 cm; constraint one card. Worked check: three correct words out of three, not assumed every-user access.

Each supplies fact/source/limit and measurable user criterion/constraint. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 identifies another needed source; NE for missing evidence, not universal leadership certification.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Life Science B / Biotechnology Basics Time Three meetings of 45 minutes; 135 total Domains C, S, A; technology applications are considered, not operated Big idea Models help us explain living systems but have limits; technology choices affect people. Student objective I can label cell parts, model complementary DNA bases, and explain a benefit, risk, and dignity safeguard. Why Science literacy helps people understand food and medicine without overstating evidence. Catholic connection Faith and reason, human dignity, and responsible service; verified sources. Models are not scientific proof of God or a substitute for moral reasoning. Local standards / evidence CST-S3: individual cell function and complementary-base explanation; CST-A1: labeled model with a stated limitation; CST-C1: distinguish evidence from a belief claim; CST-C2: benefit/risk/access analysis. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; four local codes only. Technology None. Optional prepared-slide microscope demonstration adds instrument observation only. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; letter matching and diagrams. No genetics vocabulary assumed; no previous rotation required. Prep / cleanup First packet 20 minutes; repeated 10 minutes; cleanup 4 minutes each meeting included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Make teams of at most three (⅘/7/9). Copy the teacher fact cards and case cards below. Read them; no external research or missing handouts needed.
  2. Cut each team's eight base cards: A,A,T,T,C,C,G,G. Students may instead write these letters on eight paper rectangles.
  3. Put dry nonfood materials in trays. Do not prepare fruit extraction, alcohol, candy models, body samples, or cultures. The original observation/model goals remain; extraction skill is deliberately not assessed.
  4. Optional microscope: adult uses sealed, commercially prepared plant/animal slides only; no cheek cells, blood, pond water, or broken-glass handling.

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Cell: basic unit of living things. Membrane: boundary regulating entry/exit. Nucleus: DNA-containing compartment in typical plant/animal cells. Organelle: specialized cell structure. DNA: molecule carrying inherited information. Biotechnology: using living systems or their parts to make useful products/processes.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND AND FACT CARDS
docs.text:
• Typical plant and animal cells both have membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes. Plant cells also have a cell wall; green photosynthetic plant cells have chloroplasts.
  • Mitochondria participate in releasing usable energy from nutrients; ribosomes build proteins. The nucleus is not a literal brain.
  • Bacteria do not have a membrane-bound nucleus. Mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus; most other human cells contain nuclear DNA. Some DNA is also in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
  • In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and C with G. The "ladder" model omits scale, chemistry, and many cellular processes. Many traits involve several genes and environment; DNA does not determine a person's worth.
  • Biotechnology includes fermentation and producing useful substances with cells. Classroom paper models are not experiments demonstrating a treatment's effectiveness.

Common misconception: every cell has DNA inside a nucleus. The examples above show why this absolute is false.

If asked, "Does a DNA code prove a designer scientifically?" Answer: Catholics believe in a Creator; scientific models describe observable molecular processes. The analogy to code is useful but is not a test proving a theological claim.

docs.title: Fictional case cards - all necessary information supplied
docs.text:
A - Food process: A fictional cooperative uses yeast to make bread rise. Its proposal reduces waste by better batch planning. Benefits: more usable food; risks: contamination and allergic ingredients; safeguards: qualified food-safety supervision and clear ingredient labels. We do not prepare/taste food.

B - Medicine process: A fictional laboratory uses engineered microbes to produce a useful protein. Potential benefit: more treatment supply. Questions: safety testing, price, access, and waste containment. This card does not establish approval or effectiveness of any medicine.

C - Crop proposal: A fictional drought-tolerance crop might use less irrigation. The claimed saving is a hypothesis, not measured fact. Ask for comparable field data and effects on local farmers/ecosystems. Do not infer that every genetic modification is beneficial or harmful.

Teacher key: several reasoned decisions are defensible. Require a benefit, a risk/unknown, affected people, and a safeguard; do not grade agreement with a predetermined commercial policy. Specific Church positions on embryo, cloning, or stem-cell cases are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching; those cases are outside this bounded lesson.

docs.title: Meeting 1 - cell models
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce wonder and dignity without ranking bodies by health/ability.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Read fact cards; model membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes on board.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student draws a plant or animal cell and labels the five shared parts; plant model adds wall and, for a green leaf cell, chloroplasts.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Teams compare models; check labels against fact cards, revise one error or document an accurate comparison.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Each explains two functions and one model limit to a partner; optional teacher prepared-slide demonstration uses this time instead, not extra time.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: explain membrane/nucleus distinction and why a nucleus is not a brain.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Clean up, retain drawings.

docs.title: Meeting 2 - DNA matching model
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Review cell exceptions and distinguish observation/model/belief.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Demonstrate A-T and C-G complementary pairing; write sequence ATCG.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams build four rungs from eight cards, label backbone rails, then twist paper model gently. Rotating student explains each pair.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Each student independently completes complements: ATCG -> TAGC; CCTA -> GGAT. Check and explain one correction.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Discuss what model omits and why genes plus environment are more complex than a one-letter personality code.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: one valid base pair, a cell exception, and a model limitation.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Store cards and models.

docs.title: Meeting 3 - biotechnology and ethical reasoning
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Explain technology decisions need both evidence and ethical consideration.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Adult models case A: benefit, risk, affected people, safeguard.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams examine B or C using only supplied facts; list unknowns, not invented medical claims.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Each student writes/dictates a four-part recommendation. Grade 5 uses sentence frames; Grade 6 explains a tradeoff or missing evidence.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Neighboring-team exchange; revise one safeguard to better respect access or dignity.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: distinguish one scientific claim from one ethical judgment and identify information needed before implementation.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Collect individual evidence and clean up.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: Which label describes a function rather than a literal city part? What breaks the "every cell has a nucleus" claim? Which facts support your recommendation? Who might be excluded if price is ignored? What still requires a qualified expert?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student labels five cell parts, correctly gives at least 7 of 8 complementary letters, states one model limitation, and makes a recommendation containing benefit, risk/unknown, affected people, and safeguard. Grade 6 adds a specific evidence need and tradeoff. A pretty model or group consensus alone is insufficient.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: No colored paper: pencil symbols suffice. Letters confuse: keep reference A-T/C-G visible. Model becomes literal: revisit limitations before continuing. Ethical debate becomes personal: use fictional cooperative/lab, not classmates' diagnoses or family decisions.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Dry paper only; no unknown chemicals, alcohol, tasting, toothpicks, tissue sampling, live cultures, or DNA collection. Adult alone handles optional sealed slides/microscope. No medical advice or questions about students' genetic/health information.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: five-part diagram template, paired letters, oral reasoning. Grade 5 challenge: compare plant and animal models. Grade 6: same base model with exceptions; challenge explain why a multi-factor trait cannot be inferred from our four-rung model. Use high-contrast symbols and a scribe; preserve the same conceptual evidence.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: The complete primary lesson is indoors, device-free, and independent of seasons. No microscope changes the objective: modeling, not instrument observation.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: Count scissors, cap markers, return cards, recycle unused scraps, retain labeled models and individual ethics exits.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Explored: cells, DNA models, and biotechnology choices. Did: labeled cells, paired bases, and evaluated fictional proposals. Learned: models have limits and benefits need evidence. Catholic connection: dignity and honest reasoning. Ask: "What did your DNA model leave out?" No routine homework or home extraction.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Energy B / Renewable Energy Lab Time Three meetings of 45 minutes; 135 total Domains C, S, E, M Big idea Renewable sources involve tradeoffs; a model's performance is not electrical efficiency. Student objective I can compare sources, test a rotor modification fairly, and defend a resource-aware design choice. Why Communities make energy choices under cost, land, reliability, and environmental constraints. Catholic connection Stewardship considers neighbors and future generations; Laudato Si' source. No one energy policy is inferred from a pinwheel. Local standards / evidence CST-S2: individual variables/control statement; CST-E2: before/after model tests; CST-M2: each student's table/graph; CST-C3: individual stewardship tradeoff. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; four local program codes. Technology Recommended: primary hand-fanned rotor path uses no electrical device; guarded tabletop fan optional for more repeatable tests. This models wind-to-motion, not electricity generation. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; count rotations, keep time, compare repeated measurements. No circuit assembly or energy-efficiency calculations required. Prep / cleanup First kit 25 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; cleanup 4 minutes/meeting included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Make ⅘/7/9 teams of at most three. Adult inspects commercial classroom pinwheels: securely enclosed axle ends, no exposed sharp pins or detachable small tips.
  2. Mark one rotor blade so a return to the same position counts one full rotation. Each team uses the same rotor before and after modification.
  3. Make one paper hand fan/team (folded cardstock). Mark 30 cm distance between fan and rotor; use seated work and a predictable fanning pace, acknowledging imperfect airflow control.
  4. Optional adult-operated guarded fan: stable stand, 75 cm rotor distance, low setting, no extension cords through walkways. Never insert materials into its guard.
  5. Copy source cards below. Prepare a fictional community brief: "Supply useful energy year-round while considering cost, neighbors, habitats, and winter conditions." No outside research/homework.

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text:
Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25 Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Data/graph sheet 1/student/unit 10 15 20 25 Safe enclosed-axle pinwheel 1/team, reusable 4 5 7 9 Cardstock fan; source-card sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Thin paper, A4/letter 1/team for four 2 x 4 cm tabs and design sketch 4 5 7 9 Ruler; blunt scissors; marker 1 each/team, reusable 4 5 7 9 Tape 0.25 m/team/unit 1 m 1.25 m 1.75 m 2.25 m Timer 1/teacher; class runs synchronized trials 1 1 1 1 Guarded tabletop fan, optional 1/class, adult-controlled 1 1 1 1

No heat lamps, water turbines near electricity, unprotected wiring, or bare LEDs. Optional solar electricity demonstration requires a separate adult-reviewed manufacturer kit and specified supply/load; it is not part of this timed lesson or required purchases.

docs.title: VOCABULARY AND SOURCE CARDS
docs.text:
Energy: capacity to cause change/do work; units include joules and kilowatt-hours. Power: rate of energy transfer; watts. Renewable: replenished on human-use timescales. Rotor: rotating blade assembly. Performance: measured result of a test. Tradeoff: gain in one criterion with a cost in another.

Source Model fact card Tradeoff to consider Solar Photovoltaic panels transform light into electricity; output depends on conditions. Darkness/clouds, land/materials, storage or other supply Wind Moving air turns a rotor; a generator can transform motion into electricity. Variable wind, siting/habitat, maintenance Hydro Moving water drives turbines and generators. Ecosystems, available flow, effects of dams Fossil fuels Chemical energy is transferred through combustion. Finite fuels, emissions, transport Nuclear Nuclear reactions release energy; uranium fuel is generally classified nonrenewable. Waste, construction, fuel and safety systems

These basic descriptions are models, not site-specific feasibility evidence. Renewable does not mean impact-free. Nuclear fuel did not form by the same process as fossil fuels.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
Our fan input ultimately uses muscular energy (or purchased electricity for the optional fan), not a demonstrated renewable electricity source. Counting turns per ten seconds compares rotor response under specified conditions. It does not measure joules, watts, voltage, or efficiency; efficiency would require comparable energy input/output measurements.

Common misconception: fastest rotor is always the best generator. Useful output, loads, durability, and conditions also matter.

If asked, "Did we make free electricity?" Answer: No. We observed wind-to-motion transfer in a model; no generator or energy meter is used.

docs.title: Meeting 1 - sources and test planning
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Read stewardship/community brief; ask who an energy decision affects.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Sort the five source cards; distinguish energy from power and renewable from impact-free.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams make a comparison chart; each student chooses two sources and a different tradeoff for each.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Demonstrate count of full rotor turns in 10 seconds. Plan same rotor, fan distance, operator/pace, interval, and room location.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Each writes change variable (tabs), measured response (turns/10 s), and two controls; practice counting.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: one energy/power distinction and one source tradeoff.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Store kits.

docs.title: Meeting 2 - compare and redesign
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Review controls and honest unsuccessful tests.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Measure 30 cm fan distance and run one unrecorded practice to coordinate counters.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Run three baseline trials, 10 seconds each; record every count. Fanner remains the same for comparison; swap roles only after that comparison block.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Attach four equal 2 x 4 cm paper tabs with matched tape pieces, clear of axle. Run three modified trials under same conditions; adult checks secure tabs.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Each graphs or compares baseline/modified counts; retain zero turns. Identify airflow inconsistency as a limitation.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual conclusion cites two counts and one uncertainty; no "percent efficiency" claims.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Remove tabs and inventory kits.

docs.title: Meeting 3 - communicate a design recommendation
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Revisit community brief; rotor evidence alone cannot choose a town's energy supply.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Explain a two-criterion decision table: reliability and effects on people/resources; list information still needed.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams sketch a revised rotor or a source combination; clearly separate tested result from proposed untested features.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Neighboring-team exchanges: explain data, ask one tradeoff question, revise recommendation. Nine teams use paired exchanges, not long public talks.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Each student annotates recommendation with evidence, limitation, and one fairness/stewardship concern.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: why rotor turns are not electrical efficiency and one needed real-world measurement.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Clean up, retain evidence.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: What stayed the same? Where did the model's input energy originate? Why can a zero count be valuable? What could winter change about a solar proposal? Whose needs would a cheap-but-unreliable choice ignore?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student names two controls, records six counts, compares using actual numbers, and explains one uncertainty and stewardship tradeoff. Grade 5 compares ranges/largest counts. Grade 6 calculates means and explains why a three-trial difference does not establish general superiority.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: Rotor sticks: stop, adult checks axle; do not force/bend sharp fasteners. Too fast to count: lower airflow or move hand fan farther and repeat both conditions. No rotor: use fictional counts baseline 8/9/7; tabs 6/8/7, labeled simulated; objective shifts to data interpretation, not building/testing a physical rotor. No electric fan: primary hand-fan route remains complete.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No exposed pins, projectiles, heat lamps, fire, mains wiring experiments, batteries, or water/electrical combinations. Adult operates optional guarded fan. Keep paper/tape out of guards, secure rotor/tabs, and stop when a part loosens. Student models are not installable generators.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: large marked blade, partner counter, table with trial numbers. Grade 5 challenge: compare count ranges. Grade 6: mean worked example and tradeoff matrix; challenge explain a better airflow control and why voltage alone would still not measure efficiency. Provide seated fans and alternative roles.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: All primary testing is indoors, independent of sun, snow, or temperature. Outdoor weather is discussed as a design constraint, not required exposure.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: Stop optional fan, count pinwheels, remove loose tabs, recycle scraps, store fan away from paper and retain individual tables.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Explored: energy sources and wind-model performance. Did: tested a rotor before/after and compared evidence. Learned: performance and efficiency are different. Catholic connection: wise care for resources and neighbors. Ask: "What tradeoff would your community need to investigate?" No routine homework or home electrical construction.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Design B / Biomimicry Design Time Three 45-minute meetings; 135 total Domains C, S, E, A; measurement supports the investigation Big idea A natural form can inspire a design, but performance must be tested in its new context. Student objective I can observe a form, sketch a purposeful model, compare two designs, and revise using evidence. Why Designers combine observation, art, science, and tests rather than copying an attractive shape blindly. Catholic connection Wonder and stewardship, without claiming nature is perfect or proving God through a prototype; verified sources. Unsupported attributed saint quotation removed. Local standards / evidence CST-S3: individual form/function and model-limit explanation; CST-E2: before/after tested redesign; CST-A1: observational sketch; CST-A2: purposeful pattern/form choice and critique; CST-C3: material tradeoff. Five local codes only. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; optional approved printed photographs add context, not required internet research. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; observe, draw, fold, count loads. No prior rotation, ratios, or biological research assumed. Prep / cleanup First kit 20 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; cleanup 4 minutes/meeting included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Make ⅘/7/9 teams of at most three. On board draw a broad flat leaf with veins and a cylindrical stem with outer boundary; identify drawings as illustrative, not measured plant specimens.
  2. Provide an optional approved leaf/stem photo if available; otherwise use the illustrative drawings and state that students are interpreting a supplied model rather than observing a real specimen.
  3. Prepare two strips of equal paper 8 x 20 cm/team and two stable supports 10 cm apart, inside a catching tray. Adult prepares ten sealed 10 g load packets/class for serial tests.
  4. Brief: "Design a small paper bridge for a fictional garden model. Span 10 cm, use one strip, hold a centrally placed paper platform, and minimize new material." No claim of real habitat intervention.

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text: Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25 Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Sketch/exit sheets 2/student/unit 20 30 40 50 Paper strips 8 x 20 cm 2/team/unit, initial plus revision 8 10 14 18 Matching low supports 2/team 8 10 14 18 Catching tray; ruler; marker; blunt scissors 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Paper central platform, 3 x 3 cm 1/team 4 5 7 9 Tape 0.25 m/team/unit 1 m 1.25 m 1.75 m 2.25 m Sealed 10 g packets 10/class, adult supervised serial tests 10 10 10 10 Timer; board form drawings 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Biomimicry: design inspired by living systems. Form: shape/arrangement. Function: what a part does. Model: simplified representation. Criterion: test for success. Revision: evidence-based change. Tradeoff: improvement with a cost elsewhere.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
Different plant forms perform different functions; no adaptation is a perfect universal design. Our folded/cylindrical paper shapes are analogies, not accurate biological structures. Geometry affects a paper strip's resistance to bending. Fair comparisons keep paper size/material, span, load placement, and loading sequence constant.

Common misconception: looking like a leaf makes a bridge stronger. Similar appearance is not performance evidence.

If asked, "Did plants invent bridges?" Answer: No. Designers interpret living forms to generate ideas, then test a new construction with different materials and purposes.

Retain the original unit's optional research topics: burr-inspired hook-and-loop fasteners, kingfisher-inspired train forms, gecko-inspired adhesion, lotus-inspired surfaces, and animal thermal/water management. Their specific inventor stories, commercial claims, and quotations are VERIFICATION REQUIRED from reliable sources before extension use; no invented source cards or mandatory research homework.

docs.title: Meeting 1 - observe and design
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce wonder, stewardship, and the fictional garden-model brief.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Model close observation: boundary, repeated veins/ridges, proportion; distinguish observation from claimed function.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student sketches the supplied form with three feature labels and one unanswered question; note drawing/model versus real specimen.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Teams propose two paper forms: flat, pleated/ridged, or rolled tube. Select one using span/material criteria; sketch before building.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Construct first paper bridge; each student explains the feature being translated and where analogy breaks.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: form/function inference and one model limitation.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Store dry models and clean up.

docs.title: Meeting 2 - test and redesign
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Review fair comparison and safety cap.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Adult demonstrates central platform and 10 g increments, maximum 100 g, stopping at instability.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Serial adult tests for all teams; waiting teams trace force paths and predict outcomes. Record last safe load and any instability without deliberate destruction.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Use second equal strip to change form/fold only; sketch before/after. Hold span, paper, platform, and loading sequence constant.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Adult retests nine teams at most, about 40 seconds/team; no speeches during load tests.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Each student cites original/revised loads and states whether evidence supports improvement or is inconclusive.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Return weights/supports and clean up.

docs.title: Meeting 3 - purposeful visual communication
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Distinguish a functional form from decoration and unsupported "best design" claims.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Demonstrate a visual panel: observed form -> translated feature -> tested result -> limitation.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student prepares a labeled panel with deliberate layout, not artistic-talent scoring.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Neighboring teams interpret panels without coaching; record which labels/sequence were clear.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Each student revises one visual choice or justifies a tested clear choice; add resource tradeoff.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit explains design, evidence, limitation, and material stewardship.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): File panels, recycle scraps, tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: What did you observe versus infer? What property did the model actually test? How did the same paper behave in another form? Which visual label helped your reader? What tradeoff came with an extra fold?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student labels three observed/model features, states an analogy limitation, compares two safe demonstrated loads, and revises a purposeful visual panel using reader feedback. Grade 5 uses count/mass comparisons. Grade 6 defends control variables and why a 100 g capped result cannot establish ultimate breaking strength or general biological superiority.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: Paper immediately bends: record zero safe added load and revise form. Both reach cap: neither is proven stronger; report equal demonstrated capacity under this test. No packets: use identical lightweight paper squares and report counts, not invented grams. No photos: label interpretation of teacher model, not specimen observation.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Adult alone loads; low supports, tray, 100 g cap, no body-weight tests, sharp fasteners, field collection, live animal handling, food specimens, or outdoor exposure. Student garden bridges are tabletop models, not real infrastructure or habitat installations.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: sketch frame and precreased paper, oral explanation. Challenge: compare flat/ridged forms. Grade 6: same core with control checklist; challenge propose a durability criterion not tested here. Scribe, large symbols, and alternate builder/observer roles preserve assessment.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Supplied forms and paper tests run indoors in any season. No field walk or device required.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: Adult counts ten packets, collect supports/trays/scissors, flatten recyclable drafts, retain before/after sketches and visual revisions.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Explored: nature-inspired forms and tested design. Did: sketched, compared paper bridges, and revised visual explanations. Learned: resemblance is not proof of performance. Catholic connection: wonder and stewardship. Ask: "What did your model test, and what could it not prove?" No routine homework; optional conversation only.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / B / Data Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes Objective / why / big idea I can graph five fictional counts totaling 20 and interpret a comparison without measuring anyone's faith. Graphs describe defined categories, not human worth. Domains / Catholic connection M, T, C; gratitude may be private/voluntary; dignity means no spiritual ranking. Local standards CST-M2: graph/comparison; CST-T3: private-data boundary; CST-C2: opt-out. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement None; graph paper primary; optional approved spreadsheet only if already working. Difficulty / entry Introductory; teach axes/scale; percentages scaffolded for Grade 6. Prep / cleanup Light: first 10 min, repeat 5 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Category Data.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations. Seat tool teams ⅘/7/9. Copy invented dataset: nature 6, helpful actions 5, learning 4, creative play 3, quiet time 2. Exactly one category per fictional response; these are not school/class beliefs. Do not execute any personal gratitude/faith survey. Draw blank axes 0-6, one square = one response, horizontal categories; pilot five bars.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Graph paper; paper exit; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Ruler; marker; dataset sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper consumable; tools reusable, no account/device required.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Category: group defined for counting. Frequency: count. Axis: graph reference line. Provenance: where data came from. Common misconception: graph counts generosity/grace. If asked, "May I share my thanks?" Privately/voluntarily, but not this dataset. Key: 6+5+4+3+2 = 20; nature minus quiet = 4; nature 6/20 = 30%, then 25/20/15/10%, sum 100%. No pie chart required; five bars enable comparison.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "What can these fictional counts tell us?" Brief thanksgiving reflection without disclosure.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model axes/one-unit scale, total and honest "fictional" title.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each makes all five bars, labels axes/count units and total; partners check heights without doing work for them.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Compare greatest/least/difference; diagnose deliberately missing category in teacher graph and fix. Grade 6 uses percentage scaffold.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual graph, total 20, difference 4, private-data exclusion and respectful opt-out explanation.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Cap/count tools, save graphs, reuse paper backs and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Where did data come from? Are categories overlapping? Can a bar show grace?" Each has five correct bars/labels/total, numerical comparison and privacy/ choice reason. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains another representation limit; NE if missing, not handwriting/art grade.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Total wrong -> sum original counts; retain corrected work. Graph scale changed midway -> redraw consistent zero-based scale. No graph paper -> ruled axes. No personal survey, private names/prayers, health promise, public uploading or spiritual ranking. Stop/report accidental disclosure.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: labeled axes, one-square units, oral/scribed interpretation. Grade 6/challenge: verify percentages total 100 and explain sampling limits. Indoor paper path is complete without devices.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Keep individual graphs, note needed reteaching; count tools. Explored: category data. Did: graphed an invented dataset. Learned: honest interpretation/privacy. Catholic connection: voluntary gratitude and dignity. Ask: "What can your graph not tell us?" No routine homework or home spiritual tracker.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / B / Service Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes Objective / why / big idea I can define a user criterion and design/test a clear choice-based activity card. Gifts should meet stated needs, not presumed disability or poverty. Domains / Catholic connection C, E, A; service respects dignity and recipient choice; no unsourced Vincent biography needed. Local standards CST-C2: choice/access; CST-E1: criterion; CST-A2: purposeful visual design. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement None; dry paper card primary. Difficulty / entry Introductory; show icon/text pairing and spacing. Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Activity Cards.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review accommodations/contact; seat ⅘/7/9 tool teams. Supply fictional brief: "A reading-table visitor wants a simple activity, may choose drawing or wordplay, and may decline. No name/prayer/health data needed." Each pupil creates one two-choice card: DRAW a favorite imaginary place / MAKE three words from STREAM / PASS is welcome. Adult recipient organization approval would be needed before distribution; classroom peer test is not real recipient validation. Criterion: peer locates both choices and PASS at 50 cm unaided.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Cardstock; paper evidence; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Ruler; marker set; brief sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Cardstock/paper consumable; tools reusable; no bought gifts/electronics.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Criterion: checkable requirement. Choice: user decision. Hierarchy: visual importance/order. Consent: freely given permission. Common misconception: a gift must be accepted to count as service. If asked, "Can we make a medical aid?" No; this is an activity communication card, not a patient-use/food-contact/assistive/safety device. Worked wordplay examples: TEAM, STAR, RAM use available letters once per word. Three labels should be distinct; two choices plus PASS = three options.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "What did the visitor actually request?" Introduce dignity/choice.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model two-choice layout, high contrast and 50 cm test.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each sketches two layouts, chooses one and makes card with original icons, clear instructions and PASS.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Partners locate three options without coaching; record found/not yet, revise spacing/wording, repeat. Do not infer emotional benefit.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Each explains criterion/constraint (one card), visual purpose/revision and recipient approval/decline safeguard.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save cards/tests, cap/count tools, sort scrap and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Can someone choose neither? What directs the eye? What did your test show?" Each has three-option test, purposefully revised layout and criterion/dignity decision. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 defends layout tradeoff; NE for untested work.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: Too much text -> shorten while keeping choice/PASS. No cardstock -> paper same count. No approved partner -> store classroom prototypes; never claim delivery. No clinical/powered/food-contact items, private surveys, identifiable media, sharp tools or mandatory donations. Stop/report unsafe conditions.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Grade 5/support: large words, icon outlines, dictation and pre-folded card. Grade 6/challenge: compare two layouts for access and explain untested recipient needs. Indoor desk plan; no off-site service required.

docs.title: CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Store prototypes pending adult approval, keep individual tests, count tools. Explored: service gift design. Did: tested a two-choice card. Learned: clear options/consent. Catholic connection: dignity in service. Ask: "How could someone decline?" Optional conversation; no routine homework.

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Reference Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / B / Communication Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes Objective / why / big idea I can design a readable four-panel Advent resource and justify its time/privacy choices. Technology should serve purpose, not demand attention/data. Domains / Catholic connection T, A, C; Advent prepares for Christ; responsible time/resources and voluntary reflection. Four activity panels are not official weekly theme assignments. Local standards CST-T3: intentional use/privacy; CST-A2: layout; CST-C3: time/material reason. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Requirement Optional; paper primary preserves communication/ethics; approved slides may produce an actual digital version. Difficulty / entry Introductory; teach visual hierarchy and equal panels. Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; device setup extra if chosen; cleanup 4 min.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Review contact/accommodations. Religion teacher confirms local seasonal timing; core content below needs no quotation, song or stock image. Seat tool teams ⅘/7/9. Copy four panels: Pause (quiet reflection may stay private), Notice (observe a useful classroom tool), Share (offer a turn), Care (reuse paper). Each is an optional classroom invitation, not fasting requirement or faith score. Pilot fold into four equal panels. Optional IT-pretested school slides: four slides, title/text/original drawing only, save school-only; no personal accounts.

Item Allocation 10 15 20 25 Paper panel sheet; evidence sheet; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Ruler; marker set; content sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9 Computer with approved slide editor, optional 1/team 4 5 7 9 Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

Paper consumable; tools reusable; software is access, not material.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Intentional use: use for a chosen purpose. Hierarchy: visual priority. Privacy: control of personal information. Stewardship: responsible care. Common misconception: more notifications mean more spiritual growth. If asked, "Are these official weekly Advent themes?" No; devotional resource choices, not universal liturgical assignments. Four two-minute invitations = 8 minutes, not a collected personal screen-time survey.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "Could a tool support reflection without collecting it?"
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model four panels/title/body contrast and eight-minute example.
  3. 11-25 (14 min): Each makes four-panel layout, original image and one brief invitation/panel; approved digital teams actually create/test slides if chosen.
  4. 25-35 (10 min): Peer finds Pause/Share without coaching, reads one instruction; revise visual order/text, retest and record.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual layout purpose, privacy exclusion and time/resource tradeoff; name actual paper/digital route.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save school-only if digital, cap/count tools, save panels and tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "What does the user need first? Why no personal journal input?" Each supplies four coherent panels, reader-backed visual revision and privacy/ time rationale. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 compares tool tradeoff; NE for missing; paper never called digital production.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY
docs.text: No devices -> paper route unchanged objective. Too much text -> one action per panel. Unapproved content -> use supplied invitations, no fabricated quote. No private prayers, personal usage tracking, compulsory fast, public posts, unlicensed music/images or flashing effects. Stop/report unsafe data use.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Make teams of at most three (⅘/7/9), rotating designer/operator/tester. Prepare one screen template/team from the component list below.
  2. Copy reference events and tests below. No downloaded templates or unspecified resource cards are needed.
  3. If devices are chosen, teacher/IT verifies current platform requirements and age/privacy approval, individual school-managed access, project saving, and Companion/emulator connection. Never share one password among children or require a personal Google account.

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Interface: what the user sees/acts on. Event: action triggering instructions. Condition: test with true/false outcomes. State: current values/display. Prototype: model to learn from. Data minimization: collect only what is genuinely needed.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
A paper operator can execute events by moving labels; a real computer executes programmed blocks. Both can expose unclear design, but only a real-app run supplies programming/operation evidence. Test expected versus actual output; users should not need the creator to explain every control.

Common misconception: attractive screens are functioning apps.

If asked, "Can we publish this?" Answer: Not in this unit. School approval, privacy review, accessibility, and tested behavior must precede any publication.

docs.title: Complete reference project - classroom kit help
docs.text:
Fictional user: a student locating a classroom supply, without entering names.

Designer components: TitleLabel ("Kit helper"), ChoiceBox (text input; prompt "Type ruler or tape"), FindButton ("Find"), ClearButton ("Clear"), ResultLabel (initially "Choose a supply"). Arrange top-to-bottom with large labels; do not communicate through color alone.

Reference Blocks/paper events:

When FindButton.Click:
  if ChoiceBox.Text = "ruler":
    set ResultLabel.Text to "Rulers: tray A"
  else if ChoiceBox.Text = "tape":
    set ResultLabel.Text to "Tape: tray B"
  else:
    set ResultLabel.Text to "Type ruler or tape"

When ClearButton.Click:
  set ChoiceBox.Text to ""
  set ResultLabel.Text to "Choose a supply"

Input is case-sensitive in this starter: Ruler takes the fallback branch. Students may improve clear instructions or deliberately add case-handling after core tests. Do not silently claim the starter handles all spellings.

Test Event / input Expected result 1 Find / ruler Rulers: tray A 2 Find / tape Tape: tray B 3 Find / empty Type ruler or tape 4 Find / crayon Type ruler or tape 5 Clear after any input Empty ChoiceBox; Choose a supply 6 Find / Ruler Type ruler or tape in starter

Teacher key: no data is retained or transmitted by this design. Persistent storage is not needed. Optional future TinyDB work needs a separate verified example; the former TinyDB1.Tag property example is removed.

docs.title: Meeting 1 - events and first prototype
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce fictional user and dignity/privacy purpose.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Demonstrate components and Find/ruler event on board or pretested device.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student sketches a screen, labels all five components, and predicts Find/tape output.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Teams create the paper screen or real Designer layout. Device users create a new school-managed project and rename components to match the reference.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Trace one Find event, rotating operator; discuss what is model versus actual app.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit names trigger, condition, output.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Save/store projects, tidy.

docs.title: Meeting 2 - user-centered visual design
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Review each student's event explanation.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Criteria: locate Find/Clear without coaching; read labels at comfortable seated distance; no private input.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student suggests two layouts and justifies a visual hierarchy (title, action, output).
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Teams select/revise layout; keep one screen and reference functionality.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Neighboring-team user test: point to Find/Clear; record confusion and one proposed revision.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit explains an accessible label and why student names are unnecessary.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Save/store and clean up.

docs.title: Meeting 3 - implement and trace conditions
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Read reference events and identify three branches.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Teacher models nested if/else blocks or paper decision cards; demonstrate empty input.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams implement exactly the reference; each member handles one branch. In paper route operator changes ResultLabel according to written events.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Execute tests 1-4; record expected/actual separately and rotate operator.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Correct a mistaken branch and rerun affected test. Preserve failed result.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Each independently traces crayon input and proposes a correction to an intentionally reversed ruler/tape result.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Save/store; clean up.

docs.title: Meeting 4 - full testing and revision
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce repeatable user testing, not popularity voting.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Model Clear reset and case-sensitive test 6; explain limits.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams run all six tests; each student records at least two tests personally.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Another team tries without explanation; record label confusion and test result.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Revise one visual label or branch and rerun the affected test, with expected behavior stated first.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit gives before/after evidence and an honest remaining limit.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Save/store; clean up.

docs.title: Meeting 5 - demonstrate and assess
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Review what may honestly be called programmed/operated versus simulated.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Prepare one screen plus raw test table; no new features.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Pair adjacent teams; each explains purpose, event trace, and design revision. Nine teams use an extra three-team group, with each member getting a brief turn.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Teacher reviews individual evidence while teams demonstrate Find/invalid/Clear to peers. All students execute a trace; device operators are recorded separately.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Each student completes the final three-input trace (ruler, empty, Clear) and one dignity/privacy explanation.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Summarize one capability and one limit; no unsupported "mastered app development" claim.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Export/save only through approved school storage; clean up.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: Which event starts this branch? What happens with an empty string? Can a user identify the result without color? Which data should this tool never request? What does a paper test fail to demonstrate?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student accurately traces three final cases, explains one corrected bug, cites a before/after user test, and identifies a privacy/access safeguard. Grade 5 uses the reference branches. Grade 6 defends an additional spelling/empty-input handling choice with two tests. Real programming credit additionally requires observed block editing and execution; paper route earns design/algorithm evidence only.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: Login/connection fails: switch to supplied paper screen and events; mark shifted objective. Empty output: inspect matching component names and clicked event. Button seems inert: check Blocks association, not decoration. Too much ambition: defer screens, storage, sensors, sound, and publication. No printer: copy five components and tests from board.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No personal accounts/password sharing, private health/prayer entries, GPS/camera/microphone/texting, public uploads, or app installation outside approved tools. Adult/IT controls device setup and charging. Review interfaces for respectful language; nobody's faith or ability is ranked by app scores.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: movable output cards and highlighted matching text, oral trace. Challenge: predict Ruler. Grade 6: three-branch trace scaffold; challenge normalize case or add another supply and test both valid/invalid inputs. Large print, keyboard access, and a scribe preserve reasoning goals.

docs.text: Paper screen, operator, event cards, and six tests are a complete five-meeting indoor route. This is not an actual mobile app.

docs.text: Revenue: money received. Cost: money spent. Surplus: revenue minus cost, not guaranteed impact. Capacity: work possible within limits.
