docs.title: Complete fictional enterprise packet
docs.text:
"A community reading table offers original bookmark cards. Some visitors pay, others choose a free card; no one records names or asks income. The organizer has $10 starting funds and 30 production minutes." Goal: clear pickup system and affordable offer, not a promised reduction in poverty. Canvas fields: user, offered value, payer, free-access policy, resources, cost, workflow, output check, untested outcome.

Planning allowances, not retailer quotes: paper $0.20/card, printing $0.30/card, setup $2.00/batch; price \(1.50 paid card. Scenario A produces 10 cards, 8 paid/2 free: variable cost 10x\)0.50=$5, total \(7; revenue 8x\)1.50=$12; surplus $5. Free cards cost resources despite no revenue. Scenario B same batch, 4 paid/6 free: revenue \(6, surplus -\)1. Five paid sales cover \(7 (5x\)1.50=$7.50), but demand is not guaranteed. Fictional production time 2 min/card: 10x2+5 setup = 25 min, leaving 5 min buffer. Twelve cards -> 29 min. These are assumptions to test, not observed school production rates.

Workflow test uses six order tokens in sequence: PAID BOOK, FREE ART, PAID ART, FREE BOOK, PAID BOOK, PASS. Paper stations: order -> choose -> pickup, with no identifiable records. Criterion: route 5 requests correctly plus PASS without confusion; peer locates free choice without asking permission. Record actual routing successes/time, not profit or social improvement.

docs.title: Meeting 1: purpose and business model
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "Who benefits, and who might be excluded?" Explain dignity.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Read brief/canvas; model payer versus beneficiary and no-name policy.
  3. 11-24 (13 min): Each drafts user/value/access choice; teams complete canvas, distinguish stated facts from guesses.
  4. 24-35 (11 min): Work Scenario A with calculator/check; compare starting funds and production limits.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual revenue $12/cost $7/surplus $5 and a fairness concern.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save dated logs/canvas and count tools.

docs.title: Meeting 2: capacity and prototype
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Recall assumptions versus observed evidence.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model Scenario B and 25-minute capacity calculation.
  3. 11-24 (13 min): Build three-station counter labels and four sample bookmark cards; each chooses visual feature serving reader, not extra costly materials.
  4. 24-35 (11 min): Run six-token workflow; rotate all pupils; record correct routes/PASS and actual elapsed time.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual budget comparison, capacity check and one observed confusion/limit.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save tokens/prototype and raw results, return tools.

docs.title: Meeting 3: revise and evidence-limited impact
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Identify one test issue.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Explain output (cards/routed requests) versus untested outcome.
  3. 11-24 (13 min): Revise labels/order; recalculate chosen fictional paid/free scenario; do not collect real customer data.
  4. 24-35 (11 min): Repeat six-token test unchanged otherwise; compare success/time, not fabricated benefit.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Each submits before/after recommendation, fair-access choice and required real-user evidence.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Save both versions, count kit, tidy.

docs.title: Meeting 4: pitch and tradeoff defense
docs.text:
1. 0-4 (4 min): Name what is modelled, not launched.
  2. 4-11 (7 min): Model 90-second pitch: user, offer, numbers, test, ethics, limit.
  3. 11-24 (13 min): Each prepares budget/result evidence and caption; teams rehearse.
  4. 24-35 (11 min): Paired exchanges, each pupil speaks 45-90 seconds and answers one evidence question; trio fits, no nine six-minute plenary talks.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual corrected budget, supported decision, tradeoff and next approval need.
  6. 41-45 (4 min): Reuse prototypes, return tools, save logs, recognize specific work.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: "Are free cards costless? Does routing prove social impact? What if only four people pay?" Each has correct A/B budgets, capacity sum, baseline/retest results and evidence-limited fair-access pitch. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 tests a changed assumption; NE if missing.

docs.title: Complete fictional brief, interface and key
docs.text: "A fictional clinic information kiosk user wants to find the general information desk, choose paper directions and leave without giving a name. The clinic user may decline the kiosk entirely." No real clinic layout or medical advice. Four screens: HOME ("Information only; no names; Directions / Paper / Exit"); DIRECTIONS ("Fictional desk: room A; Back / Exit"); PAPER ("Ask staff for a paper map; Back / Exit"); CLOSED ("You may ask staff directly; Home"). Paper events: Directions from HOME -> DIRECTIONS; Paper from HOME -> PAPER; Exit from any open screen -> CLOSED; Back from DIRECTIONS/PAPER -> HOME; Home from CLOSED -> HOME. Invalid event leaves screen unchanged with "Use a labeled control"; no hidden data. Criterion: locate Directions/Paper/Exit without coaching, complete six correct event transitions; constraints: four paper screens, no personal input, no medical content. Tests: HOME/Directions -> DIRECTIONS; Back -> HOME; Paper -> PAPER; Exit -> CLOSED; Home -> HOME; HOME/Back -> unchanged. Math: six transitions with one error = ⅚ correct, not a medical accuracy rate. Fictional resource comparison: 4 sheets at $0.10 = $0.40 versus 8 sheets $0.80; reuse same base, but fewer screens may need clearer navigation.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: kWh: unit of energy, not instantaneous power. Provenance: origin/ context of record. Mean: total divided by count. Confound: other factor affecting comparison. Common misconception: a lower second week proves a campaign worked. If asked, "Can we delete unusual values?" No; flag, verify against original, keep both versions and reason. A missing reading is not zero.

docs.title: Complete dataset and key
docs.text:
Invented classroom record, not school measurement. Fictional campaign occurs between weeks; occupancy/weather records unavailable.

Day Week A kWh Week B kWh Monday 12 11 Tuesday 14 13 Wednesday 13 12 Thursday 11 10 Friday 15 14

Totals 65/60 kWh; means 13/12 kWh; ranges both 4 kWh; difference 5 kWh. That is about 7.7% of 65 if explicitly taught, not necessary Grade 5 evidence. Working-copy intentional error: Tuesday A typed 41; raw says 14. Correction log records old 41/new 14/source/reason; never alter raw. Graph: grouped bars, weekdays horizontal, kWh 0-16 vertical, one-unit grid, two distinguishable patterns/labels, zero baseline. Hypothetical protocol: facilities staff records daily usage for matched occupied weekdays, method/unit/date/context; raw locked, working copy versioned. No claim of executed monitoring. Proposed action: reusable reminder label; criterion reader finds message, not guaranteed kWh reduction.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS
docs.text:
Check contact/accommodations; seat ⅘/7/9 tool teams. Draw supplied stage cards, not unknown specimens. Germination: living seed embryo -> root emerges -> shoot/leaves -> growing seedling, given suitable water/oxygen/temperature. Butterfly: egg -> larva/caterpillar -> pupa -> adult, living throughout normal development. Card sequence is generalized model, not live time-lapse. No growing requirement or claimed instant result within 45 minutes.

docs.title: VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text: Embryo: young organism in seed. Germination: beginning growth from seed. Metamorphosis: major developmental change. Symbol: meaning expressed through a representation. Common misconception: seed must die or caterpillar wholly dissolves. Both processes involve living organisms; tissues reorganize in metamorphosis. If asked, "Does every seed grow?" No; viability/conditions matter. Key: four ordered stages each; biological development is neither ice melting nor creation of new chemical substance alone; models omit time and internal detail.

  4. 25-35 (10 min): Partner reads sequence and asks one biology question; revise misleading "dead seed" or vague arrow, record old/new caption.
  5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual accurate explanations of both processes, model limit and scientific-versus-Easter-symbol statement.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Welcome and observation / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea S, A; a detail we notice is different from a question we want to investigate Student objective / why "I can show a detail and ask a question." Scientists begin by noticing and wondering. Catholic connection Wonder at creation and respectful listening; use the source guidance in the routines below. Local standards CST-S1: observed detail/question; CST-A3: picture/oral communication. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 minutes included

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Make 5/7/10/12 active pair/trio teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits at 10/15/20/25 pupils. Draw one large leaf with visible branching lines on each kit's half-sheet. Alternatively use an adult-inspected clean large leaf; pictures avoid allergies.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: large leaf drawing 5 8 10 13 Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: timer, roster, crayon and one demonstration drawing reused from a kit. No letter cards, slideshow, purchased journal or printing required.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text: Observe: notice a detail. Question: something we want to find out. Represent: show an idea with a picture, gesture or words. Misconception: a guess is a detail we saw. Point to the actual drawing. If asked "Why does a leaf have lines?" Say that living leaves have veins that transport water and other materials; our drawing is a model, not a live leaf.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Invite wonder and a short original prayer if customary. Say C-STREAM is a time to notice, make, test and care; acronym recall is not the target.
  2. 4-8: Model "I see a line" versus "I wonder what the line does." Point to the evidence. Draw the detail, not a perfect leaf.
  3. 8-17: Partners inspect, swap pointing roles and each draw/select a detail. Ask "What can you point to?" Begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child points to a genuine detail and asks/selects one question. Offer "What does this part do?" or "Are all leaves alike?" Record support.
  5. 21-25: Two children share; retain dated sheets; count drawings and crayons; clear tables. Thank partners for listening.

docs.title: Success, access and SAFETY
docs.text: Success: each child connects a picture/gesture to an actual detail and a question. Do not score enthusiasm, letters or drawing realism. Support: offer two details; scribe an oral question. Challenge: ask how a question could be checked. Large pictures only for mouthing/allergy concerns; no taste, close smelling or collecting. Fully indoors.

docs.title: If things go wrong and family copy
docs.text: No leaf/drawing: draw a plain leaf with three branching lines on the board. Child only guesses: ask where the claimed feature appears; keep the question. Early finish: compare a partner's representation. Follow the routines' cleanup. Family: We noticed a detail and asked a question. Ask, "What did you actually see, and what do you still wonder?" No routine homework or supplies required.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / title K / Movement and instructions / Exploring Movement with Sphero Time Two meetings, each 25 minutes, including cleanup Meaningful domains C, T, M Big idea A tool responds to input; an algorithm is an ordered set of steps. Student objective "I can predict a two-step path, try it, and fix one step." Why Clear directions and checking results help us use tools responsibly. Catholic connection Include every partner in making decisions; tools should benefit people, not exclude them. CCC 2405, teacher paraphrase. Local standards CST-C2, CST-T1, CST-T2, CST-M1; local program codes, never official benchmarks. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology requirement Optional: picture-grid pathway is primary; real Sphero driving extends tool input/output. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Beginner / Light: 10 minutes for paper kits; optional robot setup 20 minutes plus charging / 3 minutes inside each meeting

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Make 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 students: pairs, with a final trio for odd enrollment. Prepare ⅝/10/13 kits; the extra kit at 15/25 is a reserve. Assign chooser, mover, and checker; swap roles after each trial.
  2. Draw one 3-by-3 grid per pair, with 10 cm squares. Mark the lower-left square START and the upper-left square FINISH. Draw another target one square right of START. No printing is necessary.
  3. Make four large cards per pair: two upward arrows, one right arrow, one STOP hand. Here arrows mean one square up the page/right on the page, not a robot's facing direction.
  4. Draw a paper robot at least 8 cm wide per pair. Place kits at seated tables and write a roster with columns A (algorithm), I (input/output), H (real hardware drive), P (real programming).
  5. Optional hardware: use one school-approved, charged Sphero and one paired tablet. Before children arrive, open the installed Sphero Edu version, select the robot, enter Drive, aim/calibrate toward the far end, and test its lowest practical speed and stop control. Keep a 1 m clear demonstration lane and an adult beside it. If pairing or safe stopping fails, omit hardware. A substitute need not troubleshoot Bluetooth during class.

docs.title: Supplies and exact quantities
docs.text:
Supply / allocation 10 15 20 25 Per student: half-sheet observation paper; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Per pair/team: grid; large paper robot 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Per pair/team: four command cards 20 32 40 52 Class: large demonstration grid and robot 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each Teacher: roster, timer 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each

Optional class supplies, any enrollment: one robot, one tablet, one roll painter's tape. There is no class-set purchase or family donation requirement. Reuse grids/cards in meeting 2.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
• Input: what we give a tool; point to an arrow or control.
  • Output: what the tool does; move the paper robot.
  • Algorithm: steps in order; point left to right along cards.
  • Debug: find a mismatch, change a step, try again.

A paper model follows the stated grid rule because a person moves it. In Drive mode an adult steers continuously; this is operating hardware, not writing a program. Real robots can drift, lose connection, or respond to sensors; they do not necessarily execute a command exactly.

Misconception: "Robots know what I want." Explain that our model needs explicit steps; a machine depends on controls, software, sensors, and conditions.

If asked, "Can robots think?" "Some machines use complicated software to choose actions. This classroom robot responds to its controls. It is not a person."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Keep children seated outside the optional robot lane. No chasing, racing, throwing, body maze, beanbag toss, or robot on a table edge. Stop the robot before retrieving it. Adult handles charging and battery compartments; inspect for damage. Use large paper pieces, not coins or tiny tokens. Offer seated pointing instead of body movement. Never physically guide a child's hands without permission.

docs.title: Meeting 1: input and output (25 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Invite a brief prayer for including others. Show two arrow choices: "Which way will our robot move?"
  2. 3-7 (4 min): Model one arrow, one-square output, and STOP. Optional adult Drive demonstration replaces the last two minutes, not adds time. Name the difference between a card model and a real steering control.
  3. 7-16 (9 min): Pairs try UP then STOP and RIGHT then STOP from the same START. Swap roles every trial. Each child chooses and predicts one move before a partner executes it. Teacher begins individual I checks while circulating.
  4. 16-20 (4 min): Finish remaining I checks: child points to input and predicted/observed output. Accept pointing, speech, or drawing; do not repeat already documented checks.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Ask "What did we give it? What did it do? How did we include our partner?"
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Collect cards, park paper robots, return crayons; adult stops and stores optional hardware.

docs.title: Meeting 2: sequence and debugging (25 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Recall input/output; show START and FINISH two squares up.
  2. 3-6 (3 min): Model UP, RIGHT: it misses FINISH. Ask "Which step needs changing?" Change RIGHT to UP; reset and retest.
  3. 6-15 (9 min): Pairs build UP, UP, STOP. Mover follows cards only. Each child then tries the intentionally wrong UP, RIGHT path and changes one card. Third child receives a full chooser turn, not just checker duty. Teacher starts individual A/count checks now.
  4. 15-20 (5 min): Finish remaining individual checks while partners rehearse: each child orders two arrows, predicts the endpoint, and corrects one wrong card. Record A and count two moves aloud/on fingers; no 25-child serial exit line.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Share one correction and one fair-turn action.
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Reassemble four-card kits, collect grids and individual drawings, clear tables.

docs.title: Evidence and what success looks like
docs.text:
Record I and A separately as independent / prompted / not yet. Success is a correct prediction of two one-square moves and a correction that reaches the pictured target, plus identifying a tool input/output. Neat writing, knowing left/right on one's body, or driving speed are not assessed.

H may be recorded only for a child who actually controls the real robot and stops it safely; an adult demonstration is observation, not child operation. P stays not assessed in this unit. No-device success demonstrates algorithms and model input/output, not operating or programming real hardware.

docs.title: Questions, support, and troubleshooting
docs.text:
• "What happens if we change the order? Did the output match your prediction?"
  • Support: offer two pictured choices; cover unused squares; child points while adult moves the token. Avoid screen or motor demands.
  • Challenge: design a three-command route and explain one correction; no speed competition.
  • Wrong route: reset to the same START, read one card at a time, and fix only the first mismatch.
  • Confused arrows: hold the page in one fixed orientation and point to the destination square.
  • Robot drift/disconnection: adult stops, checks aim once, then returns to paper; do not report a paper success as hardware success.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: the seated grid is the full lesson in any weather. No outdoor or internet requirement.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text: We predicted and corrected picture instructions and practiced fair turns. Ask: "Show me two steps and one way to fix them." Real robot driving was optional and was recorded separately from algorithm learning. No homework or device purchase.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / title K / Observation / Wonder Walk Time 25 minutes, including transitions and cleanup Domains / big idea C, S, A / Observations tell what we notice; questions tell what we want to find out. Student objective / why "I can show two details I noticed and ask one question." Careful looking helps us study and care for creation. Catholic connection Leave living things undisturbed and reuse materials; stewardship is a responsibility, not permission to take everything. CCC 2402, paraphrase. Local standards CST-C3, CST-S1, CST-A1; local, not official. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty None / Beginner Prep / cleanup Light: 10 minutes / 3 minutes within lesson

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Default indoor plan: seat pairs at tables. Provide one clean fallen leaf and one smooth rock at least 5 cm across per pair. Use large teacher-drawn leaf/rock pictures if allergies, mouthing, or availability make specimens unsuitable. Say that a drawing is a representation, not a specimen.
  2. Fold a half-sheet into two observation boxes for each child; put crayons within reach. Draw an eye and a question mark on the board.
  3. With 10/15/20/25 students, make 5/7/10/12 teams (pairs/final trio) and prepare ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment. A third child receives their own paper and a turn with each object.
  4. Optional outdoor path: school policy permits it only with required adult coverage, accessible dry route, safe weather, and no icy surfaces. Choose two stops within a two-minute walk. If clothing/transit would exceed the four-minute allowance, use indoors. Check headcount at exit, each stop, and return; do not assume 25 children can be supervised outdoors by one adult.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Allocation 10 15 20 25 Per student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Per team: large leaf/picture; large rock/picture; tray 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Optional per team: magnifier 5 8 10 13 Teacher/class: eye/question drawings; roster; timer 1 set 1 set 1 set 1 set

Outdoor only: one rigid paper backing per child (10/15/20/25); no collection bags or camera needed. Teacher checks specimens and supplies handwashing access.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text:
Observe: notice with safe senses; point to eyes. Detail: a small part you notice, such as a vein or speckle. Question: something to investigate. Stewardship: careful use and care.

A detached leaf was part of a living plant; a rock was not. Do not classify living things by movement alone or demand a living/nonliving judgment about a detached leaf. Plants are alive although they do not walk. Observation can include accessible hearing, touch of approved items, or description; sight is not the only valid pathway.

Misconception: "My guess is something I saw." Distinguish "I see lines" from "I think water goes through them."

If asked, "Why does a leaf have lines?" "The lines include veins that carry water and other materials. We can see a pattern; our drawing alone does not prove what is inside."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No tasting, unknown plants, wild mushrooms, animal remains, feathers, nest disturbance, or smelling unknown materials closely. Adults inspect/clean specimens; pictures are equivalent observation targets when needed. No looking at the Sun through eyes or magnifiers. Keep magnifiers out of direct sun; wash hands after specimens. No collection or picking. Cancel outdoor work for cold, ice, storms, unsafe heat, or insufficient staffing.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Brief prayer for care of creation. Model "I notice a line" and "I wonder where it goes." Explain safe looking and gentle hands.
  2. 3-5 (2 min): Indoors: distribute trays and demonstrate passing. Outdoors: walk to first stop and count children.
  3. 5-11 (6 min): Look at first object/stop. Each child points to one detail, then draws it in box 1 or dictates while adult sketches. Ask "What do you actually notice?"
  4. 11-17 (6 min): Pass second object/observe second stop without moving away from the group. Add a second detail in box 2. Partner asks one question using "I wonder..." or chooses between teacher's two question pictures. Teacher begins recording individual detail/question evidence now.
  5. 17-19 (2 min): Indoors: return trays. Outdoors: return inside and count children. Keep drawings.
  6. 19-22 (3 min): Finish remaining individual checks during paired sharing: each child shows two details and a question. Do not repeat documented checks or require 25 serial speeches. Ask "How did we care for the things we studied?"
  7. 22-25 (3 min): Collect reusable materials, wash hands, save drawings. Teacher adds one question to the Wonder Wall later, not extra class time.

docs.title: Evidence and success
docs.text: On the roster record two observed details and one question for every child: independent / prompted / not yet. A child may point, dictate, sketch, or choose a picture; do not judge realistic drawing skill. Successful evidence is specific ("three lines," "bumpy edge"), not just "I liked it." One stewardship action is returning materials or leaving an organism untouched.

docs.title: Questions and contingencies
docs.text:
• "Which detail can you show me? Which idea would we need to test?"
  • Support: use large drawings, tactile approved leaf models, oral description, two pictured choices, or a seated observation partner.
  • Challenge: compare the two objects using a visible feature and ask a testable question.
  • No specimens/magnifiers: use large teacher drawings and naked-eye observation; report observations of the drawings honestly.
  • Too many questions: collect one per child orally; the adult may jot a key word rather than a full sentence.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: use the default table lesson unchanged at -10 F. A nearby window is optional, not a required outdoor view.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text: We drew or described two observed details, asked a question, and practiced leaving creation undisturbed. Ask: "What did you notice, and what do you still wonder?" A safe window observation is optional; nothing must be brought from home.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Structures / two meetings of 25 minutes each Domains / big idea C, E, M; the base and arrangement affect whether a structure stays standing Student objective / why "I can count blocks, test a low tower, change its base and test again." Evidence helps builders improve. Catholic connection Care for shared tools and others' work; skilled work can serve people. Local standards CST-C3: resource care; CST-E2: before/after test; CST-M1: count up to ten chosen blocks. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 10 minutes / 4 minutes in each meeting

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use 5/7/10/12 active pair/trio teams and ⅝/10/13 budgeted kits. Inspect blocks; test one low six-block model; draw a two-attempt picture record. KEVA is optional branding; ordinary large stable wooden blocks work.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: 20 large blocks 100 160 200 260 Kit: tray/mat 5 8 10 13 Student: sheet; crayon, per meeting 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: timer, roster and one shared measuring ruler. Demonstrate using a budgeted kit, then return it. Retain the first meeting's sheets at school.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text: Base: bottom supporting parts. Stable: stands without a hand holding it. Test: check against a criterion. Redesign: change and test again. Misconception: tallest means best. Criterion is ten seconds unaided, with the same six blocks, not maximum height. If asked why a tower falls: identify slipping, leaning or a changed support; do not promise widening always wins.

docs.title: Meeting 1: a fair starting test, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Discuss buildings serving people and caring for shared supplies.
  2. 4-8: Model six blocks on a low base. Teacher times ten seconds, hands away.
  3. 8-17: Partners build with six selected blocks, swap turns, count and test. Teacher gives a common start/stop signal; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child counts the chosen set, points to the base and reports standing/falling. Record actual results, including falls.
  5. 21-25: Draw/retain a first-attempt picture; count blocks back; clear trays.

docs.title: Meeting 2: change and retest, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve drawings, not unverifiable memories. Restate six blocks/ten seconds.
  2. 4-8: Demonstrate changing only base arrangement with the same blocks.
  3. 8-17: Each partner chooses a base change, rebuilds and observes the same timed test. Rotate the trio's builder turn; start individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child indicates the change, counts the set and compares two outcomes. Ask "What stayed the same? Did your change help in this test?"
  5. 21-25: Save dated evidence, return all 20 kit blocks, thank partners, clear.

docs.title: Success, support, challenge and SAFETY
docs.text: Record counting, observed result and tested change separately. Falling is evidence, not failure of a child. Support: a three-block model and prompted count, with reduced criterion recorded. Challenge: repeat the six-block test to check reliability, not height. Build seated below shoulder height; no throwing, walking gallery, shaking another model or standing on furniture.

docs.title: Troubleshooting, indoor alternative and family copy
docs.text: Missing first sheet: run a fresh first test, label it today, then compare. No blocks: groups <=3 may share kits using the routines; do not claim a paper picture is a tested tower. Repeated collapse: use flat blocks on a wider base. All work indoors. Family: We counted blocks and compared a ten-second test before and after a change. Ask, "What changed, and what did the test show?"

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Service design / three 25-minute meetings Domains / big idea C, E, A, M; a useful design must meet a user's stated need and a test Student objective / why "I can plan a tray, carry two empty cups, change a part and retest." Engineers use evidence to serve people. Catholic connection Listen to a requested need; respect people rather than assuming incapacity. Local standards CST-C2: need/inclusion; CST-E1: carrying criterion; CST-E2: test/redesign; CST-A1: plan; CST-M1: count two cups. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes first kit, 5 reset / 4 per meeting

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use 5/7/10/12 active teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits. On each desk mark a 30 cm path. Tell this complete fictional request: "Our classroom helper asks for a tray to move two empty cups from one mark to the other without either falling." Precut smooth cardboard and tape; pretest a flat tray at slow walking-hand speed.

Kit/student allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: two cups; two 20 cm cardboard squares 10 each 16 each 20 each 26 each Kit: ten craft sticks; ten 10 cm tape strips 50 each 80 each 100 each 130 each Kit: storage tray 5 8 10 13 Student: plan/evidence sheet; crayon, per meeting 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: ruler, timer, roster, pencil; adult-only scissors. Demonstrate with a budgeted kit. Store work by kit number; no family materials or purchased unit.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Need: a requested problem. Criterion: what the model must do. Plan: drawing before making. Redesign: a change informed by a test. A rim may retain cups but can use extra material; test rather than promise. Misconception: decoration proves a helper works. Ask about the same two cups and path. If asked about helping a real person, say this is a desk model only. No liquid, loaded glasses, high shelves, climbing, wearables, pets, infants, disability simulation or trial of an actual assistive device.

docs.title: Meeting 1: ask, plan and try, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Read the fictional request; each child names who asks and what they need.
  2. 4-8: Demonstrate two cups/path; draw a flat-tray plan and the pass condition.
  3. 8-17: Children draw a plan, count two cups and try moving them on a flat piece. Swap chooser/mover/checker roles; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child points to their plan and explains/indicates the criterion, not just appearance. Record whether both cups remained aboard.
  5. 21-25: Date drawings; store dry labeled kits; count and clear.

docs.title: Meeting 2: make and collect a first result, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve plans and re-read the request.
  2. 4-8: Model folding a low edge and attaching it with precut tape.
  3. 8-17: Build from the two cardboard pieces, at most ten sticks and ten strips. Each child handles an appropriate construction step and observes a slow test.
  4. 17-21: Record cups aboard, 0/½, and where a cup moved. Child shows a result on the plan; drawing/pointing is sufficient.
  5. 21-25: Retain the first-result sheets and dry models; reset trays.

docs.title: Meeting 3: evidence-led redesign, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve results. A missing result is collected freshly, not invented.
  2. 4-8: Model changing one edge, keeping the same cups/path and slow movement.
  3. 8-17: Partners propose one change, retest and swap roles. Count cups remaining and begin each child's evidence check.
  4. 17-21: Each child points to a changed part, compares two results and explains whether it met the requested need. Keep unsuccessful results too.
  5. 21-25: Save evidence, remove reusable sticks, sort dry scraps and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, troubleshooting and access
docs.text:
Check requested need, plan, two-cup count and tested change separately. Ask "What stayed the same? Which part changed first? Who requested this?" Support: adult-started folds, two choices, dictated explanation. Challenge: explain a material tradeoff without claiming real-device safety. Insufficient cardboard: fold stiff school cardstock to the same size and record the material used. No stored model: rebuild a simple first version and take a fresh result. All work is indoors; never turn a missing kit into an unsafe real-person challenge.

Family: We planned a desk model, moved two empty cups and retested one change. Ask, "What did your test show?" Models are not real assistive devices; no homework, donation or home testing.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Structures / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, E, M; a deck crosses a gap and supports hold it up Student objective / why "I can show supports, test a deck, change it and retest." Bridges provide access; models help us reason safely. Catholic connection Name someone a safe crossing could serve; inclusion is not a structural test. Local standards CST-C2: access need; CST-E1: gap/load criterion; CST-E2: retest; CST-M1: count supports/load. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and quantities
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use 5/7/10/12 active teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits. Place two equal-height large blocks 5 cm apart on each tray, with one 20-by-10 cm cardboard deck. Pretest one identical large wooden block as load; no tiny cars/coins required. The criterion is spanning the gap and holding this load for three seconds.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: two supports + one load block 15 24 30 39 Kit: two cardboard deck pieces 10 16 20 26 Kit: tray; ruler 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: timer/roster, demonstration from one kit. No school-owned specialty set assumed.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text: Support: holds up a deck. Deck: crossing surface. Gap: open space. Retest: repeat the same check after a change. Folding can change stiffness. Misconception: any short plank spans any gap. Use the supplied long deck, not a six-inch gap with a short plank. If asked about a real bridge, explain that our model cannot establish safety for people.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Draw two places across a stream; ask who needs access. State criterion.
  2. 4-8: Show supports/deck, count two supports and one load; place the load gently at the deck's center for three timed seconds, then remove it.
  3. 8-17: Partners test version 1, fold the second deck into a shallow channel and retest. Keep support gap, load and location the same. Swap roles; begin individual checks and record a fall honestly.
  4. 17-21: Each child indicates support/deck, counts the parts, and reports before/after results and a changed feature. Ask "What stayed the same?"
  5. 21-25: Save dated sketches, return/count blocks and rulers, flatten reusable cardboard, clear trays. No walking or sequential whole-class load queue.

docs.title: Success, SAFETY, support and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Success is identifying parts/criterion and comparing two actual tests, not a pretty or successful bridge alone. Desk models only; no person/pet weight, throwing, tall supports or fingers under the load. Adult-inspected smooth blocks. Support: prestarted folds, adult placement directed by the child. Challenge: repeat to check whether the result agrees. Missing blocks: two equal-height closed books and one identical large classroom load per kit, pretested by the teacher; record the substitute material. No safe load: defer load evidence, teach parts only and report the change. Fully indoors in any weather.

Family: We counted supports and compared two same-load bridge tests. Ask, "What changed and what stayed the same?" No homework or model use by people.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Algorithms / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, T, A; ordered instructions can deliver a respectful message Objective / why "I can explain how people choose steps, predict two moves and fix a wrong step." Clear instructions help us communicate. Catholic connection Gratitude and care for a recipient; no forced family disclosure or presumed need. Local standards CST-C2: respectful recipient; CST-T2: prediction/correction; CST-A3: message. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional ScratchJr extension, paper primary / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits for 10/15/20/25 pupils; active teams 5/7/10/12. Draw a 3-by-3 grid, START lower-left and recipient one square right and one up. Draw four large cards: RIGHT, UP, DOWN, STOP. Arrows refer to the page. Use an 8 cm paper token with a child's drawn gratitude image.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: grid; token 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Kit: four large cards 20 32 40 52 Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: timer/roster; model with one budgeted kit. No word cards, projector or account.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Algorithm: steps in order. Predict: say where steps will end. Debug: find and correct an error. Message: idea for another person. Misconception: a motion-lines drawing is executable code. A person follows our paper rules; that is an algorithm model, not software execution. If asked about computers, explain that real programs must be run on a device. Desk grids, large parts, no body maze, small tokens or public student uploads.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Choose a school helper or trusted recipient; draw/describe a thankful message without sharing private details. Original prayer optional.
  2. 4-8: Model RIGHT, DOWN, STOP missing the target. Reset; replace DOWN with UP and test again. STOP is not a movement. Explain the human process: name the delivery goal, break it into two moves, then put the moves in order.
  3. 8-17: Partners predict RIGHT, UP, STOP, follow cards, reset and fix the intentionally wrong path. Rotate each planner/mover turn; begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child predicts the endpoint, changes one wrong card and explains/points to the message's meaning and recipient. Ask who chose the instructions and have the child show the goal, smaller moves and their order.
  5. 21-25: Share two messages without personal information; store four-card kits, retain dated records and clear.

docs.title: Success, support, troubleshooting and extension
docs.text:
Record prediction, tested correction and communicated meaning separately. Ask "Which step changed? Did the output match?" Support: two pictured choices and adult movement directed by the child. Challenge: test reversed order. Misoriented grid: fix page orientation before retesting. Missing cards: draw arrows on ordinary paper. Entire primary lesson works indoors without devices.

Optional digital extension: only after regular-teacher compatibility/ access preflight, replace practice time with an already-open ScratchJr project. Attach a green-flag start followed by two blue movement blocks; tap the flag, observe, change a direction and rerun. Each child must execute to receive software evidence; observing or paper movement does not qualify. Installed controls: ScratchJr interface. If setup fails, return to paper and mark execution unassessed.

Family: We communicated thanks and corrected picture instructions. Ask, "Which card did you change?" No home app, purchase or routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Service art / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, A; visual choices help a recipient understand a message Objective / why "I can choose a picture for someone, explain it and make it clearer." Art communicates care. Catholic connection Respect the recipient's wishes; gifts are not proof that a person needs rescuing. Local standards CST-C2: dignity/recipient; CST-A2: purposeful choice; CST-A3: explanation/revision. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Teacher offers a card for a school helper or child-chosen trusted person. Arrange school-approved delivery first; if acceptance is unknown retain it as a communication model. Precut four paper shapes at least 5 cm per child. Fold one sheet into a card; a second sheet is the plan.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Student: two sheets 20 30 40 50 Student: four large shapes 40 60 80 100 Student: crayon 10 15 20 25 Kit: glue stick, pairs/final trio plus reserve 5 8 10 13

Teacher: timer/roster, adult scissors, one sample made from budgeted materials.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text: Recipient: person the message is for. Plan: picture of the idea. Choice: feature selected for a reason. Revise: make meaning clearer. Misconception: more decorations make the best gift. Judge communicated meaning, not polish or expense. If asked whether this is engineering, say today's target is art/service; no functional engineering test is claimed.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Discuss caring without assuming every recipient likes the same gift. Ask "Who is it for, and what message will it carry?"
  2. 4-8: Show a simple unclear drawing, add one meaningful feature and explain why. Model a plan with no required words.
  3. 8-17: Each child plans and makes a card; partners point to the main idea and give one respectful suggestion. Revise a feature; begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child identifies recipient and a purposeful shape/color/ picture choice, then indicates a change making the message clearer.
  5. 21-25: Retain evidence/arrange approved delivery, count shapes, cap glue, collect crayons and clear.

docs.title: Success, SAFETY, access and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Record recipient awareness, choice/reason and communication revision. Do not grade handwriting, expense, artistic realism or personal piety. Support: large ready-folded card, two picture choices, adult scribing. Challenge: explain how spacing/contrast helps the recipient. No sequins, glitter, ribbon, food, unsafe tiny stickers or public names/images. No recipient permission: keep the card in class; no external visit. No glue: draw shapes directly and assess the same design choices. All work indoors; no family donation or required home delivery.

Family: We made and revised a thoughtful visual message. Ask, "Why did you choose that picture, and what did you change?" No routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Evidence reflection / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, A; an enjoyable memory and a demonstrated skill are different Objective / why "I can show evidence of one discovery and explain it." Honest reflection helps us choose what to practice. Catholic connection Thank others and report what we actually demonstrated; do not exaggerate. Local standards CST-C1: honest claim/evidence; CST-A3: communicate/revise. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional approved documentation camera; no device needed / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Retrieve one dated work sheet per child if available. Otherwise use the fresh paper test below; never invent an earlier result. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits with a 3-by-3 grid, large paper token and RIGHT/UP/STOP cards.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: grid; token 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Kit: three cards 15 24 30 39 Student: evidence half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: roster/timer and demonstration from one kit. No treats, certificates, photo collection or slideshow required. Optional camera use follows school consent.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text: Evidence: work/result supporting a claim. Demonstrate: show a skill. Favorite: something enjoyed. Practice: work on a skill not yet secure. Misconception: attending means mastery. A partner's result does not prove this child's understanding. If asked about a missing portfolio, collect a new dated demonstration and label it today, not as a past event.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Celebrate effort; contrast "I liked robots" with "I predicted this path."
  2. 4-8: Model explaining a dated result. For fresh evidence demonstrate RIGHT, UP, STOP from the lower-left square and reset.
  3. 8-17: Each child chooses existing evidence and rehearses its explanation, or predicts/follows the fresh route. Swap turns; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child shows one actual result, explains it and changes a drawing/ gesture if the listener cannot understand. Record any prompted evidence.
  5. 21-25: Neighboring partners share concurrently; retain dated sheets, return cards/crayons and clear. No 25-child presentation queue.

docs.title: Success, access, SAFETY and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check claim matches actual evidence and communicates a meaning. Favorite activity, certificate and attractive drawing are not skill evidence. Support: two sample explanations and pointing. Challenge: name a limit or next practice step. Desk-only large paper pieces; no snack/allergy or body-maze activity. Child cannot recall: use the fresh route, not a leading invented memory. No prior work: the supplied paper test is the complete indoor pathway. Optional camera documents evidence but does not substitute for observing it.

Family: We celebrated an actual discovery and named something to practice. Ask, "What can you show me, and what does it show?" Home work is optional.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Light and design / two 25-minute meetings Domains / big idea C, S, T, A; materials transmit light differently and artists choose materials for a purpose Objective / why "I can compare three materials and explain a tissue placement choice." Fair tests inform design. Catholic connection Report actual results; a classroom light symbol is not scientific proof of a belief. Local standards CST-C1: evidence/symbol distinction; CST-S2: comparison; CST-T1: flashlight input/output; CST-A2: design choice. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None for digital devices / guided / 15 minutes first kit / 4 per meeting

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, 5/7/10/12 active teams. Inspect secured flashlight battery covers; teacher alone handles cells. Precut a 10 cm rigid clear plastic square with smooth edges, tissue square and cardboard square per kit. Mark lamp/material/white-screen positions at 10 cm intervals. Pretest at normal room lighting; adjust screen position for visible results, then keep it fixed.

Allocation for both meetings 10 15 20 25 Kit: flashlight; each of 3 test squares; white screen 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Student: large precut paper frame; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Student: two tissue art squares 20 30 40 50 Student: four 5 cm tape strips 40 60 80 100

Teacher: timer/roster, scissors for advance preparation, demonstration from one kit. Total tissue test/art squares: 25/38/50/63. Keep first results at school.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Source: makes light. Transmit: lets light through. Opaque: blocks transmission in this test. Symbol: represents a meaning, not a measured fact. Clear plastic transmits much light; tissue scatters/transmits some; cardboard usually blocks it. Describe actual outcomes, not guaranteed brightness. Misconception: tissue is fully transparent. If asked whether paper makes light, explain it reflects/transmits source light; it is not itself a light source. No Sun viewing, beams at eyes, flames, lasers, glass, tubes, loose wrap, accessible batteries or student circuit building. Keep the room safely lit.

docs.title: Meeting 1: material comparison, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Identify lamp as source; distinguish a taught faith symbol from an observation.
  2. 4-8: Model flashlight switch input/output and one material at fixed marked distances. Look at the screen, not into the beam.
  3. 8-17: Partners predict and compare all three squares, holding lamp, screen and material positions constant. Swap roles; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child classifies one actual outcome as clear/fuzzy/blocked and identifies a kept-same condition and flashlight control.
  5. 21-25: Date results, switch off lamps, return three squares and clear.

docs.title: Meeting 2: evidence-informed art, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve results; if absent run a fresh tissue/cardboard comparison.
  2. 4-8: Model tissue placement in a precut frame; choose a position to make a pattern readable. No required holiday date or devotional history.
  3. 8-17: Each child chooses and tapes tissue placement, compares its light effect at the marked position and revises one choice after peer feedback.
  4. 17-21: Child explains/points to the purposeful choice and distinguishes what the test showed from a classroom meaning of the symbol.
  5. 21-25: Retain evidence, switch off/count lights, collect dry scraps and clear.

docs.title: Success, access, troubleshooting and reported holdings
docs.text:
Assess prediction/result, kept-same condition, input/output and artistic reason separately; color beauty is not mastery. Support: two material choices, adult placement directed by child, tactile shapes. Challenge: compare repeat tests. No visible result: teacher adjusts screen before issuing kits; record adjustments. No secured lights: use inspected source/class demonstration and record student operation unassessed; never improvise a battery circuit. All work indoors.

Reported OLP holding, preserved: 8 Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135. Count, completeness, location, manufacturer age/power guidance and condition remain unverified. See reported holdings. Only a pretested adult-operated demonstration is optional; the flashlight minimum is unchanged, no loan or student circuit objective is added.

Family: We compared light through materials and made a purposeful art choice. Ask, "What did you observe, and what did your picture mean?" No homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Stars and models / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea S, A, M; a drawn pattern represents stars but does not make light or show actual distances Objective / why "I can count five star dots and explain that my picture is a model." Models help communicate ideas while leaving things out. Catholic connection Wonder at creation and truthful explanation; no physical cause for the biblical star is claimed. Local standards CST-S3: model/limit; CST-A1: representation; CST-M1: count 3-5 dots. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Draw five separated dots, numbered for the teacher only, in a simple zigzag on one kit card. It is an invented pattern, not an official constellation. Budget ⅝/10/13 cards for active 5/7/10/12 pair/trio teams.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: five-dot model card 5 8 10 13 Student: sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: timer/roster, demonstration from one card. No stickers, glitter, glue, night visit, Sun viewing or device required.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and source
docs.text: Star: makes its own light. Pattern: arrangement we recognize. Model: representation with limits. The Sun is a star; stars remain present in daytime even when difficult to see. Our dots are not stars at equal real distances; a crayon does not produce light. Source inspected October 4: NASA stars, teacher paraphrase. Misconception: stars physically have five points. Say pointed paper shapes are symbols; real stars are not paper cutouts. If asked about Magi, use only the school's approved religion material; number, travel time and astronomical explanation are not needed or asserted here.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Invite wonder; compare a real light-producing star with a picture.
  2. 4-8: Model one-to-one counting of five dots and drawing their arrangement. Explain the picture does not show actual size/distance.
  3. 8-17: Partners point/count and each make a model with 3-5 dots. Swap roles; child chooses spacing to help a partner recognize it. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child counts their dots and explains/points to a model limit: not actual stars, not producing light, or not real distances.
  5. 21-25: Neighbor partners interpret the pictures; retain dated work, return cards/crayons and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, SAFETY and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check count matches dots, recognizable representation and one limit separately. Ask "What is real in the sky? What can this picture not tell us?" Support: three large dots, tactile raised paper marks/adult scribing. Challenge: same five dots drawn differently, explaining that lines are our drawing choice. No Sun/night observations or dark room. Child draws pointed stars: accept the symbol, then explicitly distinguish shape from the real object. No dark paper: ordinary paper works; no supply purchase is necessary. The entire model pathway is indoors and independent of weather or nighttime access.

Family: We counted a star-pattern model and explained what it cannot show. Ask, "Does your picture make light like a star?" No required evening outing.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Observation and practice goals / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, M, A; a goal needs an action and evidence, not a wish or promise Objective / why "I can record what I observe in the sky and choose a way to check it again." Repeated records help us compare conditions. Catholic connection Honest observations and patient practice, not a claim that God guarantees a particular result. Local standards CST-C1: truthful record; CST-S1: observation; CST-S3: weather representation; CST-M2: symbol record; CST-A3: communicate goal. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 5 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. From a safe indoor window away from the Sun, identify sky as mostly clear, partly cloudy or mostly cloud covered. Draw three large cloud-coverage symbols per kit. Make no temperature/wind inference from appearance. If pupils cannot view the sky, teacher supplies a dated first-hand description and labels it teacher observation, not the child's measurement.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: three large symbols 15 24 30 39 Student: dated record sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12. Teacher: timer, roster, class record sheet with date and observation time. Store it for Week 20, not at home.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text: Observation: what was seen/described now. Record: saved information. Goal: skill to practice. Prediction: expected future result, not today's observation. One record cannot establish a seasonal pattern or forecast. Misconception: a drawing of a sunny sky means it is warm. Explain we have not measured outdoor temperature. If asked about tomorrow, label any answer a guess.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Reframe goals as checkable practice. Ask "How could we show learning?"
  2. 4-8: Model selecting today's sky symbol and dating the record; distinguish observation from a picture of preferred weather.
  3. 8-17: Observe safely or listen to the labeled teacher report; each child chooses/draws a matching symbol and describes the evidence. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child explains today's record and chooses the goal "record the sky again and compare" with a pointing/drawing reminder. Do not award future mastery.
  5. 21-25: Save individual/class records for Week 20, collect symbols/crayons, clear. No compulsory between-class or home observation.

docs.title: Success, access, SAFETY and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check record matches actual report, child distinguishes now from a guess and states a checkable next action. Support: two symbol choices, read-aloud/tactile symbols and adult scribing. Challenge: identify what was not measured. No outdoor exposure, Sun viewing, climbing to windows or forced sensory task. No visible sky/teacher report: use an explicitly invented practice picture, mark model data and defer actual-weather evidence. Week 20 provides a fresh real record when possible; never invent the previous observation.

Family: We practiced a weather record and a checkable goal. Ask, "What did you observe, and how will you check it again?" No homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Practice and evidence / four meetings, each 25 minutes Domains / big idea S, T, E, A, M; practice means checking results, not collecting a station stamp Objective / why "I can retest, compare records, explain a pattern and fix instructions." Transfer makes skills usable. Catholic connection Fair turns and honest reporting; no claim that everyone mastered every field. Local standards CST-S1: actual observation; CST-T2: correction; CST-E2: retest; CST-A2: purposeful readable pattern; CST-M2: weather/pattern representation. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional pretested robot extension, paper primary / guided / 15 minutes per prepared kit / 4 each meeting

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. One challenge occupies the whole class per meeting; no five-station rotation or passport. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits for 5/7/10/12 active teams. Every meeting uses 10/15/20/25 student half-sheets/crayons plus one teacher timer/roster. Demonstrate with a budgeted kit; return it before practice.

Meeting / kit allocation 10 15 20 25 19: 20 large blocks; one tray 100 / 5 160 / 8 200 / 10 260 / 13 20: three sky-symbol cards 15 24 30 39 21: three circles and three squares, >=5 cm 15 each 24 each 30 each 39 each 22: grid; >=8 cm token; four command cards 5 / 5 / 20 8 / 8 / 32 10 / 10 / 40 13 / 13 / 52

For 20 retrieve Week 18's dated sky record if it is a real observation. If missing, prepare to record at this meeting's beginning and again at minute 17; label both date/time. Do not invent yesterday's weather. For 22 draw a 3-by-3 grid with START lower-left; cards RIGHT, UP, DOWN, STOP.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text: Retest: repeat a check. Record: saved information. Repeat: recurring unit in a pattern. Debug: correct instructions. Misconception: visiting a station proves mastery. Each child supplies the specific evidence below. If asked why weather did not change, explain that unchanged observations are valid; two records cannot establish a season. Pattern drawings are representations; paper routes are not software/hardware operation.

docs.title: Meeting 19: structure retest, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Recall a low six-block tower's ten-second unaided criterion.
  2. 4-8: Model a base change with the same six blocks and timing.
  3. 8-17: Partners test, change base and retest; swap roles and begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child indicates a change and compares two actual results, including a fall. Save a two-result drawing.
  5. 21-25: Count blocks, retain dated evidence, clear trays.

docs.title: Meeting 20: two weather records, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Safely observe sky/cloud coverage away from the Sun; date/time a first record if no actual previous class record exists.
  2. 4-8: Model mostly clear/partly cloudy/mostly covered symbols. Explain that a forecast, preferred picture or room temperature is not this observation.
  3. 8-17: Children select/draw today's symbol and compare a prior actual record when available. Identify matching/different features; begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Make a second timed observation if using the same-day route. Each child compares the two labeled records and states what was observed.
  5. 21-25: Save records with dates/times; collect cards/crayons and clear.

docs.title: Meeting 21: a readable repeat, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Name circle/square and a repeated unit, not a favorite color.
  2. 4-8: Model circle-square-circle-square and predict next circle-square.
  3. 8-17: Partners arrange/extend six pieces; swap turns and change spacing to make the pattern readable to a partner. Begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child selects the next two shapes and explains/points to why the spacing or arrangement helps communication.
  5. 21-25: Save a drawing, count three of each shape per kit, clear.

docs.title: Meeting 22: sequence correction, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Target is one square right and one up from START.
  2. 4-8: Model RIGHT, DOWN, STOP missing it; reset and correct DOWN to UP.
  3. 8-17: Every child predicts, follows and corrects the path in a full turn; partners move only by the shown rule. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child shows endpoint and tested correction; save individual evidence.
  5. 21-25: Repack grids/tokens/cards, retain evidence and clear.

docs.title: Success, SAFETY, access and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Record four separate checks across the unit, not one participation score. Support: a modeled choice, large tactile shapes, adult-directed movement or scribing. Challenge: fair repeated test, record limitation, new repeat or reversed route. No height contests, small tokens, body mazes, unknown nature items, Sun viewing or outdoor prerequisite; structures stay low and seated. No sky view: labeled teacher observation, or explicitly model data with actual-weather evidence deferred. Missing blocks: shared <=3 groups, same test. All minimum pathways are indoors and device-free.

Optional robot extension is a separately pretested teacher choice; charge/aim and verify compatible controls before class. Replace, do not add, work time; actual operation/execution evidence requires each child's real device turn. If equipment fails, paper evidence remains computational thinking only.

Family: We checked structure changes, two weather records, a readable repeat and picture instructions. Ask about one actual result, not a station stamp. No homework or donations.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Truthful learning display / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, T, A; a display communicates actual evidence and protects private information Objective / why "I can show a result and help someone understand it." Clear explanations share learning with our community. Catholic connection Faith and reason support truthful inquiry; gratitude does not replace evidence. Local standards CST-C1: honest result; CST-T3: private-information/adult-help scenario; CST-A3: audience explanation/revision. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional approved photography; none needed / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and quantities
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use actual school event dates, not a presumed calendar week. Retrieve one dated test/observation sheet per child. Missing work has a fresh route: 3-by-3 grid, START lower-left, target right then up; RIGHT/UP/STOP cards. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: grid; large token; three cards 5 / 5 / 15 8 / 8 / 24 10 / 10 / 30 13 / 13 / 39 Student: display/evidence sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Teacher: two hypothetical sharing cards 2 2 2 2

Teacher: timer/roster, demonstration from a kit and an approved classroom display space. Visitors, public photography, outside contact and personal names are not required. Draw a house icon to represent a fictional person's home address, and an anonymous shape pattern. Read their meanings aloud; no actual address or student data is written or requested.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Evidence: actual work/result. Audience: person interpreting the display. Explain: tell what a result means. Revise: make a message clearer. Misconception: a favorite photograph proves every skill. A child must identify what was actually demonstrated. If asked whether prayer proves a science claim, say our faith reflection and test result are different kinds of statement. If asked about sharing, a home address stays private; ask the trusted school adult before public sharing. An anonymous pattern is not personal information, but school permission still applies to publication. Seated desk models, large paper parts; no public names/images without approval.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Invite thanks for school/community and state the truthful-display goal.
  2. 4-8: Model a result plus explanation. If no work exists, run RIGHT, UP, STOP freshly; date it today and do not claim a robot ran. Read the two hypothetical sharing cards and model keeping the address private.
  3. 8-17: Each child prepares a display from a real record or performs the fresh route. Partner asks "What does this show?" Begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child points to evidence, explains its meaning and revises one mark/drawing/gesture when the audience is confused. Each child chooses which hypothetical card is private and names the adult to ask before sharing.
  5. 21-25: Pairs share concurrently; save dated evidence, put displays in the approved space, return materials and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, support and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check actual result, truthful limitation, understandable communication and private-information/adult-help choices; never collect a child's home details. Ask "Did you do this, observe it or predict it? What would you still practice?" Support: pointing/dictation and two explanatory choices. Challenge: name what the evidence cannot establish. No portfolio: use the supplied fresh route; do not send the child home to obtain a photograph. No display area: keep individual sheets in a class envelope. Indoors, no visitor/device prerequisite.

Family: We explained one real result and revised its presentation. Ask, "What evidence does your picture show?" Optional family conversation only.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / title K / Algorithms for service / Dash Robot Friends Time Two 25-minute meetings; no extra delivery meeting Domains / big idea C, T, M / Ordered instructions can be tested and corrected to reach a useful destination. Student objective / why "I can plan three steps, find a wrong step, and try again." We check a tool's results before relying on it to help people. Catholic connection Choose a welcoming message that respects the recipient; share roles fairly. CCC 2405, paraphrase about using skills to benefit people. Local standards CST-C2, CST-T1, CST-T2, CST-M1; local, never official. Official benchmark alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty Optional / Beginner with prior two-arrow experience Prep / cleanup Light: 10 minutes for paper; optional hardware Moderate: 20 minutes plus charging / 3 minutes each meeting

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Make 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 children (pairs/final trio). Prepare ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment. Seat everyone at tables; no classroom delivery routes among feet.
  2. Per team draw a 4-by-2 grid of 10 cm squares. START is lower-left; FRIEND is the square two right and one up. Draw a large paper Dash, four arrows (two RIGHT, one UP, one deliberately wrong DOWN), and STOP.
  3. Make one half-sheet kindness card per child. Students can draw a welcome symbol or dictate a message; the intended recipient may decline it.
  4. Mark a roster A (algorithm), I (input/output), P (real program), H (real hardware operation). Reuse Sphero vocabulary but explain that the page grid, not robot orientation, defines arrows.
  5. Optional: reserve school-approved Dash access only if available; no loan assumed. Use one charged robot/tablet in an adult-controlled clear 1 m demonstration lane. The vendor lists Blockly and Path, not Blockly Jr. Before class, the teacher tests the actual installed Blockly interface: connect Dash, assemble a start/run sequence with two short forward moves and a quarter-turn, and run/stop safely at low speed. Calibrate distance/turn to the lane and make a screenshot/drawing of the three tested blocks. If controls, app compatibility, or safe stopping are uncertain, omit hardware; do not substitute invented button names.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Allocation 10 15 20 25 Per student: kindness half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Per team: grid; large paper Dash 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Per team: five command cards 25 40 50 65 Teacher/class: large grid, marker, timer, roster 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each

Optional, whole class: one Dash, one tablet, one roll painter's tape. Never attach cards where they could obstruct wheels/sensors; put the message at the destination instead. No new consumables are needed for meeting 2.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text:
Sequence: steps in order. Command: one instruction. Debug: locate and fix a mismatch. Input/output: instructions given / observed result.

The paper model uses one-square moves; Blockly forward distance and robot turns use different units and a heading. A person moving a paper robot is acting out an algorithm. Real programming requires a saved block sequence executed by software; steering in Drive mode is not programming. Wheels may slip or a battery may fail: a correct program does not guarantee an exact physical path.

Misconception: "Dash is my friend and knows who needs kindness." People choose recipients and make ethical decisions; the classroom machine has no human feelings.

If asked, "Why did it miss?" Check the start heading, distance, surface, connection, and code. A missed target is evidence to investigate, not a child's failure.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No robot racing/chasing, real medicine delivery, riding, or free driving near children. Adult manages lane, charging and stop control. Keep feet/hands outside lane; retrieve only when stopped. No blindfolded or walking "human robots." Use large paper tokens. Seek permission before physical help or delivering messages.

docs.title: Meeting 1: plan a delivery (25 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Pray for kindness; choose a pictured welcome gesture that respects another person.
  2. 3-7 (4 min): Model RIGHT, RIGHT, UP on the page. Count three moves and identify input/output. If hardware is prepared, adult demonstrates the tested sequence for two of these minutes; state the different units.
  3. 7-15 (8 min): Each team member lays three arrows and predicts the destination before partner execution. Swap planner/mover/checker after every trial.
  4. 15-20 (5 min): Each child draws/dictates a welcoming card; teacher checks individual prediction and three-move count during work.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Ask "Who chooses the message? Does the robot decide what is kind?"
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Store five-card kits, messages and grids; stop and store optional Dash.

docs.title: Meeting 2: test, debug, and communicate (25 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Reestablish START and FRIEND. Recall that different inputs change outputs.
  2. 3-6 (3 min): Run RIGHT, RIGHT, DOWN on the page. Identify the first mismatching command; replace DOWN with UP, reset, retest.
  3. 6-15 (9 min): Pairs/trio test and correct that sequence, each child taking a planner turn. Teacher begins individual prediction/correction checks while circulating. At the correct target, offer the message to the pictured recipient; actual sharing is optional.
  4. 15-20 (5 min): Finish remaining checks: child orders three cards, predicts endpoint, changes the wrong third card and shows the corrected endpoint. No serial class exit line. Optional prepared hardware replaces up to two minutes of team work, never individual evidence; select a child to edit the tested block and run it under adult control.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Ask "What changed? What stayed the same? How did our message include someone?"
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Count cards back, clear tables, return drawings; adult stores hardware.

docs.title: Individual evidence and success
docs.text:
Record A: predicted three-card route and one successful correction; I: identified instruction and observed result. Use independent / prompted / not yet; accept pointing, oral explanation, moving cards, or a drawn path. Fair role-sharing and a respectful message are C evidence; artistic polish is not assessed.

P is demonstrated only by a child who edits a real block sequence and runs it on Dash; H only by a child who actually uses the robot's controls safely. Others' status is not assessed, even when they watched a demonstration. No-device students can meet the algorithm objective, not real hardware operating/programming objectives.

docs.title: Questions, support, troubleshooting, indoor fallback
docs.text:
• "Which command made the mismatch? How do you know? Why do we reset before retesting?"
  • Support: use two cards first, offer UP/DOWN picture choices, let the child point while an adult moves pieces.
  • Challenge: invent a different three-step route and an intentional error for a partner; do not require loops before ordered steps are secure.
  • Wrong start: reset to the marked square; a changed starting place is a changed test condition.
  • No hardware/app fails: finish the page-grid lesson; accurately label evidence as algorithm/model work.
  • Crowded class: 12 teams run concurrently at seated tables with one reserve kit; optional hardware remains a teacher station.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: this is an entirely indoor lesson in all weather.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text: We designed a welcoming delivery route, tested it, and corrected an instruction. Ask: "Which step did you change, and what happened?" Real robot programming was optional and recorded only for children who performed it. No homework or equipment purchase.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Requested-need design / two 25-minute meetings Domains / big idea C, E, A; serving a user means listening and balancing criteria Objective / why "I can plan a stand, test it and explain a change." A useful design needs more than an appealing appearance. Catholic connection Dignity means asking what is wanted, not stereotyping age, illness or disability. Local standards CST-C2: requested need; CST-E1: two criteria/limits; CST-E2: retest; CST-A1: plan; CST-E3: tradeoff explanation. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes first kit, 5 reset / 4 each meeting

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use this complete fictional request: "The reader wants our folded paper book to stand open for ten seconds, without holding, and wants its picture visible." Pretest a small folded-cardboard stand on a desk. Do not tape across the picture. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits for active 5/7/10/12 teams.

Kit/student allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: two smooth 20 cm cardboard squares 10 16 20 26 Kit: folded paper book; storage tray 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Kit: ten sticks; ten 10 cm tape strips 50 each 80 each 100 each 130 each Student: plan/result sheet; crayon, per meeting 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher: timer/roster, ruler, adult scissors. Draw a large circle on the open book as the picture; measure a <=20 cm model. Store first-test records at school.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Request: stated need. Criterion: success condition. Constraint: limit. Tradeoff: one choice can help a feature while making another harder. A higher front edge may support the book but obscure its picture; test both. Misconception: everyone in a group needs the same aid. Use only this fictional request. If asked to give the stand to a real person, explain it is a classroom model, not an approved assistive device. No wearables, cords, infant/pet trials, loaded cups, body weight, reaching high shelves or simulated disability.

docs.title: Meeting 1: request, plan and first test, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Read the request; children identify both success conditions.
  2. 4-8: Show simple folded support, ten-second timed test and picture visibility.
  3. 8-17: Each child draws a plan; partners build within the ten-stick/tape allowance and test the model. Swap builder/tester turns; begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Record standing yes/no and visible picture yes/no. Child points to the plan and identifies a requested feature, not a supposed disability.
  5. 21-25: Date/save records, label dry models by kit, count and clear.

docs.title: Meeting 2: improve and defend a tradeoff, 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve actual two-criterion results; missing results are freshly tested.
  2. 4-8: Model changing a front support while keeping book/test time the same.
  3. 8-17: Partners change one feature and retest both criteria. Rotate each child's choice/test turn; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child compares results and explains/points to a tradeoff: support versus visible picture, or material use versus function.
  5. 21-25: Save evidence, reclaim sticks, sort dry cardboard, clear trays.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Record requested need, plan, two test outcomes, change and tradeoff separately. Ask "What did the reader request? Did both criteria work? What got harder?"
