docs.title: OLP Snap Circuits classroom guide
docs.text: Reported stock: 8 individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135, reported 2026-10-04. This means eight student activity kits, not eight six-kit classroom packs. See the holdings record. Physical inspection and classroom approval are still required.

docs.title: Before teaching: release the hardware pathway
docs.text:
Allow 30 minutes for first inspection/pretesting, plus time to obtain any missing instructions or parts; allow 15 minutes for repeat preparation. Leave a prepared kit, approved diagram, component list and this guide for a substitute. A substitute must not invent a circuit or approve unfamiliar parts.

  1. Label the individual kits SC01-SC08. Record the actual manufacturer model, instruction/workbook edition, contents, condition, location and checker. OHM-135 is the supplier item number, not a verified manufacturer model.
  2. Read the matching in-box manufacturer instructions. Select one documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project with a complete return path. Record its project/page number and component IDs on the teacher's setup card. Use the same project in every station; do not mix modules from different systems.
  3. Verify manufacturer age guidance for the actual pupils, battery access, holder protection and the school's electrical-safety requirements. The supplied holder is not assumed equivalent to a screw-secured, current-protected AA holder. If it does not meet school requirements, use the protected-AA alternative or paper route, not improvised covers or protection.
  4. Adult installs only the battery type/count specified for that project. Record b = fitted cells per station and the chemistry/voltage. Count fitted cells as stations * b; reserve complete kits need their own checked cells. Keep replacement cells separately in adult-controlled storage. Do not assume the kit uses the earlier lessons' two-AA allocation.
  5. Pretest the documented switch-OFF/light-off and switch-ON/light-on states twice. An LED project is allowed only if the matching instructions document polarity and required current limiting; never substitute a bare LED for a lamp.
  6. Teach power isolation, not just switch OFF: before changing snap connections, the adult disconnects the battery holder from the build as directed by the manufacturer. Pupils do not handle cells or holder contacts. Adult checks the complete approved layout before reconnecting power.
  7. Issue only the approved project's parts, grid, component list and diagram. Leave motors/fan blades, sound modules, extra loads and unused holders stored. No free wiring, shorts, series/parallel extensions or assumed sensors.

Stop conditions: missing matching instructions, unsuitable age rating, unapproved holder/protection, missing parts, failed pretest, warmth, smell, damage or leakage. Mark the kit OUT OF SERVICE, tell the responsible adult and use a named alternative. A lit lamp alone does not certify safe wiring.

The supplier description lists switches, lamps, LEDs and battery holders and recommends upper elementary. It describes a six-kit classroom pack, not OLP's eight individual kits. It does not verify OLP's exact model, battery allocation or school approval. This guide provides original teaching routines, not a replacement for that model's manufacturer instructions or a claim of official standards alignment.

docs.title: Station capacity: no group larger than three
docs.text:
Use balanced pairs/trios, not a singleton. Each kit is one hardware station. The teacher demonstration uses a station kit before pupil work, not a ninth kit.

Pupils Teams (size distribution) Hardware stations Hardware waves Unissued kits available as reserves 10 4 (two trios, two pairs) 4 1 4 15 5 (five trios) 5 1 3 20 7 (six trios, one pair) 7 1 1 25 9 (seven trios, two pairs) 5 2 3

These numbers assume all eight kits pass preflight. Reserves are not automatically complete or powered. Recalculate when a kit is out of service; do not increase team size or mark a paper turn as electrical operation. One wave cannot serve more than 24 pupils with eight kits.

docs.title: The 25-pupil rotation
docs.text:
Assign teams 1-5 to wave A (15 pupils) and teams 6-9 to wave B (10 pupils). Provide nine team work areas but only five dry hardware stations. Waiting teams work on their own prediction, diagram and audience/design task. The timed lessons include one minute for transfer/reset; supplies move, not live circuits. Adult isolates power and checks stations before the second wave.

Each hardware wave gives a team 12 minutes in Grades 3-4 or 14 minutes in Grades 5-6: follow the approved build, adult inspection, individual switch tests, and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Every child contributes a designated snap connection to the isolated team build and then operates the switch for two OFF/ON cycles. Rotate connector/tester/recorder; a role label alone is not evidence. The teacher checks each team before energizing and again after a repair. Never create a live short as the fault.

At smaller enrollments, all teams use wave A; wave B is extra retesting, feedback and individual checking time, not an additional meeting. If inspections or motor/access needs take longer, record unfinished physical evidence and schedule a supervised completion turn. Do not rush a safety check or report that every child operated a kit unless observed.

docs.title: Individual evidence sheet: draw or copy onto paper
docs.text:
No printer, account, app or additional workbook purchase is required. Each pupil records:

Check Pupil response / teacher observation Full path Label battery, switch, light and conducting return path Prediction OFF -> expected output; ON -> expected output Test OFF/ON observations for cycle 1 and cycle 2 Open-path repair Gap, one approved correction and observed retest result Design/message Intended user/reader; one choice and specific feedback Evidence level Physical contribution and switch test observed / prompted / not yet; paper reasoning recorded separately

Teacher key for the approved simple switched light: OFF opens the path and the light is off; ON closes the path and the light is on. If observation differs, report the actual result. Disconnect power; adult checks the diagram, contacts and cells. Do not substitute parts or bypass protection.

docs.title: Protected-AA alternative: separate equipment, not a Snap conversion
docs.text:
Keep the original protected circuit option if already verified and available. Do not attach Snap parts to its supply or LittleBits modules.

  • Grades 3-4: screw-secured covered 2-AA holder with documented protection, matching cells, switch, enclosed current-limited 3 V LED module and three insulated leads. Pretest holder + -> switch -> module +; module - -> holder -.
  • Grades 5-6: enclosed, current/short-circuit-protected switched 2-AA holder, push switch, adult-prepared sleeved red LED/220-ohm ¼-watt series-resistor assembly and three insulated leads. Pretest the complete series return path. Supply OFF before reconnection; adult checks before ON.

Use the same station/wave counts above. Add one complete spare: ⅚/8/6 kits at 10/15/20/25 pupils, 10/12/16/12 fitted AA cells, and 15/18/24/18 leads. This is a selected-path allocation, not a change to the shared purchasing BOM. For Grades 5-6 retain the original four-state evidence: supply OFF with button released/pressed -> off/off; supply ON with button released/pressed -> off/on. Snap's slide switch instead uses two OFF/ON states repeated twice; do not claim push/release behavior or four independently controlled states from that route.

docs.title: Safety and return
docs.text:
Adult supervision, dry seated stations, counted small parts and teacher-managed power throughout. No button/coin cells, household/mains/USB power, soldering, cutting wires, exposed fan blades, battery-terminal shorts or take-home circuits. Never mix cell types/old and new cells or recharge disposable cells. Use manufacturer-directed isolation and adult handling of damaged/hot cells.

Reserve the lesson's final cleanup block: isolate power, count issued parts and cells against each station list, return parts to SC01-SC08, flag discrepancies, and store in a dry adult-controlled location away from water. Adult removes cells for long storage as directed. Only diagrams and paper art go home. Kindergarten remains adult-demonstration only after preflight; no new student circuit-building objective is introduced.

docs.title: Student progress tracker
docs.text: Retain the useful fall/winter/spring growth conversation, but track taught objectives rather than enthusiasm or generic participation. October 2026. Use assessment, rubrics and Local Standards.

docs.title: Lesson evidence roster
docs.text:
Student Date/grade/unit/lesson Objective/local code Exact action/words or artifact Mode/access support ½/¾ or NE Feedback/next check [One row per child; extend to actual enrollment, including 25] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]

Levels: 1 Beginning, 2 Developing, 3 Meets Expectation, 4 Extends Learning. Use the lesson's specific descriptors. NE means no adequate evidence yet (absence, unavailable equipment, missed check); it is not a zero. Ordinary read-aloud, gesture, bilingual response, scribe and motor assistance do not lower achievement. Record conceptual hints separately.

docs.title: Termly growth summary
docs.text:
Student/objective/local code Fall evidence/date/level Winter evidence/date/level Spring evidence/date/level Next teaching [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]

Examples of appropriate evidence by grade, not new official benchmarks:

Grade Possible individual evidence when corresponding objective taught K Points/sorts by an observed feature; shows a two-action sequence; tells one detail 1 Names the problem/user; compares two results; explains one design choice 2 Records an equal-condition comparison; explains a changed sequence 3 Shows common test conditions and links one redesign to the result 4 Measures in the specified unit and uses results to justify an improvement 5 Compares two designs using taught criteria/constraints 6 Defends a choice with evidence, cost/tradeoff and a taught ethical consideration

This is not an independent progression specification: use the shared grade progression and local definitions for expected outcomes. Real program/robot execution is only recorded when actually demonstrated on a working device. Never fill those cells from an unplugged activity.

docs.title: Workload and privacy
docs.text:
During hands-on time sweep the roster; pair a simultaneous point/show/draw exit response with short targeted conversations. At 25, record unobserved children NE and collect later rather than assuming all groups mastered the concept. Review at project completion and termly; do not require daily long checklists. At expected-mastery checkpoints, retain two dated observations on separate occasions as required by Local Standards, including an individual demonstration and changed context/follow-up explanation. Both must meet the target; one lesson rating is not end-of-grade mastery. Store named records under the school's actual privacy practice. Do not publish names, scores or photographs in newsletters without verified permission.

Behavior/engagement notes may inform support but remain separate from subject mastery. Report "measured the span accurately; next compare repeated trials," not "participates well, therefore proficient."

docs.title: C-STREAM substitute teacher guide
docs.text: C = Catholic identity, R = religion/faith integration, A = arts including music, M = mathematics. Thank you for leading hands-on learning. October 2026. Use the actual scheduled lesson, not a generic assurance that every old lesson is ready. Readiness review.

docs.title: Twenty minutes before class
docs.text:
Minutes Do this 0-4 Read objective, background/vocabulary and native timed steps; identify each child's evidence prompt 4-8 Find the kit at the location supplied by school; count student/team/class/teacher items for enrollment 8-12 Read SAFETY; check accommodations, materials condition and actual school emergency/office contact 12-16 Perform the exact lesson model/pretest, then place counted trays and assign roles 16-20 Draw/read aloud short steps; rehearse individual check, cleanup and the named fallback

School must fill lesson/date [ ], kit/actual location [ ], office/contact [ ], accommodations [ ], emergency instructions [ ] before handoff. Do not assume "STREAM closet," iPads, apps, loan kits or a quick-reference card exists.

Grade 3 example: rebuilt Week 10 Bridge Engineering. Use its precise quantities/span/load/check and 40-minute period. If its kit or prep test fails, use the fallback below and record the changed objective. This guide does not certify all legacy lessons.

docs.title: SAFETY: stop rather than improvise
docs.text: No button cells, latex balloons, projectile activities or neodymium magnets in K. No unknown chemicals, food experiments, glass, hot surfaces, unsafe cold exposure or electrical repair. Teacher controls batteries/clip leads/small loads. Do not use unfamiliar electric/magnetic equipment without a verified pretest. Stop, isolate unsafe materials, move to a seated safe task and notify the responsible school adult. Injury, suspected ingestion of a battery/magnet or other urgent danger requires the school's emergency escalation immediately. Do not send pupils hunting for missing dangerous parts.

docs.title: Fallback A: paper structure comparison
docs.text:
Objective: Compare flat and folded paper under the same span and load. Big idea: Shape can affect a structure; a fair comparison keeps test conditions the same. Catholic connection: Reliable design serves people; shared resources are used responsibly. No "God is an engineer" comparison. Technology Requirement: None. Difficulty: introductory comparison. Prep: 10 minutes if counted stock/supports exist; cleanup included below. Vocabulary: span = gap between supports; load = what a structure supports; compare = notice how results are alike/different.

Background/misconception: Folded and flat paper may respond differently. The result can be the same under a small load; report that honestly. A collapse is information, not failure of the student. If asked why a fold matters, show the changed shape; do not promise that every fold always improves it.

Scope/material Rate 10 pupils 15 20 25 Student response paper (or oral response) 1/child 10 15 20 25 Team paper 2/team 8 10 14 18 Team index-card test loads 10/team 40 50 70 90 Team ruler 1/team 4 5 7 9 Stable support books/blocks 2/team 8 10 14 18 Teacher 2 demonstration sheets, 10 cards, timer, evidence roster One class set in addition to team issue quantities

Pencils/crayons are school basics. Total paper at 25 = 25 + 18 + 2 = 45 sheets; total cards = 90 + 10 = 100. No scissors, coins, tape, devices or donations. Books/supports must be confirmed; without them use fallback B, not an unsafe stack.

Before class: Set stable supports 10 cm apart on each desk; lay one sheet flat across. Fold the second lengthwise into an accordion with adult modeling. Try adding cards one by one at the center in both tests; reset with the same gap and count. Test before class; reduce the gap if neither supports even one card and record that shared change. No escalating to heavy falling weights. K adult places loads; child still predicts/points/compares.

docs.title: Exact native timing (choose the grade column)
docs.text:
Step K 25 1-2 30 3-4 40 5-6 45 What to do/say Hook/purpose 0-3 0-3 0-4 0-4 "What might a fold change?" Explain objective and stewardship Model/vocabulary/safety 3-7 3-8 4-10 4-11 Align supports, show flat/folded examples, demonstrate one load placement Build/test first comparison 7-14 8-18 10-24 11-27 Students take turns placing paper/cards; count or point to result Improve/retest 14-19 18-23 24-32 27-36 Change one paper shape; keep gap/load placement. "What stayed the same?" Individual check 19-22 23-27 32-37 36-41 "Show the result. What stayed the same in the test?" Cleanup/close 22-25 27-30 37-40 41-45 Count cards/rulers/supports, retain dry paper, clear desks, brief thanks

Meets: Each child identifies the observed comparison (including equal results) and shows one common condition. For K, adult reads/models and accepts pointing/gesture. Use Show, Try, Tell. Support: Pre-fold paper, steady supports, scribe or allow a large gesture. Challenge: Repeat the comparison and explain whether it supports the first result; older pupils can compare equal-material versions without untaught ratios. At 25: Nine seated teams, rotating turns; check children during tests plus simultaneous show/draw exit. Mark unobserved evidence NE and leave a follow-up. Troubleshoot: Sliding supports -> stabilize or stop that test; equal results -> record them, not "wrong"; time short -> stop new construction, keep check/cleanup. Family copy: "We compared paper structures using the same gap and loads. Ask: 'What stayed the same, and what changed?' Optional: discuss a folded object already nearby. No home project needed."

docs.title: Fallback B: no devices, no consumable supplies, or unsafe weather
docs.text:
Objective: Make and distinguish a direct observation from a guess. Materials: A familiar safe classroom object/view already present; no handling of hazardous objects. Technology: None. Prep: 2 minutes. Vocabulary/background: Observe = notice directly; guess/inference = an idea that needs more evidence. "Looks wooden" does not prove material composition.

Follow the same native timing columns above: 1. Hook: "What can we actually notice about this desk/door/window view?" 2. Model one observation and one inference; safety: seated, no climbing/touching. 3. Each child notices/points/tells one feature; partners compare. 4. Identify which claim can be checked by looking; refine it. 5. Each child shows one observable feature (older pupils distinguish a guess). 6. Restore room, finish the evidence notes and close.

Meets: Child points/names an observable feature; for a stated older-grade inference objective also explains why a guess needs evidence. Read aloud, model, allow gesture/gaze/home-language response. Challenge: propose a safe way to check a guess. Record objective change; no claim of engineering/programming mastery. Cleanup: no materials to collect; reset seating and leave evidence/NE. Family: "We practiced observing carefully. Ask: 'What did you notice directly?'" At -10 F remain indoors; if there is no safe view, use an ordinary indoor object.

docs.title: Device/supply contingency and return note
docs.text:
Paper algorithms preserve sequence/debugging concepts, not real programming or robot-operation mastery. Defer those objectives if devices fail; do not invent accounts or app permissions. Technology Plan.

Leave lesson/steps completed, actual individual evidence or NE, objectives changed/deferred, restock counts, broken parts OUT OF SERVICE, safety/source questions and the next check. Named evidence stays under school privacy practice. See handoff template and Local Standards; official alignment and unverified Church/supplier claims are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: 📝 Teacher Self-Evaluation for C-STEM Excellence
docs.text:
This local self-evaluation tool helps teachers reflect on Catholic identity, hands-on learning, inclusion and instructional planning. It does not establish NCEA/Cognia certification, accreditation or compliance with official standards.

October 2026 status: Treat the following as legacy/local reflection prompts, not a verified official NCEA, Minnesota or Archdiocesan instrument. Attribution, quoted wording and the numbered characteristics/factors are VERIFICATION REQUIRED against a primary source before claiming official alignment. Teacher reflection is separate from student achievement. Use objective-linked evidence and Local Standards, including authentic arts/music (A) and mathematics (M). Do not grade students for apparent joy, participation, interior faith or family practice.

docs.title: 📋 Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: Self-assessment tool for teachers to evaluate and improve their C-STEM instruction

Frequency: Complete at the beginning and end of each semester, or after each unit

Scoring: Honestly rate your current practice to identify areas for growth

docs.title: 🎯 Part 1: Ten Local Reflection Themes
docs.text:
Legacy attribution to NCEA and the italicized wording below: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. These prompts are not an official certification checklist.

Rate your alignment with each characteristic:

  • 4 = Consistently exemplify this characteristic

  • 3 = Usually demonstrate this characteristic

  • 2 = Sometimes demonstrate this characteristic

  • 1 = Rarely or never demonstrate this characteristic

docs.text:
"Integrate Catholic identity into every aspect of the curriculum"

Indicator Self-Rating (1-4) Faith is woven throughout lessons, not just in opening/closing prayer Students see faith and science as complementary Catholic teaching is meaningfully connected to STEM content Scripture is used appropriately in STEM lessons Catholic scientists/heritage are highlighted Average Score: /4

"Leverage community and industry partnerships"

docs.title: 🙏 Educator's Prayer for C-STEM Teaching
docs.text:
Lord, help me to be a faithful teacher of Your truth. May I integrate faith and reason seamlessly, Showing my students the harmony of Your creation.

Give me patience to nurture every learner, Creativity to engage curious minds, And wisdom to connect learning to service.

Help me cultivate wonder in my classroom, That students may see Your glory in all we study. May I never tire of learning and growing So that I may better serve Your children.

Through Christ our Lord, Amen.

docs.title: 🙋 C-STREAM Volunteer Guide
docs.text:
Location: Our Lady of the Prairie Catholic School · Belle Plaine, MN · Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis

Thank you for volunteering in our C-STREAM classroom! This guide will help you support hands-on, faith-integrated STEM learning.

October 2026 safety/access note: The teacher retains responsibility. Confirm school screening, safeguarding, supervision, emergency and privacy requirements before volunteering; any claimed Archdiocesan requirement needs source verification. Share only accommodation information necessary for your assigned role. No button cells, latex balloons or projectile activities; no neodymium magnets in K. Do not repair electrical gear or handle batteries without the teacher's assigned procedure. Stop hazards and notify the teacher; suspected battery/magnet ingestion requires immediate emergency escalation. Use materials kit counts and the substitute safety guide.

docs.title: You ARE here to:
docs.text: ✅ Support students as they work ✅ Encourage when things don't work the first time ✅ Ask questions that help students think ✅ Assist with materials and supplies ✅ Celebrate effort and creativity ✅ Model curiosity and wonder

docs.title: You are NOT expected to:
docs.text: ❌ Know all the answers (it's okay to say "Let's find out together!") ❌ Do the work for students ❌ Teach the lesson (the teacher leads instruction) ❌ Grade or evaluate student work ❌ Discipline students (refer behavior issues to the teacher)

docs.title: ⏱️ Typical C-STREAM Session
docs.text: Time What's Happening Your Role Opening (2-3 min) Prayer, wonder question Participate, model reverence Introduction (5-10 min) Teacher explains activity Listen, prepare materials Hands-On Time (15-25 min) Students build/create/explore Circulate, assist, encourage Sharing (3-5 min) Students share work Listen, celebrate Closing (2 min) Cleanup, closing prayer Help with cleanup

docs.title: Instead of... Try...
docs.text: Instead of... Try... "That's wrong" "Tell me about your design" "Do it this way" "What happens if you try...?" "That won't work" "Interesting! What do you think will happen?" "Let me fix it" "What could you change?" "Good job!" "I noticed you tried 3 different ways—that's perseverance!"

docs.title: Great Questions to Ask
docs.text:
To spark thinking:

  • "What are you trying to make?"

  • "What's your plan?"

  • "What do you think will happen?"

When they're stuck:

  • "What have you tried so far?"

  • "What could you try next?"

  • "Who could you ask for ideas?"

After testing:

  • "What happened?"

  • "What worked well?"

  • "What would you change?"

Faith connections:

  • "What does this teach you about God's creation?"

  • "How could this help someone?"

  • "What are you grateful for in this project?"

docs.title: Before Class
docs.text:
• Set out materials at stations

  • Count supplies (enough for each group)

  • Test technology if applicable (iPads charged, apps open)

  • Prepare any teacher-requested materials

docs.title: During Class
docs.text:
• Circulate among groups

  • Distribute additional supplies as needed

  • Help with technology issues (basic troubleshooting)

  • Encourage struggling students

  • Redirect off-task behavior gently ("What's your next step?")

  • Take photos if requested (check photo policy first!)

docs.title: After Class
docs.text:
• Help students clean up their areas

  • Sort and organize materials

  • Count/inventory supplies

  • Wipe down tables if needed

  • Debrief with teacher (What went well? Any concerns?)

docs.title: Kindergarten (25-minute sessions)
docs.text:
• Need lots of support — Stay close, help with fine motor tasks

  • Short attention spans — Keep them focused on one step at a time

  • Encourage exploration — Mistakes inform learning; observe the specific concept and safety rules

  • Celebrate everything — "Look what you made!"

docs.title: Grades 1-2 (30-minute sessions)
docs.text:
• Building independence — Let them try before helping

  • Reading support — They may need instructions read aloud

  • Partner work — Help them collaborate nicely

  • Encourage iteration — "What if you tried it again?"

docs.title: Grades 3-4 (40-minute sessions)
docs.text:
• More independent — Step back, observe, intervene less

  • Group dynamics — Help ensure everyone participates

  • Deeper questions — Push their thinking with "why" and "how"

  • Documentation — May need help recording their process

docs.title: Grades 5-6 (45-minute sessions)
docs.text:
• Very independent — Your role is mostly material support

  • Complex projects — Ask about their design thinking

  • Leadership opportunities — Can they help others?

  • Critical thinking — Challenge them to go deeper

docs.title: A student is frustrated
docs.text:
1. Acknowledge feelings: "This is tricky, isn't it?"
  2. Normalize struggle: "Real engineers face problems too!"
  3. Focus on process: "What have you tried?"
  4. Suggest a break: "Take a breath, then look again"
  5. Celebrate effort: "I see you're not giving up!"

docs.title: A project "fails"
docs.text:
1. Reframe it: "That's data! Now you know what doesn't work."
  2. Connect to learning: "What did you learn from this?"
  3. Encourage iteration: "How could you change it?"
  4. Share stories: "Even famous inventors failed many times!"

docs.title: Students are arguing
docs.text:
1. Stay neutral: "What's the disagreement about?"
  2. Facilitate: "Can you each share your idea?"
  3. Problem-solve: "Is there a way to try both?"
  4. Involve teacher if needed

docs.title: You don't know the answer
docs.text:
1. Be honest: "Great question! I'm not sure."
  2. Model learning: "Let's think about this together."
  3. Ask the student: "What do YOU think?"
  4. Check with teacher if needed

docs.title: A student is off-task
docs.text:
1. Redirect gently: "What step are you on?"
  2. Give a job: "Can you be the materials manager?"
  3. Move closer: Sometimes proximity is enough
  4. Involve teacher for persistent issues

docs.title: Technology doesn't work
docs.text:
1. Basic troubleshooting: Restart app, check connections
  2. Use the teacher's named backup; paper algorithms do not demonstrate real programming/robot execution
  3. Pair students: Share working devices
  4. Stay calm: Tech problems happen to everyone

docs.title: ✝️ Faith Integration Tips
docs.text: C-STREAM isn't just STEM—it's Catholic STEM! Help students make faith connections:

docs.title: Simple Connections
docs.text:
• "Isn't it amazing that God created all of this?"

  • "How does this show God's love for us?"

  • "Engineers help people—just like we're called to do!"

  • "What can this teach us about being patient like God is with us?"

docs.title: When Students Struggle
docs.text:
• "God doesn't give up on us, and we don't give up on our projects!"

  • "Making mistakes is part of how God helps us learn."

  • "Let's ask God to help us figure this out."

docs.title: During Teamwork
docs.text:
• "How are we showing kindness to our teammates?"

  • "Jesus worked with a team too—his disciples!"

  • "Using our talents together is how we serve God."

docs.title: Print and keep with you! ✂️
docs.text:
C-STREAM VOLUNTEER QUICK GUIDE

DO:

  • Ask questions, don't give answers

  • Encourage every attempt

  • Let them struggle a little (productive struggle!)

  • Celebrate effort, not just success

  • Connect to faith when natural

SAY:

  • "Tell me about your design"

  • "What could you try next?"

  • "That's great problem-solving!"

  • "How does this help us appreciate God's creation?"

WHEN STUCK:

  • "What have you tried?"

  • "What's one thing you could change?"

  • "Can you ask a classmate?"

REMEMBER:

  • It's okay not to know the answer

  • "Failure" is learning

  • Process matters more than product

  • You're modeling curiosity!

docs.title: ❓ Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: What if I'm not good at science/technology? A: That's okay! You're here to support and encourage, not teach. Your enthusiasm matters more than expertise.

Q: Can I help my own child's class? A: Usually yes! Check with the teacher about classroom policies.

Q: What if a student says something about faith I don't know how to answer? A: It's fine to say, "That's a great question! Let's ask [teacher] or you could ask your parents."

Q: Should I post photos on social media? A: Please don't post photos of students without explicit school permission. Many families have privacy concerns.

Q: How often should I volunteer? A: Whatever works for you! Weekly, monthly, or special events—all help is appreciated.

Q: What if I can't make my scheduled time? A: Let the teacher know as soon as possible so they can adjust plans.

docs.title: 🙏 Volunteer Prayer
docs.text:
Before serving:

Lord, thank You for the opportunity to serve these children. Help me encourage their curiosity, celebrate their efforts, and point them toward You in all they learn. Give me patience when things are challenging and joy in their discoveries. Amen.

docs.title: ✨ Wonder and Curiosity Guide
docs.text:
This resource provides strategies for cultivating the sense of wonder that is foundational to Catholic STEM education.

October 2026 teaching/source note: Preserve the observation/questioning practices; numerical claims, quotations and historical/theological attributions below are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before classroom copying. An observation does not experimentally prove a theological conclusion. Invite gratitude without grading spontaneous awe or interior belief. Use concrete stewardship/dignity decisions, not a literal comparison of God to an engineer/scientist/artist. Magnet demonstrations require age-appropriate large encapsulated ferrite equipment; no neodymium magnets in K. See safety and kits.

"Approaching education from the perspective of wonder, exploration, and faith will ignite the love of learning."

docs.title: 📋 Overview
docs.text:
Wonder is the starting point of both scientific inquiry and faith. When we marvel at God's creation, we are drawn to understand it more deeply through science and to worship the Creator who made it.

The Wonder Cycle: 

     +----------------------+
     |                      |
     v                      |
  WONDER          GRATITUDE/WORSHIP
     |                      ^
     v                      |
 CURIOSITY         UNDERSTANDING
     |                      ^
     v                      |
  INQUIRY ---------------►-+

docs.title: 🌟 What is Wonder in Catholic Education?
Wonder vs. Simple Curiosity
docs.text: Simple Curiosity Catholic Wonder "How does that work?" "How amazing that God designed this!" Satisfied by an answer Deepened by understanding Leads to knowledge Leads to knowledge AND worship Self-focused learning Learning as response to God

docs.title: Wonder as Gateway to Faith and Science
docs.text:
Wonder serves as a "privileged gateway into the divine order of things." When students wonder at creation:

  • They are drawn to study it (science)

  • They are drawn to praise the Creator (faith)

  • They see that faith and science lead to the same truth

docs.title: 1. Wonder Questions
docs.text: Start lessons with questions that evoke awe:

docs.title: For Young Children (K-2)
docs.text:
• "Have you ever watched a butterfly and wondered how it knows how to fly?"

  • "Isn't it amazing that tiny seeds grow into huge trees?"

  • "Why do you think God made so many different kinds of animals?"

  • "Have you ever wondered why the sky changes colors?"

docs.title: For Grades 3-5
docs.text:
• "How is it possible that your heart beats 100,000 times every day without you thinking about it?"

  • "What do you wonder about when you look at the stars?"

  • "Did you know there are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on Earth?"

  • "How do birds know where to fly when they migrate thousands of miles?"

docs.title: For Grades 6-8
docs.text:
• "Scientists estimate there are 37 trillion cells in your body, all working together. How is that possible?"

  • "The same mathematical patterns appear in shells, flowers, and galaxies. Why do you think that is?"

  • "What would it be like to be the first person to discover something no one knew before?"

  • "How can studying atoms help us understand the universe?"

docs.title: 2. Wonder Moments
docs.text:
Build "wonder pauses" into your lessons:

Before Instruction: "Before I tell you how this works, take a moment to wonder about it. What do you notice? What surprises you?"

During Activities: "Stop and look at what you created. Isn't it amazing that you figured that out?"

After Learning: "Now that you understand this better, does it make you wonder about anything else?"

Connecting to Faith: "When I learned this, I was amazed at how God designed creation. What amazes you?"

docs.title: 3. The "Wow" Collection
docs.text:
Create a classroom practice of collecting "wows":

Daily Wow Board: Students can add observations that made them say "wow" throughout the week.

Wonder Journal: Students keep a journal where they record things that amaze them about creation.

Wow Sharing: Begin or end class with students sharing something that made them wonder.

docs.title: 4. Mystery Before Explanation
docs.text:
Present phenomena before explaining them:

Traditional Approach: "Today we're going to learn about magnets. Magnets have two poles..."

Wonder Approach: Show two magnets attracting and repelling "Watch this... Why do you think that happens? What do you wonder about this?" Let students observe and question before explaining

docs.title: 5. Connecting Wonder to the Creator
docs.text:
Explicitly connect wonder to faith:

Example Script: "Scientists have discovered that butterfly wings have tiny scales that create their beautiful colors. When I learned this, I was amazed at how detailed God's creation is—even in things we can barely see! What does this tell us about God?"

Reflection Questions:

  • "What does this tell us about the Creator?"

  • "Why do you think God made the world with so much detail and beauty?"

  • "How does understanding this make you feel about God?"

  • "What might you say to God about what you learned today?"

docs.title: Opening Wonder (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Purpose: Spark curiosity and connect to faith

Activities:

  • Wonder question

  • Mystery object/phenomenon

  • "What do you notice? What do you wonder?"

  • Brief moment of awe at creation

Prayer Connection: "Lord, open our eyes to the wonders of Your creation today."

docs.title: Sustained Wonder (During Instruction)
docs.text:
Purpose: Maintain engagement and curiosity

Techniques:

  • Pause for "wow moments" when content is particularly amazing

  • Ask "Isn't that amazing?" and mean it

  • Share your own wonder: "When I first learned this, I couldn't believe..."

  • Point out complexity and beauty: "Think about how intricate this is..."

docs.title: Reflective Wonder (Closing)
docs.text:
Purpose: Deepen learning and connect to faith

Activities:

  • "What was the most amazing thing you learned today?"

  • "What new questions do you have now?"

  • "How does what you learned today make you think about God?"

  • "What do you want to explore more?"

Prayer Connection: "Thank You, Lord, for the wonder of [specific content]. Help us to keep wondering and learning about Your creation."

docs.title: 🎨 Creating a "Place of Wonder and Awe"
docs.text: Transform your STEM space into a wonder-inducing environment:

docs.title: Physical Environment
docs.text:
• Display "wonder questions" on walls

  • Include images of amazing natural phenomena

  • Create a "wonder corner" with intriguing objects

  • Use natural light when possible

  • Include plants or natural elements

  • Display student "wow" discoveries

docs.title: Learning Environment
docs.text:
• Welcome questions without judgment

  • Model curiosity yourself

  • Celebrate "I wonder..." statements

  • Allow time for observation

  • Connect discoveries to the Creator

  • Create space for quiet wonder

docs.title: Spiritual Environment
docs.text:
• Include religious imagery connecting faith and creation

  • Display quotes from Catholic scientists

  • Post relevant Scripture verses

  • Pray with wonder and gratitude

  • Reference patron saints of science

docs.title: Life Sciences
docs.text:
• "Did you know that you started as a single cell smaller than a dot?"

  • "How do plants 'know' to grow toward light?"

  • "Why do you think there are so many different species of beetles?"

  • "How does your body know how to heal a cut?"

docs.title: Earth Sciences
docs.text:
• "What do you think the Earth looked like a million years ago?"

  • "How did mountains form?"

  • "Why does the moon change shape?"

  • "What's at the center of the Earth?"

docs.title: Physical Sciences
docs.text:
• "Why does ice float when most things sink?"

  • "How can sound travel through walls?"

  • "What makes fire?"

  • "Why is the sky blue?"

docs.title: Technology/Engineering
docs.text:
• "How did people solve this problem before technology?"

  • "What if you could invent anything—what would help people most?"

  • "How do computers 'think'?"

  • "What makes a bridge strong?"

docs.title: Space
docs.text:
• "How far away is the nearest star?"

  • "What do you think is beyond the edge of the universe?"

  • "How many galaxies do you think exist?"

  • "What would it be like to stand on Mars?"

docs.title: From Wonder to Praise
docs.text:
Help students see the natural connection between wonder and worship:

Wonder Statement → Worship Response

Wonder Worship "The human body is so complex!" "Thank You, God, for making us so wonderfully." "The universe is so vast!" "How great is our God who made all this!" "This pattern is so beautiful!" "Lord, You are an amazing artist." "How can this work so perfectly?" "Your wisdom, God, is beyond understanding."

docs.title: Scripture Connections for Wonder
docs.text:
Psalm 19:1 - "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands."

Psalm 139:14 - "I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well."

Job 12:7-10 - "But ask the animals, and they will teach you, or the birds in the sky, and they will tell you; or speak to the earth, and it will teach you, or let the fish in the sea inform you. Which of all these does not know that the hand of the Lord has done this?"

Sirach 42:15-17 - "Now I will recall God's works; what I have seen, I will describe... The clear vault of the sky shines forth like heaven itself, a vision of glory."

docs.title: ✨ Teacher Self-Assessment: Wonder
docs.text:
Rate yourself:

Indicator Rating (1-4) I genuinely wonder at the content I teach I communicate wonder to my students I ask wonder-provoking questions I allow time for students to wonder I connect wonder to the Creator My classroom environment promotes wonder Students express wonder and curiosity

Goal for cultivating more wonder:

Guide Version: 2.0 Framework: C-STREAM Based on: Catholic Educational Philosophy & Wonder-Based Pedagogy

docs.title: 2026-27 curriculum review
docs.text:
Reviewed beginning October 4, 2026. This is a local curriculum-development review, not an Archdiocesan approval or certification of official standards coverage.

Current generated program totals are regenerated with the lesson/material maps rather than inferred from filenames or old report snapshots. They describe documents and planned evidence/use—not observed student outcomes or physical school holdings.

Start with the executive review, then choose the relevant grade review and read the actual lesson before teaching. The audits distinguish baseline concerns from revised lessons; complete written instructions do not replace a counted kit, local safety/access checks or an actual classroom trial.

Completed reference library: all 251 K-6 documents now have complete conditional written pathways. See the K closeout and source-verified external candidates. The other three band reviews likewise document closure of their written package queues. Remaining physical/source/pilot gates are explicit in the school release checklist.

docs.title: Before scheduling
docs.text:
1. Choose one schedule and one rotation, not all available tracks.
  2. Check revision, technology, materials and open concerns in the lesson audit.
  3. Use the local progression to select the younger/older grade expectation.
  4. Prepare the actual kit and verify accommodations and school safety procedures.
  5. Collect one individual piece of evidence, even when students work in teams.
  6. Record what students demonstrated; do not infer mastery from participation.

Hold any unresolved P0 activity. Substitute a documented safe lesson that meets a stated objective rather than improvising with unknown materials, unavailable equipment or unsuitable weather.

docs.title: Executive curriculum review
docs.text: School: Our Lady of the Prairie, Belle Plaine, Minnesota; Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis. Planning year: 2026-27. Review/completion work: October 4, 2026.

docs.title: Overall judgment
docs.text:
The baseline was a substantial useful activity bank, not a uniformly usable, verified academic program. The completed repository now provides 251 complete conditional lesson references, intentional local K-6 progression, individual planned evidence, scalable materials, realistic periods, source boundaries, teacher/family systems and automated consistency checks.

This is document completion, not an Archdiocesan approval, full state-subject coverage certification, physical-kit inspection or classroom-outcome study. The school release checklist identifies the checks a repository review cannot perform.

docs.title: Preserved structure and completed lessons
docs.text:
Band Weekly files Bi-weekly files Complete references K 20 17 37 1-2 40 34 74 3-4 37 34 71 5-6 35 34 69 Total 132 119 251

All original lesson URLs, baseline dispositions/priorities and meeting allocations are preserved. The final state is 251 rebuilt packages, 0 improved-only, 0 unchanged outlines. Audit history is not erased or downgraded to imply formal safety closure.

Across all alternatives the library represents 345 teaching meetings. That is not one pupil's year. Choose one weekly/bi-weekly track and rotation; compare actual meetings with school holidays. Native periods remain 25/30/40/45 minutes.

The current generated summary gives map/resource totals. The validation record and band reviews document content, timing, quantity and evidence checks rather than inferring readiness from a filename.

docs.title: Standards environment and traceability
docs.text:
For 2026-27, verified Minnesota implementation editions are science 2019, arts 2018, ELA 2020 and social studies 2021. Mathematics 2022 begins full implementation in 2027-28; retain the 2007 planning baseline unless the school intentionally transitions early. CSTA 2026 was published in July 2026 and uses different elementary organization from 2017.

The 18 CST competencies are locally created, not fabricated Archdiocesan benchmarks. They survive lesson changes and support 126 grade targets/stages. The local map contains 929 planned evidence links.

The external matrix provides 29 narrow, source-verified candidates using sixteen identifiers across twenty-six lessons. A separate register records twenty-four inspected arts/CSTA identifiers. State-agency arts copies retain MDE-copy/school review; CSTA is national, not automatically adopted Minnesota guidance.

Final MDE tables inaccessible through normal retrieval are not replaced with guessed science/math/ELA/social-studies numbers. The program complements primary subjects; a topic resemblance, device or local code cannot certify official coverage. Obtain school-issued OMCE guidance before claiming institutional alignment.

docs.title: Classroom practicality
docs.text:
Every reference supplies native-period directions, exact class-size quantities, individual evidence, safety/access, troubleshooting, cleanup and family copy. No package requires hidden institutional knowledge as its written minimum; actual kits, software, room, contacts and approvals still need local confirmation.

The eight reported individual OHM-135 Snap Circuits kits are preserved as reported—not inspected—stock. Four selected Grades 3-6 routes use matching manual/project checks and bounded hardware waves. Snap is not automatically equivalent to protected-AA or modular electronics; K remains optional adult demonstration only.

The original conditional first-year budgets remain $229.52 / $476.04 / $854.32 / $2,367.84. They fund a modest core on stated cohort/stock assumptions, not every optional item in every alternative track. Prices/specifications and actual replenishment require local checks. Do not purchase every catalog row.

Technology labels describe the selected primary pathway, not every extension. Paper reasoning can preserve computational concepts but cannot establish actual software, sensor, robot or electrical operation. Declare what was deferred.

docs.title: What to do next at school
docs.text:
1. Select the actual schedule/rotation and next reference, not the entire bank.
  2. Complete the counted-kit, safety/access and pretest release checks.
  3. Pilot younger/older references; measure real preparation/cleanup and supply use.
  4. Gather individual evidence, with two dated observations at local mastery checkpoints.
  5. Finish authorized official-source/institutional review before restoring stronger claims.

There is no remaining written-package queue to disguise as "future improvements." Remaining release work is real school/source/pilot evidence, explicitly separated from the repository checks and recorded in the implementation plan.

docs.title: Source-verified external alignment candidates
docs.text:
Combined candidate matrix | Verified benchmark register | Authority and implementation register

This matrix is separate from the local standards map. It provides exact external identifiers, individual grades, lesson tasks, planned evidence and claim boundaries. It is not full subject coverage, school/diocesan approval or proof that students mastered a benchmark.

docs.title: Minnesota arts, 2018
docs.text:
The state-agency Perpich workbook was directly inspected, including exact Kindergarten and Grades 1-6 rows. The workbook defines grade 0 as K and shows arts area, grade, strand, anchor standard and benchmark in each identifier. The inspected identifiers are listed individually in the register, not manufactured from a grade pattern.

The workbook itself identifies MDE's hosted Excel as the official version. The source-verified state-agency copy therefore retains a MDE-copy corroboration and school-review hold for formal institutional claims. Its 2018 edition is the implemented arts reference for 2026-27.

A visual-design topic is insufficient. Proposed links require actual child-created or child-directed art, appropriate artistic foundations and the specific evidence the benchmark expects. A mechanical redesign alone is not artistic revision; a picture in a lesson is not evidence of art creation.

docs.title: CSTA national computer science, 2026
docs.text:
The publisher's current viewer and its ordinary public index/detail responses were inspected directly. The exact identifiers, grade placement and clarifications are recorded in the register. Retrieval used the same unauthenticated read operations as the public viewer, not restricted materials or a login bypass.

Elementary grades have separate identifiers; Grade 6 uses the 6-8 band. Do not reuse the 2017 elementary bands as 2026 grade organization. This is a verified national framework, not automatically adopted Minnesota or Archdiocesan standards.

Respect the full scope:

  • Grade 2 algorithm creation includes sequence, events and repetition.
  • Grade ¾ mappings cover sequence, events, repetition and selection across one or more algorithms, with the appropriate written/visual representation.
  • Grade 5's representation includes variables and the required structures.
  • The selected middle-school correctness benchmark needs a given algorithm, specified inputs, expected/actual outputs and verification by trace or execution.
  • Paper can evidence permitted tracing/conceptual work, but never actual software execution or robot/sensor operation.

Partial practice is described as partial or omitted from a full benchmark claim. A named code, apparatus or teacher demonstration cannot supply missing individual evidence.

The matrix gives each grade's evidence rather than assigning both grades in a band the same external expectation. Access supports can preserve a target; when an alternative changes it, record the scope and deferred evidence.

docs.title: Unavailable official tables
docs.text:
Normal retrieval of final MDE science, mathematics, ELA and social-studies tables did not provide readable source documents. Browser-verification HTML is not the underlying standard, and a repealed rule or NGSS/Common Core identifier is not a substitute. No guessed external number is published. Use the local framework for the taught enrichment outcomes and withhold unsupported official coverage claims pending authorized source access.

The school release checklist identifies the remaining institutional/source checks without blocking documented safe local learning simply because an unsupported external claim is withheld.

docs.title: Regeneration and verification
docs.text:
.\scripts\Build-CurriculumMaps.ps1
.\scripts\Build-ExternalAlignment.ps1
.\scripts\Build-ExternalAlignment.ps1 -ValidateOnly

The external builder checks exact source IDs/URLs/editions, grade placement, lesson existence/band, required scope/evidence, authority boundaries, duplicate links and generated-matrix freshness against the source-verified register. Editorial task/evidence review and actual classroom assessment remain separate.

docs.title: Family communication system
docs.text: October 2026. C-STREAM is Catholic identity + science + technology + religion/faith integration + engineering + arts (including music) + mathematics. C shapes purpose/dignity/stewardship; R is explicit faith teaching/reflection. Music belongs within A; M means mathematics. Art involves observation, composition, form, performance or communication, not decoration alone.

docs.title: One copy system, not competing guides
docs.text:
1. At unit launch, complete the newsletter block.
  2. At completion, change planned verbs to what students actually did and include a specific result/skill. Send an additional update when objectives change.
  3. Keep the teacher-only trace: lesson path, objective, selected local code, individual prompt and evidence threshold. Verify official/Church source claims separately. VERIFICATION REQUIRED for unverified quotations, diocesan requirements or biographies.
  4. Copy through the school's actual approved newsletter/email/paper route. Provide translation/read-aloud support as locally arranged; no invented platform.
  5. Keep learning at school. No routine homework, purchases, donations, accounts, outdoor exposure, home device, photo submission or event attendance required. All home activities below are optional, ungraded and can be skipped.

Existing entry points Weekly Parent Sheet and Parent Communication Guide use the same block. Do not send two contradictory versions. If an exceptional required home task is proposed, document why it cannot reasonably happen in class, obtain school approval and provide an equally accessible school alternative; the default remains no routine homework.

docs.title: Ready-to-adapt unit examples for every grade
docs.text: These are example copy, not claims that these units have already been taught or an independent scope/sequence. Adapt to the actual band lesson and assessed objective. Do not claim device programming if the class used paper.

docs.title: Kindergarten - Notice and make patterns
docs.text:
What we explored: Repeating patterns and careful observation. What students did: Sorted large classroom objects, built a two-part pattern and drew or pointed to its next part. What they learned: To notice a repeating unit and show what comes next. Our Catholic connection: We practiced caring for shared materials and giving each classmate a turn as we explored creation with gratitude. Ask your child: "Can you show the two parts of your pattern and what comes next?" Try this at home, optional: Make a clap-pause-clap-pause pattern together for one minute; use silent hand motions if sound is uncomfortable. No supplies.

Teacher trace: each child completes/explains a pattern orally or by pointing; adult modeling/read-aloud replaces independent reading. Select the matching arts/math code from Local Standards.

docs.title: Grade 1 - Sound and rhythmic phrases
docs.text:
What we explored: How a pattern of sound and silence makes a rhythmic phrase. What students did: Compared gentle tapping sounds and composed a four-beat phrase using claps and pauses. What they learned: To repeat a phrase and explain one intentional sound/silence choice. Music was an artistic activity, not just background noise. Our Catholic connection: We used our gifts to listen to and include one another; a silent pattern was an equally welcome response. Ask your child: "Can you perform your four beats and show where the pause is?" Try this at home, optional: Echo one four-beat phrase with hands or silent motions for a minute. No instruments or recording required.

Teacher trace: individual phrase/repetition, not participation or singing talent; select the taught A/math/science competency only where evidenced.

docs.title: Grade 2 - Directions and debugging
docs.text:
What we explored: Algorithms: ordered instructions, and how to fix an error. What students did: Used large arrow cards to move a paper pointer on a desk grid, tested the route, and changed an incorrect turn. What they learned: To explain how the changed instruction affected the route. This was unplugged computing, not a claim that software was programmed. Our Catholic connection: We considered how clear, respectful directions help other people and why responsibility matters when using tools. Ask your child: "Which arrow did you change, and where did the pointer go after that?" Try this at home, optional: Give a seated partner two safe hand-motion instructions, then reverse them and compare. No blindfold, walking maze or food.

Teacher trace: individual sequence trace and correction; actual device execution is assessed later if it is a separate objective.

docs.title: Grade 3 - Paper bridges and fair comparisons
docs.text:
What we explored: How changing a paper structure can change its performance. What students did: Planned, built, tested and improved paper bridges under common test conditions. What they learned: To name an observed result, keep test conditions the same, and explain a change using evidence, even when a bridge collapsed. Our Catholic connection: We considered how reliable structures serve people and why using shared materials responsibly matters. Ask your child: "What stayed the same in your two tests, and what did you change?" Try this at home, optional: Look at the shape of an ordinary book spine or folded paper already nearby and talk about what a fold might change. No building, weights, purchase or homework submission required.

Teacher trace: use the rebuilt bridge lesson and its exact individual check; this copy does not impose a different span/load.

docs.title: Grade 4 - Indoor insulation and evidence
docs.text:
What we explored: Comparing how materials affect temperature change. What students did: Used a teacher-prepared indoor comparison, measured at the same planned times and represented results on paper. What they learned: To compare temperature changes with units and describe what was held constant. Conclusions were limited to the classroom test. Our Catholic connection: We considered responsible resource use and how good evidence can inform care for people and creation. Ask your child: "Which comparison result supported your claim, and what stayed the same?" Try this at home, optional: Discuss why a familiar blanket may help keep a person warm. No heating, outdoor experiment or materials needed.

Teacher trace: publish this only after the planned safe indoor investigation; no claim about outdoor testing, hot liquids or guaranteed material performance.

docs.title: Grade 5 - Closed electrical paths
docs.text:
What we explored: What happens when a protected low-voltage circuit path is closed or opened. What students did: Took supervised turns connecting a protected AA pack and current-limited light module, then opened the path and compared outputs. What they learned: To identify a complete path and explain the observed change. Drawing a circuit alone was not the practical test. Our Catholic connection: We discussed using knowledge responsibly and caring for equipment and people rather than wasting energy or taking unsafe shortcuts. Ask your child: "What changed when the path opened, and which observation showed that?" Try this at home, optional: Point to a familiar room-light switch and discuss its purpose without opening it, handling batteries or touching wiring.

Teacher trace: each child's actual supervised circuit action and explanation; record any missing hands-on evidence as NE.

docs.title: Grade 6 - Design choices for people
docs.text:
What we explored: How criteria, cost and user needs influence a design. What students did: Compared classroom paper/model prototypes and communicated a design choice using measured evidence and a clear visual explanation. What they learned: To defend a choice and name a tradeoff or limitation. Our models were not certified devices or real-world solutions. Our Catholic connection: Human dignity and stewardship informed whom the design included and how resources were used. Ask your child: "Which result supported your choice, and who might need a different design?" Try this at home, optional: Discuss one familiar door handle or container: who might find it easy or difficult to use? No disability simulation, purchase or alteration of household equipment.

Teacher trace: individual evidence/tradeoff explanation; select only practiced engineering, arts, math and Catholic competencies.

docs.title: Project/events/donations and privacy
docs.text:
The school provides required materials and class work time. An optional event celebrates the same evidence, not family-funded polish. Invitations include a non-attendance route (in-class sharing or a generic newsletter summary). Requests for clean recyclables say explicitly: "Donations are optional; every student will have school-provided supplies." Staff screen all donated items.

Use anonymous/general class descriptions by default. Student names, images, audio, scores and identifiable work require the school's verified consent/ privacy process; no public upload or personal account is assumed.

docs.title: Parent simulation
docs.text: A teacher can answer "What is my child learning?" with: a specific concept, student action, individual success evidence, Catholic decision and next learning step. A bare "fun craft" or "used an iPad" is insufficient. Progression/official alignment belongs to the shared review; local codes are not state or diocesan accreditation claims.

docs.title: Curriculum gap analysis
docs.text:
A gap can be missing content, insufficient depth, missing individual evidence, an unsuitable prerequisite, or an unusable teaching procedure. The existence of a file or tag does not close it. The detailed band reviews and audit rationale fields provide the lesson-level evidence.

Autonomous K closure: all 37 K documents are complete references, with dated weather comparison, hypothetical privacy/adult-help scenarios, requested book criteria/tradeoffs and formerly audit-only individual checks implemented. Every K primary-material term is cataloged; twelve arts candidates have exact source-verified identifiers. This closes those document-level gaps, not actual school stock, official full-subject coverage or observed mastery.

All-grade closeout: the other 214 lesson documents are also complete conditional references. Fair retests, individual checks, grade-specific support/challenge, complete timed sequences and explicit material/pathway boundaries replace the earlier package queues. Baseline weaknesses remain historical evidence, not a claim that every old defect is still active. Full external subject coverage and actual mastery remain separate checks.

docs.title: Program-wide gaps and controls
docs.text: Area to investigate Baseline concern or evidence limit Improvement and closure evidence Official standards No structured, verified benchmark-to-task-to-assessment map in the baseline Source register and local map added; official benchmark alignment remains VERIFICATION REQUIRED until reviewed against the applicable version. Grade progression Combined-grade activities do not automatically define seven distinct expectations Local K-6 performance progression; collect individual evidence at the younger/older expectation rather than awarding mastery for exposure. Pacing Legacy planner/menu totals double-count time and extend beyond the claimed year Corrected calendar and document-level meeting records; compare the chosen track with the actual school timetable. Substitute usability General guide refers to quick-reference packets without proving they exist Revised reference lessons and common template; complete remaining scheduled P1 lessons and conduct actual kit walkthroughs. Early readers Written journals, vocabulary and independent directions can hide a reading prerequisite Model, point, draw, tell and manipulate; verify an emerging reader can meet the objective without another child doing the thinking. Devices and computing Equipment/app use can be mistaken for computational thinking Require an algorithm trace/debugging explanation; distinguish that from real digital execution and hardware operation. Indoor access Nature, weather and growth topics do not guarantee an indoor pathway Specify the indoor procedure and objective; prepared data/models must not be described as a child's firsthand measurement. Materials/cost Specialty kits and assumed school stocks obscure a minimum budget Normalized core inventory, budget ceilings and kits; verify local stock and distinguish optional legacy equipment from core purchases. Assessment Group products and participation can hide individual understanding A named oral/drawn/demonstrated evidence check and objective-linked rubric for each scheduled lesson. Catholic identity Prayers, metaphors, saint references and technological enthusiasm are not enough Students give an age-appropriate reason about truth, dignity, stewardship or service; verify historical/scriptural attributions. Arts Digital tools and decoration can replace genuine artistic learning Observational sketches, purposeful form/pattern, communication, feedback and artistic revision; assess the stated art objective, not polish. Homework/equity Take-home continuation can make household support a hidden prerequisite No routine homework; class evidence and optional no-purchase family questions. Safety "Safe materials," unspecified samples and small electrical parts are not sufficient controls Exact approved supplies, adult-only steps, stop rules and local policy checks; hold unresolved P0 activities. Year A/B continuity A returning student's changed project does not prove more sophisticated reasoning Reestablish prerequisites in either entry year; preserve a small portfolio and increase independence/evidence, not simply product size.

docs.title: Content questions that must not disappear
docs.text:
The repository has named activities in physical, life and Earth science, structures, weather, light/circuits, robots/coding, art and service. This is evidence of available contexts, not complete subject coverage. Use the lesson map to locate intended evidence, then check the following across the selected schedule and both rotation entry years:

Competency Minimum closure evidence Electricity before middle school A safe, age-appropriate complete/open-circuit investigation with an explanation; neither a craft light nor a robot alone proves understanding. Data interpretation Each student interprets a table, graph or organized comparison appropriate to the grade. Measurement progression Count/compare -> consistent unit -> record/compare -> repeated measurements -> justified precision and limitations. Engineering redesign An actual second test after a justified change, not only a drawing of an imagined improvement. Life science Observations or an explicitly labeled model explain living things, change or interdependence; plants need follow-up time. Earth/space science Evidence/modeling of weather, seasonal change or systems, with a scientifically accurate explanation. Physical science Students investigate an effect such as force, motion, light, sound, energy or circuits rather than only name it. Unplugged computing Students trace, predict, debug or revise instructions; later grades encounter loops/conditions/data as appropriate. Technology ethics A reasoned decision about users, accessibility, resources, privacy or impacts; not just a device rule list. Catholic scientific heritage A verified, relevant example with a distinction between biography, Church teaching and scientific evidence. Stewardship A concrete decision about reuse, waste, care or service and a student explanation. Hands-on mathematics Quantities/measurements/data used to reason about the activity, not decorative numbers. Student choice A choice within understandable criteria/constraints, followed by a reason. Independent and collaborative work Team activity plus an individual check; roles do not permanently assign one child all reasoning or tool use. Communication A drawing, model, oral explanation or display communicates evidence to an audience and receives feedback. Learning from failure Students describe what a test showed, change an appropriate feature and try again without blaming the student.

Do not "fill a gap" by adding another topic title. Identify the exact grade, rotation, meeting, student action and evidence; reduce competing activities if necessary. The scope and sequence prioritizes fewer, better investigations.

docs.title: Band-level evidence and next work
docs.text:
• Kindergarten: nonreader access, short-period routines, observation/manipulation and safe indoor options.
  • Grades 1-2: oral-to-recorded explanation, instructional sequences, measured comparison and accessible design choices.
  • Grades 3-4: fair tests, data, real redesign and grade-appropriate arithmetic.
  • Grades 5-6: systems, evidence quality, computing, inclusive design and justified tradeoffs.

See the implementation plan for priorities and teaching-release gates. A desk review cannot certify that any of these competencies has been mastered by actual students.

docs.title: 1. Completion and boundaries
docs.text:
All 61 remaining lesson packages have been fully rebuilt, not relabeled or supplemented with a generic appendix. Their main legacy plans were replaced with coherent teacher-facing instructions. The 13 earlier rebuilt lesson bodies are byte-for-byte preserved. The current inventory is 74 complete documented references, with no improved or unchanged revision rows and no remaining HOLD/REVIEW package gaps in the 61 replacements.

This is documented/local-validation completion, not observed classroom outcomes, school approval, device availability or a promise that every child will meet every criterion. Actual stock, equipment condition, local policy, accommodations and a classroom pilot remain conditional. These are ordinary implementation checks, not a newly invented repository backlog.

Owned changes: the four Grades 1-2 lesson folders, their four READMEs, this review and the 74-row audit. No shared resources, standards, maps, navigation, other grade bands, nested agents or commits were changed by this completion work. Shared purchasing, official standards mapping and program integration belong to the parent.

Before editing, the current review, audit, all 74 lessons and four READMEs were frozen in the session artifact folder grades12-completion-baseline. Individually authored replacement records, staged packages and local check results are also retained in session artifacts, not committed tooling.

The exact 19-column header is:

docs.title: 3. What was completed in the main teaching plans
docs.text:
Each of the 61 replacements includes:

  1. A native-period overview with objective, purpose, Catholic classroom connection, local codes, technology requirement, prep and cleanup.
  2. Concrete before-class actions, a reusable kit allocation and a board-ready record layout. No missing worksheet or independent web research is required.
  3. A complete physical supply table for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils, distinguishing student, kit and class quantities. Teams of at most three use 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 table kits; scarce-device/circuit lessons state their separate three-kit wave route.
  4. Concise vocabulary/background, a specific misconception and an actual "If asked" response.
  5. Every original meeting explicitly timed 0-3 / 3-7 / 7-20 / 20-26 / 26-30. The final four minutes are cleanup, not borrowed extra time. The 13 references keep their original complete native timings.
  6. A usable individual record and distinct Grade 1/Grade 2 criteria. The teacher checks during practice and comparison; there are no 25-child speeches hidden in a six-minute exit block.
  7. Visible SAFETY, nonreader/physical/sensory access, a support path, a bounded challenge, specific troubleshooting, an indoor default and optional family copy.

The shared format is a teaching structure, not identical content: steps, tests, materials, questions, evidence and troubleshooting are individually authored for the actual context. A leaf observation, lamp path, squirrel habitat, arithmetic game, service invention, musical phrase and portfolio explanation are not all described as paper engineering.

docs.title: Safety and accuracy closures
docs.text:
Unsafe original options are removed from the replacement instruction, not retained under a permissive new label:

  • No flames, glass mirrors, student sharp puncturing, Sun viewing/focusing or eye-directed beams.
  • No high-shelf reaching, body attachments, real mobility/medical-device testing, heavy tower loads, catapults, lever launches or live butterfly acquisition/release.
  • No loose high-powered magnets, filings or exposed tiny clips; the magnet task uses counted encased tools and a sealed sample.
  • No latex balloon drums, mouth-shared instruments, forced loud sound, food gifts, child fasting requirements, compulsory donations or unsafe litter collection.
  • Protected lamp paths use matched closed AA packs, current-limited modules and designated connections with power OFF. No bare-cell improvisation, mains power, bare LEDs, student cell replacement or shorting pack terminals.
  • Pupa and dormant processes are living processes, not biological Resurrection. Soil is not plant food; no guaranteed germination date is invented. Paper stars do not emit light or show true stellar distances.
  • Model data, teacher-observed data, real pupil observations, predictions and faith imagery are explicitly distinguished. Unexpected, equal or unsuccessful results remain honest results.
  • Unsupported scientist origin stories, Magi counts/professions/travel, Saul/Paul renaming, unverified saint anecdotes and attributed quotations are omitted. The only new historical contexts are the short source-checked Mendel/abbey and Agnesi/mathematics-service paraphrases below.

docs.title: Grade 1
docs.text:
Entry does not require reading, writing paragraphs, past rotation attendance or a personal device. Teacher-read icons, pointing, drawing, large materials and child-directed partner actions make the reasoning accessible. Record actual operator separately: a partner's hardware/software operation does not demonstrate the child's independent operation.

Expected evidence where actually taught:

  • Represent two observed details; ask a question; distinguish a clearly modeled/observed feature from a guess.
  • Count relevant objects once, align measurement starts, compare same-unit lengths and extend an AB unit.
  • Name a user need, show a safe test and identify a changed feature.
  • Order/run a short sequence on the chosen route, with actual hardware/app operation recorded only after a personal turn.
  • Convey a purposeful visual/musical idea and respond to a specific clarity comment.
  • Explain a protective/resource-care/inclusion action rather than only recite a prayer.

Signature: Bridge Building, a preserved reference, and the measured extension Strong Bridges. The child explains the span/load comparison and a tested change; no strongest-child ranking.

docs.title: Grade 2
docs.text:
Grade 2 rechecks the same foundations, then adds interpretation, controlled comparison and defended choices. Another robot brand is not inherently a higher cognitive level.

Expected evidence where actually taught:

  • Explain an observation/model/faith distinction and an evidence limit.
  • Record comparable lengths with units, repeated outcomes and a kept-same condition.
  • Distinguish criterion from constraint, interpret a before/after display and defend a tradeoff.
  • Explain an executed code correction, reset/calibration or finite repeat; trace a human-selected if/then without claiming autonomous sensing.
  • Represent/check quantity relationships within already taught bounds and explain a strategy, not race to an answer.
  • Justify an artistic or musical revision for purpose/audience rather than decorative polish.

Signature: Invention Labs is now a complete four-meeting reference:

  1. Hear one of two real bounded classroom-user requests; distinguish criterion/material limit; sketch alternatives.
  2. Build and run two baseline trials with role turns and separate child records.
  3. Change one feature; run two equivalent trials; interpret successes out of two before/after.
  4. Recommend a design in a seated table fair using results, a limitation and a tradeoff.

The original four meetings and baseline P0 are preserved. A partial/nonworking prototype can provide honest test evidence; it does not earn an invented success.

docs.title: Earth science, physical science, life science and authentic arts
docs.text:
• Earth/space: star/source/model limitations, indoor winter and seasonal references, and Weather Watchers. The latter records the same view at the start, minute 7 and minute 20, including no change/unknown visibility; it does not prefill rainy records or claim a forecast. Precipitation's Earth-water relationship is distinguished from a complete water-cycle model.
  • Physical: shadow/reflection, ramp path/runout, safe magnetic attraction, chain reliability, actual protected lamp input/output, vibrating strip pitch and musical phrase.
  • Life: plant needs/care and dated evidence, squirrel habitat connections, visibility-model limits, plant/butterfly stage relationships and seasonal representation.
  • Arts/music: observational representations, deliberate contrast/form, audience critique/revision, Sound Engineering's quiet four-beat phrase and Easter Joy's purposeful rhythmic/gesture composition. These are not just decorative coloring or hymn copying.
  • Service: listened-to classroom requests, fair quantities, bounded function tests and recipient-focused messages. Cards without a functional test are not called engineered products.

These are local opportunities, not complete coverage of every topic or every official primary-subject benchmark.

docs.title: 6. C/S/T/E/A/M balance
docs.text:
Count a file once per domain only when its mapped code has an actual student action and individual criterion. Do not count tags, acronym recital, equipment sitting nearby or every minute of a multimeeting file. Catholic incidence needs honest-evidence/model distinctions, dignity/inclusion/service or resource care beyond prayer alone. Arts needs purposeful representation/pattern/critique, mathematics needs actual quantity/measurement/pattern/data reasoning, and engineering needs a stated problem/test decision.
