Domains overlap; columns do not sum to 74. Counts are neither minute shares nor observed mastery. The six files without a mapped C code are not counted merely for gratitude/classroom tone. The resulting program is not all paper construction: tested engineering is deliberately narrower than model/art making, math is explicit, and real physical/life/Earth inquiry and music remain.

docs.title: 7. Technology, materials and workload
docs.text:
Primary digital requirement Current files Native meetings represented Meaning None 63 84 No digital dependency; may still need real physical tools/circuit equipment Required 10 13 Actual stored robot/ScratchJr execution is the objective Recommended 1 1 Digital Art uses real Undo/revision controls; paper supports A, not those controls Optional 0 0 No unnecessary camera/video/celebration requirement remains

The 13 required meetings are 390 inventory minutes, not a child's annual screen time. Software is listed separately as ACCESS, never as a physical supply.

The 61 replacements contain 659 material-allocation rows / 2,636 numeric class-size cells. Every new quantity cell was checked against student, kit or class allocation at all four enrollments. Cards, blocks, supports, rulers and trays are reused; paper includes two sheets per child per meeting. Consumables have stated whole-package allocations and construction/revision reserves where needed.

The four folder summaries link optional Grades 1-6 routines and state balanced trio/pair distributions explicitly: 10 pupils = 3+3+2+2; 15 = five trios; 20 = six trios plus a pair; 25 = seven trios plus two pairs. These do not replace complete lesson instructions or pair-specific kit allocations. Limited hardware follows the written wave/shared-test route, with actual individual operation evidence; groups are not enlarged to four and watching is not scored as operation.

Robot/circuit scarcity is not concealed. Three complete kits can serve two four-minute waves for 10/15 pupils or three for 20/25, up to three table teams per wave. Individual actions are checked during turns. One/two/no complete kits permit fewer actual turns; pending evidence is recorded unassessed, not replaced by watching or paper mastery.

Prep estimates are planning values, not measured labor: many reusable-kit setups are 10-15 minutes; first dot-card/pattern/silhouette sets have honest moderate estimates; robot charging is extra manufacturer time. Plant care stays at school with a named adult. The new planting package schedules contact-handwashing during practice (about 25 seconds per child at a visible sink, one waiting maximum), rather than hide a 25-child queue in four-minute cleanup; where that cannot be supervised the adult handles mix/seeds and pupils direct.

No mandatory home purchase, internet, donation, animal acquisition or routine homework is added. Shared cost tiers, normalized purchasing/alias integration and actual reported holdings are parent-owned in the materials plan. A cheap paper route supports genuine low-tech evidence but is never advertised as equivalent to physical robots, app controls, circuits or sound production.

Family copy describes the intended taught sequence, not an outcome observed during this review. Before sending it, select the actual route and collected evidence; replace any primary hardware/live-observation sentence when the class used a fallback or a child has unassessed operation evidence. docs.title: Bounded CSTA 2026 national candidate
docs.text:
The parent's normal public request verified E1-ALG-IM-03, individual Grade 1, in the current CSTA 2026 viewer, publisher detail record 350296, source NAT-01. The boundary is explaining how changing algorithm steps or their order can change the outcome; writing computer code is not required.

One CS candidate is recorded in the external CSV, using the existing exact 14-column header alongside the two retained arts candidates. Its workbook_sheet is the CSTA public viewer and workbook_row is the publisher record ID, not an Excel row.

Grade / national code Existing task and individual evidence Scope boundary 1 / E1-ALG-IM-03 Sphero Coding Adventures, meeting 2: original run, shorten a roll instruction, predict/rerun, compare travel, and answer the teacher's "what changed and why" question. Retain the child's original/revised action record, two outcomes and explanation of their relationship. Only the individual's explained algorithm change counts. The literal tabletop-card route may supply algorithm reasoning when an actual before/after comparison and explanation are collected. Mere card ordering, watching a teammate or pointing to a block is insufficient. Paper does not demonstrate robot operation.

Grade 2 full E2-ALG-PS-01 is not asserted. It requires sequence, events and iteration all to be evidenced, not just a stored sequence. ScratchJr's short Green Flag/motion/End task does not require repetition; other robot tasks introduce finite repeats but do not explicitly require and assess creation of an event-response algorithm. Optional demonstrations and a Run button alone do not establish every structure. The omission is not based on absent nested loops, variables or conditions; those are not Grade 2 requirements. No complete priority lesson or native meeting was reopened for a label.

Status: SOURCE VERIFIED - NATIONAL FRAMEWORK SCHOOL REVIEW REQUIRED. The two earlier arts candidates keep their separate MDE-copy/school-review conditions. The primary audit remains the fixed local-code contract.

docs.text:
Use the fixed local eighteen-code catalog. Codes are local program competencies, not MDE, OMCE, CSTA or Church numbers. Every audit row has 2-5 unique CST-[CSTEAM][1-3] codes. The lesson's scheduled action/individual prompt, not a tag or prayer alone, justifies each selected code.

Competency Grade 3 core/support Grade 4 challenge Inquiry Observe, predict, name changed/kept-same conditions, record whole-number results Repeat/compare variation, explain confounding or sample limits Systems Label parts, living stages, arrows, inputs/outputs Explain model omissions, alternate paths or tradeoffs Computing Trace sequence/repeat/condition; actually edit/run when equipment works Boundary/reset/debug explanation and model-versus-operation limits Design State criterion/constraint, test and change a feature Defend revision against equal conditions and access/resource tradeoffs Art/music Labeled observation/model, purposeful layout or four-beat choice Specific critique, revised composition and meaning/readability tradeoff Math Whole counts, cm/mm, totals/differences, labeled tables/bars Repeated ranges, budget alternatives, measurement precision, not forced ratios Catholic action Honest reporting, fair turns, requested service, stock care Explain inclusion/privacy/stewardship decisions and supported claim limits

Neither grade's core requires decimal division, percentages, means or efficiency ratios. Challenge is deeper reasoning, not unsupported secondary-school algebra. Oral/pointing/dictated/motor-assisted evidence is valid where it preserves the concept; neatness, speed, excitement, private faith and prayer intensity are not competency proxies.

Participation/group products are not individual mastery. At local expected- mastery checkpoints, two dated observations on separate occasions, including individual demonstration and changed-context explanation, are required. These documents plan opportunities; they do not report actual pupil outcomes.

docs.title: CSTA 2026 national candidates: scope check, not a new coverage claim
docs.text:
The parent verified the current publisher's CSTA 2026 viewer, including E3-ALG-PS-01 (Grade 3, detail record 350270) and E4-ALG-PS-01 (Grade 4, detail record 350271). The former requires sequence, events, iteration and selection; these may span multiple algorithms. The latter requires written everyday-language representations covering all four structures across multiple algorithms; formal pseudocode/flowcharts are not required. These are national framework codes, not evidence of Minnesota adoption.

No national CS row was added to the external CSV in this follow-up:

  • Scratch Programming and Game Design provide sequence, events and selection, but their required scoring algorithms have no iteration structure. Repeating four inputs during a test is not itself student creation of an iterative algorithm.
  • Sphero provides sequence/repeat representations, but its required route does not require selection. Its Grade 4 representation evidence alone does not cover all four.
  • Multiple algorithms may legitimately provide combined coverage, but a full candidate needs a documented, individually attributable evidence set joining all required structures and, for Grade 4, the written everyday-language representations. The inspected unit records do not establish that combined set for each learner; generic local T2 labels cannot substitute for it.

The four visual-arts rows remain the only external matches currently declared. This is a conservative omission, not a claim that the band lacks useful CS practice or cannot later document combined evidence. Completed lessons, priorities, objectives and timings were not altered merely to add standards labels. No full CS subject coverage, state adoption or pupil attainment is claimed.

Baseline findings are not erased: CSV status remains 45 KEEP + IMPROVE, 24 REBUILD and priority remains 41 P0, 24 P1, 4 P2. revision=rebuilt records a complete teaching package, not school approval, a classroom trial, a live device test, an electrical inspection, clinical validation, diocesan certification or observed student learning.

docs.title: Source-verified individual-grade Visual Arts practice
docs.text:
The parent and this follow-up directly inspected the state-agency Perpich 2018 arts workbook, source MN-05, worksheet MN2018ArtsEdStandardsVisualArts, on 2026-10-04. Rows 74/76 contain Grade 5 codes 5.5.2.3.⅕.5.2.4.1; rows 87/89 contain Grade 6 codes 5.6.2.3.⅕.6.2.4.1. Row 87 permits abstraction, symbolism or naturalism; it does not require all three. These are verified official source entries, unlike the local CST catalog. MDE-copy corroboration and school review remain required.

The external-alignment CSV contains these four arts matches and the separately scoped national CS rows below. It uses the exact Kindergarten external header, with individual grade 5 or 6, not the combined band. Each row names the actual task, individual evidence, existing path, edition, source, sheet and row. These are complete practice matches for the specified art route, not inferred science/math codes or certification of every pupil's performance.

Grade / verified code / row Existing lesson and actual practice Individual evidence and route limit 5 / 5.5.2.3.1 / 74 Giving Season Making: sketch two compositions; make and redesign a welcome-card art object using an original image, hierarchy and contrast. Original/revised layout, two reader checks and the child's before/after visual-choice reason. Count only artistic redesign; a readable title or consent decision alone is insufficient. Primary paper route. 6 / 5.6.2.3.1 / 87 Christmas Electronics: create a purposeful original light-symbol artwork/label, including the supplied star/wreath representation choices, and distinguish meaning from electrical mechanism. A peer interprets the symbol without coaching; the individual explains a visual choice and what it communicates. The child's own symbolic paper art counts, including the paper-art fallback; switch operation, a component diagram or the word "symbol" alone does not. Protected-AA operation remains a separate four-state assessment. 6 / 5.6.2.4.1 / 89 Gratitude Design: create original image/text compositions; a peer interprets action/reason and asks a question; revise the visual communication and retest. Initial/revised card, reader interpretation/question and an individual reason linking the change to intended thanks. Consent or spelling correction alone is not meaning-focused artwork revision. Primary paper route. 6 / 5.6.2.4.1 / 89 Advent Technology: create four panels with original imagery; reflect with a peer on interpreting Pause/Share and the invitation; revise visual order/image-text meaning and retest. Individual first/revised layout, peer interpretation and reader-backed explanation. Paper is the primary art route. Optional digital art counts only after an actual produced file and the same collaborative revision; privacy/time reasoning alone is not the arts evidence.

Not claimed: although row 76's Grade 5 artist-statement benchmark is source verified, these selected routes do not explicitly require and assess an artist statement using art vocabulary. A generic design explanation is not promoted to that benchmark. No science/math number, broad "art" tag, presence of a computer or theoretical symbolism is used as alignment evidence. No lesson body, meeting count, local-code set or Snap/protected-AA route was changed to manufacture a match.

docs.title: Substantive changes and preserved purposes
docs.text: Family / example Completed change and retained learning Experimental Design Six actual ramp trials, variables/two controls, repeatable distances, worked mean and limit; no chemistry/projectiles. Structural Engineering / Bridges Low supports, adult 20/40 g comparisons, force paths, form/retest and equal-unit ratios; no destructive loading or pretend breaking strength. Optics Actual reflection/refraction observations, annotated rays and bounded two-mirror periscope; no Sun/laser/glass route. Astronomy / Space Science Verified NASA Earth-Sun fact card, consistent distance-only model and clearly fictional mission budget. No unchecked star counts/current-role/news dependencies. Social Entrepreneurship Complete fictional cost/revenue/capacity/canvas/workflow packet, fair-access alternatives and output/outcome distinction; no brand advertising, real sales or promised impact. Health Technology Four dry information-interface meetings, complete fictional brief/six events, visual hierarchy, consent and usability retest; no clinical testing, bodies as patients, sensors or efficacy claims. Body Systems / Life Science Accurate gas/circulation cards, blood-color limits, cell exceptions and eight-base complement; no pulse/breath assessment, extraction, samples/cultures or medical disclosure. Environmental Monitoring Preserved invented raw record, verified working-copy correction, ten bars/totals/means, confounds and evidence-limited proposal; not real monitoring or causal savings. Ecosystems Food-to-consumer arrows, annotated form, energy/matter distinction, bounded perturbation and habitat/access area tradeoff; no wild collection or perfect-balance claim. Outside projects remain separately approved. New Life Technology / seasonal messages Genuine visual/music composition, eight-beat rhythm checks and audience revision; safe optional digital production. Resurrection remains distinct from biology and artistic emotion is not a clinical outcome. Goals / gifts / exhibitions Measurable school-task milestones and buffers, recipient choice, specific message/reader tests and scaled paired defenses; no private spiritual/health goals or 25 plenary talks.

docs.title: Grades 5 and 6: progression and remaining coverage limits
docs.text:
Either year may come first. Check cm/g/counts, sequence/if-else, observation versus inference and model labels rather than assuming attendance or judging reading speed. Teach the missing skill in the model window.

Competency Grade 5 support/evidence Grade 6 increment Measurement/testing Large ruler/unit guides; actual repeated values; name changed/measured/two controls Compare variation/confounds, equal units, explain what was not measured Mathematics/data Scaffold totals, labeled zero-based graphs, budget steps Means/ranges/ratios with worked example; denominator, capacity and uncertainty Computing Trace event/reset/guard using large cards; each device pupil edits/runs Exact boundaries, state/local-variable behavior, test coverage and access tradeoffs Life/Earth/physical systems Directed model labels, cell/seed exceptions and observed versus reference Distinguish energy/matter, omissions, causal uncertainty and additional evidence Engineering Criterion/constraint, original/retest evidence, one justified change Defend material/cost/space/access tradeoff and remaining validation Art/music Intentional visual form/sequence and four-beat composition; reader critique Defend hierarchy/motif choices and revise without promising universal interpretation Catholic ethics/service Honest reporting, stated need, consent, resource care Distinguish output/outcome, source type, privacy/access and unsupported inference Communication Oral/drawn/scribed result/limit and caption revision Defensible recommendation, evidence quality and next test; not more ornate presentation

Repetition is purposeful only when constraints/evidence advance: A route versus B reset/sensor decision; A bridge form versus B room access; A controlled weather comparison versus B provenance/cause limits; A basic app events versus B conditional tests. Repeated seasonal cards/galleries should not displace investigation or music/science/coding practice.

Coverage still supplemental: paper algorithms do not prove real programming; models do not establish microscopy/clinical competence/real environmental monitoring. The preserved circuits do not certify Ohm's-law/current-measurement proficiency. Longer research, source comparison, sustained observation, advanced autonomy, app persistence and externally validated service would need additional approved instructional time, not missing core instructions.

docs.title: Technology plan and physical gates
docs.text:
Current audit distribution: 51 None, 3 Optional, 9 Recommended, 6 Required. None/Optional/Recommended describe primary-path digital needs, not equipment-free operation. Paper routes honestly assess local reasoning; digital production/ robot measurements/circuit operation are separately recorded.

The six Required packages now contain complete executable reference blocks: Gratitude Coding, Advanced Scratch, App Inventor, Scratch Games, Advent Coding, App Design. If school-approved working setups exist, pupils assemble/edit/actually run the starter and compare expected/actual tests. Paper fallback explicitly changes to algorithm/interface reasoning and defers runtime evidence; it never quietly certifies programming. The coding choice in Passion Projects follows the same rule. Optional digital message routes actually produce a file when chosen.

Teacher/IT must confirm current age/privacy policy, approved school-managed individual access, compatible editor/Companion/emulator, save and device capacity before class. Never shared passwords, personal/home account requirements, public uploads, private inputs, tracking, camera/GPS/microphone or cloud database in core. At 25 pupils, nine simultaneous setups require actual stock; insufficient devices means the specified shared route or documented deferred operation, not an invented queue or automatically treating observers as operators.

docs.title: Executable shared-kit routes without larger groups
docs.text:
The six new Required programming packages, three new optional BOLT packages and the coding choice in Passion Projects now include ten specific three-setup alternatives, alongside their original one-setup/team routes. Passion Projects uses its coding waves in meetings 2-3 while science/music continue their own complete paths. Choose one allocation, never add both. The teacher demo uses an issued setup; no extra device/kit or holding is assumed.

Keep the balanced distributions in the optional Grades 1-6 reference routines: 10 = two trios/two pairs; 15 = five trios; 20 = six trios/one pair; 25 = seven trios/two pairs. This guide does not replace any package's own supplies, code/test key, native numbered steps or safety conditions.

With three actually approved/pretested setups, teams 1-3 use 11-19, teams 4-6 19-27, teams 7-9 27-35. These windows occupy the existing combined steps 3-4 period; the 0-11 introduction/model, 35-41 individual check and 41-45 cleanup remain unchanged. At 10/15 pupils, two waves suffice and the last eight minutes support retests. Three waves take 24 minutes and cover up to nine groups without making any group larger than three.

Every operator has up to two minutes for a meaningful code change and actual execution, with two minutes/team for approved transitions, reset and checking. The exact edits/tests are in the lesson: list index repair, square/clone parameter changes, app reset/branch repair, game reset cases, Advent state reset, four real sensor readings, a bounded robot endpoint/retest pair or the Passion Projects labelled <4/<3 guard comparison. Waiting pupils complete their own specific traces/design/data records, not passive watching. The two-pupil robot teams use their spare third turn to retain three trials per condition.

Preloading the complete printed reference, approved account switching, surface/supervision checks and turn timing are advance preparation and must be piloted on actual equipment. This shared route teaches editing/ executing a provided program, not independent from-scratch construction. With only one/two safe working setups, that many teams use each window; remaining operation checks are booked later and recorded paper-only/NE. Do not rush accommodations, share passwords, turn a partner's action into another child's operation evidence or claim all children executed if they did not. The eleven preserved references, especially Snap's actual eight-kit/five-station/ two-wave plan, are unchanged by these new alternatives.

The audit now names 15 registered access references across required/optional Scratch, App Inventor, Sphero and Snap-manual routes. Their resource-register status is NOT A PHYSICAL INVENTORY PRICE, never a fabricated device holding, software price or approval. journal/portfolio are declared aliases for prepared dated learning records; preparing/storing those records still needs the counted paper/tools and teacher time.

docs.title: Snap Circuits and protected-AA references
docs.text:
Preserved Snap plan uses eight reported individual OHM-135 classroom kits, not eight multi-kit packs or confirmed inspected inventory. At 10/15/20: ⅘/7 teams and stations; at 25: nine teams, five stations, two 14-minute waves, with controlled reset/reserves and individual physical turns. Selected manufacturer-approved slide-switch/lamp project is two states, tested twice. No assumption about battery count, push button, LED resistor or protection from the kit name. Model/manual/power/safety gates and the parent-owned classroom guide remain unchanged; this pass did not approve the stock.

The audit's kit name resolves to the separate reported OHM-135 holding, not a priced generic circuit kit. Eight is a school-reported quantity, not physically verified, and no price is invented. Access: matching Snap Circuits manual resolves to the manufacturer-instruction resource; it is not a generic project-diagram purchase.

The separate protected-AA supply/push-switch/LED-resistor route retains its four-state key. No mixing supplies/modules, bypasses, shorts, coin cells, mains/USB substitutions, soldering or take-home circuits. Qualified adult inspection and isolation precede changes. Warm/damaged/leaking/smelly parts: stop, isolate, report OUT OF SERVICE. Without safe physical kits, reasoning/ design can proceed, electrical operation is deferred.

For that separate route, canonical procurement names are Protected switched 2-AA circuit pack, AA alkaline cell, Adult-prepared sleeved LED/resistor assembly and Insulated clip lead. The qualified adult must confirm the actual holder's enclosed contacts/switch/short protection, compatible 3 V cells, red LED/220-ohm ¼-watt series resistor/polarity/sleeves and three-lead path. The specific assembly is not silently replaced by a generic LED module; none of these names makes it compatible with Snap modules. Reference bodies, quantity tables, actual state keys and station/wave timings remain unchanged.

docs.title: Audit-only material and resource reconciliation
docs.text:
All 69 audit lists, including the 11 reference rows, now use selected physical/resource/holding terms. Only materials changed in this normalization; the other 18 audit fields are preserved. Compatible concurrent masking-tape, hardware and ACCESS declarations were retained. Dated records use the declared prepared-resource format, not a fictional notebook or software purchase. Exact software/manual ACCESS names are not priced physical supplies. OHM-135 is a separate reported holding with actual model/manual/preflight checks, not a newly priced or confirmed classroom pack. docs.title: Adhesive type clarification
docs.text:
All newly rebuilt paper/cardboard kits now specify masking tape, not a generic Tape/Glue item. The two new optional robot floor-lane rows specify Removable floor-marking tape; an adult checks the actual product's adhesion/removal compatibility with the school's surface. The registry's FLOORTAPE type is not an automatic masking/painter-adhesive equivalent. Quantities and tests are unchanged. The app's short tape input is explicitly a fictional masking-tape category, not unspecified adhesive.

The audit also records masking tape for preserved reference paper/cardboard mounting and includes the already-written masking-tape rows in Sphero Mastery and Environmental Science. This is a procurement clarification, not a change to the eleven reference bodies or their timing/evidence. Masking/floor-marking tape is not electrical insulation, a replacement for sleeved leads, short-circuit protection, or permission to mount anything on the Snap grid. The Snap no-extra-mounting-tape gate and separate protected-AA specifications remain unchanged.

New lesson tables separate per-student records, shared team tools and teacher-only loads/optics/devices. Teams of at most three: ⅘/7/9 at 10/15/20/25. Consumable/reusable distinctions, cut/pour/load preparation, actual role turns and cleanup are specified. Same kits are reused across alternative schedules; do not sum all four tracks into a single classroom purchase order.

The new 58 packages contain 285 supply rows checked at all four sizes: 1,140 table cells / 1,172 numeric quantity comparisons (compound paper/ pencil cells contain two quantities). Exact decimal scaling is checked rather than floating-point equality. Useful quantities at 25 include:

  • Ramp investigations: nine ramps/balls/trays/rulers, 18 books; six trials/team.
  • Serial structure comparisons: four shared 10 g packets/class, adult 20/40 g cap; nine low trays; no nine sets of dangerous maximum loads.
  • Optics: 18 plastic mirrors/supports, nine channels/cups/trays; 900 mL adult-poured water, no water near power. One teacher graduated measuring cup portions it before class; transparency does not imply volume calibration.
  • Class kit service: 27 kit sheets + 25 individual evidence sheets = 52; nine folders/rulers/labels, accepted/deferred status recorded.
  • Core standalone computing: nine working setups if all teams execute simultaneously, or three preloaded approved setups in the defined waves. Apps need tested device/emulator access; no loan/holding is guaranteed.
  • Shared robot lanes: three optional setups and 6 m removable floor-marking tape, instead of nine setups/18 m at 25 pupils. Actual space, surface, supervision and stopped reset/turn timing must be checked.

Preparation estimates are planning estimates, not observed stopwatch results. Most paper packages need 10-20 minutes; first optics/structures/capstone/code kits may need 25-30. Device approval and first electrical inspection are additional work, not concealed inside a 20-minute substitute arrival. Prebuild/inspect reusable kits, then use repeat preparation and actual school location/contact. Adult serial tests budget roughly one minute/team; pilot throughput locally and defer evidence rather than compress safety.

docs.title: Planning allowances retained from reference-kit audit

docs.title: What remains conditional
docs.text:
The workbook itself says the MDE-hosted Excel is the official version. The directly inspected state-agency copy establishes its displayed codes and content; a final MDE-copy corroboration and school curriculum review remain required before a formal program-wide official-alignment claim.

Each proposed link was matched to the rewritten lesson's actual directions and evidence check. It is not a claim that pupils already demonstrated the benchmark. A table row must meet its stated scope:

  • Original art requires a child-created or child-directed representation. Merely selecting a supplied picture does not prove art creation.
  • A stated choice must concern the child's own artwork. Counting points or watching a teacher is not sufficient.
  • Image/object distinctions are visual-arts evidence, not proof of full science-standard coverage.
  • The music link requires a student-directed choice and sharing of an actual musical sound. Silent gestures or only rests can satisfy the local pattern route but do not establish that external sound-sharing benchmark.

The CSV status deliberately separates source verification from institutional review and classroom outcomes. The generated local-standard map retains its general external-alignment verification hold and links here for these narrowly checked candidates.

Method: one document credit for a required/current minimum pupil task, not a tag, prayer alone, optional hardware, decorative craft or station visit. Counts overlap and are not minutes or subject-standard coverage. Reflection can earn communication/truth credit but is not a new scientific investigation.

Weekly slot Credited domains Required task basis 1 S,A Actual detail/question and representation 2-3 C,T,M Fair turns, input/output, algorithm, move count 4 C,S,A Care, observed details/question and sketch 5-6 C,E,M Resource care, stable test/retest and counting 7-9 C,E,A,M Requested tray criterion, plan, two-cup comparison 10 C,E,M Access need, same-load retest, support/load count 11 C,T,A Respectful gratitude message and tested correction 12 C,A Recipient dignity, purposeful art and clarification 13 C,A Honest actual evidence and communicated result 14-15 C,S,T,A Evidence/symbol distinction, fair light test, tool and design 16 S,A,M Model/real distinction, representation and dot count 18 C,S,A,M Honest observed sky record and checkable practice 19-22 S,T,E,A,M Retest, two weather records, readable repeat and debugging 23 C,T,A Truthful evidence display, private-data scenario, communication 24-25 C,T,M Welcoming message, three-command correction and count 26-27 C,E,A Requested book criteria, plan, retest and tradeoff 28 C,A,M Honest flat/solid distinction, pattern and count 29-31 C,S,A,M School care, actual dated comparisons and sketches/counts 33 C,S,A Belief/biology distinction and ordered visual model 34 C,A Honest skill record and handoff communication Bi-weekly sessions Credited domains in order 01-05 CSA; CSM; CEM; STA; CSEM 06-10 CA; CAM; CSA; CTA; SM 11-15 CSA; CSEA; CSA; CSA; CTA 16-17 CSEM; CA Domain Weekly /20 documents Bi-weekly /17 documents C 17 15 S 8 11 T 6 3 E 5 4 A 16 12 M 10 6

Hardware operation/programming, circuits, loops/conditions and measured outdoor weather are not K mastery claims. Those are deliberate handoff/extension boundaries, not credits awarded from pictures or apparatus present.

docs.title: 4. Signature design and reference readiness
docs.text:
Engineering Helpers is now a complete three-meeting reference: plan a tabletop tray, move the same two empty cups over 30 cm, record and retest one change. No real assistive device, infant/pet or high-shelf trial. In spring, Helping Hands advances to requested book-standing/picture-visibility criteria and a tradeoff.

All 37 references are document-complete, locally conditional. No document is asserted to have passed an actual classroom/substitute trial. The older eight references' first-pass desk scores are historical editorial judgments, not measured outcomes; the second pass uses explicit instruction/arithmetic checks rather than manufacturing new student-performance scores.

docs.title: 5. Materials, grouping and reported holdings
docs.text:
Use K reference routines. 10/15/20/25 pupils form 5/7/10/12 active pair/trio teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve at odd enrollment. Use no singleton "pair." Limited-kit groups <=3 require ⅘/7/9 kits with every child receiving a full decision/test turn.

Exact quantities live in each lesson; do not issue nine generic kits to all pair-based lessons. Examples: 260 blocks for a full structure allocation; 15 germination cups/36 seeds; 4.2 L contained water; 104 child/teacher life-cycle cards. Timings include individual checks and cleanup, but freezing, charging, ongoing plant care and actual school hygiene rules require advance arrangements.

The expanded catalog and material-usage index now identify every K primary term. Optional robots/hosts remain explicit in the lessons and technology plan, not mandatory primary-material purchases. Paper resources are assembled from separately priced stock; zero additional item-purchase cost is not free paper or zero teacher preparation. Budgets do not guarantee every K pair-based kit or all annual consumables for a 32-meeting year.

docs.title: Reported OLP holdings
docs.text: Preserved school report: 8 Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135. See reported-holdings data and the shared holdings record. Count, completeness, condition, location, manufacturer age/power guidance and school safety permission remain unverified. K uses only an optional preflighted adult demonstration in the light unit. No K student-circuit objective or loan requirement is inferred. Eight reports are not nine ready student stations.

docs.title: 6. Sources and official mapping
docs.text:
Local CST codes are stable program competencies, not official benchmarks. The external-candidate matrix verifies four exact 2018 arts identifiers and twelve planned task/evidence links across eleven K lessons against the state-agency workbook. MDE-copy corroboration, school review and actual mastery remain separate. No guessed science/math code replaces inaccessible final tables.

Directly inspected content sources include NASA stars, USDA monarch biology, CCC 638-645, and the verified teaching register. Inherited unverified biographies/quotations were omitted from the 29 new minimum paths. Devotional tradition, classroom interpretation and scientific evidence are not interchangeable. The original growing references retain their verified UMN/USDA sources and ongoing-care preflight.

docs.title: 7. Family communication
docs.text: Each rewritten reference includes a copy-ready concept/action/question and optional family conversation. Use only the lessons actually taught. Weather copy now distinguishes actual versus model records; privacy copy uses hypothetical examples; art copy explains choices; portfolios identify demonstrated skills rather than attendance. No purchase, donation, home device, parent teaching, private family disclosure or routine homework is required.

docs.title: 8. Validation and remaining release gates
docs.text:
The autonomous validator checked 29 new references, 37 new 25-minute meeting sequences and 360 class-size quantity comparisons. All 37 audit records are complete; frozen baseline judgments/paths/meetings/minutes match. Global map regeneration and publication checks are recorded in Validation. Source verification is not institutional approval.

Scenario Current document result and remaining condition Nonreader Modeled oral/picture directions, pointing/dictation and child-directed action; no reading/handwriting mastery assumption Substitute in 20 minutes Prepared-kit gate and named fallback; first-time cards, seed/ice preparation and charging are advance work No devices All 37 minimum pathways continue; actual hardware/software evidence remains separately unassessed/deferred Minnesota January Indoors; actual sky/teacher-source/model data labeled; plant care and water arrangements still need school checks 25 pupils Exact pair/trio/reserve allocations and circulating individual checks; real room, staffing and hygiene capacity untested Limited funding Primary supplies normalized, shared-kit alternatives stated; actual holdings/specifications/prices and annual consumption still need verification Parent explanation Specific concept, action, Catholic reasoning, evidence and next step; no invented observed outcomes

Remaining document-package backlog: 0 for K. Remaining release work is school-specific preflight and classroom trials, exact science/math/MDE-copy verification and primary-subject coverage review. Hold any newly found unsafe condition; when a fallback changes the target, record missing evidence rather than claiming success. All 22 baseline P0 entries remain historical priorities, not formally closed safety or diocesan approvals.

docs.title: K-6 C-STREAM learning progression
docs.text:
Local planning framework, dated 2026-10-04 for 2026-27. Not MDE/Archdiocese-approved. Use the fixed meanings in Local Standards and external-version limits in Standards Sources.

These are observable end-of-grade targets, not new external benchmarks and not evidence of existing curriculum coverage. Each grade increases the student's agency, precision, explanation and ability to consider others. Earlier skills remain in use. I/D targets guide formative assessment; M checkpoints require the individual evidence described below. Access supports are always allowed.

For K-1, demonstrate and give short oral/picture instructions; accept pointing, acting, construction and dictated explanations. For 2-3, add labels, repeated tests and simple comparisons. For 4-6, add independent plans, evidence, limitations and justified tradeoffs, not merely larger projects.

docs.title: Catholic integration: reason, dignity and stewardship
docs.text:
End of grade CST-C1: faith/reason and honest evidence CST-C2: dignity/service/inclusive ethical design CST-C3: stewardship/resources/work K Tell or show one thing actually observed; connect careful noticing with the taught idea of wonder at creation. Offer a classmate a usable turn/role and identify someone a simple design could help. Return a shared tool, sort a reusable piece and tell why materials need care. 1 Distinguish an observation from a guess in a demonstration; report an unexpected result honestly. Describe a user's need and make one change that helps the user participate. Choose a reusable material and describe careful work as a way to care for gifts and people. 2 Compare a prediction with a recorded result and explain why truthful results matter, even when disappointing. Explain how a design helps a person and identify a feature that might make it hard for another person to use. Compare two material choices for waste and function; carry out and explain a less-wasteful choice. 3 Use recorded evidence to revise an explanation; explain in simple terms that study of creation and taught faith need not compete. Ask a user-centered question, adapt a feature and explain the adaptation without stereotyping the user. Keep a simple resource record and explain a reuse decision that protects function and respects others' work. 4 Separate an evidence-based claim from a taught faith/ethical reflection; acknowledge a limitation and credit an idea. Compare solutions for access, safety and service; justify an inclusive choice using a realistic user scenario. Compare waste, durability and repair possibilities; defend a responsible choice under a material limit. 5 Explain how a claim is supported or challenged by evidence; distinguish scientific explanation, uncertainty and Catholic ethical judgment. Identify a possible unintended harm or exclusion and propose an appropriate safeguard before testing. Evaluate material use and possible effects on people/creation; explain why skilled work and service matter beyond winning. 6 Defend an honest, limited conclusion, correct an error and explain the taught compatibility of faith/reason without treating faith as test data. Defend a service-oriented design using evidence about user needs, accessibility and privacy/safety; identify a remaining ethical tradeoff. Recommend a resource/work plan considering durability, waste, repair and effects on people/creation; acknowledge a tradeoff.

Evidence examples: Individual oral observation versus prediction (K-1); explanation of one inclusive/resource choice (2-3); annotated ethical design decision with evidence and a limit (4-6). Assess understanding and actions, not private belief or spiritual maturity.

docs.title: Science: inquiry, investigations and systems
docs.text:
End of grade CST-S1: observations/questions/evidence CST-S2: investigations/testing/variables CST-S3: physical/life/Earth systems/models K Show a detail or change using senses safely; ask a question about what was noticed. Make a pictured/oral prediction, follow a teacher-set safe test and show the result. Make or describe a simple representation of an observed physical object, living thing or weather feature. 1 Record two observations with pictures/marks and use them to answer a simple question. Compare two teacher-set conditions and identify what was different and what was observed. Identify important parts of a physical, living or Earth/space example and show a relationship using a model. 2 Ask a testable question, record observations and explain an answer using at least one recorded result. With a scaffold, change one feature, keep another consistent and repeat a test to compare results. Use a labelled model to explain a simple change in a physical, life or Earth/space system. 3 Use repeated observations or simple data to describe a pattern and explain how it answers the question. Identify the changed feature, measured outcome and a feature kept consistent; carry out repeated safe trials. Describe interacting parts and cause/effect in models across physical, life and Earth/space contexts. 4 Support a claim with recorded results and distinguish the result from an explanation or new question. Plan a fair comparison, record repeated measurements and explain why a controlled feature matters. Use a model to predict a system change and compare that prediction with observation in each science context. 5 Compare evidence from more than one trial/source, notice disagreement and propose a useful follow-up question. Identify changed, measured and controlled variables; describe a repeatable method and one source of uncertainty. Explain a physical, life or Earth/space interaction with a model and identify an important feature the model omits. 6 Defend a claim with relevant data, address conflicting evidence and state what the investigation cannot establish. Conduct and explain a safe, repeatable controlled investigation; discuss variation and a justified improvement to the method. Use and revise models in physical, life and Earth/space contexts to explain/predict change, identify a limit and compare with evidence.

Evidence examples: Observation sketch and explanation (K-1); individual description of changed/consistent features and trial record (2-3); investigation plan, evidence-supported claim and model limitation (4-6). Across the year, collect physical, life and Earth/space examples for CST-S3; one context is insufficient. A craft labelled "science" is not a scientific explanation.

docs.title: Technology and computing: tools, algorithms and impacts
docs.text:
End of grade CST-T1: tools/input-output/troubleshooting CST-T2: algorithms/loops/conditions/debugging CST-T3: data/digital citizenship/technology impacts K Select and safely demonstrate a tool for a task; show what action causes an observable result. Put at least three pictured actions in order, follow them and locate one misplaced action with support. Sort objects by an observable feature and identify, in a scenario, information to keep private and an adult to ask for help. 1 Explain a tool's job and describe an action/input and result/output; check an obvious problem safely. Give a precise sequence, identify a repeated action and correct a step that produces the wrong result. Record a simple sort/count and explain a safe, kind choice in a teacher-provided technology scenario. 2 Trace input, action and output in a simple system; describe a problem and test one likely cause. Represent a sequence and repeated group of steps; follow a simple if/then choice and correct an error. Explain a simple data display, distinguish private from shareable information and acknowledge another person's idea. 3 Compare tools for a purpose and trace a system's input/output; document a check rather than changing parts at random. Write/arrange instructions with a loop and condition, trace two possible cases and explain a correction. Collect anonymous task data, explain what it shows and choose responsible sharing/credit in a realistic scenario. 4 Break a system problem into parts and test causes in order; explain how each check narrows the problem. Decompose a task, represent loops and conditions, and use a trace to locate and repair an error. Identify missing/misleading data and explain a technology benefit, possible harm and protective action. 5 Choose a tool/system for function and access; document input/output checks and a justified troubleshooting sequence. Compare algorithms for the same task, test contrasting inputs and revise for correctness and clarity. Evaluate data relevance and collection limits; explain privacy, credit and access decisions in a technology use case. 6 Defend a safe tool/system choice and use documented checks to distinguish likely causes from unsupported guesses. Design and explain a decomposed algorithm with repetition and conditions; test usual and boundary cases and justify debugging revisions. Evaluate a data-informed technology proposal for accuracy, privacy, accessibility and social effects; justify safeguards and a tradeoff.

Evidence examples: Individual tool explanation and movement-card trace (K-1); loop/choice demonstration and privacy scenario (2-3); algorithm trace, troubleshooting log or technology-impact recommendation (4-6). Local algorithms can be unplugged. Claim actual device programming only after individually checking executable work on a device; cards alone do not establish it.

docs.title: Engineering: requirements, iteration and decisions
docs.text:
End of grade CST-E1: problems/criteria/constraints CST-E2: build/test/redesign CST-E3: tradeoffs/communicate solutions K Name a problem and show what a solution should do using a teacher-given material limit. Build a simple model, try it and identify/change a part that did not work. Show a design choice and give a reason using words, pointing or a demonstration. 1 Identify a user, one success criterion and one material/time limit before building. Test a prototype against a stated criterion, change a feature and try again. Compare two choices for the task and explain a preferred choice with a demonstrated result. 2 Distinguish what a solution must accomplish from a limit on making it; sketch a possible solution. Record before/after results and explain how a change addressed a weak part. Compare two options against a criterion and explain what is gained or given up. 3 State a user's problem, an observable criterion and a constraint; explain why a proposed design addresses them. Run the same success test on two versions and explain an improvement using recorded results. Present a solution with a labelled model/sketch, results and one remaining weakness. 4 Write measurable criteria and constraints with a scaffold; use them to compare possible designs before construction. Use repeated measurements to revise a prototype; explain whether the change improved the stated criterion. Compare alternatives using performance evidence and a material/cost limit; explain a tradeoff to an audience. 5 Prioritize a user's criteria within time, materials and safety limits; justify a plan before building. Document multiple versions and comparable tests; justify a revision and distinguish improvement from an untested change. Recommend a design using more than one criterion, evidence and an acknowledged resource/access tradeoff. 6 Define and justify a user-centered problem, measurable success criteria and resource, safety and access constraints. Conduct and document evidence-driven iterations under constraints; explain unresolved failure and a justified next test. Defend a solution using performance, cost/resources, ethics/access and tradeoffs; answer a critical question with evidence.

Evidence examples: Individual demonstration of a changed part (K-1); before/after record and reason (2-3); criteria sheet, test record and defended recommendation (4-6). A failed prototype can provide strong learning evidence. Failure during engineering is information, not failure of the student.

docs.title: Art: observation, purposeful design and communication
docs.text:
End of grade CST-A1: observational sketches/models CST-A2: purposeful pattern/form/design CST-A3: artistic communication/critique/revision K Draw or construct a representation with a noticed detail and identify what it shows. Create a repeated pattern or selected shape/form and describe one choice. Explain what an artwork/model communicates and respond to one respectful suggestion. 1 Represent important parts observed in an object and explain their placement. Choose pattern, color or form for a stated purpose rather than adding it without a reason. Describe an intended idea and make a change after a specific helpful comment. 2 Make a labelled sketch/model that another person can use to identify parts or relationships. Use shape, pattern or composition to guide attention or support a function; explain the choice. Explain how a visual feature communicates an idea; give specific kind feedback and show a revision. 3 Use observed detail and relative sizes in a drawing/model to clarify a relationship. Compare two arrangements/forms and choose one for meaning, appearance or function with a reason. Present an intended message, identify a feature that supports it and revise using audience feedback. 4 Use labelled views or an annotated model to explain observed structure while distinguishing imagined features. Select visual features for purpose/audience, test alternatives and explain how the choice affects meaning or use. Give criterion-based feedback and revise a work to clarify meaning while explaining the decision. 5 Represent an observed system with purposeful views, relative scale and annotations; identify a representation limit. Compare form, pattern or composition alternatives for function and aesthetic intent; justify a purposeful choice. Compare interpretations, critique specific choices respectfully and document a revision consistent with intent. 6 Produce an accurate observational representation suited to an audience; distinguish measured, estimated and symbolic features. Defend pattern/form/design choices considering aesthetic intent, function, audience and constraints. Communicate a complex idea artistically, use respectful evidence-based critique and explain how revision strengthened or changed intent.

Evidence examples: Observed-detail explanation (K-1); annotated sketch and reason for composition (2-3); alternative designs, critique and explained revision (4-6). Do not grade realism or neatness unless explicitly taught and relevant. This visual/design strand does not certify complete arts coverage.

docs.title: Mathematics: quantities, representation and reasoning
docs.text:
Targets use the mathematics already taught in the primary classroom. Numbers, units and operations are chosen accordingly; advanced content must not become a hidden prerequisite. A scaffold is instruction, not proof of mastery of an untaught operation.

End of grade CST-M1: count/compare/measure CST-M2: data/pattern representation CST-M3: grade-appropriate quantities/operations/reasoning K Count a small set with one-to-one matching and compare length, amount or number directly. Sort objects, show a simple repeating pattern or object graph, and describe a visible comparison. Model joining/separating small quantities or compare shapes/amounts; show how the answer fits the task. 1 Count needed materials, compare quantities and measure a length with equal nonstandard units without gaps. Make a tally/picture display or represent a repeat and explain what a symbol/unit stands for. Use taught addition/subtraction with objects or drawings to solve a material/count problem and explain the strategy. 2 Estimate and measure a task quantity with a taught standard unit/tool; record the unit. Create a labelled table/picture/bar display of simple data and describe a comparison or pattern. Use taught quantities/operations in a practical problem; explain the strategy and check with a model or estimate. 3 Choose an appropriate taught unit, measure consistently and compare repeated measurements. Organize repeated-test data in a labelled table/graph and describe how a result changes. Use taught equal-group/measurement reasoning to solve and check a project problem, stating what quantities mean. 4 Measure with appropriate precision, record units and explain why a tool/unit suits the question. Choose a suitable display, label its scale/units and use it to support a comparison without distorting the data. Apply taught whole-number or fraction/measurement reasoning to a project problem and explain why the result is reasonable. 5 Estimate, repeat measurements and explain variation/rounding appropriate to the task and tool. Represent data clearly, identify an unusual value and distinguish a pattern from a claim the data cannot support. Use taught fraction/decimal or multi-step reasoning for materials, measurement or cost; check the answer and units. 6 Choose units/tools and a justified measurement method; explain precision, repeated results and limits. Choose and defend a data/pattern representation, interpret variation and identify a limitation or misleading presentation. Solve and defend a taught multi-step quantities problem, using ratio/rate reasoning only after prerequisites; check units and reasonableness.

Evidence examples: Count/compare demonstration (K-1); measurement record and explained representation (2-3); checked practical calculation and interpretation of data (4-6). A graph in a group poster is not proof that every student can interpret it.

docs.title: Separate planned instructional-stage matrix
docs.text:
This matrix is a local intended progression, not an audited lesson-coverage map or a student-results record. Every code recurs every year.

  • I - Introduced: model and encounter the foundation; collect a formative check.
  • D - Developing: guided practice with increasing independence.
  • R - Reinforced: revisit and transfer prior learning at the new grade target; continue formative checks. It does not mean the skill is finished.
  • M - Expected mastery checkpoint: plan individual assessment of that grade's target. M never means a student has mastered it merely by exposure.
Local code K 1 2 3 4 5 6 CST-C1 I D R M R R M CST-C2 I D M R R R M CST-C3 I D R M R R M CST-S1 I D M R R R M CST-S2 I D D R M R M CST-S3 I D R M R R M CST-T1 I D M R R R M CST-T2 I D D R M R M CST-T3 I D D R R M M CST-E1 I D M R R R M CST-E2 I D R M R R M CST-E3 I D D R R M M CST-A1 I D M R R R M CST-A2 I D R M R R M CST-A3 I D D R M R M CST-M1 I M R R R R M CST-M2 I D M R R R M CST-M3 I D R M R R M

The checkpoints are local instructional choices, not state/diocesan deadlines. All Grade 6 M entries refer to the local Grade 6 target, not mastery of a whole national 6-8 band or the entirety of a subject.

docs.title: Turning a plan into verified learning
docs.text:
1. Select a small number of primary codes for each lesson; do not claim all eighteen because students built something.
  2. Give each participating grade its own target and success criterion. An older student's answer or a mixed-grade team's product does not establish younger students' competence.
  3. Rotate meaningful roles and include a brief individual demonstration or explanation. Track who supplied which evidence, not just team completion.
  4. At M checkpoints, apply the individual mastery rule: two dated occasions, including an individual performance and a changed context or follow-up explanation, both meeting the grade target. Record missing evidence as not yet assessed, not mastered.
  5. Map actual lessons and evidence separately for weekly/bi-weekly schedules and A/B rotations. A second rotation may revisit a code with a harder task; it must not defer a grade's essential target until the student has left it.
  6. If time, weather, devices or materials change, preserve the target and valid assessment, not necessarily the activity. Use indoor alternatives, unplugged representations or another meeting when they retain the assessed skill. Do not relabel a materially different skill as equivalent.
  7. Flag unmet targets and uncertain external mappings for parent integration. This plan alone does not prove that any existing schedule can yet deliver and assess all targets within its available meetings.

Two to four primary codes per lesson is a useful planning limit, not a mandated quota. Short checks can overlap when each skill is actually demonstrated. Keep evidence in the school-approved assessment system; do not collect personal or family data merely to make a project feel authentic.

docs.title: Lesson quality audit
docs.text:
The baseline contains 251 lesson documents. Multi-week documents represent more than one meeting; the audit is a document-level review, not a count of 251 activities to teach in one school year.

Band Baseline documents Review and scored examples Complete baseline/revision records K 37 Kindergarten review CSV 1-2 74 Grades 1-2 review CSV 3-4 71 Grades 3-4 review CSV 5-6 69 Grades 5-6 review CSV

Combined lesson map includes skills/local standards, assessment evidence, materials, technology, preparation, cleanup, scope, baseline disposition and revision state. Follow lesson_path relative to the documentation root to read the actual teacher instructions.

docs.title: Dispositions
docs.text:
Baseline status Meaning KEEP Strong enough as written for its intended context; still check local inventory and students. KEEP + IMPROVE Valuable concept; identified instructions, evidence or classroom support need improvement. REBUILD Keep the learning objective; rebuild weak, unsafe or impractical lesson design. REPLACE Another activity better meets the objective under the school's constraints. REMOVE Documented duplication, developmental mismatch, safety, cost or insufficient learning value warrants retirement.

No activity is removed merely because a reviewer prefers a different project. P0/P1/P2/P3 indicate baseline priority, not proof that a problem remains after a revision. unchanged, improved and rebuilt identify the subsequent work; consult the band review for release conditions.

docs.title: Quality score
docs.text:
Score each applicable dimension from 0 to 3:

  • 0: absent, inaccurate or unsafe.
  • 1: named, but insufficient instructions or evidence.
  • 2: teachable with a clearly identified remaining support/check.
  • 3: explicit, developmentally appropriate and independently usable.
Dimension Evidence needed for a strong score Academic rigor Correct explanation and a testable, observable learning target. Age appropriateness Prerequisites and response mode fit each grade, including nonreaders. Catholic integration Truth, dignity, stewardship or service changes students' thinking/actions; not only a prayer. Standards alignment Claimed local competencies connect to actual student work; official claims pass the source gate. Hands-on learning Students manipulate, observe, measure or construct, not merely watch. Engagement Meaningful choices and a comprehensible problem, not entertainment alone. Substitute friendliness No hidden kit, content knowledge, account or classroom-location assumptions. Instruction clarity Numbered steps and realistic times include assessment and cleanup. Low-tech access Technology category is explicit; a fallback states any objective change honestly. Cost efficiency Quantities and reusable/consumable distinctions support an affordable pathway. Preparation Specific steps and honest first-use/repeat-use time estimates. Assessment Individual evidence measures the objective, not attendance, handwriting or decoration. Differentiation Practical support/challenge and access alternatives preserve the objective. Safety Specific hazards, adult-only steps, stop rules and local-policy checks. Scalability Quantities, roles and testing logistics work for 10/15/20/25 students. Family communication Plain-language learning, Catholic connection and an answerable child question. Progression Prior skill, grade-specific expectation and next step are explicit.

For a numeric summary, report earned / (3 x applicable dimensions) together with the scored dimensions and rationale. Do not average unscored dimensions as zeros or compare summaries using different denominators. Scores are editorial judgments, not measured student outcomes.

Safety, accuracy and access are gates, not averageable weaknesses. A high engagement score cannot offset an unresolved unsafe procedure. Classroom piloting and individual mastery checks remain necessary.

docs.title: Evidence and limits
docs.text:
Band reviewers inspect the lesson text rather than treating front-matter tags as evidence. Domain exposure counts may overlap: one measured bridge test can support engineering and mathematics. An exposure count is not a percentage of instructional minutes or a finding of subject-standard mastery. The band reviews state their counting assumptions and unresolved issues.

See the implementation plan for teaching-release gates and the traceability guide for official benchmark verification.

docs.title: Local K-6 C-STREAM standards
docs.text:
Local program framework. Planning date: 2026-10-04. School year: 2026-27. These are original school-program competencies, not official MDE or Archdiocesan standards and not approved by either body. They integrate Catholic identity with science, technology, engineering, art and mathematics without replacing the school's religion or primary subject curricula.

The fixed contract is 18 codes: three per domain. Keep codes and meanings stable when projects, materials, schedules or rotations change. Religion/faith is integrated in the Catholic domain and across practice; there is no additional CST-R* domain. Grade-specific performance targets are in Learning Progression, not new standard codes.

docs.title: Competency catalog
docs.text:
Evidence examples are possible individual checks, not mandatory projects or claims that existing lessons already assess these skills.

Code Competency and observable intent Examples of individual evidence CST-C1 Faith/reason and honest evidence. Use reason to study creation; distinguish an observation, prediction, explanation and taught faith connection; report results truthfully, including uncertainty. K-1: tell what was actually seen rather than hoped for. 2-3: revise a prediction using a recorded observation. 4-6: defend a claim, identify a limit, and explain why honest inquiry is compatible with the taught Catholic view. CST-C2 Dignity/service/inclusive ethical design. Respect every person's worth; identify a real need, include others, and consider who benefits or might be excluded or harmed. K-1: offer an accessible role or adapt a shared tool. 2-3: explain how a design helps its user. 4-6: evaluate an access/privacy concern and justify a safer, more inclusive design. CST-C3 Stewardship/resources/work. Care for creation and shared resources; use materials responsibly; value careful work and gifts used in service. K-1: sort reusable scraps and explain their care. 2-3: choose less wasteful materials without losing function. 4-6: compare resource use, durability and effects on people; explain a work/service connection. CST-S1 Observations/questions/evidence. Ask investigable questions; observe, record and use evidence to explain a phenomenon without overstating a conclusion. K-1: point out an observed change. 2-3: explain a pattern with recorded observations. 4-6: support a claim with data, uncertainty and a useful follow-up question. CST-S2 Investigations/testing/variables. Predict, plan and conduct safe tests; increasingly identify what changes, what is measured and what stays consistent; repeat and compare results. K-1: show a prediction and follow a teacher-set test. 2-3: identify the one changed feature. 4-6: present a repeatable investigation, controlled variables and a limitation. CST-S3 Physical/life/Earth systems/models. Observe and model age-appropriate physical, living and Earth/space systems; use models to explain relationships and identify their limits. K-1: depict an observed object, living thing or weather change. 2-3: label interacting parts. 4-6: use a model to explain a change and describe what it omits. Collect physical, life and Earth/space examples across the year. CST-T1 Tools/input-output/troubleshooting. Select and use appropriate tools safely; describe a system's input and output; diagnose problems using evidence rather than random changes. K-1: select a ruler or safe tool and describe its job. 2-3: trace an input/action/output. 4-6: explain a systematic troubleshooting sequence. A non-digital tool can support local evidence but not an external device-use claim. CST-T2 Algorithms/loops/conditions/debugging. Create, follow, represent and improve instructions; progress from sequence to repetition and conditions; locate and correct errors. K-1: give and fix movement-card instructions. 2-3: trace a loop and an if/then choice. 4-6: test an algorithm on contrasting inputs and explain a correction. Devices are optional for this local competency unless the chosen objective requires execution on one. CST-T3 Data/digital citizenship/technology impacts. Represent and question data; protect privacy, credit ideas and communicate responsibly; evaluate technology's benefits, limitations and effects on people. K-1: sort anonymous objects and recognize private information in a scenario. 2-3: explain a data display and a safe sharing choice. 4-6: evaluate data quality, access, privacy and a technology tradeoff. CST-E1 Problems/criteria/constraints. Define a user-centered problem, observable success criteria and real limits before choosing a solution. K-1: name what a model must do and one limit. 2-3: distinguish a success requirement from a material limit. 4-6: write and justify measurable criteria and constraints for a user. CST-E2 Build/test/redesign. Make a prototype, test against criteria, record what happened, and improve deliberately using evidence. K-1: identify a weak part and make a change. 2-3: compare before/after tests. 4-6: document iterations and distinguish measured improvement from an attractive but untested change. CST-E3 Tradeoffs/communicate solutions. Compare alternatives, explain design choices and limitations, and communicate an evidence-supported recommendation to an audience. K-1: show a choice and give a reason. 2-3: compare two options against a criterion. 4-6: defend a recommendation using performance, cost/resources, access and tradeoffs. CST-A1 Observational sketches/models. Observe closely and represent form, parts, relationships and details in drawings or made models that help understanding. K-1: show a noticed detail. 2-3: label a drawing/model so someone else can interpret it. 4-6: use multiple views, relative sizes or annotations for an accurate visual explanation. Artistic polish is not the criterion. CST-A2 Purposeful pattern/form/design. Use pattern, shape, form, composition, color or texture intentionally for an aesthetic or functional purpose; explain choices. K-1: create and describe a repeat or form. 2-3: choose visual features to direct attention or support function. 4-6: compare alternatives and justify choices for purpose and audience. Decoration alone is not evidence. CST-A3 Artistic communication/critique/revision. Convey ideas visually or artistically; discuss meaning and intent, give respectful specific feedback, and revise while preserving or clarifying purpose. K-1: explain an idea and respond to a helpful comment. 2-3: describe how a visual choice communicates meaning. 4-6: give criterion-based critique and show a reasoned revision. CST-M1 Count/compare/measure. Count or compare relevant quantities; estimate and measure with appropriate tools and units; consider precision and repeated measurements as appropriate. K-1: count materials and compare lengths. 2-3: record a measurement with units. 4-6: choose a tool/unit, repeat a measurement and explain precision appropriate to the task. CST-M2 Data/pattern representation. Organize quantities and patterns in objects, drawings, tables or suitable graphs; interpret a representation without distorting its message. K-1: make a tally or object graph. 2-3: label a table/bar display and explain a pattern. 4-6: choose a defensible representation, identify an unusual value and avoid unsupported conclusions. CST-M3 Grade-appropriate quantities/operations/reasoning. Use quantities, operations and relationships already taught or explicitly scaffolded in classroom mathematics; explain strategies, units and reasonableness in practical problems. K-1: show a quantity or joining/separating strategy. 2-3: justify a count, equal-group or measurement calculation. 4-6: solve and check an appropriate multi-step problem; use fractions, decimals or ratios only when their prerequisites are taught.

docs.title: What counts as demonstrated learning?
docs.text:
Use a short observation, explanation, drawing, model, data record or performance. Offer oral, pointing, tactile, large-format, scribed or assistive responses where they preserve the skill being assessed. Reading stamina, handwriting, speech fluency, fine-motor speed and expensive supplies are not proxies for competence.

Local assessment level Decision rule Beginning Student attempts the task but cannot yet demonstrate the stated grade target, even with the offered support. Record the next support. Developing Student demonstrates part of the target, or needs a conceptual prompt/model to complete it. Meets expectation Student demonstrates the full stated grade target and explains/shows the relevant reasoning, using permitted access supports but without an adult or peer supplying the answer. Extends learning Student meets the target and transfers, critiques or improves it in a new appropriate situation. More complicated or prettier work alone is not extension.

Mastery rule: A group product, exposure, attendance, participation, or a single lucky result cannot establish individual mastery. At an expected-mastery checkpoint, collect at least two dated observations on separate occasions, including an individually attributable demonstration and a changed context or follow-up explanation. Both must meet the grade target. This is a local assessment policy, not an external agency requirement. If evidence is missing, record not yet assessed; if it is partial, record developing and reteach.

Assess Catholic competencies through understanding of taught ideas and observable truthful, respectful, responsible choices. Do not grade prayer intensity, private belief, a child's perceived holiness, family religious practice, or willingness to disclose personal circumstances. Distinguish a student's design critique from the worth of the student.

docs.title: Traceability contract for integration
docs.text:
A future lesson/assessment record should identify:

  1. Local code and grade target from this catalog/progression.
  2. Grade, schedule and rotation, unit and lesson; combined grades retain separate success criteria.
  3. Student action and evidence: what each learner will do, how the teacher will check it, and what meets expectation.
  4. Instructional stage: introduced, developing, reinforced or expected-mastery checkpoint, separate from the student's assessed result.
  5. External mapping, if claimed: source/edition, exact verified number and grade/band, paraphrased requirement, matching task, individual assessment and evidence location. Label unresolved rows VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

Until lesson tasks and assessments are inspected, a source connection is only a candidate, not a verified alignment. Do not infer official science alignment from CST-S*, CSTA alignment from CST-T*, or OMCE approval from CST-C*. See Standards Sources.

docs.title: Scope limits
docs.text:
• Eighteen competencies are a durable integrated-skills framework, not all religion, science, CS, engineering, arts, mathematics, ELA or social studies standards. They do not certify complete subject coverage.
  • CST-S3 requires physical, life and Earth/space contexts over time; one bridge or robotics unit cannot stand for the entire science program.
  • Local art emphasizes observation, visual design and communication; it does not represent full dance, music, theater or media arts provision.
  • Unplugged computing can assess algorithms. It cannot by itself prove actual device operation, executable programming, online research or digital-tool use when an external benchmark specifically requires those actions.
  • Mathematical sophistication follows the primary math curriculum. Extension for an older student must not become an unsupported prerequisite for a younger student in a combined-grade class.
  • The planned progression is a design target, not a finding that every existing lesson or rotation already supplies it.

docs.title: Materials and equipment plan
docs.text: Planning estimates dated October 2026, USD; NOT vendor quotations. Supplier price, protection, ingredients, availability and school stock are VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Do not order an unspecified product solely because its name appears here.

docs.title: What these budgets cover
docs.text:
The normalized inventory CSV distinguishes required starter materials, high-value additions and optional legacy devices. The first three packages serve one cohort of up to 25 students through a modest 17-meeting low-tech core. Reusable equipment can serve grades K-6 sequentially, not seven classes simultaneously. The enhanced package adds consumable allocations for seven sequential 25-student cohorts and optional standalone robots. Different schedules or heavier consumable use need a revised annual allocation. None of these packages claims coverage of all 251 legacy lesson documents, specialty kits, every commercial curriculum or a full replacement of primary science/math/arts instruction.

Planned inventory/resource use groups exact references by canonical identity, grades and distinct lesson documents. These counts answer where an item/resource is planned without relabeling a catalogue occurrence as physically verified use. Select a schedule/rotation before annual costing; alternative tracks are not additive demand.

Existing inventory assumptions, not verified holdings: school provides 25 pencils, 25 blunt scissors, shared crayons/markers, board/chalk or whiteboard, 18 stable books/support blocks for bridge stations, a teacher timer, access to handwashing and normal table-cleaning supplies. No device, printer, app license, family donation, commercial kit or loan is assumed. If these basics are missing, price them before approval or run safe pre-cut/oral alternatives; the ceiling does not magically supply them.

docs.title: OLP holdings and circuit use
docs.text: The separate reported holdings record includes eight individual Snap Circuits kits. The classroom guide supplies model-specific preflight gates and a two-wave plan for 25 pupils. docs.title: A genuine low-tech core, not teacher demonstrations
docs.text:
This operations core is a purchasing/use-case model, not a competing pacing guide. Teachers use the shared scope and band lessons to select meetings. Grade-appropriate variants use the same reusable stock with increasing evidence.

Core use case Starter materials Individual learning, not merely a group craft Observation and scientific questions Paper, pencil, familiar classroom object K points/tells a detail; older pupils distinguish observation from inference Sorting/data/measurement Cards, rulers, cups Each child sorts/counts/compares; older pupils record units and explain data Structures and paper bridges Paper, sticks, tape, supports Each child predicts, tests, explains one observed result and a redesign Algorithm/debugging Large paper arrow cards and desk grid Each child follows, edits or explains a sequence; not claimed as software mastery Arts/design Paper/cardstock, existing crayons, cards Observational drawing, composition and visual communication with a stated artistic choice Music/sound Hand/body percussion, cards, dry cups Each child composes/repeats a short rhythmic phrase; safe volume and silent pattern route Habitat/stewardship models Paper, cups, cardstock Each child explains a need or evidence-based resource choice; no outdoor prerequisite Closed-path electricity Nine protected AA packs, modules and leads Grades 1-6 take turns completing/opening paths and explaining the output; K observes enclosed light with adult handling

A possible 17-meeting consumption model is observation 2, structures 4, measurement/data 2, algorithms 3, arts/music 3, habitat/stewardship 1, circuits 2. This explains inventory use estimates; it is not verified legacy coverage or a mandate to use the same complexity in every grade. Paper stock allows up to 20 sheets per pupil; issue no more than 1 m tape per team per build, retain arrow cards, reuse dry cups/sticks and keep models in school.

The completion passes added named physical, prepared and teacher-tool identities, plus unambiguous aliases. Separate access/prepared/component resources contain 32 identities without invented standalone hardware prices. Budget join: Select the 37 purchase rows from the configuration table below by item_id; use that column's purchased quantity, not every inventory row's quantity_25. Recurring figures are annual estimates only for the stated cohort/consumption basis: one cohort in the first three configurations, seven sequential cohorts enhanced. docs.text:

docs.title: Safety and donation screening
docs.text:
No button cells, latex balloons or projectile activities in the operational core. No neodymium magnets in K; no loose high-strength magnets at any core station. Teacher controls AA cells, circuit clips, small test loads and enclosed magnets. Do not purchase electrical parts lacking verifiable protection. Stop unsafe equipment and report to the responsible school adult. Suspected battery/magnet ingestion needs urgent emergency escalation.

Optional clean dry cardboard from school/store/family sources can reduce use; school provides purchased paper/cardstock if none is donated. Reject food-soiled containers, chemical packaging, sharp metal/glass, mold, unknown batteries, loose magnets, latex and dangerous tools. Donating or fundraising never gates participation or grades.
